episodes.notes: Documented chiefly through Mughal chronicles, which are written from the victor's court perspective. Local heroic memory should be presented respectfully but separated from details not found in early sources.

episodes.title: Rana Kumbha Raises the Fortress of Kumbhalgarh
episodes.era: Mewar, 15th century CE
episodes.region: Kumbhalgarh and Chittor, Rajasthan
episodes.logline: Rana Kumbha strengthened Mewar with mountain forts and monuments, including Kumbhalgarh and the Vijay Stambha at Chittor. The episode can focus on builders, guards, and musicians working together to make a realm resilient.
episodes.moral: Strength is not only won in battles; it is built in stone, art, and preparation.

sources.citation: Kumbhalgarh inscription/prashasti of Maharana Kumbha, V.S. 1517 / 1460 CE, published in Epigraphia Indica, Vol. XXIV
sources.note: Primary inscriptional basis for Kumbha's genealogy, titles, and Mewar building-patronage claims.

sources.citation: Ranakpur inscription of V.S. 1496 / 1439 CE, edited by G.H. Ojha, on Kumbha's reign and patronage
sources.note: Contemporary epigraphic evidence for Kumbha's authority and religious-cultural patronage.

sources.citation: Dasharatha Sharma, Rajasthan Through the Ages, Vol. I, chapters on 15th-century Mewar
sources.note: Modern historical synthesis for context around fortification, politics, and culture.

episodes.notes: Kumbha's patronage is inscriptionally grounded. Later bardic accounts about numbers of forts and dramatic episodes should be treated as tradition unless tied to epigraphy or architecture.

episodes.title: Amoghavarsha's Court Gives Kannada a Classic Voice
episodes.figure: Amoghavarsha I Nrupatunga and the Rashtrakutas
episodes.era: Rashtrakuta Empire, c. 814-878 CE
episodes.region: Manyakheta/Malkhed and the Deccan
episodes.logline: In the Rashtrakuta age, Amoghavarsha's court helped shape Kavirajamarga, one of the earliest surviving works on Kannada poetics. The story can show a ruler valuing language, learning, and calm statecraft as part of imperial strength.
episodes.moral: A kingdom's glory grows when it protects its language and scholars.

sources.citation: Kavirajamarga, attributed to Nrupatunga Amoghavarsha, 9th century, esp. opening verses on Kannada literary regions
sources.note: Primary literary source for the courtly cultivation of Kannada poetics.

sources.citation: Sanjan copper plates of Amoghavarsha I, Saka 793 / 871 CE, published in Epigraphia Indica, Vol. XVIII
sources.note: Epigraphic evidence for Amoghavarsha's Rashtrakuta rule and titles.

sources.citation: A.S. Altekar, The Rashtrakutas and Their Times, chapters on Amoghavarsha I and Rashtrakuta culture
sources.note: Scholarly synthesis for political setting and literary patronage.

episodes.notes: Kavirajamarga is associated with Amoghavarsha/Nrupatunga, but scholars debate whether he personally authored it or sponsored it. Present the achievement as courtly patronage rather than a guaranteed one-man authorship.

episodes.title: Harsha's Great Assembly of Learning and Giving
episodes.era: Pushyabhuti/Vardhana rule, 7th century CE
episodes.region: Kanauj and Prayaga, north India
episodes.logline: Harsha gathered monks, scholars, envoys, and common people at grand assemblies where debate and generosity were celebrated. A child-safe episode can show banners, books, and gifts, not battlefield rivalry.
episodes.moral: The best rulers make space for learning, dialogue, and care for others.

sources.citation: Banabhatta, Harshacharita, trans. E.B. Cowell and F.W. Thomas, chs. VII-VIII
sources.note: Court biography for Harsha's lineage, courtly world, and royal self-presentation.

sources.citation: Xuanzang, Da Tang Xiyu Ji / Si-yu-ki, trans. Samuel Beal, Book V, accounts of Kanauj and Prayaga assemblies
sources.note: Near-contemporary traveller's account describing Harsha's public assemblies and donations.

sources.citation: R.C. Majumdar, The History and Culture of the Indian People, Vol. III: The Classical Age, chapter on Harsha
sources.note: Modern synthesis comparing literary and travel accounts.

episodes.notes: Harshacharita is a court panegyric and must be balanced with Xuanzang's outsider account and modern scholarship. Harsha's conflict with Pulakeshin II is already covered in batch 1, so this episode focuses on assemblies and culture.

episodes.title: Rudrama Devi Rules in Her Own Name
episodes.figure: Rani Rudrama Devi of the Kakatiyas
episodes.era: Kakatiya kingdom, c. 1262-1289 CE
episodes.region: Warangal and Telangana-Andhra region
episodes.logline: Rudrama Devi governed as a sovereign in a world that expected kings, not queens. Inscriptions and a foreign traveller remember a capable ruler whose authority was recognized across her realm.
episodes.moral: Leadership comes from courage, responsibility, and ability—not from expectations about who should lead.

sources.citation: Malkapuram inscription of Rudrama Devi, 1261 CE, published in South Indian Inscriptions / Epigraphia Andhrica collections
sources.note: Epigraphic evidence for Kakatiya genealogy, grants, and Rudrama Devi's royal authority.

sources.citation: Chandupatla inscription, 1289 CE, Nalgonda district, recording events at the end of Rudrama Devi's reign
sources.note: Important inscription for the later phase of Rudrama Devi's rule and conflict with Ambadeva's circle.

sources.citation: Marco Polo, Travels, Book III, ch. on Mutfili/Motupalli region, Yule-Cordier translation
sources.note: Foreign traveller's account of a just queen in the region, commonly identified with Rudrama Devi, though the identification needs a note.

episodes.notes: Rudrama Devi's sovereignty is inscriptionally documented. Marco Polo's queen is widely associated with her, but because the travel account uses regional names, the identification should be presented as probable rather than the sole proof.

episodes.title: Warangal's Stone Gateways Stand for Kakatiya Resilience
episodes.figure: Prataparudra and the Kakatiya city of Warangal
episodes.era: Kakatiya kingdom, late 13th-early 14th century CE
episodes.region: Warangal, Telangana
episodes.logline: Warangal's great fort, gateways, and planned sacred spaces show the engineering confidence of the Kakatiya capital. Even when armies pressed the city, its stones remembered a society skilled in building, trade, and administration.
episodes.moral: A city's strength is made by planners, artisans, farmers, and defenders together.

sources.citation: Amir Khusrau, Khaza'in-ul-Futuh, trans. Muhammad Habib, section on Malik Kafur's Warangal campaign of 1310
sources.note: Contemporary Persian account noting Warangal's political importance and the campaign context.

sources.citation: Ziauddin Barani, Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi, trans. in Elliot and Dowson, Vol. III, account of Ulugh Khan's Warangal campaign, 1323
sources.note: Later 14th-century chronicle evidence for Prataparudra's Warangal and its final Delhi Sultanate confrontation.

sources.citation: Archaeological Survey of India, Warangal Fort protected monument documentation, Telangana
sources.note: Archaeological basis for the fort, gateways, temple remains, and urban layout.

episodes.notes: This episode should avoid vilifying adversaries and should not turn the siege accounts into graphic violence. The documented focus is the Kakatiya capital's architecture and resilience; later local legends around hidden treasures should be excluded unless sourced.

episodes.title: Sukaphaa Crosses the Patkai and Begins the Ahom Story
episodes.figure: Chaolung Sukaphaa and the early Ahom kingdom
episodes.era: Ahom founding tradition, 1228 CE onward
episodes.region: Patkai hills, Charaideo, and the Brahmaputra valley, Assam
episodes.logline: Sukaphaa led his followers across mountains into the Brahmaputra valley and built alliances that began the long Ahom story. The episode can show migration, friendship-making, rice fields, and a new capital at Charaideo.
episodes.moral: A lasting home is built by courage, patience, and respect for neighbours.

sources.citation: Ahom Buranji, trans. G.C. Barua, early chapters on Sukaphaa's migration and settlement at Charaideo
sources.note: Court chronicle tradition for Sukaphaa's journey, alliances, and founding memory.

sources.citation: Edward Gait, A History of Assam, 2nd ed., chapters I-II on the Ahom arrival and early state
sources.note: Scholarly synthesis using Buranjis and colonial-era archival comparison.

sources.citation: S.K. Bhuyan, Studies in the History of Assam, essays on Ahom Buranjis and early Ahom polity
sources.note: Context for how Buranji materials should be read critically.

episodes.notes: The broad Ahom founding tradition is preserved in Buranjis compiled and transmitted over time, so precise dates and speeches should be handled cautiously. Batch 1 already covers Lachit Barphukan; this episode is about the much earlier founding.

episodes.title: Ahilyabai Holkar Rebuilds with Compassion
episodes.era: Holkar rule, 1767-1795 CE
episodes.region: Maheshwar, Malwa, and pilgrimage networks across India
episodes.logline: Ahilyabai Holkar governed from Maheshwar with a reputation for justice, public works, and support for sacred and civic places across India. The episode can show roads, wells, ghats, and careful listening in court.
episodes.moral: Power is noblest when it repairs, protects, and serves.

sources.citation: John Malcolm, A Memoir of Central India, Vol. II, sections on Ahalya Bai Holkar's administration and public character
sources.note: Early 19th-century account preserving administrative reputation and examples of governance.

sources.citation: Stewart Gordon, The Marathas 1600-1818, New Cambridge History of India, chapter on Maratha state formation and Holkar power
sources.note: Modern context for Malwa politics and Ahilyabai's place in Maratha governance.

sources.citation: Madhya Pradesh District Gazetteer: Indore, sections on Maheshwar and Ahilyabai's public works
sources.note: Gazetteer evidence for built heritage, ghats, and regional memory of civic patronage.

episodes.notes: Ahilyabai belongs to the early modern period, but she is included because the seed list extends the app's 'ancient to medieval' spine into regional early-modern heroes. Avoid miracle stories and stick to governance, patronage, and documented public works.

episodes.title: Bajirao's Swift Ride to Delhi
episodes.era: Maratha Confederacy, 1737 CE
episodes.region: Deccan to Delhi corridor
episodes.logline: Bajirao I became famous for rapid cavalry movement and bold planning, especially the 1737 dash toward Delhi. A child-safe telling can follow maps, messengers, and disciplined riders who outpaced expectations.
episodes.moral: Speed matters most when it is guided by clear thinking and discipline.

sources.citation: Jadunath Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire, Vol. I, chapters on Bajirao's 1737 northern campaign
sources.note: Detailed military-political reconstruction using Persian and Maratha records.

sources.citation: G.S. Sardesai, New History of the Marathas, Vol. II: The Expansion of the Maratha Power, chapters on Bajirao I
sources.note: Maratha-focused synthesis of Bajirao's campaigns, diplomacy, and reputation.

sources.citation: Selections from the Peshwa Daftar, ed. G.S. Sardesai, letters and orders relating to the 1736-1737 northern expedition
sources.note: Administrative correspondence base for movements, planning, and campaign chronology.

episodes.notes: Popular claims that Bajirao was 'undefeated' are common but should be phrased carefully: his career is remembered for remarkable battlefield success and mobility, while each campaign still needs source-specific treatment.

episodes.title: Hampi Amazes the Travellers
episodes.era: Vijayanagara Empire, 15th-16th century CE
episodes.region: Hampi/Vijayanagara, Karnataka
episodes.logline: Foreign visitors described Vijayanagara as a vast, wealthy, carefully planned capital, and Hampi's ruins still show markets, temples, waterworks, and royal spaces. The episode can be a guided walk through a buzzing city of many skills.
episodes.moral: A great city is made by planners, farmers, artists, traders, and protectors working together.

sources.citation: Abdur Razzaq Samarqandi, Matla-us-Sadain, 1440s Vijayanagara account, trans. in India in the Fifteenth Century, Hakluyt Society
sources.note: Primary traveller's description of the capital's scale, wealth, and courtly spectacle.

sources.citation: Domingo Paes, account of Vijayanagara c. 1520, in Robert Sewell, A Forgotten Empire: Vijayanagar
sources.note: Eyewitness Portuguese account of streets, markets, waterworks, and royal ceremonies.

sources.citation: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Group of Monuments at Hampi, Brief Synthesis and criteria
sources.note: Archaeological and heritage summary of Hampi's urban, sacred, hydraulic, and defensive remains.

episodes.notes: Krishnadevaraya and Raichur are already covered in batch 1; this episode is about the capital as an urban achievement. Traveller accounts praise the city but should be balanced with archaeology.

episodes.title: Sushruta Trains the Careful Surgeon
episodes.figure: Sushruta and the Sushruta Samhita tradition
episodes.era: Ancient Indian medical tradition, text layered c. 1st millennium BCE-early CE
episodes.region: North India, later pan-Indian medical learning
episodes.logline: The Sushruta Samhita teaches that students should practise delicate cuts on fruits, gourds, and other safe models before treating people. The episode can celebrate careful training, cleanliness, and compassion in healing.
episodes.moral: Skill should be learned patiently before it is used to help others.

sources.citation: Sushruta Samhita, Sutrasthana 9 (Yogyasutriya Adhyaya), trans. K.L. Bhishagratna, Vol. I
sources.note: Primary medical text section on practical training models for surgical students.

sources.citation: Sushruta Samhita, Sutrasthana 7-8, trans. K.L. Bhishagratna, sections on instruments and surgical preparation
sources.note: Primary source for organized surgical knowledge and instrument classification.

sources.citation: Dominik Wujastyk, The Roots of Ayurveda, selections on the Sushruta Samhita and classical Indian medicine
sources.note: Modern philological context for dating, layers, and medical significance.

episodes.notes: The text is layered and not a modern surgical manual; present its historical significance without claiming uninterrupted modern equivalence. Avoid graphic medical imagery for children.

episodes.title: Nagarjuna's Middle Path of Careful Thinking
episodes.era: Early centuries CE, commonly placed c. 2nd-3rd century CE
episodes.region: Deccan/North India traditions; Buddhist scholastic world
episodes.logline: Nagarjuna taught students to examine ideas carefully and avoid extremes, shaping the Madhyamaka school of thought. The episode can show a calm debate where wisdom means asking better questions.
episodes.moral: Deep thinking begins when we question our own assumptions with humility.

sources.citation: Nagarjuna, Mulamadhyamakakarika, esp. 24.18 on dependent arising and emptiness
sources.note: Primary philosophical text expressing the central Madhyamaka insight.

sources.citation: Kumarajiva's Chinese translation of Nagarjuna's Madhyamaka text tradition, Taisho Tripitaka no. 1564, early 5th century CE
sources.note: Early textual transmission evidence for Nagarjuna's influence beyond India.

sources.citation: David Seyfort Ruegg, The Literature of the Madhyamaka School of Philosophy in India, Harrassowitz, 1981
sources.note: Scholarly guide to sources, attribution problems, and Madhyamaka development.

episodes.notes: Do not conflate the philosopher Nagarjuna with later alchemical or tantric authors named Nagarjuna. This episode is documented as intellectual history, not as a miracle biography.

episodes.title: Muziris Opens the Sangam-Age Sea Road
episodes.figure: Chera/Tamilakam ports and Indian Ocean traders
episodes.era: Sangam age and early historic trade, c. 1st century BCE-3rd century CE
episodes.region: Kerala-Tamilakam coast, especially Muziris/Muchiri
episodes.logline: At Muziris, ships from across the sea met Tamilakam's pepper, pearls, textiles, and poems of bustling ports. The episode can show dockworkers, scribes, and merchants exchanging goods and languages peacefully.
episodes.moral: Openness, trust, and skill turn a port into a bridge between peoples.

sources.citation: Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, sections 54-56, trans. J.W. McCrindle, on Muziris, Nelcynda, and pepper trade
sources.note: Near-contemporary Greco-Roman trade manual naming Muziris and western-coast commerce.

sources.citation: Pliny the Elder, Natural History, Book VI.26, on Roman shipping and Muziris-region trade
sources.note: Roman testimony for long-distance trade with the southwest Indian coast.

sources.citation: P.J. Cherian et al., Pattanam excavations reports on early historic Indian Ocean trade material from Kerala
sources.note: Archaeological context for the Muziris/Pattanam debate and maritime material culture.

episodes.notes: The exact identification of ancient Muziris with Pattanam is influential but still debated. Present the trade network as documented, and the precise site-location question as an active scholarly discussion.

episodes.title: Lokamahadevi's Virupaksha Temple at Pattadakal
episodes.figure: Queen Lokamahadevi and the Early Chalukya builders
episodes.era: Early Chalukya, c. 740 CE
episodes.region: Pattadakal, Karnataka
episodes.logline: Queen Lokamahadevi sponsored the Virupaksha temple at Pattadakal, where northern and southern architectural ideas met in stone. The episode can show architects comparing plans and carving a shared masterpiece.
episodes.moral: Beautiful things happen when different skills and traditions work together.

sources.citation: Pattadakal Virupaksha temple inscriptions of Lokamahadevi, c. 740 CE, recording the temple foundation
sources.note: Primary epigraphic evidence that Queen Lokamahadevi sponsored the temple.

sources.citation: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Group of Monuments at Pattadakal, Brief Synthesis, noting Virupaksha temple built by Queen Lokamahadevi in 740 CE
sources.note: Heritage and archaeological summary of the monument's architectural significance.

sources.citation: George Michell, Pattadakal, Oxford University Press / Archaeological Survey of India guide
sources.note: Scholarly architectural analysis of Pattadakal's temple forms and patronage.

episodes.notes: Pulakeshin II is already covered in batch 1; this episode focuses on later Chalukya temple-building and a queen's patronage. The 'victory over Kanchi' context should be stated without triumphalist hostility.

episodes.title: Martanda Varma Wins at Colachel and Builds Travancore
episodes.era: Travancore, 1741 CE and after
episodes.region: Colachel and Travancore, Kerala
episodes.logline: At Colachel, Travancore defeated a Dutch East India Company force, and Marthanda Varma later used disciplined state-building to strengthen his kingdom. The episode can show strategy, captured cannons, and former foes becoming trainers rather than enemies.
episodes.moral: A wise victory turns danger into learning and stronger institutions.

sources.citation: P. Shungunny Menon, A History of Travancore from the Earliest Times, chapters on Marthanda Varma and Colachel
sources.note: Early historical account of the battle, De Lannoy tradition, and Travancore consolidation.

sources.citation: V. Nagam Aiya, The Travancore State Manual, Vol. I, sections on Marthanda Varma and the Battle of Colachel
sources.note: State-manual synthesis of Travancore records and administrative developments.

sources.citation: A. Galletti, The Dutch in Malabar: Selections from the Records of the Madras Government, 1911, Dutch records around the Travancore conflict
sources.note: Record-based context from Dutch/colonial archival material for the European-company side.

episodes.notes: This is early modern, but included because the seed list extends through regional resistance to European companies. Treat Dutch opponents with dignity and emphasize statecraft, reform, and restraint after victory.

episodes.title: Taming the Kaveri: The Grand Anicut
episodes.era: Early Chola root, c. 2nd century CE
episodes.region: The Kaveri delta, Tamil country
episodes.logline: Long before the imperial Cholas, Karikala throws a great stone dam across the flooding Kaveri, the Grand Anicut, turning a wild river into canals and rice-plains that would one day feed an empire.
episodes.moral: The mightiest empires rest first on water, soil and patient engineering.

sources.citation: The Kallanai (Grand Anicut) across the Kaveri, among the oldest water-diversion structures still in use
Sangam poem Pattinappalai on Karikala Chola; K. A. Nilakanta Sastri, The CōĻas

episodes.chapter_part: I. Rise of the Tiger Throne

episodes.title: Chandragupta I and the Licchavi Bride
episodes.era: Founding of the Gupta empire, c. 319-335 CE
episodes.region: Magadha and the eastern Gangetic plain, Pataliputra
episodes.logline: A Magadha king weds the Licchavi princess Kumaradevi and strikes a gold coin bearing both their names, turning a marriage alliance into the seed of an empire and the start of the Gupta era.
episodes.moral: The strongest thrones rest on alliance and legitimacy, not conquest alone.

sources.citation: Prayag Prashasti (Allahabad Pillar) of Samudragupta, composed by Harishena
sources.note: Retrospective source naming Chandragupta I and the Licchavi connection.

sources.citation: The Chandragupta I-Kumaradevi 'King and Queen' gold coins, legend 'Lichchhavayah', Gupta Brahmi
sources.note: Contemporary coinage naming the queen jointly with the king - unique political propaganda.

sources.citation: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India (2008); R.C. Majumdar (ed.), The Gupta Empire (1946)
sources.note: Chronology and the downsized view of his actual territory.

episodes.notes: He was the first Gupta to claim Maharajadhiraja; his forebears Sri Gupta and Ghatotkaca were only local Maharajas. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP (Upinder Singh; Romila Thapar) DOWNSIZES his realm to Magadha, Prayaga and parts of Bihar - the vast empire is his son Samudragupta's work, so do NOT depict him ruling all India. The Gupta-era epoch (319/320 CE) is conventional and its exact founding is debated. The king-and-queen coin naming Kumaradevi is the earliest Indian case of a queen named on coinage as co-legitimizer - a strong visual anchor. Spoken name should say 'the First'.
episodes.chapter_part: I. The Rise of the Guptas

episodes.title: Chandragupta Raises the Peacock Standard
episodes.era: Founding of the Maurya Empire, c. 321-297 BCE
episodes.region: Magadha, Pataliputra, Punjab and the Gangetic plain
episodes.logline: A young challenger from uncertain origins topples the Nandas, gathers Magadha around Pataliputra, and raises the first empire to bind much of ancient India under one throne.
episodes.moral: A new order can rise when courage is joined to discipline.

sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Alexander, on 'Androcottus' (Chandragupta)
sources.note: Greek testimony establishing Chandragupta's historical reality outside later Indian legends.

sources.citation: Vishakhadatta, Mudrarakshasa, c. 4th-9th century CE
sources.note: Literary drama of the Nanda overthrow and Chanakya's plotting; useful but late and legendary.

sources.citation: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India (2008); Romila Thapar, Early India (2002)
sources.note: Modern synthesis treating his existence as secure and his origin stories as uncertain.

episodes.notes: Chandragupta founded the Maurya Empire around 321 BCE after overthrowing the last Nanda ruler, traditionally Dhana Nanda, and made Pataliputra the imperial center. KEY ACCURACY FLAGS: his origins are legendary and disputed across Buddhist, Jain and Brahmanical traditions; do NOT present the 'Mura' concubine etymology of Maurya as fact, because modern scholars reject it on Sanskrit grammatical grounds and the Puranas do not mention Mura. The peacock/Moriya connection is more plausible but still belongs to layered tradition. Chanakya's role is central in later storytelling, especially Mudrarakshasa, but there are no Mauryan court records and no contemporary narrative of the Nanda coup.
episodes.chapter_part: I. The Rise of the Peacock Throne

episodes.title: Harihara and Bukka Raise a City of Victory
episodes.figure: Harihara I and Bukka Raya I
episodes.era: Foundation of Vijayanagara, traditional date 1336 CE
episodes.region: Hampi, the Tungabhadra valley, Kampili, Hoysala country and Sringeri
episodes.logline: Two Sangama brothers turn a boulder-ringed river valley into Vijayanagara, a new capital whose origin story blends inscription, politics and sacred memory.
episodes.moral: Great beginnings are strongest when legend is balanced with evidence.

sources.citation: Sringeri Grant of 1346 CE; South Indian Inscriptions series
sources.note: Earliest hard epigraphic evidence for Harihara's sovereignty and the capital's early name.

sources.citation: Burton Stein, Vijayanagara, New Cambridge History of India I.2 (1989)
sources.note: Modern synthesis of the empire's rise and political structure.

sources.citation: Rao, Shulman and Subrahmanyam, Textures of Time (2003)
sources.note: Treats the conversion-and-return story as a legitimizing foundation tradition.

episodes.notes: Harihara I and Bukka Raya I, sons of Sangama, are securely tied to the empire's foundation, with 1336 widely accepted as the traditional date and 1346 giving the earliest firm inscriptional confirmation. KEY FACTS: early evidence points to Hoysala and Kampili political worlds, not a single simple origin; Vidyaranya and Sringeri mattered for legitimacy, but Vidyaranya became Sringeri pontiff only later, so do NOT show him as a fully proven mastermind personally reconverting the brothers in 1336. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP stresses gradual consolidation by local powers, not an instant religious revival. Accuracy flag for the whole chapter: include the four dynasties, Sangama, Saluva, Tuluva and Aravidu, and avoid framing Vijayanagara simply as a Hindu bulwark against Islam.
episodes.chapter_part: I. The City of Victory Rises

episodes.title: The Village That Began Everything
episodes.era: Neolithic and Chalcolithic Mehrgarh, c. 7000-3300 BCE
episodes.region: Mehrgarh, Kachi Plain, Balochistan, at the foot of the Bolan Pass
episodes.logline: In mud-brick rooms beside the Bolan Pass, South Asia's earliest known farmers grow grain, tend cattle, drill teeth, spin cotton, and begin the long road to Harappan cities.
episodes.moral: Great cities begin with patient hands in small villages.

sources.citation: J.-F. Jarrige et al., Mehrgarh: Field Reports 1975-1985 (1995)
sources.note: Primary excavation record for settlement, burials, craft and radiocarbon sequence.

sources.citation: L. Costantini, 'The Beginning of Agriculture in the Kachi Plain' in South Asian Archaeology 1981 (1984)
sources.note: Evidence for early crops and cotton at Mehrgarh.

sources.citation: R. Macchiarelli et al., 'The Earliest Evidence of Dental Drilling in Mehrgarh, Pakistan,' Nature 440 (2006)
sources.note: Recent scientific evidence for proto-dentistry.

episodes.notes: Mehrgarh Period I, c. 7000-5500 BCE, had aceramic mud-brick houses, wheat and barley, sheep, goats and cattle; later phases added pottery, copper, beads and early cotton evidence. The 2006 Nature study of drilled molars shows unexpected medical skill, while Bhirrana's very early TL dates are important but debated as a separate pre-Harappan Hakra phase. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT call Mehrgarh the world's oldest farming site, do NOT say its people spoke any known language, and do NOT conflate this precursor village with the later Mature Harappan cities.

episodes.title: Babur's Thunder at Panipat
episodes.era: First Battle of Panipat, 21 April 1526
episodes.region: Panipat, Delhi and Agra
episodes.logline: On a dusty plain north of Delhi, Babur chains carts, fires cannon, and defeats Ibrahim Lodi to begin a new empire.
episodes.moral: New power must be matched by discipline and responsibility.

sources.citation: Babur, The Baburnama, trans. W.M. Thackston, Freer Gallery/Smithsonian, 1996
sources.note: Eyewitness memoir for Babur's tactics, artillerymen and the battle's aftermath.

sources.citation: Jos Gommans, Mughal Warfare: Indian Frontiers and High Roads to Empire 1500-1700, Routledge, 2002
sources.note: Recent military synthesis cautioning that organization and politics mattered alongside artillery.

sources.citation: Gulbadan Begum, Humayun-Nama, trans. A.S. Beveridge, Royal Asiatic Society, 1902
sources.note: Early Mughal family perspective on the founding generation and Kabul's reaction.

episodes.notes: Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat on 21 April 1526 using Central Asian tulughma flanking tactics, chained carts, matchlocks and Ottoman-style field artillery under Ustad Ali Quli and Mustafa Rumi. Recent military scholarship warns that cannon alone did not create victory: Lodi factional weakness, Babur's veteran command structure and tactical discipline also mattered. The Baburnama is the core eyewitness source, while later Persian accounts inflate numbers; do NOT claim exact Lodi troop totals, and do NOT move Babur's later Khanwa skull-tower story to Panipat.

episodes.title: Pulakeshin I Builds the Red Rock Fort
episodes.era: Early Chalukya rise, c. 543-566 CE
episodes.region: Vatapi (Badami), Malaprabha valley, Karnataka
episodes.logline: On a red sandstone bluff above a lake, Pulakeshin I turns Vatapi into a fortress and gives a local Deccan house the confidence of kings.
episodes.moral: Great beginnings are built with courage and careful foundations.

sources.citation: Badami cliff inscription, Saka 465 / c. 543 CE, published in D.C. Sircar, Select Inscriptions, Vol. 2
sources.note: In-situ primary source for the fort, titles and early Chalukya power at Vatapi.

sources.citation: Mahakuta pillar inscription, c. 595 CE, Epigraphia Indica Vol. IV
sources.note: Primary genealogy from Pulakeshin I through his successors, with courtly exaggeration.

sources.citation: Hemanth Kadambi, 'The Chalukyas of Badami: In Conversation,' Sahapedia (2018)
sources.note: Recent landscape-focused interpretation of Chalukya power in the Malaprabha region.

episodes.notes: Pulakeshin I is securely placed in the mid-sixth century because the Badami cliff inscription records the fort of Vatapi in Saka 465, usually converted to 543 CE, though the inscription proves fort-building more directly than a single founding day for the dynasty. His Ashvamedha and Hiranyagarbha claims show how a rising family used ritual language to announce sovereignty, while recent landscape work argues that Chalukya power grew from older local agrarian and settlement networks rather than appearing overnight. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT treat divine descent claims as genealogy; do NOT confuse him with Pulakeshin II; do NOT state 543 CE as an exact coronation date.

episodes.title: Lakhbaksh Starts the Tower of Delhi
episodes.era: Early Delhi Sultanate, c. 1192-1210 CE
episodes.region: Delhi, Mehrauli, Lahore and the old Ghurid frontier
episodes.logline: A Turkic slave-general breaks from the Ghurids, rules from Delhi and Lahore, and begins the sandstone tower that still marks the first Sultanate horizon.
episodes.moral: Power is strongest when it builds more than it conquers.

sources.citation: Minhaj-i-Siraj Juzjani, Tabaqat-i Nasiri, completed 1260
sources.note: Near-contemporary Persian history preserving the early Mamluk succession.

sources.citation: Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque inscription, c. 1199-1206
sources.note: Site inscription recording Aibak's mosque and its reused temple material.

sources.citation: Peter Jackson, The Delhi Sultanate: A Political and Military History (Cambridge University Press, 2003)
sources.note: Modern synthesis stressing the gradual formation of the Sultanate under Aibak and Iltutmish.

episodes.notes: Aibak, a Turkic slave of Muhammad of Ghor, became governor after Tarain in 1192 and asserted independence after his master's assassination in 1206, ruling only until his death in a polo accident at Lahore in 1210. He began the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque and the first storey of the Qutb Minar, but the Sultanate's formal shape hardened later under Iltutmish. Recent work by Jackson and Finbarr Barry Flood cautions that temple-column reuse at Mehrauli was both violent appropriation and complex material translation involving Indian craftsmen. Do NOT claim Aibak built the whole Qutb Minar or that the Sultanate was founded on one precisely documented day.

episodes.title: The Yuezhi Cross a Thousand Mountains
episodes.era: Yuezhi migration and settlement in Bactria, c. 176-30 BCE
episodes.region: Gansu, the Ili Valley, Sogdia and Bactria
episodes.logline: Driven from the grasslands by Xiongnu power, the Greater Yuezhi cross Central Asia and settle in Bactria, where one clan will become the Kushans.
episodes.moral: A people in exile can carry the seeds of a new world.

sources.citation: Sima Qian, Shiji, chapter 123, Zhang Qian's mission
sources.note: Earliest outside account of the Yuezhi in Bactria and their five-part political structure.

sources.citation: Hou Hanshu, chapter 88, trans. John Hill, Through the Jade Gate to Rome (2009)
sources.note: Chinese account of the Yuezhi defeat, migration and later Kushan rise.

sources.citation: Craig Benjamin, The Yuezhi: Origin, Migration and Conquest of Northern Bactria (2007)
sources.note: Modern synthesis of the migration and Bactrian settlement, with caution on ethnicity.

episodes.notes: The Greater Yuezhi were forced west after Xiongnu attacks around 176-174 BCE, moved through the Ili region, displaced Sakas, and entered Bactria around the mid-2nd century BCE. Zhang Qian found them settled and prosperous about 128 BCE, divided among five yabghu groups, one of which was Guishuang, the later Kushan clan. RECENT FINDINGS: modern Central Asian archaeology and ancient-DNA work have made older simple identifications with Tocharians insecure. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say the Yuezhi were definitely Tocharian; do NOT confuse them with later Mongol movements; the skull-cup story is in Chinese sources but cannot be archaeologically verified.
episodes.chapter: The Kushan Empire and the Silk Road

episodes.title: Simhavishnu Ends the Kalabhra Night
episodes.era: Pallava revival, c. 555-600 CE, with dates debated
episodes.region: Kanchipuram, Tondaimandalam and the Kaveri frontier
episodes.logline: After a shadowed age in Tamil history, Simhavishnu restores Pallava power from Kanchipuram and turns the court toward conquest, Vishnu worship and Sanskrit learning.
episodes.moral: A revival begins by turning memory into disciplined action.

sources.citation: Udayendiram copper plates of Nandivarman II
sources.note: Retrospective Pallava record naming Simhavishnu, his Vaishnava affiliation and campaigns.

sources.citation: Kasakudi copper plates of Nandivarman II, South Indian Inscriptions, Vol. II
sources.note: Full Pallava genealogy and eulogistic account of the dynasty's revival.

sources.citation: Rajan Gurukkal, Social Formations of Early South India (2010); K.A. Nilakanta Sastri, A History of South India (2008 reprint)
sources.note: Modern reassessment of the Kalabhra period and Pallava chronology.

episodes.notes: Simhavishnu, son of Simhavarman III, is the first imperial Pallava ruler whose power clearly reached beyond Kanchipuram, probably extending south toward the Kaveri and challenging Pandyas and Lanka-linked powers. The evidence is mostly retrospective copper plates, not inscriptions issued by Simhavishnu himself, and scholarly dates range roughly from the mid-6th to early 7th century. KEY RECENT FINDING: modern scholars such as Rajan Gurukkal warn that the Kalabhra 'dark age' was partly a later Brahmanical and dynastic framing; do NOT portray the whole period as cultural collapse. Do NOT state the legendary Ashwatthama or Naga ancestry in Pallava plates as fact.
episodes.chapter: The Pallavas and the Bhakti Dawn
episodes.chapter_part: I. Kanchi Rises from the Kalabhra Haze

episodes.title: The River That Taught the Stars
episodes.era: Kerala astronomical roots, c. 683-1295 CE
episodes.region: The Nila or Bharathappuzha valley, Tirunavaya, Tirur and Ponnani, Kerala
episodes.logline: Along the Nila River, memorized number-verses, almanacs and scholar-houses prepared the ground for Kerala's later leap toward infinity.
episodes.moral: Great discoveries grow from patient traditions.

sources.citation: Haridatta, Grahacara-nibandhana, c. 683 CE
sources.note: Early Kerala astronomical text using the Katapayadi numeral system and the Parahita computation tradition.

sources.citation: Govinda Bhattathiri, Muhurtaratnam; Paramesvara's commentary on it
sources.note: Lineage evidence linking later Kerala astronomers to an older Nila-valley tradition.

sources.citation: K.V. Sarma, A History of the Kerala School of Hindu Astronomy (1972); Kim Plofker, Mathematics in India (2009)
sources.note: Modern reconstruction of the early Kerala lineage and its mnemonic techniques.

episodes.notes: Start before Madhava. Haridatta's Parahita system, dated by its 683 CE epoch, and the Katapayadi system show a local technology for turning numbers into memorable syllables. Govinda Bhattathiri represents the later astrological-astronomical tradition that Paramesvara says his own family inherited. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP FLAG: Sarma's lineage remains the standard framework, but many personal details come from internal textual references, not inscriptions. Do NOT treat folklore from Ithihyamala as documentary biography, and do NOT pretend the Kerala school appeared suddenly from nowhere.
episodes.chapter_part: I. The Country of the River

episodes.title: The Queen at the Coin Pass
episodes.era: Early Satavahana rise, c. 70-50 BCE
episodes.region: Naneghat pass, Western Ghats, Maharashtra
episodes.logline: At a toll pass between seaports and the Deccan, a Satavahana queen records sacrifices, genealogy, and some of the earliest digit shapes behind modern numerals.
episodes.moral: Names carved with care can outlive armies.

sources.citation: Georg Buhler, 'The Naneghat Inscription,' Epigraphia Indica Vol. 4 (1883)
sources.note: Primary publication of the Naneghat cave inscription and royal portrait record.

sources.citation: Richard Salomon, Indian Epigraphy (Oxford University Press, 1998)
sources.note: Guide to Brahmi, Prakrit inscriptions and palaeographic caution.

sources.citation: Andrew Ollett, Language of the Snakes (University of California Press, 2017)
sources.note: Recent synthesis of Satavahana Prakrit, chronology and epigraphic culture.

episodes.notes: Naneghat linked coastal ports such as Sopara and Kalyan to inland centers such as Nasik, Ter and Pratishthana. Queen Nayanika, also read Naganika by some scholars, probably ruled as regent after Satakarni I and recorded Vedic sacrifices, gifts, genealogy and damaged royal portraits in Maharashtri Prakrit Brahmi. Recent work stresses careful palaeography and new documentation, while Kanaganahalli finds have sharpened early Satavahana chronology. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT claim the inscription contains zero or a full place-value system; it preserves early digit shapes for some numbers. Do NOT call it Buddhist or give a fixed date beyond the c. 2nd-1st century BCE range.
episodes.chapter: The Satavahanas and the Sangam Age
episodes.chapter_part: I. Roads Through the Red Earth

episodes.title: Tarabai Outlasts Aurangzeb
episodes.era: Maratha resistance and regency, 1700-1708 CE
episodes.region: Satara, Kolhapur, the Deccan, Malwa and Gujarat
episodes.logline: After Rajaram dies, Tarabai holds a mobile kingdom together and keeps Maratha resistance alive until Aurangzeb's exhausted armies fade.
episodes.moral: Leadership can survive when courage serves a larger duty.

sources.citation: Khafi Khan, Muntakhabu-l-Lubab, sections on the late Deccan war
sources.note: Hostile Mughal-side testimony for Maratha resistance after Rajaram's death.

sources.citation: G.S. Sardesai, New History of the Marathas, Vol. II, chapters on Tarabai and Shahu
sources.note: Synthesis drawing on bakhars and Marathi administrative materials.

sources.citation: Stewart Gordon, The Marathas 1600-1818 (Cambridge UP, 1993)
sources.note: Modern account of the succession crisis, Tarabai's regency and state formation.

episodes.notes: Tarabai, daughter of Hambirrao Mohite and widow of Rajaram I, acted as regent for her son Shivaji II from 1700 as Mughal armies pressed Satara and the Deccan. KEY FACTS: Maratha raids reached Malwa and Gujarat before Aurangzeb died at Ahmadnagar in 1707; Shahu's release then split Maratha politics, and Tarabai's Kolhapur court survived after the Battle of Khed in 1708. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP FLAG: Gordon, Guha and Deshpande treat her as a strategic political actor later marginalized by Peshwa-centered memory. Do NOT claim she personally led every raid from horseback; some battle details come from retrospective bakhars and must be treated cautiously.

episodes.title: Guru Nanak and the River That Spoke
episodes.era: Founding Sikh tradition, c. 1469-1539 CE
episodes.region: Rai Bhoi di Talvandi, Sultanpur Lodhi, Kartarpur and the Punjab
episodes.logline: After vanishing at the Bein River, Nanak returns with a message beyond Hindu and Muslim labels and builds a singing, working community at Kartarpur.
episodes.moral: Truth grows when people share work, song and bread.

sources.citation: Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak's hymns including the Babur Vani passages
sources.note: Primary evidence for Nanak's teaching and rare historical anchors in the 1520s.

sources.citation: Varan Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 1, c. 1600-1636
sources.note: Early Sikh account before many later janamsakhi elaborations.

sources.citation: W.H. McLeod, Guru Nanak and the Sikh Religion (1968); S.S. Padam ed., Sakhi Mahal Pehle Ki (2014)
sources.note: Modern source criticism and the recently published early tradition.

episodes.notes: Nanak was born in 1469 at Rai Bhoi di Talvandi, worked at Sultanpur Lodhi under Daulat Khan Lodi, and settled around 1521 at Kartarpur, where the sangat, shared labor and langar became the seed of Sikh community life. Recent source criticism is vital: the Guru Granth Sahib preserves his own hymns, while janamsakhis were written after his death and often expand miracle stories. Sakhi Mahal Pehle Ki, published by S.S. Padam in 2014 and linked to an older tradition, lacks many famous travel episodes, so do NOT claim exact four-udasi routes, Mecca conversations, or the three-day river disappearance as verifiable biography; tell them as Sikh tradition around a securely attested teacher.
episodes.chapter: The Sikh Gurus and Ranjit Singh

episodes.title: The Doctor Who Built a Science House
episodes.era: Colonial Bengal and the founding of IACS, 1867-1876
episodes.region: Calcutta, Bengal Presidency
episodes.logline: Mahendralal Sarkar turns public donations into India's first independent research institute, proving that Indians can build science on their own terms.
episodes.moral: Institutions begin when one person refuses to wait for permission.

sources.citation: Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science founding deed and minute books, 1876, IACS Archives, Kolkata
sources.note: Primary institutional record for the association founded on 29 July 1876.

sources.citation: Mahendralal Sarkar, Calcutta Journal of Medicine, from 1868
sources.note: Shows Sarkar's medical and scientific advocacy in print.

sources.citation: Deepak Kumar, Science and the Raj 1857-1905, Oxford University Press, 1995
sources.note: Places IACS within colonial exclusion from official scientific bodies and Indian public science efforts.

episodes.notes: Mahendralal Sarkar, the second MD graduate of Calcutta Medical College, campaigned from 1867 until the Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science opened on 29 July 1876 in Calcutta. This is a SOCIAL and INSTITUTIONAL innovation story: a science institution funded by Indian public subscription rather than colonial patronage. It later gave C.V. Raman the laboratory space where the Raman Effect was found. Recent work by Deepak Kumar and Projit Mukharji reads Sarkar's project as both scientific self-strengthening and part of colonial Bengal's medical politics. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT claim IACS was the first non-European science institution in the world; the safer attested claim is first Indian-run independent research institution. Sarkar also defended homeopathy, so present him as a complex medical reformer, not a modern laboratory scientist in every respect.
episodes.chapter_part: I. The Dawn of Indian Research

episodes.title: The Rope That Measured the Sacred Fire
episodes.figure: Baudhayana and the Sulbasutra cord measurers
episodes.era: Vedic ritual geometry, c. 800-500 BCE
episodes.region: The Vedic heartland of northern India
episodes.logline: Priests stretch cords across fire altars and turn ritual craft into some of India's earliest recorded geometry.
episodes.moral: Careful measurement can turn devotion into discovery.

sources.citation: Baudhayana Sulbasutra; Sen and Bag, The Sulbasutras (INSA, 1983)
sources.note: Primary geometric rules for altar construction, including the diagonal rule and a square-root approximation.

sources.citation: Kim Plofker, Mathematics in India (Princeton University Press, 2009)
sources.note: Modern synthesis that separates real Vedic geometry from priority myths.

sources.citation: George Thibaut, On the Sulvasutras, Journal of the Asiatic Society of Bengal 44 (1875)
sources.note: Early scholarly study of the sulba textual tradition.

episodes.notes: The Baudhayana Sulbasutra preserves practical cord-geometry for constructing ritual altars, including the rule that a rectangle's diagonal makes the areas made by its two sides and an impressively close approximation of the square root of 2. Recent scholarship stresses that the date is a linguistic and cultural range, not a fixed year, and that the manuscripts are much later than the ideas. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT claim Baudhayana proved the Pythagorean theorem before Pythagoras; the text states a construction rule without Greek-style proof, and Old Babylonian tablets already knew the relationship. Baudhayana as a person is traditional and essentially biographical silence.

episodes.title: The Brahmin Prince Who Made a Kingdom
episodes.era: Early Ahom state formation, r. 1397-1407 CE
episodes.region: Habung, Charaideo and Charagua in Upper Assam
episodes.logline: Raised outside the court and recalled in crisis, Sudangphaa turns a shaken Tai clan realm into a kingdom with coronation rites, borders and counselors.
episodes.moral: Institutions can rescue a realm when bloodlines alone cannot.

sources.citation: Satsari Assam Buranji, in G.C. Barua, Ahom Buranji (1930)
sources.note: Primary chronicle tradition for Sudangphaa's accession, the Patkai frontier and court reconstruction.

sources.citation: Deodhai Assam Buranji, ed. S.K. Bhuyan
sources.note: Priestly chronicle preserving ritual and coronation traditions around Ahom kingship.

sources.citation: H.K. Barpujari, ed., The Comprehensive History of Assam, Vol. 2 (1992)
sources.note: Modern synthesis of the transition from Mong Dun Shun Kham to a more formal Ahom state.

episodes.notes: Sudangphaa, remembered as Bamuni Konwar because he was raised in a Brahmin household, is best used to show state formation rather than romance. Buranji tradition places his reign in 1397-1407, after a period of regicide and instability, and credits him with restoring authority, strengthening the Burhagohain and Borgohain structure, creating the singarigharutha coronation ceremony, building Charagua and fixing the Patkai frontier after conflict with Mong Kawng. ACCURACY FLAGS: his childhood recovery story and speeches are chronicle tradition; do NOT present every detail as contemporary fact. The wider sources problem matters here because early Ahom events were written down retrospectively, and recent scholarship warns that the earliest centuries carry calendar and genealogy uncertainties.
episodes.chapter_part: I. Golden Gardens Become a Kingdom

episodes.title: Vijayalaya Seizes Thanjavur
episodes.era: Rise of the Imperial Cholas, c. 850 CE
episodes.region: Thanjavur, Kaveri delta, Tamil country
episodes.logline: A chieftain under the Pallavas, Vijayalaya seizes Thanjavur from the Muttaraiyar and raises the tiger banner, founding a line that would one day rule an ocean.
episodes.moral: Great empires begin with one bold, patient beginning.

sources.citation: K. A. Nilakanta Sastri, The CōĻas, 'The Rise of the Cholas'
Tiruvalangadu copper-plate grant (genealogy of the Chola line)

episodes.chapter_part: I. Rise of the Tiger Throne

episodes.title: Samudragupta's Hundred Victories
episodes.era: Gupta expansion, c. 335-375 CE
episodes.region: From the Gangetic plain across the Deccan; the pillar at Prayaga (Allahabad)
episodes.logline: Court poet Harishena carves Samudragupta's conquests onto Ashoka's old pillar: nine northern kings uprooted, twelve southern kings captured and freed, a horse-sacrifice revived, and a warrior-king who has himself struck in gold playing the veena.
episodes.moral: True greatness is measured not only in battles won but in the culture a ruler nurtures.

sources.citation: Prayag Prashasti (Allahabad Pillar) of Harishena, in situ at Allahabad Fort; J.F. Fleet, Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum Vol. III (1888)
sources.note: The sole primary source for Samudragupta's campaigns.

sources.citation: Samudragupta's gold coins: Archer, Lyrist (veena), Battle-Axe, Tiger-Slayer and Ashvamedha types
sources.note: Contemporary coinage; the Lyrist type shows him as poet-king (Kaviraja).

sources.citation: Daud Ali, Courtly Culture and Political Life in Early Medieval India (2004); Upinder Singh (2008)
sources.note: Reads the Prashasti as royal ideology; critiques the 'Napoleon of India' label.

episodes.notes: TWO DIFFERENT LOGICS: the northern (Aryavarta) kings were ANNEXED; the southern (Dakshinapatha) kings were captured then RE-INSTATED as tributaries (graha-moksha-anugraha), not annexed. He revived the Vedic Ashvamedha (first since the Kanvas) and struck a coin of himself playing the veena. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP rejects V.A. Smith's 'Napoleon of India' (1904) as Eurocentric - his was a mandala/concentric-sovereignty polity, not a European bureaucratic empire. His own poems do not survive (legendary). The pillar is a eulogy, not a survey.
episodes.chapter_part: I. The Rise of the Guptas

episodes.title: Kautilya's Manual of Spies and Kings
episodes.era: Mauryan statecraft tradition and later Arthashastra compilation
episodes.region: Pataliputra and the imagined machinery of imperial rule
episodes.logline: In a world of forts, treasuries, allies and secret agents, the Arthashastra imagines how a ruler might keep order before the strong swallow the weak.
episodes.moral: Power needs wisdom, restraint and watchfulness to serve the people.

sources.citation: Patrick Olivelle, King, Governance, and Law in Ancient India: Kautilya's Arthasastra (OUP, 2013)
sources.note: Current standard translation and dating discussion.

sources.citation: Thomas R. Trautmann, Kautilya and the Arthasastra: A Statistical Investigation (Brill, 1971)
sources.note: Statistical evidence that the text is composite rather than a single real-time work.

sources.citation: R.P. Kangle, The Kautiliya Arthasastra, 3 vols. (University of Bombay, 1960-65)
sources.note: Classic edition representing the traditional Kautilya attribution.

episodes.notes: Use the Arthashastra's vivid material: the seven limbs of the state, spies disguised as ascetics or merchants, taxation near one-sixth of produce, mines, forts, treasuries and mandala diplomacy. CRITICAL RECENT-SCHOLARSHIP FLAG: do NOT portray the book as Chanakya's real-time notebook written beside Chandragupta. Trautmann found the text statistically heterogeneous; Olivelle places its likely compilation around 50 BCE-50 CE, with possible older Mauryan material and a Kautilya attribution functioning as a traditional nom de plume. It may reflect Mauryan-compatible political thought, but whether its elaborate spy system was actually implemented is uncertain.
episodes.chapter_part: I. The Rise of the Peacock Throne

episodes.title: Hampi the Boulder Crowned Capital
episodes.era: Vijayanagara capital at its height, 14th-16th centuries CE
episodes.region: Sacred Centre, Royal Centre and agricultural zones of Hampi, Karnataka
episodes.logline: Among granite hills and the Tungabhadra, Hampi grows into a sacred, royal and agricultural city whose streets astonish visitors from Persia and Portugal.
episodes.moral: A city can be designed as both home and sacred landscape.

sources.citation: Abdur Razzaq, Matla-us-Sadain, 1443
sources.note: Persian ambassador's account of seven walls, gardens and unmatched urban splendour.

sources.citation: Domingo Paes, Narrative, c. 1520-22, in Robert Sewell, A Forgotten Empire (1900)
sources.note: Portuguese eyewitness comparison of the city to Rome.

sources.citation: Fritz and Michell, Hampi Vijayanagara (Marg, 2003)
sources.note: Vijayanagara Research Project documentation of sacred, royal and agrarian zones.

episodes.notes: Hampi's core stretched across roughly 25-33 sq. km in a granite boulder landscape, with the Virupaksha sacred centre, the Royal Centre, Mahanavami Dibba, elephant stables, markets and an agricultural buffer. RECENT FINDINGS: the Vijayanagara Research Project, directed by John M. Fritz and George Michell from 1980 to about 2012, mapped more than 1,600 standing or ruined structures and many minor features, creating the benchmark archaeological atlas. Razzaq's seven walls and Paes's Rome comparison are powerful foreign impressions, but do NOT treat every number or comparison as census-grade fact. The Kishkindha associations are sacred geography, not historical geography, even though they shaped the site's meaning.
episodes.chapter_part: I. The City of Victory Rises

episodes.title: The City That Drew Itself in Straight Lines
episodes.era: Early to Mature Harappan urban transition, c. 2700-1900 BCE
episodes.region: Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Rakhigarhi, Dholavira and Kalibangan
episodes.logline: Across a vast Bronze Age world, builders lay streets to the compass, fire bricks in one ratio, and turn scattered towns into a shared urban language.
episodes.moral: Order can be built into the very bricks of daily life.

sources.citation: J.H. Marshall, Mohenjo-daro and the Indus Civilization (1931)
sources.note: Foundational excavation record for Mohenjo-daro's plan and brickwork.

sources.citation: J.M. Kenoyer, Ancient Cities of the Indus Valley Civilization (1998)
sources.note: Modern synthesis of city planning and craft standardisation.

sources.citation: R.S. Bisht, 'Dholavira: A New Horizon of the Indus Civilization,' Puratattva 20 (1991)
sources.note: Primary report on Dholavira's distinctive tripartite city plan.

episodes.notes: Mature Harappan urbanism, usually dated c. 2600-1900 BCE, used 1:2:4 baked bricks, street grids, citadel and lower-town planning, and regional variants such as Dholavira's citadel, middle town and lower town. Kalibangan preserves an earlier ploughed field, while Rakhigarhi excavations since 2013 make it one of the largest known Harappan sites. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT call this a Harappan Empire, do NOT invent a central king, do NOT treat the debated granaries as certain, and do NOT identify Kalibangan fire altars as Vedic sacrifices.

episodes.title: The Princess Who Wrote History
episodes.era: Gulbadan Begum's memoir, c. 1587
episodes.region: Kabul, Agra, Fatehpur Sikri and the Hajj route
episodes.logline: Asked by Akbar to remember the past, Gulbadan Begum writes the only first-person Mughal court memoir by a woman.
episodes.moral: History grows wiser when more voices are allowed to speak.

sources.citation: Gulbadan Begum, The History of Humayun (Humayun-Nama), trans. A.S. Beveridge, Royal Asiatic Society, 1902
sources.note: Primary memoir, surviving in a single incomplete Persian manuscript.

sources.citation: British Library, Add MS 24063, Humayun-Nama manuscript record
sources.note: Physical manuscript basis for Gulbadan's text.

sources.citation: Ruby Lal, Vagabond Princess: The Great Adventures of Gulbadan, Yale University Press, 2021
sources.note: Recent reassessment of Gulbadan as an author and traveller, not merely a source for Humayun.

episodes.notes: Gulbadan Begum, Babur's daughter and Humayun's half-sister, wrote her Humayun-Nama for Akbar around 1587 after living through exile, family conflict, return and a seven-year Hajj journey from 1575 to 1582. Ruby Lal's recent work highlights her literary agency and the neglected story of Mughal women leading an imperial pilgrimage. The text survives in one incomplete manuscript with early folios missing; do NOT treat remembered dialogue or childhood scenes as verbatim transcripts, and do NOT reduce her to only Humayun's biographer.

episodes.title: Mangalesa Lets the Rock Speak Kannada
episodes.era: Badami cave patronage, c. 597-610 CE
episodes.region: Badami cave temples, Karnataka
episodes.logline: In Cave 3 at Badami, royal gifts and sacred images turn sandstone into one of the Deccan's earliest dated voices in Kannada.
episodes.moral: A people's language becomes stronger when it is honored in public.

sources.citation: Badami Cave 3 inscription of Mangalesa, in Epigraphia Indica and DHARMA Epigraphy Project
sources.note: Primary monument inscription for the cave endowment and early Kannada-script record.

sources.citation: George Michell, Pattadakal, Oxford University Press / ASI (1997)
sources.note: Standard art-historical context for Early Chalukya architecture.

sources.citation: Hemanth Kadambi, 'Early Calukya Architecture and Archaeology,' Sahapedia (2011)
sources.note: Recent reassessment of Badami-Aihole-Pattadakal monuments and dating cautions.

episodes.notes: Badami Cave 3, associated with Mangalesa, combines Sanskritic royal culture, early Kannada documentary practice and a spectacular Vishnu iconographic program, including Varaha, Trivikrama and Anantasayana. DHARMA's recent digital editions and Kadambi's archaeological synthesis make it safer to describe the cave as part of a royal landscape of fort, lake and cliff rather than as an isolated shrine. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT call this the oldest Kannada inscription, because Halmidi and other records are older; do NOT claim Mangalesa personally carved the cave; do NOT give 578 CE without qualification, since cave dating is debated.

episodes.title: Iltutmish Wins a Throne and a Caliph
episodes.era: Mamluk consolidation, 1211-1236 CE
episodes.region: Delhi, Lahore, Tarain, Sindh, Bengal and Baghdad
episodes.logline: Iltutmish turns a fragile conquest into a recognized sultanate with coins, iqta grants, a caliphal diploma, and a daughter he dares to name heir.
episodes.moral: Legitimacy must be earned in symbols and in service.

sources.citation: Minhaj-i-Siraj Juzjani, Tabaqat-i Nasiri, volumes on Iltutmish
sources.note: Main near-contemporary account of Iltutmish's court and succession.

sources.citation: Silver tanka and copper jital coinage of Iltutmish, British Museum and Indian Museum collections
sources.note: Physical evidence for titles, currency and claims to sovereignty.

sources.citation: Sunil Kumar, The Emergence of the Delhi Sultanate 1192-1286 (Permanent Black, 2007)
sources.note: Recent interpretation of early Sultanate institutions as fluid and negotiated.

episodes.notes: Iltutmish defeated Aram Shah in 1211, beat Yildiz at Tarain in 1216, overcame Qabacha by c.1228, and received Abbasid recognition in 1229. He issued the silver tanka and copper jital, expanded the iqta system, completed much of the Qutb Minar, and was remembered for preferring Razia over weaker sons. Recent scholarship treats the iqta order and succession story as less tidy than later textbooks suggest; Minhaj is essential but not neutral. Do NOT claim Iltutmish single-handedly created every Sultanate institution, or that Razia's nomination survives as an undisputed formal decree.

episodes.title: Kujula Kadphises Forges the Kushan Crown
episodes.era: Founding of the Kushan dynasty, c. 30-80 CE
episodes.region: Bactria, Kabul, Gandhara and Taxila
episodes.logline: Kujula Kadphises unites the five Yuezhi chiefs, borrows the coin language of Greeks and Indians, and turns a migrant clan into a kingdom.
episodes.moral: A founder succeeds by joining old loyalties to new ambition.

sources.citation: Hou Hanshu, chapter 88, trans. John Hill (2009)
sources.note: Primary Chinese narrative of Kujula attacking the other yabghu and founding Guishuang rule.

sources.citation: Rabatak inscription, published by Joe Cribb and Nicholas Sims-Williams, JONS 160 (1995/96)
sources.note: Names Kujula as the great-grandfather of Kanishka and anchors the dynasty.

sources.citation: Osmund Bopearachchi, Monnaies greco-bactriennes et indo-grecques (1991); Joe Cribb and David Jongeward coin studies
sources.note: Key numismatic work on Indo-Greek, Indo-Parthian and early Kushan transitions.

episodes.notes: Kujula Kadphises, the Guishuang yabghu, probably united the Yuezhi groups around the 1st century CE and expanded through Kabul, Gandhara and Taxila. His coins overstruck or imitated Indo-Greek issues of Hermaeus while adding Kharoshthi legends, a political language that turned borrowed symbols into Kushan legitimacy. RECENT FINDINGS: numismatic die studies separated the unnamed Soter Megas series from Kujula and linked it more securely to Vima Taktu. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT call Kujula a Buddhist patron like Kanishka; do NOT claim precise dates or a proven age of eighty-plus as fact.
episodes.chapter: The Kushan Empire and the Silk Road

episodes.title: Mahendravarman's Vow Without Mortar
episodes.era: Mahendravarman I's reign, c. 600-630 CE
episodes.region: Mandagapattu, Mamandur, Kudimiyamalai and Kanchipuram
episodes.logline: A king who writes farce, studies music and cuts shrines from living rock declares that his new temple will use no brick, wood, lime, mortar or metal.
episodes.moral: Innovation begins when imagination refuses old limits.

sources.citation: Mandagapattu Tirumurti temple inscription of Mahendravarman I
sources.note: Primary rock inscription proclaiming a shrine made without brick, wood, lime, mortar or metal.

sources.citation: Kudimiyamalai music inscription, South Indian Inscriptions, Vol. II, No. 68
sources.note: Early musicological inscription associated with Mahendravarman's courtly world.

sources.citation: Mahendravarman I, Mattavilasa Prahasana, ed. M. Lockwood and A. Vishnu Bhat (1981)
sources.note: Sanskrit farce set in Kanchipuram and reflecting its religious plurality.

episodes.notes: Mahendravarman I was a warrior, artist, playwright and temple innovator. His Mandagapattu inscription is the famous engineering claim that the temple was made without brick, wood, lime, mortar or metal, marking the Pallava rock-cut turn; his Mamandur inscription connects him with plays, while the Kudimiyamalai inscription preserves rare early music theory. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP: Marilyn Hirsh and R. Champakalakshmi stress the king's creative patronage while warning that his Jain-to-Shaiva 'conversion' is better read as a shift in patronage, not a simple doctrinal drama. Do NOT attribute all Mamallapuram monuments to him, and do NOT retell Periya Puranam miracles as biography.
episodes.chapter: The Pallavas and the Bhakti Dawn
episodes.chapter_part: I. Kanchi Rises from the Kalabhra Haze

episodes.title: Madhava at the House of the Ilanchi Tree
episodes.era: Founding generation of the Kerala school, c. 1340-c. 1425
episodes.region: Sangamagrama, probably Kudallur near the Nila-Kunti confluence, Kerala
episodes.logline: From a small river settlement, Madhava becomes the remembered founder whose followers credit him with series that reached beyond the mathematics of his age.
episodes.moral: A quiet village can change the world's questions.

sources.citation: Madhava, Venvaroha, 1403 CE, ed. K.V. Sarma (1956)
sources.note: Dated surviving astronomical work establishing Madhava's historical identity.

sources.citation: Nilakantha Somayaji, Tantrasangraha, 1500-1501; Jyeshthadeva, Yuktibhasa, c. 1530-1550
sources.note: Later Kerala texts repeatedly attribute the infinite series tradition to Madhava.

sources.citation: P.P. Divakaran, The Mathematics of India (2018); C.T. Rajagopal and M.S. Rangachari, Archive for History of Exact Sciences 18 (1978)
sources.note: Recent and classic analysis of Madhava's location, methods and attributed verses.

episodes.notes: Madhava's biography is a sources problem: no contemporary inscription records his birth or death, and his famous mathematical series survive through later attributions rather than autograph proof-texts. His surviving works such as Venvaroha and Sphutacandrapti are astronomical. Divakaran favors Kudallur near the Nila-Kunti confluence over the popular Irinjalakuda identification; present the location as probable, not certain. ACCURACY FLAG: do NOT call Madhava the inventor of calculus or sole author of all later Kerala mathematics; say his school preserved reliable attributions to him for specific infinite series used in astronomy.
episodes.chapter_part: I. The Country of the River

episodes.title: The Potsherds Speak at Keezhadi
episodes.era: Vaigai valley urbanism, c. 3rd century BCE-3rd century CE; earlier dates contested
episodes.region: Keezhadi near the Vaigai River, Sivaganga district, Tamil Nadu
episodes.logline: Under the fields near Madurai, brick structures, dice, ornaments and Tamil Brahmi potsherds reveal a literate urban world while a fierce dating debate continues.
episodes.moral: Good history welcomes discovery without outrunning proof.

sources.citation: Tamil Nadu State Department of Archaeology, Keezhadi Excavation Reports, Seasons 4-8
sources.note: Official reports for finds, trenches, AMS samples and site interpretation.

sources.citation: Iravatham Mahadevan, Early Tamil Epigraphy (Harvard Oriental Series, 2003)
sources.note: Standard reference for Tamil Brahmi scripts and dating.

sources.citation: T.S. Subramanian, reports on Keezhadi excavations in The Hindu, 2019-2025
sources.note: Detailed public reporting on excavation phases and the ASI/TNAD dispute.

episodes.notes: Keezhadi was located by ASI archaeologist K. Amarnath Ramakrishna after a Vaigai survey and excavated from 2014 onward, with later phases by the Tamil Nadu archaeology department. Finds include brick structures, graffiti, Tamil Brahmi sherds, terracotta figures, dice, iron objects, punch-marked coins and ornaments; a museum opened in 2023. RECENT FINDINGS: AMS samples have been cited for early dates, but the crucial question is whether inscribed sherds belong to the same secure layer. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say the 6th century BCE literacy claim is proven, do NOT identify the site as ancient Madurai, and do NOT treat an unpublished or disputed report as consensus.
episodes.chapter: The Satavahanas and the Sangam Age
episodes.chapter_part: I. Roads Through the Red Earth

episodes.title: Balaji Vishwanath Writes a New State
episodes.era: Rise of the hereditary Peshwa, 1713-1720 CE
episodes.region: Satara, Pune and Mughal Delhi
episodes.logline: A Konkan accountant becomes Peshwa and turns Maratha power into a recognized fiscal and constitutional system.
episodes.moral: Institutions can outlast the victories that create them.

sources.citation: Peshwa Daftar, Balaji Vishwanath letters and early Shahu-period documents
sources.note: Primary Modi-script administrative evidence for the early Peshwa system.

sources.citation: Khafi Khan, Muntakhabu-l-Lubab, account of the Syed Brothers and Delhi politics
sources.note: Persian narrative context for the 1719 Mughal settlement.

sources.citation: Andre Wink, Land and Sovereignty in India (Cambridge UP, 1986)
sources.note: Key interpretation of chauth, sardeshmukhi and Maratha sovereignty claims.

episodes.notes: Balaji Vishwanath became Peshwa in 1713 and in 1719 helped the Syed Brothers at Delhi while securing Mughal recognition of Maratha chauth and sardeshmukhi rights in the six Deccan provinces, plus the release of Shahu's mother Yesubai. KEY FACTS: his office became hereditary when Bajirao succeeded in 1720, shifting real power from Satara toward Pune. RECENT FINDINGS: modern state-formation work reads this as a fiscal-military constitution rather than a simple heroic rise. Do NOT present colorful bakhar stories about secret persuasion or Shahu's recognition as unverified fact.

episodes.title: Guru Angad Shapes the Living Letters
episodes.era: Second Guru and early Sikh literacy, c. 1539-1552 CE
episodes.region: Khadur Sahib, Tarn Taran district, Punjab
episodes.logline: Lehna becomes Angad and gives the growing community a clear script, schools and songs that ordinary Punjabi children can learn.
episodes.moral: A shared alphabet can turn faith into a living school.

sources.citation: Guru Granth Sahib, 62 hymns of Guru Angad
sources.note: Textual and manuscript evidence of early Gurmukhi use.

sources.citation: Varan Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 1
sources.note: Early Sikh source crediting Angad's role in the script tradition.

sources.citation: Richard Salomon, Indian Epigraphy (1998); Gurinder Singh Mann, The Making of Sikh Scripture (2001)
sources.note: Modern account of Gurmukhi's structure and early manuscripts.

episodes.notes: Guru Angad, born Lehna in 1504, succeeded Guru Nanak in 1539 and worked from Khadur Sahib, where tradition remembers akharas, free schools, and a disciplined langar. His innovation was not magic invention but standardization: Gurmukhi drew on Landa, Sharda and local scripts, then became a stable 35-letter system suited to Punjabi and to preserving the Gurus' hymns. The Goindval Pothis and other late 16th-century manuscripts are important material evidence. ACCURACY FLAG: do NOT say Angad invented writing or created Gurmukhi in a single moment; say he codified and spread a script that made Sikh scripture and Punjabi literacy durable.
episodes.chapter: The Sikh Gurus and Ranjit Singh

episodes.title: The Chemist Who Made Swadeshi Medicine
episodes.era: Swadeshi science and industry, 1896-1944
episodes.region: Calcutta, Edinburgh and Maniktala
episodes.logline: Prafulla Chandra Ray turns a home laboratory into Bengal Chemical, joining modern chemistry with the dream of Indian industrial self-reliance.
episodes.moral: Knowledge serves best when it also builds livelihoods.

sources.citation: Prafulla Chandra Ray, Life and Experiences of a Bengali Chemist, 2 vols., 1932 and 1935
sources.note: Primary memoir for Ray's training, teaching and Bengal Chemical.

sources.citation: Prafulla Chandra Ray, History of Hindu Chemistry, vols. 1-2, 1902 and 1908
sources.note: Ray's own scholarly recovery of earlier Indian chemical traditions.

sources.citation: John Lourdusamy, Science and National Consciousness in Bengal 1870-1930, Orient Longman, 2004
sources.note: Recent study of Ray's pedagogy, nationalism and student network.

episodes.notes: Ray returned from Edinburgh to Presidency College, published his 1896 study of mercurous nitrite, and in 1901 founded Bengal Chemical and Pharmaceutical Works from modest rooms in Calcutta. This is an ECONOMIC and SCHOLARLY innovation story: an Indian pharmaceutical enterprise making medicines and chemicals, and a historian-chemist using Sanskrit sources in History of Hindu Chemistry. His students included Meghnad Saha and S.N. Bose. Recent scholarship by Lourdusamy and Projit Mukharji stresses the mix of modern lab science, swadeshi industry and historical recovery. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say Ray invented mercurous nitrite from nothing; say he systematically synthesized and studied it in an Indian laboratory. Do NOT portray him as an armed freedom fighter; his nationalism was industrial, educational and scholarly.
episodes.chapter_part: I. The Dawn of Indian Research

episodes.title: The Teacher Who Wrote in Silence
episodes.era: Formal Sanskrit grammar, c. 400-350 BCE
episodes.region: Salatura and Gandhara, near the northwestern crossroads
episodes.logline: Panini compresses Sanskrit into thousands of tiny rules and creates a grammar that behaves like a machine.
episodes.moral: A sharp rule can hold a whole world of speech.

sources.citation: Panini, Ashtadhyayi; S.C. Vasu translation (1891)
sources.note: Primary grammar whose sutras demonstrate the formal rule system.

sources.citation: Patanjali, Mahabhashya, c. 150 BCE
sources.note: Early commentary proving Panini's authority before the Common Era.

sources.citation: George Cardona, Panini: A Survey of Research (1976; reprint 1997)
sources.note: Authoritative modern research survey on date, method and interpretation.

episodes.notes: Panini's Ashtadhyayi is a compact generative grammar of Sanskrit, traditionally linked to Salatura in Gandhara and usually placed around the mid-4th century BCE by recent arguments from coin references and linguistic chronology. The text cites earlier grammarians, so it is a summit of a long tradition rather than a lone miracle. Recent work includes Rishi Rajpopat's 2022 Cambridge thesis on rule-conflict resolution, but that does not change the ancient date. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT claim Panini invented computer science or formal language theory; say his grammar anticipates features later admired by linguists. Lion stories and Chanakya links are late legend.

episodes.title: Suhungmung Opens the Eastern Gates
episodes.era: Expansion under Suhungmung, r. 1497-1539 CE
episodes.region: Sadiya, Dikhow, Chutia territories and Upper Assam
episodes.logline: Suhungmung absorbs the Chutia kingdom, its officers and its crafts, changing a frontier power into a larger Assamese state.
episodes.moral: A wise victor learns from the people he conquers.

sources.citation: Snake Pillar inscription of Suhungmung, early 16th century, Sivasagar
sources.note: Oldest surviving Ahom-language inscription and a key anchor for the reign.

sources.citation: Satsari Assam Buranji, in G.C. Barua, Ahom Buranji (1930)
sources.note: Chronicle account of the Chutia campaigns and Ahom expansion.

sources.citation: Arupjyoti Saikia, The Unquiet River (OUP, 2019)
sources.note: Recent environmental and political history of the Brahmaputra valley, useful for expansion and incorporation.

episodes.notes: Between about 1513 and 1524 Suhungmung's reign brought the Chutia kingdom around Sadiya under Ahom control, adding territory, nobles, scribes, frontier offices and specialized artisan khels to the state. He also adopted the title Swarganarayana, showing a new Hinduized royal idiom while the dynasty remained rooted in Tai traditions. RECENT FINDING / SOURCE FLAG: the Snake Pillar inscription gives rare material evidence for Ahom writing in this period, while Christian Daniels and Arupjyoti Saikia stress how uncertain earlier foundation dates remain. Do NOT call the Chutia people passive subjects; the episode should show incorporation, conflict and cultural transfer, not a simple replacement story.
episodes.chapter_part: I. Golden Gardens Become a Kingdom

episodes.title: The Chola Village Chooses Its Guardians
episodes.era: Chola administration under Parantaka I, c. 919-921 CE
episodes.region: Uttaramerur, Tamil Nadu
episodes.logline: At Uttaramerur, village rules were carved in stone: who could serve on committees, who was disqualified, and how names were chosen by the pot-ticket method. This is an episode about fairness, responsibility, and public trust.
episodes.moral: A strong community needs clear rules and honest service.

sources.citation: Uttaramerur Vaikunta Perumal Temple inscription of Parantaka I, year 12, kudavolai committee rules
sources.note: Primary source for qualifications, disqualifications, and committee selection procedure.

sources.citation: Uttaramerur inscription of Parantaka I, year 14, supplementary village assembly regulations
sources.note: Primary continuation/refinement of local governance rules.

sources.citation: K.A. Nilakanta Sastri, The Cholas; South Indian Inscriptions editions by E. Hultzsch/H. Krishna Sastri
sources.note: Scholarly translation and administrative context.

episodes.notes: This was not modern universal democracy; it was a structured village assembly with property, learning, age, and conduct qualifications. Present it accurately as local self-governance.
episodes.chapter_part: I. Rise of the Tiger Throne

episodes.title: Chandragupta II and the Fall of the Shakas
episodes.era: Gupta zenith, c. 375-415 CE (Shaka conquest c. 409 CE)
episodes.region: Malwa, Gujarat and Saurashtra; the Udayagiri caves near Vidisha
episodes.logline: Vikramaditya ends three centuries of foreign Shaka rule in western India, wins the sea-ports, and has the earth-lifting Boar of Vishnu carved at Udayagiri - the god's power mirrored in the king's.
episodes.moral: A ruler's grandest monument is the order and freedom he leaves his people.

sources.citation: Udayagiri Cave 6 inscription of Chandragupta II, Gupta Era 82 (c. 401 CE)
sources.note: The only monument where he is directly named; edited by Michael Willis.

sources.citation: First Gupta silver coinage (rupaka), modeled on Western Kshatrapa coins after the conquest; COININDIA
sources.note: Numismatic proof of the Shaka absorption (~409 CE).

sources.citation: Michael Willis, The Archaeology of Hindu Ritual (Cambridge, 2009)
sources.note: Standard study of Udayagiri and the Varaha as royal-religious ideology.

episodes.notes: His throne-name was Vikramaditya. The defeat/annexation of the Western Kshatrapas (last king Rudrasimha III) is dated c. 388-409 CE - marked by when Shaka coinage CEASES (~409) and the first Gupta SILVER coins appear. Winning Gujarat's ports fed the prosperity Faxian later saw. The Udayagiri Varaha (Cave 5) equates the king with Vishnu lifting the Earth. The 'Navaratna' (nine gems, incl. Kalidasa) court is LEGENDARY - only in much later texts; present as tradition, not fact. Spoken name should say 'the Second'.

episodes.title: Five Hundred Elephants for Seleucus
episodes.era: Seleucid-Mauryan treaty, c. 305-303 BCE
episodes.region: The Indus frontier, Gandhara, Arachosia and the Hindu Kush
episodes.logline: When Seleucus Nicator marches east to reclaim Alexander's frontier, Chandragupta answers with a treaty of lands, marriage ties, an ambassador, and five hundred elephants that shake the Hellenistic world.
episodes.moral: The wisest victories can end in treaties, not endless war.

sources.citation: Appian, Syriaca 55
sources.note: Primary Greek account of Seleucus crossing the Indus, making treaty and contracting a marriage alliance with Sandrocottus.

sources.citation: Strabo, Geographica XV.2.9
sources.note: Greek source for the marriage alliance and ceded eastern satrapies.

sources.citation: Paul J. Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (Harvard University Press, 2014)
sources.note: Modern study of Seleucid space, diplomacy and the eastern frontier.

episodes.notes: The treaty after the Seleucid-Mauryan war gave Chandragupta control of Gandhara, Arachosia, Gedrosia and the Paropamisadae, while Seleucus received 500 war elephants and sent Megasthenes to Pataliputra. The elephants later mattered at Ipsus in 301 BCE.
