ACCURACY FLAGS: the exact war and treaty dates fall in a debated 305-303 BCE range, with treaty dates sometimes placed as late as 303-298 BCE; the marriage alliance is real in Greek sources, but epigamia may mean formal intermarriage or permission for elite intermarriage, so do NOT invent a named Seleucid princess romance. The Kandahar Greek Edict under Ashoka later confirms Mauryan control in the region.
episodes.chapter_part: II. The Empire Meets the World

episodes.title: The Tanks That Fed an Empire
episodes.figure: Kamalapura Tank and the Bukka Aqueduct
episodes.era: Vijayanagara hydraulic works, especially 15th-16th centuries CE
episodes.region: Kamalapura, Anegundi, the Royal Centre and Tungabhadra canals
episodes.logline: In a dry stone landscape, tanks, aqueducts, pipes and channels carry water into fields, palaces and rituals, letting a vast capital survive.
episodes.moral: Civilization depends on patient care for water.

sources.citation: Kamalapura Tank inscription, 15th century
sources.note: Describes the large perennial tank that watered the suburb and fields.

sources.citation: ASI Hampi excavation reports, 1970s-2020s
sources.note: Excavation evidence for terracotta pipes, channels, drains and water structures.

sources.citation: Nagaveni A., Tanks of Kamalapura, AIIR Journal (2018)
sources.note: Recent study of tank construction phases and inscriptional record.

episodes.notes: Vijayanagara received limited rainfall, so its survival depended on Kamalapura Tank, the Bukka Aqueduct near Anegundi, rock-cut channels, sluices, terracotta pipes, stepped tanks and agricultural canals. KEY FACTS: Kamalapura irrigated fields and fed the Royal Centre; the Bukka Aqueduct is a standing stone-channel system; underground pipes near royal buildings show concealed plumbing. RECENT FINDINGS: 2026 ASI work near Hazara Rama reported stone drainage channels, a 23-metre canal and related remains, extending the water map into the ceremonial core. Do NOT state peak population figures like 500,000-750,000 as census facts; they are estimates from foreign accounts and urban footprint.
episodes.chapter_part: I. The City of Victory Rises

episodes.title: The Invisible Government of Harappa
episodes.era: Mature Harappan civic organisation, c. 2600-1900 BCE
episodes.region: Major Harappan cities from Sind and Punjab to Gujarat and Haryana
episodes.logline: A civilization with standard bricks, weights and streets leaves no palace, no royal portrait, and no conqueror's boast, forcing historians to imagine power without a visible throne.
episodes.moral: Leadership is not always carved as a crown.

sources.citation: G.L. Possehl, The Indus Civilization: A Contemporary Perspective (2002)
sources.note: Key synthesis arguing against a simple imperial model.

sources.citation: J.M. Kenoyer, 'Early City-States in South Asia' in The Archaeology of City-States (1997)
sources.note: Important argument for heterarchical city-state models.

sources.citation: R. Coningham and R. Young, The Archaeology of South Asia (2015)
sources.note: Recent overview of governance debates and material evidence.

episodes.notes: Harappan cities show no confirmed palace, royal inscription, victory stele or named ruler; instead historians infer administration from maintenance-heavy drains, public buildings, seals, weights and cross-regional standards. The dominant modern model is heterarchical or multi-centred governance, perhaps merchant and ritual elites coordinating through shared norms, but hierarchy did exist in burials and access to goods. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say there was no government, do NOT claim an egalitarian utopia, and do NOT name any Harappan ruler because no personal names are deciphered.

episodes.title: The City Akbar Built and Left
episodes.era: Fatehpur Sikri as imperial capital, c. 1571-1585
episodes.region: Fatehpur Sikri, near Agra
episodes.logline: Akbar raises a red sandstone capital around a Sufi blessing, fills it with debate, and then leaves it for the frontier.
episodes.moral: A great city is built from vision, but must answer history's needs.

sources.citation: Abul Fazl, Akbarnama, vol. III, trans. H. Beveridge, Asiatic Society, 1939
sources.note: Court account of Sikri, Salim Chishti, construction and Akbar's reign.

sources.citation: Father Antonio Monserrate, The Commentary of Father Monserrate, trans. J.S. Hoyland and S.N. Banerjee, 1922
sources.note: Jesuit eyewitness for Akbar's court and religious debates.

sources.citation: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Fatehpur Sikri, List no. 255, inscribed 1986
sources.note: Archaeological and architectural record for the surviving city.

episodes.notes: Fatehpur Sikri was built from about 1571 after the birth of Prince Salim and served as capital until Akbar shifted toward Lahore in 1585. Its trabeate red sandstone architecture, Diwan-i-Khas, Panch Mahal and Ibadat Khana show a deliberate imperial language of synthesis and debate. Recent scholarship treats the abandonment as primarily strategic, tied to the northwest frontier, with water stress as only part of the story; do NOT repeat the simple legend that the city was deserted only because its wells failed, and do NOT present miracle tales around Salim Chishti as court record.

episodes.title: Pulakeshin II Holds the Narmada Line
episodes.era: Chalukya-Harsha frontier, c. 618-620 CE
episodes.region: Narmada frontier, Aihole and Vatapi
episodes.logline: When Harsha's northern power presses south, Pulakeshin II makes the Narmada a frontier that even court poets remember with a pun.
episodes.moral: Defending a boundary can shape the map of an age.

sources.citation: Aihole Prashasti of Ravikirti, Saka 556 / 634 CE, Epigraphia Indica Vol. VI; DHARMA INSBadamiCalukya00005
sources.note: Primary Chalukya claim that Pulakeshin checked Harsha at the Narmada.

sources.citation: Xuanzang, Great Tang Records on the Western Regions, trans. Samuel Beal (1884)
sources.note: Independent near-contemporary testimony that Harsha did not subdue the southern kingdom.

sources.citation: Daud Ali, Courtly Culture and Political Life in Early Medieval India (2004)
sources.note: Recent reading of prashastis as literary political performance, not battle reports.

episodes.notes: The Aihole inscription says Pulakeshin II dashed the mirth of Harsha, while Xuanzang independently shows that the Deccan remained outside Harsha's effective reach. The safest story is a Narmada standoff or checked advance, not a fully described pitched battle, because Ravikirti wrote court poetry about fifteen years later and Banabhatta's Harshacharita is silent on the defeat. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say Harsha fled in terror; do NOT invent battle details such as elephants drowning; do NOT treat the Aihole prashasti as neutral reportage.

episodes.title: Razia Sultan Rides Through the Gate
episodes.era: Mamluk Delhi, 1236-1240 CE
episodes.region: Delhi, Kuhram and Tabarhinda in north India
episodes.logline: Her coins call her Sultan, and for four fierce years Razia governs in her own name while nobles fear the woman they cannot control.
episodes.moral: A rightful voice may sound revolutionary in an unjust room.

sources.citation: Minhaj-i-Siraj Juzjani, Tabaqat-i Nasiri, account of Razia's reign
sources.note: Principal near-contemporary narrative, shaped by elite court assumptions.

sources.citation: Coins of Razia with Arabic and Nagari legends, Indian Museum and American Numismatic Society examples
sources.note: Primary evidence that she used the sovereign title Sultan.

sources.citation: K.A. Nizami, 'Razia Sultana', Encyclopaedia of Islam, 2nd edition; Peter Jackson (2003)
sources.note: Modern correction of the title and critical reading of the succession story.

episodes.notes: After Iltutmish's death, Razia displaced Ruknuddin Firuz in November 1236, ruled directly, appointed Jamal-ud-Din Yaqut as Master of Horses, fought rebel governors, was overthrown after Malik Altuniya's revolt, and died in October 1240 while trying to regain Delhi. Her coins are the strongest evidence for her authority and for using Sultan rather than Sultana. Recent numismatic and gender-history work emphasizes sovereign titulature over romance. Do NOT claim a love affair with Yaqut, do NOT present unveiling stories as certain, and do NOT call her merely queen-consort.

episodes.title: Vima Kadphises Strikes the Gold Dinar
episodes.era: Kushan gold coinage and Mathura expansion, c. 100-127 CE
episodes.region: Mathura, Purushapura, Kapisa and the Indo-Roman trade routes
episodes.logline: Vima Kadphises mints heavy gold coins on a Roman-scale standard, turning Kushan power into money that could travel between four worlds.
episodes.moral: Trust is the hidden metal inside every coin.

sources.citation: Mathura statue inscription of Vima Kadphises, published in D.C. Sircar, Indian Epigraphy (1965)
sources.note: Primary evidence for Vima's royal titles and Mathura presence.

sources.citation: David Jongeward, Joe Cribb and Peter Donovan, Kushan, Kushano-Sasanian, and Kidarite Coins (ANS, 2015)
sources.note: Recent catalogue of Kushan coin weights, types and sequences.

sources.citation: Pliny the Elder, Natural History 6.26 and 12.41
sources.note: Roman complaint about gold flowing east for Indian and Asian luxuries.

episodes.notes: Vima Kadphises issued Kushan gold coins of roughly 7.8-8.0 grams, near the Roman aureus standard, in an age when Roman bullion moved east for spices, textiles and silk. His coins show him at a fire altar and often carry Shiva with Nandi, while his Mathura statue presents a Central Asian ruler in boots and coat inside an Indian political landscape. RECENT FINDINGS: Jongeward-Cribb-Donovan and Robert Bracey's die studies refine the ruler sequence and coin chronology. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT call him the first Indian ruler ever to use gold; his innovation was standardized imperial gold coinage, not the invention of gold money. Do NOT invent direct Roman embassies.
episodes.chapter: The Kushan Empire and the Silk Road

episodes.title: Mamalla Takes Vatapi
episodes.era: Pallava-Chalukya war and Vatapi campaign, c. 630-654 CE
episodes.region: Kanchipuram, Manimangalam and Vatapi (Badami)
episodes.logline: Narasimhavarman Mamalla answers his father's defeat by driving north, taking Vatapi in 642 CE, and turning a Chalukya boast into a Pallava legend.
episodes.moral: A setback can become strength when patience waits for the right hour.

sources.citation: Kuram copper-plate grant of Paramesvaravarman I, South Indian Inscriptions, Vol. I
sources.note: Pallava account of victories over Pulakeshin and the destruction of Vatapi.

sources.citation: Xuanzang, Da Tang Xiyuji, Book X, on Kanchipuram c. 640 CE
sources.note: Eyewitness account of Kanchi's religious institutions and prosperity during Mamalla's reign.

sources.citation: Culavamsa, chapters 41-44
sources.note: Sri Lankan record of Manavarman's Pallava alliance and Narasimhavarman's Lanka expeditions.

episodes.notes: Narasimhavarman I, called Mamalla or Great Wrestler, defeated Chalukya forces near Kanchi and sent Paranjothi north to capture Vatapi in 642 CE; Pallava forces likely held the city until the Chalukya recovery around 654 CE. Xuanzang's visit around 640 CE gives an independent portrait of a prosperous Kanchipuram with Buddhist monasteries and Hindu temples. RECENT DEBATE: the Chalukya record gap after 642 strongly suggests Pulakeshin II died in the crisis, but no Chalukya inscription says exactly how. Do NOT state with certainty that Pulakeshin died in a named duel or that miracle stories from later hagiography caused the victory.
episodes.chapter: The Pallavas and the Bhakti Dawn
episodes.chapter_part: II. Wrestlers, Exiles and Crowned Boys

episodes.title: Paramesvara Watches Fifty Five Years
episodes.era: Drigganita reform and observational astronomy, c. 1393-1443
episodes.region: Alathiyur and the Nila valley, Kerala
episodes.logline: Refusing to trust old tables blindly, Paramesvara compares eclipses with the sky for decades and rebuilds computation around observation.
episodes.moral: Truth improves when tradition listens to evidence.

sources.citation: Paramesvara, Drigganita, 1431 CE; Grahanamandana, epoch 1411 CE; Goladipika, 1443 CE
sources.note: Primary texts for the observation-based correction program.

sources.citation: David Pingree, Census of the Exact Sciences in Sanskrit, Series A vol. 4 (1981)
sources.note: Manuscript census listing Paramesvara's large surviving corpus.

sources.citation: K. Ramasubramanian, M.D. Srinivas and M.S. Sriram, Current Science 66:9 (1994); Plofker (2009)
sources.note: Modern account of Kerala model modifications beginning with Paramesvara.

episodes.notes: Paramesvara, the confirmed direct pupil of Madhava, belonged to the Vatasseri family at Alathiyur. His Drigganita, literally sight-computation, corrected the older Parahita constants through eclipse observation and helped shape Kerala almanac practice. KEY FACTS: Grahanamandana uses a 1411 epoch, Drigganita was completed in 1431, and Goladipika in 1443; the often-cited 55-year span is inferred from text dates and observation references. Do NOT claim modern laboratory science, but do highlight the unusually explicit empirical correction tradition and his cyclic-quadrilateral circumradius result later seen in Europe with Lhuilier.

episodes.title: The Coin That Crushed the Sakas
episodes.era: Satavahana restoration, c. 60-130 CE depending on chronology
episodes.region: Western Deccan, Nasik, Malwa, Saurashtra and Pratishthana
episodes.logline: A king praised by his mother as restorer of Satavahana glory defeats the Saka satraps and stamps his own authority over Nahapana's silver coins.
episodes.moral: Victory is strongest when evidence bears its mark.

sources.citation: R.G. Bhandarkar, 'Inscriptions at Nasik,' Epigraphia Indica Vol. 8 (1906)
sources.note: Nashik Cave 3 prashasti of Gautami Balashri and related records.

sources.citation: E.J. Rapson, Catalogue of Indian Coins in the British Museum: Andhras, etc. (1908)
sources.note: Classic treatment of Satavahana and Nahapana coinage and overstrikes.

sources.citation: Shailendra Bhandare, 'Numismatic Evidence and Satavahana Chronology,' South Asian Studies (2006)
sources.note: Recent revised chronology based on coins and hoards.

episodes.notes: Gautamiputra is known above all from the Nashik prashasti commissioned by his mother Gautami Balashri in his son Pulumavi's reign. It says he destroyed the Sakas, Yavanas and Pahlavas, uprooted the Khakharata line of Nahapana, and restored Satavahana glory. The Jogalthambi hoard of thousands of Nahapana coins overstruck with Gautamiputra's name gives rare material proof of political reversal. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP: Bhandare, Shimada and Ollett have narrowed but not settled the date debate. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT treat courtly eulogy as literal conquest of every enemy, do NOT say eka-bamhana has one agreed meaning, and do NOT claim the hoard fixes an absolute reign date.
episodes.chapter: The Satavahanas and the Sangam Age

episodes.title: Palkhed Without a Pitched Battle
episodes.era: Maratha-Nizam conflict, 1727-1728 CE
episodes.region: Pune, Berar, Khandesh, Gujarat, Palkhed and Mungi-Shevgaon
episodes.logline: Bajirao refuses the Nizam's heavy army a grand battle and wins by speed, water, supplies and strategic patience.
episodes.moral: The smartest victory may be won before swords cross.

sources.citation: Selections from the Peshwa Daftar, ed. G.S. Sardesai, letters for the 1727-1728 campaign
sources.note: Administrative correspondence for movements and negotiations.

sources.citation: Treaty of Mungi-Shevgaon, 6 March 1728
sources.note: Documented settlement recognizing Maratha claims after the Palkhed campaign.

sources.citation: Stewart Gordon, Marathas, Marauders, and State Formation (OUP, 1994)
sources.note: Modern reading of campaigns as revenue and sovereignty operations, not pure conquest.

episodes.notes: In 1727-1728 Bajirao answered Nizam-ul-Mulk's challenge by avoiding a set-piece battle, striking Berar, Mahur and Washim, threatening Burhanpur, and trapping the Nizam near Palkhed before the 6 March 1728 treaty. KEY ACCURACY FLAGS: this is not the already existing 1737 Delhi ride; it is a distinct logistics story about mobile cavalry and a heavier artillery army. Recent scholarship warns against turning Bajirao into an always-undefeated legend; do NOT ignore earlier setbacks or the Nizam's own logistical mistakes.

episodes.title: Guru Amar Das Builds the Steps of Equality
episodes.era: Third Guru and social reform, c. 1552-1574 CE
episodes.region: Goindval on the Beas River, Punjab
episodes.logline: At Goindval, the old Guru builds a baoli, seats rich and poor in one langar, and teaches that women may lead and widows need not burn.
episodes.moral: Equality becomes real when it is practiced before every meal.

sources.citation: Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Amar Das's Var Suhi and other hymns
sources.note: Primary text for his anti-sati teaching and devotional program.

sources.citation: Goindval Pothis, late 16th century
sources.note: Pre-canonical Sikh manuscript collections tied to Guru Amar Das's family.

sources.citation: Gurinder Singh Mann, The Making of Sikh Scripture (2001); Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh, Sikhism: An Introduction (2011)
sources.note: Recent scholarship on manuscripts, women and reform.

episodes.notes: Guru Amar Das became Guru in 1552, established Goindval, and built the 84-step baoli as both sacred and civic water infrastructure. His hymns condemn sati by redefining the true sati as spiritual fidelity, not a widow's death; tradition also credits him with opposing purdah, appointing women through the piri system, organizing 22 manjis, and strengthening dasvandh, the one-tenth community contribution. Recent scholarship highlights these as social and economic institutions, not only devotional teachings. ACCURACY FLAGS: Akbar's visit and exact conversations at langar are plausible Sikh tradition rather than firm imperial record; do NOT attach modern Anand Karaj circumambulation practices directly to his age.
episodes.chapter: The Sikh Gurus and Ranjit Singh

episodes.title: Bose Sends Invisible Waves Through Walls
episodes.era: Microwave and plant-response research, 1894-1917
episodes.region: Presidency College and Bose Institute, Calcutta
episodes.logline: Jagadish Chandra Bose builds tiny instruments, sends millimetre waves through walls, and then measures the hidden pulses of plants.
episodes.moral: Curiosity can cross the border between machines and life.

sources.citation: J.C. Bose, On Polarisation of Electric Rays by Double-Refracting Crystals, The Electrician, 1895
sources.note: Primary publication from Bose's millimetre-wave experiments.

sources.citation: J.C. Bose, Response in the Living and Non-Living, Longmans Green, 1902
sources.note: Primary source for his plant and biophysical investigations.

sources.citation: Subrata Dasgupta, Jagadish Chandra Bose and the Indian Response to Western Science, Oxford University Press, 1999
sources.note: Modern contextual biography of Bose's physics, biology and colonial setting.

episodes.notes: Bose demonstrated millimetre-range waves in Calcutta in the 1890s using apparatus he built while facing salary discrimination at Presidency College. He later studied plant responses with instruments such as the crescograph and founded the Bose Institute in 1917. This is a SCIENTIFIC and ENGINEERING innovation story: horn antennas, waveguides and a galena detector anticipated parts of microwave and semiconductor practice, while his plant work helped create a biophysical imagination. IEEE recognition in 1998 and later history-of-science work have restored his technical importance. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT claim Bose invented radio before Marconi; Bose studied the physics of waves, not commercial wireless telegraphy. Do NOT claim Marconi simply stole Bose's invention; priority and influence remain debated.
episodes.chapter_part: II. Minds That Changed the World

episodes.title: The Abandoned Boy Who Became the King's Physician
episodes.era: Early Buddhist medical tradition, c. 5th century BCE
episodes.region: Rajagriha, Takshashila and the early Buddhist world
episodes.logline: Jivaka studies every plant around Takshashila and returns with healing as his only wealth.
episodes.moral: Knowledge can turn rejection into service.

sources.citation: Pali Vinaya Pitaka, Mahavagga VIII; I.B. Horner, The Book of the Discipline, Vol. IV (1951)
sources.note: Primary Buddhist narrative of Jivaka's training and medical career.

sources.citation: Kenneth G. Zysk, Asceticism and Healing in Ancient India (Oxford University Press, 1991)
sources.note: Critical study of Buddhist medicine and early healing practice.

sources.citation: C. Pierce Salguero, The Buddhist Medicine King in Literature and History, History of Religions 48.3 (2009)
sources.note: Recent study of how Jivaka's biography changed across cultures.

episodes.notes: The Pali Vinaya presents Jivaka as a foundling raised near the Magadhan court, trained for seven years at Takshashila, and later physician to Bimbisara, Ajatashatru and the Buddha. His teacher's test, asking for a plant with no medicinal use, makes the episode vivid and socially grounded. Recent scholarship treats the narratives as valuable evidence for pre-classical medical ideas while noting Buddhist hagiography. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT make every cure literal or miraculous; parallel Pali, Sanskrit and Chinese traditions reshape the biography. Do NOT call Jivaka the founder of surgery, because Sushruta and other medical schools belong to separate traditions.

episodes.title: The Snake Pillar Speaks in Ahom Script
episodes.era: Early Ahom epigraphy, early 16th century CE
episodes.region: Sivasagar and the royal centers of Upper Assam
episodes.logline: A stone pillar with a serpent and Ahom letters becomes a rare witness to when court memory began to harden into written record.
episodes.moral: A written line can steady a kingdom's memory.

sources.citation: Snake Pillar inscription of Suhungmung, c. 1497-1539 CE
sources.note: Primary epigraphic evidence for the Ahom script and royal authority.

sources.citation: Edward Gait, A History of Assam, 2nd ed. (1926)
sources.note: Classic synthesis that cross-checked Buranjis with inscriptions, coins and material evidence.

sources.citation: Christian Daniels, 'The Foundation of the Ahom Polity Revisited,' BSOAS 86:2 (2023)
sources.note: Recent reassessment of early Ahom chronology and the limits of retrospective Buranji dates.

episodes.notes: This scholarly innovation story uses the Snake Pillar to explain the Ahom sources problem. Buranjis preserve extraordinary court memory, but much early material was recorded after the events, and the Ahom script itself seems to become visible only from the late medieval period. The Snake Pillar, associated with Suhungmung, is therefore crucial as a material anchor between chronicle and inscription. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say Sukaphaa brought writing to Assam as a proven fact, and do NOT treat 1228 as beyond dispute. Present the pillar as evidence that by Suhungmung's reign Ahom royal memory, ritual authority and script were becoming visibly inscribed in stone.
episodes.chapter_part: I. Golden Gardens Become a Kingdom

episodes.title: Rajaraja Raises Brihadisvara
episodes.era: Imperial Chola, 1003-1010 CE
episodes.region: Thanjavur, Tamil Nadu
episodes.logline: Rajaraja Chola I turned royal power into a towering temple, carefully recording gifts, workers, lamps, music, and administration on stone. The episode can show planners, artisans, and scribes building a monument together.
episodes.moral: Great works endure when vision is matched with organization and respect for skill.

sources.citation: Thanjavur Rajarajesvara/Brihadisvara Temple inscriptions, ed. E. Hultzsch and V. Venkayya, South Indian Inscriptions
sources.note: Primary records of Rajaraja's endowments, personnel, and temple administration.

sources.citation: UNESCO/ASI, Great Living Chola Temples: Brihadisvara Temple at Thanjavur
sources.note: Archaeological and architectural evidence for construction, consecration, and Chola art.

sources.citation: K.A. Nilakanta Sastri, The Cholas, Rajaraja I chapters
sources.note: Scholarly synthesis from inscriptions and Chola history.

episodes.notes: The temple is also known as Rajarajesvara in inscriptions and Brihadisvara today. Avoid anachronistic claims about construction methods not evidenced by archaeology or inscriptions.

episodes.title: Prabhavatigupta, the Regent Queen
episodes.era: Gupta-Vakataka age, c. 385-450 CE
episodes.region: The Vakataka realm of the Deccan (Vidarbha); a daughter of the Gupta house
episodes.logline: Chandragupta II's daughter, widowed young, rules the Deccan for twenty years as regent for her sons, issuing land-grants in her own name and binding the Gupta north to the Vakataka south that would one day paint Ajanta.
episodes.moral: Power held with wisdom can steady a realm as surely as any sword.

sources.citation: Poona and Riddhapur copper-plate grants issued in Prabhavatigupta's own name as regent
sources.note: Primary proof of a Gupta princess exercising sovereign authority.

sources.citation: Vakataka genealogical records; her marriage to Rudrasena II
sources.note: Establishes the Gupta-Vakataka matrimonial alliance.

sources.citation: Hans Bakker, The Vakatakas (1997); Upinder Singh (2008)
sources.note: Scholarship on her regency and the Gupta-Vakataka link to Ajanta.

episodes.notes: She married the Vakataka king Rudrasena II; after his early death she governed as regent (~405-425 CE) for her sons, issuing copper-plate land-grants in HER OWN name - a rare, ATTESTED case of a woman wielding sovereign power in ancient India, and she proudly styles herself of the Gupta (Dharana) gotra. The alliance she embodies connects the Guptas to the later Ajanta caves. A strong female-ruler story (echoing Kundavai in the Chola chapter). Keep it about governance and the alliance, not romance.

episodes.title: Megasthenes at the Wooden Capital
episodes.era: Greek embassy to Chandragupta's court, c. 300 BCE
episodes.region: Pataliputra, at the ancient Ganges-Son river system
episodes.logline: A Greek ambassador walks the long timber walls of Pataliputra, counting towers, gates and river defenses, while trying to describe an India his own world barely understands.
episodes.moral: A stranger's account can illuminate history, but must be read with care.

sources.citation: Megasthenes, Indica, preserved in Arrian, Strabo, Diodorus, Pliny and Aelian
sources.note: Lost eyewitness account surviving only as later Greek and Roman fragments.

sources.citation: ASI excavations at Bulandibagh and Kumrahar, Patna (Waddell 1895; Spooner 1912-13; Jaiswal 1951-55)
sources.note: Wooden palisade beams and the 80-pillar hall evidence tied to ancient Pataliputra.

sources.citation: Richard Stoneman, The Greek Experience of India (Princeton University Press, 2019)
sources.note: Recent assessment of Greek knowledge and Megasthenes' reliability.

episodes.notes: Megasthenes' Indica is lost and survives only in fragments quoted by later authors; Strabo called him unreliable, while modern scholars use him carefully. Tell the physical city: a parallelogram-like Pataliputra, wooden palisade with arrow slits, ditch, 570 towers and 64 gates, and a palace compared with Susa and Ecbatana. Archaeology at Bulandibagh found waterlogged wooden palisade beams, and Kumrahar revealed remains of a pillared hall, though the exact 80-pillar reconstruction and function remain debated. RECENT GUIDANCE: the Son River shifted course; satellite and geomorphological studies support the ancient confluence context. Do NOT present Megasthenes' 'seven castes' or fabulous descriptions as accurate Indian social science.
episodes.chapter_part: II. The Empire Meets the World

episodes.title: Krishnadevaraya Takes Raichur
episodes.era: Tuluva dynasty zenith and the Raichur campaign, 1520 CE
episodes.region: Raichur Doab between the Krishna and Tungabhadra rivers; Vijayanagara and Bijapur
episodes.logline: Krishnadevaraya marches on Raichur with nayaka troops, elephants and Portuguese guns, winning a dazzling victory that also hardens Deccan rivalries.
episodes.moral: Triumph needs humility, because victory can plant future danger.

sources.citation: Domingo Paes, Narrative, c. 1520-22, in Sewell, A Forgotten Empire (1900)
sources.note: Eyewitness-era Portuguese account of Krishnadevaraya and the Raichur campaign.

sources.citation: Ferishta, Tarikh-i-Ferishta, c. 1612, trans. Briggs (1829)
sources.note: Deccan Persian perspective on Raichur and the 'kiss my foot' episode.

sources.citation: Richard M. Eaton, 'Kiss My Foot,' Said the King, Modern Asian Studies
sources.note: Recent analysis of firearms, diplomacy and Raichur's long-term consequences.

episodes.notes: Krishnadevaraya ruled 1509-1529 and captured Raichur Fort from Ismail Adil Shah in 1520, using a cosmopolitan army that included nayaka contingents, Muslim cavalrymen and Portuguese gunners. KEY ACCURACY: Paes's huge army figures are foreign estimates and almost certainly exaggerated; show scale without repeating them as literal numbers. Eaton's recent scholarship reframes the battle as military theatre and diplomatic overreach, with firearms and the humiliating 'kiss my foot' demand helping sour later Deccan politics. Do NOT stage this as a Hindu army versus a Muslim enemy; Vijayanagara and the Sultanates shared soldiers, technology, diplomacy and shifting alliances.
episodes.chapter_part: II. The Zenith of the Rayas

episodes.title: The Pool at the Heart of the City
episodes.era: Mature Harappan Mohenjo-daro, c. 2500-2000 BCE
episodes.region: The citadel mound of Mohenjo-daro, Sind
episodes.logline: On a raised mound at Mohenjo-daro, masons seal a brick tank with gypsum and bitumen so water can gather at the heart of the city.
episodes.moral: Shared spaces can make a community feel whole.

sources.citation: J.H. Marshall, Mohenjo-daro and the Indus Civilization, Vol. I (1931)
sources.note: Primary excavation description of the Great Bath.

sources.citation: E.J.H. Mackay, Further Excavations at Mohenjo-daro (1938)
sources.note: Additional excavation context for the citadel complex.

sources.citation: M. Jansen, 'Mohenjo-Daro - City of the Indus Valley,' Endeavour 11 (1987)
sources.note: Modern architectural reassessment of the site.

episodes.notes: The Great Bath is about 12 m by 7 m by 2.4 m deep, lined with baked brick, gypsum mortar and bitumen, with inlet and corbelled drain features. Its citadel position and surrounding rooms suggest public or ritual importance, but no text explains its function, and conservation studies warn that salts and water-table changes threaten the monument. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT call it certainly a ritual purification pool, do NOT call it the world's first swimming pool, and do NOT say every Harappan city had one.

episodes.title: The Mansab Opens the Gate
episodes.era: Akbar's mansabdari reforms, c. 1560s-1595
episodes.region: Agra, Fatehpur Sikri and the Mughal provinces
episodes.logline: Akbar turns nobles of many backgrounds into ranked servants of one empire, measuring honor in zat and cavalry in sawar.
episodes.moral: A stronger state can grow by widening the circle of trust.

sources.citation: Abul Fazl, Ain-i-Akbari, vol. I, trans. H. Blochmann, Asiatic Society, 1873
sources.note: Primary schedule for mansab ranks, zat, sawar and cavalry obligations.

sources.citation: M. Athar Ali, The Mughal Nobility Under Aurangzeb, 2nd ed., Oxford University Press, 1997
sources.note: Foundational study of the nobility and the Akbari roots of the system.

sources.citation: Shireen Moosvi, The Evolution of the Mansab System under Akbar until 1596-7, Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society, 1981
sources.note: Specialist analysis showing the system evolved rather than appearing complete at once.

episodes.notes: The mansabdari system ranked imperial officers by zat, personal standing and salary, and sawar, the cavalry obligation they had to maintain. It integrated Central Asian, Persian, Afghan, Indian Muslim and Rajput elites, with men such as Man Singh of Amber rising to the highest service. Recent work by Moosvi and Athar Ali shows the system developed over decades and that inspections and troop obligations were often negotiated; do NOT claim Akbar instantly created a perfectly secular meritocracy, and do NOT imply rank was free of family power or court politics.

episodes.title: Vikramaditya II Spares Kanchi's Shrines
episodes.era: Late Badami Chalukya campaigns, c. 731-740 CE
episodes.region: Kanchipuram, Tamil Nadu, and Pattadakal, Karnataka
episodes.logline: After entering Kanchipuram, Vikramaditya II leaves a rare boast not of plunder, but of protecting the conquered city's temples.
episodes.moral: Strength is noblest when it chooses restraint.

sources.citation: Kailasanatha temple pillar inscription, Kanchipuram, South Indian Inscriptions Vol. I, No. 82
sources.note: In-situ primary evidence for Vikramaditya II's conduct at Kanchi.

sources.citation: Kauthem Copper Plates of Vikramaditya II, Epigraphia Indica Vol. XVIII
sources.note: Primary Chalukya grant connected with the Pallava campaign period.

sources.citation: George Michell, Pattadakal, Oxford University Press / ASI (1997)
sources.note: Context for how the Kanchi campaigns shaped Pattadakal architecture.

episodes.notes: The Kanchipuram inscription is unusually vivid because it records Chalukya triumph inside a Pallava sacred space and says Vikramaditya II did not confiscate or damage temples. Recent urban and art-historical scholarship reads this as political magnanimity and admiration for Kanchi's prestige, with later Pattadakal monuments commemorating the victory. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT call this interreligious tolerance, since both courts were largely Hindu with multiple affiliations; do NOT claim permanent Chalukya occupation of Kanchi; do NOT merge this with Pulakeshin II's earlier Pallava wars.

episodes.title: Balban Builds the Shadow of God
episodes.era: Late Mamluk Sultanate, 1266-1287 CE
episodes.region: Delhi, Multan and the Mongol frontier
episodes.logline: A former slave turns kingship into ceremony, spies on governors, breaks the Forty, and loses his heir defending Delhi from the Mongol storm.
episodes.moral: Fear may guard a throne, but it cannot soften grief.

sources.citation: Ziauddin Barani, Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi, 14th century
sources.note: Main source for Balban's court ritual, spies and noble politics.

sources.citation: Amir Khusrau, Qiran-us-Sadain, 1289, and elegies for Prince Muhammad
sources.note: Courtly evidence from a poet close to Balban's family.

sources.citation: Peter Jackson, The Delhi Sultanate (2003), chapter on Balban
sources.note: Critical reassessment of absolutism and frontier defense.

episodes.notes: Balban rose from enslaved Ilbari Turk to regent and then sultan, ruling from 1266 to 1287. Barani credits him with crushing the old corps of Forty, enforcing sijda and paibos, using barids as intelligence officers, and guarding the northwest; his son Prince Muhammad was killed fighting Mongols in 1285. Jackson cautions that Balban's absolutism was real but not absolute, since noble cooperation still mattered. Do NOT turn Barani's claim that Balban never laughed into literal biography, and do NOT imply his reforms permanently ended factional politics.

episodes.title: The Locked Rooms of Begram
episodes.era: Kushan trade at Kapisa, objects mainly 1st-2nd century CE
episodes.region: Begram or ancient Kapisa, Afghanistan
episodes.logline: Behind sealed mud-brick walls at Begram, Roman glass, Chinese lacquer and Indian ivories reveal the Kushans as brokers of the ancient world's busiest roads.
episodes.moral: Civilizations meet most quietly in the hands of traders and makers.

sources.citation: J. Hackin et al., Nouvelles recherches archeologiques a Begram (1954)
sources.note: Primary DAFA excavation publication for Rooms 10 and 13 and their objects.

sources.citation: Periplus Maris Erythraei, trans. Lionel Casson (1989)
sources.note: Contemporary merchant handbook for Indian Ocean routes linked to Kushan-era trade.

sources.citation: Roberta Tomber, Indo-Roman Trade (2008); Matthew Cobb, Rome and the Indian Ocean Trade (2018)
sources.note: Recent studies of the Roman and Indian Ocean sides of the exchange network.

episodes.notes: The Begram hoard, excavated by Joseph Hackin's DAFA team in 1936-40, contained Roman and Alexandrian glass, Egyptian bronzes, Han Chinese lacquer and more than a thousand Indian-style ivory and bone inlays. It shows Kapisa as a trade and storage hub at the meeting of the overland Silk Road, the Hindu Kush passes and Indian Ocean routes. RECENT FINDINGS: recovered and conserved Begram pieces since 2004 and Bertille Lyonnet's 2012 critique have complicated the old idea of one simple 1st-2nd century sealing event. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say Kushans sailed to Rome; do NOT treat the hoard as a simple royal treasure without noting warehouse, gift-store and dating debates.
episodes.chapter: The Kushan Empire and the Silk Road

episodes.title: The Boy from Kambuja Crowned at Kanchi
episodes.era: Pallava succession crisis and reign, c. 731-796 CE
episodes.region: Kambujadesa, Kanchipuram and the Vaikunta Perumal temple
episodes.logline: When the royal line falters, Pallava ministers find a twelve-year-old collateral prince across the sea and crown him in Kanchipuram as Nandivarman II.
episodes.moral: Legitimacy survives when a community can renew its institutions.

sources.citation: Kasakudi copper plates of Nandivarman II, South Indian Inscriptions, Vol. II
sources.note: Primary record for the succession narrative and Pallava genealogy.

sources.citation: Vaikunta Perumal temple relief panels, Kanchipuram
sources.note: Visual dynastic narrative showing the search for and coronation of Nandivarman II.

sources.citation: D. Dennis Hudson, The Body of God (2008)
sources.note: Detailed modern study of the Vaikunta Perumal temple as royal and religious narrative.

episodes.notes: After Paramesvaravarman II died without an heir, Pallava elites selected the young Pallavamalla from a collateral line associated in the plates with Kambujadesa and crowned him Nandivarman II. The Vaikunta Perumal temple's cloister panels turn this crisis into one of India's rare early dynastic autobiographies in stone. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP by Dennis Hudson dates and interprets the temple as both a palace of Krishna and a political monument. Do NOT claim the precise Kambujadesa location is certain, and do NOT accept the 54-king divine genealogy from Brahma and Ashwatthama as history.
episodes.chapter: The Pallavas and the Bhakti Dawn
episodes.chapter_part: II. Wrestlers, Exiles and Crowned Boys

episodes.title: Nilakantha Moves the Planets Around the Sun
episodes.era: Tantrasangraha and revised planetary theory, 1444-c. 1544
episodes.region: Trikkandiyur, Kelallur Illam and Kerala's scholarly network
episodes.logline: Nilakantha keeps Earth at the center of the cosmos but lets the planets circle the Sun, creating a model mathematically close to Tycho's before Tycho.
episodes.moral: Innovation can revise a tradition from within.

sources.citation: Nilakantha Somayaji, Tantrasangraha, completed 1500-1501 CE
sources.note: Precisely dated Sanskrit synthesis of planetary theory, spherical astronomy and series results.

sources.citation: Nilakantha Somayaji, Aryabhatiya-bhasya and Jyotirmimamsa, ed. K.V. Sarma
sources.note: Primary sources for his revised planetary model and observational method.

sources.citation: Ramasubramanian, Srinivas and Sriram, Current Science 66:9 (1994); K.V. Sarma and K. Ramasubramanian, Tantrasangraha translation (2011)
sources.note: Modern interpretation of the geo-heliocentric model and full translation of the text.

episodes.notes: Nilakantha is unusually well dated: his own Siddhanta-darpana gives Kali-day 1,660,181, converted to 14 June 1444. Tantrasangraha has internal chronograms for 1500-1501 and 432 verses in eight chapters. RECENT FINDING: the 1994 Current Science paper made the strongest case that his model places Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn around the Sun while the Sun circles Earth, a Tychonic-equivalent geometry. ACCURACY FLAG: do NOT call him a full heliocentrist or a Copernicus before Copernicus; he retained a geocentric cosmology while transforming the mathematical model.

episodes.title: The King Who Gathered Seven Hundred Songs
episodes.figure: King Hala and the Sattasai Poets
episodes.era: Hala tradition c. 1st century CE; anthology redaction c. 2nd-4th century CE
episodes.region: Pratishthana and the Maharashtri Prakrit literary world
episodes.logline: A Satavahana king is remembered for gathering seven hundred Prakrit love poems whose women speak frankly of longing, desire and village life.
episodes.moral: A court becomes great when it listens to many voices.

sources.citation: Peter Khoroche and Herman Tieken, Poems on Life and Love in Ancient India: Hala's Sattasai (SUNY, 2009)
sources.note: Modern English translation and introduction to the anthology.

sources.citation: Andrew Ollett, Language of the Snakes (University of California Press, 2017)
sources.note: Recent study of Prakrit literary culture and Satavahana language politics.

sources.citation: Sheldon Pollock, The Language of the Gods in the World of Men (University of California Press, 2006)
sources.note: Context for vernacular and cosmopolitan literary economies.

episodes.notes: The Gaha Sattasai, or Gatha Saptashati, is a Maharashtri Prakrit anthology traditionally attributed to King Hala. It preserves hundreds of short lyric poems, many in women's voices, and helped make Maharashtri Prakrit a prestige medium for love poetry. Manuscript traditions name many poets, and Bana cites the work by the 7th century. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP: Khoroche, Tieken and Ollett emphasize compilation, redaction and the broader language order. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT claim Hala personally wrote all 700 poems, do NOT date the received text securely to the 1st century CE, and do NOT turn early Radha-Krishna references into proof of later theology.
episodes.chapter: The Satavahanas and the Sangam Age

episodes.title: Kanhoji Angre Rules the Western Seas
episodes.era: Maratha naval power, 1698-1729 CE
episodes.region: Suvarnadurg, Khanderi, Vijaydurg, Sindhudurg, Bombay and the Konkan coast
episodes.logline: From sea forts and swift vessels, Kanhoji Angre makes European companies bargain with a Maratha admiral they called a pirate.
episodes.moral: Control of the coast can protect freedom inland.

sources.citation: British East India Company records on failed operations against Angre, 1718-1722
sources.note: European primary evidence for repeated unsuccessful attacks.

sources.citation: Arquivo Historico Ultramarino, Lisbon, Portuguese records on Angre and the Konkan
sources.note: Portuguese imperial documentation for western-coast conflict and commerce.

sources.citation: Rene Barendse, Arabian Seas 1700-1763, Vol. I (Brill, 2009)
sources.note: Recent archive-based reassessment of Angre's origins and maritime politics.

episodes.notes: Kanhoji Angre commanded Maratha coastal power from about 1698 and, after a 1713 settlement with Balaji Vishwanath, was recognized as Sarkhel with forts and coastal posts. KEY FACTS: British-Portuguese efforts in 1718, 1720, 1721 and 1722 failed, and his sea forts later formed part of the 2025 Maratha Military Landscapes evidence base. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP FLAG: Barendse complicates nationalist and European labels alike; do NOT state a certain caste or ethnic origin, and do NOT accept the European word 'pirate' without explaining the contested admiral/privateer framing.

episodes.title: Guru Ram Das Digs the Pool of Nectar
episodes.era: Founding of Ramdaspur-Amritsar, c. 1574-1581 CE
episodes.region: Ramdaspur, later Amritsar, Punjab
episodes.logline: The fourth Guru turns a dusty settlement into Ramdaspur, calling merchants, artisans and pilgrims around a new pool of nectar.
episodes.moral: A city can be built around service instead of pride.

sources.citation: Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Ram Das's hymns including the Lavan
sources.note: Primary evidence for his literary contribution.

sources.citation: Gazetteer of the Amritsar District (1892)
sources.note: Colonial record preserving the 700-rupee land-purchase tradition.

sources.citation: Pardeep Singh Arshi, The Golden Temple: History, Art and Architecture (1989); Arvind-Pal Singh Mandair, Sikhism: A Guide for the Perplexed (2013)
sources.note: Architectural and historical context for Amritsar.

episodes.notes: Guru Ram Das, born Jetha in 1534, became Guru in 1574 and developed Ramdaspur, later Amritsar, around excavated sarovars that became the center of Sikh urban life. The story is an innovation in city-making: dasvandh donations, invited craftsmen and traders, water management, pilgrimage and commerce all strengthened one another. He composed 638 hymns, including the Lavan. RECENT/ACCURACY FLAGS: the present sarovar and shrine have been rebuilt many times, though the 16th-century site is secure; the 700-rupee purchase from Tung village comes through later records; do NOT claim the modern Anand Karaj circumambulation rite was fully fixed by Guru Ram Das, because scholars place that ritual formalization in the Singh Sabha period.
episodes.chapter: The Sikh Gurus and Ranjit Singh
episodes.chapter_part: II. The Sacred Word and the Pool

episodes.title: Ramanujan Posts a Letter of Theorems
episodes.era: Ramanujan-Hardy collaboration, 1913-1920
episodes.region: Erode, Kumbakonam, Madras and Cambridge
episodes.logline: A clerk in Madras mails G.H. Hardy pages of strange theorems, and the world of number theory opens a door no one knew was there.
episodes.moral: Genius still needs someone willing to read carefully.

sources.citation: Srinivasa Ramanujan's letter to G.H. Hardy, 16 January 1913, Trinity College Library, Cambridge, MS R.1.1
sources.note: Primary surviving letter that launched the Cambridge collaboration.

sources.citation: G.H. Hardy and S. Ramanujan, Asymptotic formulae in combinatory analysis, Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society 17, 1918
sources.note: Primary partition-function paper.

sources.citation: George Andrews and Bruce Berndt, Ramanujan's Lost Notebook, 5 vols., Springer, 2005-2013
sources.note: Definitive recent edition and analysis of the final notebook material.

episodes.notes: Ramanujan's 16 January 1913 letter to Hardy contained more than a hundred results, some known and many astonishingly new. At Cambridge he worked on partitions, modular forms, continued fractions and related fields; he became FRS in 1918 and in his last 1920 letter introduced mock theta functions. This is a MATHEMATICAL and SCHOLARLY innovation story whose recent afterlife includes Andrews and Berndt's lost-notebook editions and work by Ken Ono and others linking mock theta functions to modern mathematics and physics. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT present family traditions about the goddess Namagiri giving theorems in dreams as verified fact. Do NOT say vegetarianism in England caused his death; later medical reassessment points strongly to hepatic amoebiasis contracted earlier.
episodes.chapter_part: II. Minds That Changed the World

episodes.title: What Is Health A Debate in the Forest
episodes.era: Classical Ayurveda formation, c. 1st-2nd century CE with older layers
episodes.region: Himalayan teaching scenes and north Indian medical lineages
episodes.logline: A forest gathering asks what truly benefits living beings and turns medicine into a disciplined debate.
episodes.moral: Wisdom grows when healers argue honestly.

sources.citation: Charaka Samhita; P.V. Sharma edition and translation (1981-94)
sources.note: Primary medical compendium with debate scenes, diagnosis, ethics and theory.

sources.citation: G.J. Meulenbeld, A History of Indian Medical Literature, Vols. IA-IB (1999)
sources.note: Definitive study of the layered composition and dating problems.

sources.citation: Dominik Wujastyk, The Roots of Ayurveda (Penguin Classics, 2003)
sources.note: Accessible translated selections with notes on medical ethics and practice.

episodes.notes: The Charaka Samhita frames medicine as reasoned discussion: Atreya and sages debate what benefits living beings before building systems of diagnosis, diet, ethics and treatment. Its layers likely include Agnivesa's older teaching, Charaka's redaction around the early Common Era, and Dridhabala's much later restoration of lost chapters. Recent manuscript work shows regional recensions, reminding us that Ayurveda was transmitted and revised over centuries. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT claim Charaka founded Ayurveda or wrote a single finished book in one lifetime; do NOT treat the divine origin story as history. The value is the text's explicit ethics and clinical reasoning, not a modern biomedical identity.

episodes.title: Momai Tamuli and the Paik Revolution
episodes.era: Administrative reform under Pratap Singha, 1609 CE
episodes.region: Garhgaon, Rangpur and the villages of Upper Assam
episodes.logline: A minister remembered as rising from humble service reorganizes Assam's labor, crafts and soldiers into the paik system that powers the kingdom.
episodes.moral: The strength of a state rests on how it organizes ordinary work.

sources.citation: G.C. Barua, trans., Ahom Buranji (1930)
sources.note: Chronicle material on the 1609 reorganization and offices under Pratap Singha.

sources.citation: Jahnabi Gogoi, Agrarian System of Medieval Assam (2002)
sources.note: Detailed study of paik labor, land assignments, khels and the agrarian economy.

sources.citation: H.K. Barpujari, ed., The Comprehensive History of Assam, Vol. 2 (1992)
sources.note: Modern account of Pratap Singha, Momai Tamuli and the Ahom administrative machine.

episodes.notes: Momai Tamuli Borbarua's 1609 reforms shifted labor organization from older kin-based loyalties toward functional khels of soldiers, boatmen, weavers, elephant handlers, scribes and artisans. Paiks owed rotating state service and received usufruct land, making the system both an administrative innovation and a compulsory corvee burden. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP: Jahnabi Gogoi treats this as the key economic institution behind Ahom resilience. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT romanticize the paik system as democratic or free; it excluded elites, burdened commoners and later cracked under strain, but it also made roads, forts, boats, embankments and military production possible.

episodes.title: The Shadow of the Great Vimana
episodes.era: Imperial Chola, c. 1003-1010 CE
episodes.region: Thanjavur, Chola country
episodes.logline: To crown Rajaraja's temple, the sthapatis raise a sixty-metre tower of interlocking granite and lift an eighty-tonne capstone up a mile-long earthen ramp, an engineering marvel that has stood a thousand years.
episodes.moral: Genius is patience, mathematics, and a thousand hands moving as one.

sources.citation: Engineering studies of the Brihadisvara (Rajarajesvara) vimana and its capstone
George Michell, Architecture and Art of Southern India; the temple's own craftsman inscriptions

episodes.title: Faxian's Road Through a Golden Land
episodes.era: Gupta zenith, the traveller's years c. 399-414 CE
episodes.region: The pilgrim's road from China to Pataliputra and the Gangetic plain
episodes.logline: A Chinese monk walks across the Gupta empire seeking Buddhist scriptures and records what he sees - free hospitals in Pataliputra, orderly cities, gold coins - an outsider's honest snapshot of a golden age, and of whom it truly served.
episodes.moral: A land is judged by how it treats its poorest, not only by the gold in its markets.

sources.citation: Faxian, Foguo Ji (A Record of Buddhist Kingdoms), tr. James Legge (1886)
sources.note: Eyewitness account of Gupta India, incl. the free hospitals of Pataliputra.

sources.citation: R.S. Sharma, Indian Feudalism c. 300-1200 (1965)
sources.note: The land-grant/feudalism critique: prosperity was uneven.

sources.citation: Romila Thapar, Early India (2002); Upinder Singh (2008)
sources.note: Revisionist caution: the 'golden age' as largely an elite experience.

episodes.notes: Faxian (Fa-Hien) travelled c. 399-414 CE and does NOT name the emperor (historians infer Chandragupta II). Use his real observations: charitable hospitals in Pataliputra ('the poor, destitute, crippled and diseased may repair... food and medicine given'); orderly cities; gold dinaras. BUT weave the HONEST nuance the scholarship demands: his 'no poll-tax' likely describes the elite, not all; agrahara land-grants (R.S. Sharma) concentrated land and imposed vishti (forced labour); caste hardened and women's status declined (Thapar, Upinder Singh). Show the brilliance AND the shadow.

episodes.title: Bindusara's Figs Wine and Philosopher
episodes.era: The transitional Mauryan reign, c. 297-272 BCE
episodes.region: Pataliputra, the Deccan traditions, and the Seleucid court of Antiochus I
episodes.logline: Between Chandragupta and Ashoka, Bindusara keeps the empire steady and sends west for sweet wine, dried figs and a philosopher the Greeks refuse to export.
episodes.moral: Quiet stewardship can matter as much as dazzling conquest.

sources.citation: Athenaeus, Deipnosophistai, on Bindusara's request to Antiochus I
sources.note: Greek anecdote of sweet wine, dried figs and a sophist.

sources.citation: Puranic king-lists; Divyavadana and Mahavamsa traditions
sources.note: Later textual evidence for succession and family traditions.

sources.citation: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India (2008); Paul Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)
sources.note: Modern chronology and context for Seleucid-Mauryan diplomatic ties.

episodes.notes: Bindusara, Chandragupta's son and Ashoka's father, is epigraphically invisible: no inscription from his reign has been found. Greek sources preserve his name as Amitrochates/Allitrochades, reflecting Amitraghata, 'slayer of enemies.' The famous letter to Antiochus I asking for sweet wine, dried figs and a sophist is a wonderful scene, but Athenaeus wrote centuries later; treat the diplomatic exchange as plausible and the sophist detail as possibly literary. Taranatha's much later claim that Bindusara conquered the land between the two seas is disputed, so do NOT map him as proven conqueror of peninsular India. He is best shown as the shadowed consolidator between two better-attested rulers.
episodes.chapter_part: II. The Empire Meets the World

episodes.title: The King Who Wrote Amuktamalyada
episodes.era: Krishnadevaraya's literary court, c. 1509-1529 CE
episodes.region: Vijayanagara court, Telugu literary world, Srirangam and Pandharpur devotional imagination
episodes.logline: The warrior king becomes a poet, composing Amuktamalyada and gathering Telugu masters whose fame later shines as the Ashtadiggajas.
episodes.moral: The finest rulers honor both sword and song.

sources.citation: Krishnadevaraya, Amuktamalyada, Telugu manuscripts
sources.note: Primary literary evidence for the king as author.

sources.citation: Rao and Shulman, trans., Krishnadevaraya's Amuktamalyada (Penguin Classics India, 2021)
sources.note: Recent accessible scholarly translation and interpretation.

sources.citation: Subrahmanyam, Shulman and Rao, Textures of Time (2003)
sources.note: Explains literary patronage as political culture.

episodes.notes: Amuktamalyada tells the story of Andal and Ranganatha while embedding ideas of kingship, devotion and governance. KEY FACTS: Krishnadevaraya's authorship is attested by manuscripts and internal tradition; Allasani Peddana, Nandi Thimmana, Dhurjati, Pingali Surana and others were real poets in the Telugu golden age. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP notes the poem's bridge between Tamil devotion and Telugu court literature, and the 2021 Rao-Shulman translation has made it newly accessible. Accuracy flag: the exact formal group called the Ashtadiggajas is probably a later retrospective construction, so do NOT show a perfectly documented eight-poet club sitting in an archaeologically identified hall.
episodes.chapter_part: II. The Zenith of the Rayas

episodes.title: The City That Did Not Smell
episodes.era: Mature Harappan sanitation systems, c. 2600-1900 BCE
episodes.region: Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Lothal, Dholavira and smaller towns
episodes.logline: Under the streets, covered brick drains carry bathwater and waste away from homes, proving that Harappan urban life depended on hidden civic labour.
episodes.moral: Civilization is often what a city chooses to keep clean.

sources.citation: J.H. Marshall, Mohenjo-daro and the Indus Civilization, Vol. I (1931)
sources.note: Primary plans and sections for streets and drains.

sources.citation: M. Jansen, 'Water Supply and Sewage Disposal at Mohenjo-Daro,' World Archaeology 21 (1989)
sources.note: Technical study of water and drainage infrastructure.

sources.citation: Shereen Ratnagar, The End of the Great Harappan Tradition (2000)
sources.note: Discussion of civic institutions needed to sustain urban systems.

episodes.notes: Excavated houses at Mohenjo-daro and Harappa often have bathing platforms and drains that connect to covered street drains with inspection points and soak-pits. The system was not modern sewage treatment, but it was a citywide wastewater network far beyond most Bronze Age parallels and required maintenance, norms and authority. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say every household certainly had a bathroom, do NOT compare it as equal to modern sewage, and do NOT ignore the labourers who must have cleaned and repaired it.

episodes.title: Todar Mal Counts Every Bigha
episodes.era: Dahsala revenue reforms, c. 1580-1582
episodes.region: Agra, Allahabad, Awadh, Bihar and the Gangetic plain
episodes.logline: Todar Mal's surveyors measure fields with iron-ringed rods so tax can follow crops, prices and the land itself.
episodes.moral: Fair rules begin with careful measurement.

sources.citation: Abul Fazl, Ain-i-Akbari, vol. II, trans. H.S. Jarrett, rev. Jadunath Sarkar, Asiatic Society, 1894-1908
sources.note: Primary administrative source for revenue schedules, crops and land classes.

sources.citation: Irfan Habib, The Agrarian System of Mughal India, 1556-1707, 2nd ed., Oxford University Press, 1999
sources.note: Standard modern analysis of Mughal agrarian revenue and its limits.

sources.citation: Satish Chandra, Medieval India: From Sultanate to the Mughals, Part II, Har-Anand, 2007
sources.note: Accessible synthesis of Akbar's administrative reforms.

episodes.notes: Todar Mal's dahsala system standardized measurement with the jarib, classified land, averaged ten years of yields and prices, and assessed cash revenue most effectively in the imperial heartland. Habib's quantitative work shows both the sophistication of the Ain-i-Akbari data and the gap between ideal schedules and village practice. The reform built on Sher Shah Suri and local accounting precedents; do NOT say Todar Mal invented double-entry bookkeeping, and do NOT claim the cash system functioned uniformly in every province.

episodes.title: Dantidurga Steps Through the Golden Womb
episodes.era: Rashtrakuta takeover, c. 735-756 CE
episodes.region: Achalapur, Ellora, Manpur and the Deccan
episodes.logline: A Chalukya feudatory defeats his overlord, then uses the Hiranyagarbha ritual to be publicly reborn as a Rashtrakuta king.
episodes.moral: Power lasts only when people believe it is legitimate.

sources.citation: Samangad Copper Plates of Dantidurga, Saka 676 / 754 CE, Epigraphia Indica Vol. XVIII; CII Vol. IV
sources.note: Primary evidence for Dantidurga's power and Hiranyagarbha legitimation.

sources.citation: Ellora Cave 15 inscription and Manor plates of Dantidurga, published in JBBRAS and CII
sources.note: Primary records connecting early Rashtrakuta power to western Deccan sites.

sources.citation: Ronald Inden, Imagining India (1990); Daud Ali on courtly politics
sources.note: Modern interpretation of royal ritual as public political scripting.

episodes.notes: Dantidurga's overthrow of the last Badami Chalukya ruler around 753 CE is anchored by the Samangad plates, which combine military success with the Hiranyagarbha, a Vedic 'golden womb' ceremony that advertised ritually renewed kingship. Recent work on Deccan state formation treats this not as a lone coup but as a shift in military, Brahminical and agrarian networks. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say Dantidurga killed Kirtivarman II, because the sources do not record his fate; do NOT imply the Rashtrakutas came from nowhere; do NOT reduce the ritual to private religion without its political meaning.

episodes.title: Malik Kafur Marches Beyond the Vindhyas
episodes.era: Khalji southern campaigns, 1307-1311 CE
episodes.region: Devagiri, Warangal, Dwarasamudra, Madurai and Delhi
episodes.logline: Bought for a thousand dinars, Malik Kafur leads Alauddin's armies across the Deccan and returns with tribute that changes Delhi's imagination of India.
episodes.moral: A meteoric rise can dazzle and destroy.

sources.citation: Amir Khusrau, Khazain-ul-Futuh, 1311
sources.note: Contemporary panegyric account of Alauddin Khalji's campaigns.

sources.citation: Ziauddin Barani, Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi
sources.note: Later Persian chronicle, useful but less detailed on the Deccan raids.

sources.citation: Richard M. Eaton, A Social History of the Deccan 1300-1761 (Cambridge University Press, 2005)
sources.note: Modern context for Deccan politics and Sultanate pressure.

episodes.notes: Malik Kafur, captured in Gujarat in 1299 and later Alauddin Khalji's trusted commander, led tribute-seeking campaigns against Devagiri, Warangal, the Hoysalas and the Pandyas between 1307 and 1311. These raids extracted wealth and submission but did not annex the south permanently, and Kafur was killed soon after briefly dominating politics after Alauddin's death in 1316. Recent Deccan scholarship stresses local agency and long-term political consequences. Do NOT claim he conquered south India, and do NOT state that the Koh-i-Noor was certainly taken at Warangal; that is later tradition, not contemporary evidence.

episodes.title: Kanishka's Sword on the Silk Road
episodes.era: Reign of Kanishka I, c. 127-150 CE by Falk's dating
episodes.region: Purushapura, Mathura, Kashmir, the Tarim Basin and the Gangetic plain
episodes.logline: Kanishka rules from Peshawar toward Central Asia and the Ganges, stamping coins as King of Kings while the Silk Road bends around his armies.
episodes.moral: Power is widest when it protects the roads it conquers.

sources.citation: Rabatak inscription, Cribb and Sims-Williams, JONS 160 (1995/96); revised by Sims-Williams (2008)
sources.note: Primary Bactrian evidence for Kanishka's genealogy and claimed eastern cities.

sources.citation: Hou Hanshu chapters 47 and 88, trans. John Hill (2009)
sources.note: Chinese record of Kushan-Han conflict and Central Asian context.

sources.citation: Harry Falk, The Yuga of Sphujiddhvaja and the Era of the Kushans, Silk Road Art and Archaeology 7 (2001)
sources.note: Influential argument for 127 CE as Year 1 of the Kanishka era.

episodes.notes: Kanishka I, probably beginning in 127 CE under Falk's widely used chronology, made Purushapura the main capital and claimed rule from Sindh to Saketa, Kausambi, Pataliputra and Sri-Champa in the Rabatak inscription. Chinese sources preserve a Kushan-Han conflict across the high routes into the Tarim Basin, though battle details remain Chinese court narrative rather than Kushan testimony. RECENT FINDINGS: the Rabatak inscription, found in 1993 and published in 1995/96, transformed understanding of Kushan geography; Cribb's coin studies separated Kanishka I from later Kanishkas. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say he certainly conquered or destroyed Pataliputra; Rabatak proves claimed rule or submission, not the exact military method.
episodes.chapter: The Kushan Empire and the Silk Road

episodes.title: Five Generations Across the Deccan
episodes.era: Long Pallava-Chalukya struggle, c. 618-750s CE
episodes.region: Kanchipuram, Pullalur, Manimangalam, Vatapi and the Deccan routes
episodes.logline: Across more than a century, Pallava and Chalukya courts turn the same battles into rival poems of humiliation, revenge, endurance and royal glory.
episodes.moral: History is clearest when rival voices are heard together.

sources.citation: Aihole prashasti of Pulakeshin II by Ravikirti, Saka 556 / c. 634 CE
sources.note: Chalukya victory narrative for the Pullalur campaign against Mahendravarman I.

sources.citation: Kuram copper plates and Velurpalaiyam plates of the Pallavas
sources.note: Pallava counter-narratives for the Vatapi revenge and later victories.

sources.citation: Cynthia Talbot, Precolonial India in Practice (2001); Hermann Kulke and Dietmar Rothermund, A History of India (2004)
sources.note: Modern framing of inscriptional war narratives and temple-state politics.

episodes.notes: The Pallava-Chalukya struggle began with Pulakeshin II's victory over Mahendravarman I near Pullalur around 618-619 CE, peaked with Narasimhavarman I's capture of Vatapi in 642 CE, and continued through Chalukya occupation threats and Nandivarman II's recovery with Rashtrakuta help. The Aihole prashasti and Pallava plates are political poems, not neutral reports. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP treats these inscriptions as performances of legitimacy. Do NOT present either side's metaphors, such as writing victory on an enemy's back, as literal battlefield journalism; and do NOT duplicate the Chalukya point of view without showing Pallava endurance.
episodes.chapter: The Pallavas and the Bhakti Dawn

episodes.title: The Series That Reached Pi
episodes.era: Kerala infinite series tradition, c. 1400-1550
episodes.region: Kerala manuscripts of Tantrasangraha, Yuktibhasa and Yukti-dipika
episodes.logline: Kerala mathematicians express pi, sine, cosine and arctangent as endless series, then add error terms that make infinity useful.
episodes.moral: The infinite becomes powerful when it is made precise.

sources.citation: Jyeshthadeva, Yuktibhasa, c. 1530-1550, tr. K.V. Sarma et al. as Ganita-Yukti-Bhasa (2008)
sources.note: Malayalam proof-text giving derivations of the pi and trigonometric series.

sources.citation: Sankara Variyar, Yukti-dipika, verses on Madhava's sine series and Katapayadi pi value
sources.note: Preserves quoted Sanskrit verses attributed to Madhava.

sources.citation: Victor J. Katz, Mathematics Magazine 68:3 (1995); David Bressoud, College Mathematics Journal 33:1 (2002); Plofker (2009)
sources.note: Careful modern framing of Kerala series as precursors, not full calculus.

episodes.notes: This is the core mathematical innovation story. The school knew the alternating pi over four series, arctangent series, sine and cosine series, and correction terms that made approximations fast enough to be practical; a Katapayadi verse preserved pi to 11 decimal places. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP FLAG: historians now distinguish components of calculus from calculus as a unified theory. Do NOT say Kerala invented calculus, and do NOT imply Madhava had the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, general functions, or Newton-Leibniz notation. The correct claim is stronger and cleaner: specific infinite series appeared in Kerala roughly two to three centuries before their European rediscovery.

episodes.title: The Realm of the Three Crowns
episodes.figure: The Chera, Chola and Pandya Houses
episodes.era: Sangam polities, c. 300 BCE-300 CE
episodes.region: Tamilakam, including Karur, Urayur, Kaveripattinam and Madurai
episodes.logline: Three rival Tamil royal houses appear in Ashoka's edicts and Sangam poems as a world of poets, cattle raids, ports, hill chiefs and shifting honor.
episodes.moral: A shared culture need not mean a single kingdom.

sources.citation: E. Hultzsch, Inscriptions of Asoka (Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum Vol. I, 1925)
sources.note: Ashokan references to Cholas, Pandyas, Keralaputras and Satiyaputras.

sources.citation: D.C. Sircar, Select Inscriptions Bearing on Indian History and Civilization Vol. I (1965)
sources.note: Hathigumpha inscription and early external references to Tamil polities.

sources.citation: George L. Hart and Hank Heifetz, Four Hundred Songs of War and Wisdom (Columbia University Press, 1999)
sources.note: Translation of Purananuru poems on kings, chiefs and war.

episodes.notes: Ashoka's edicts mention southern Choda, Pandya, Keralaputra and Satiyaputra realms outside direct Mauryan rule, while Kharavela's Hathigumpha inscription may refer to a Tamil confederacy. Sangam poetry names Chera, Chola, Pandya and Velir chiefs, with symbols such as bow, tiger and fish and events like Karikala's Battle of Venni. RECENT WORK by Champakalakshmi and Mahadevan reads these poems alongside archaeology and Tamil Brahmi inscriptions. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT present the three crowns as unified Tamil states, do NOT make Ashoka's mention proof of subordination, and do NOT repeat the Grand Anicut engineering story already used in the Chola chapter.
episodes.chapter: The Satavahanas and the Sangam Age

episodes.title: Chimaji Appa Opens Vasai's Gates
episodes.era: Maratha-Portuguese war, 1737-1739 CE
episodes.region: Thane, Salsette, Arnala, Tarapur and Vasai on the Konkan coast
episodes.logline: Chimaji Appa takes fort after fort until Portuguese Bassein stands isolated and the northern Konkan changes hands.
episodes.moral: Patient preparation can break the strongest wall.

sources.citation: Arquivo Historico Ultramarino, Lisbon, Portuguese records of the Vasai campaign
sources.note: Primary Portuguese accounts for the siege and loss of Bassein.

sources.citation: Chimaji Appa's Modi-script letter to Nanasaheb Peshwa on the campaign
sources.note: Maratha-side primary correspondence preserved in Deccan archives.

sources.citation: Stewart Gordon, The Marathas 1600-1818 (Cambridge UP, 1993)
sources.note: Modern context for the campaign's revenue and coastal consequences.

episodes.notes: The Vasai campaign was a methodical reduction of Portuguese positions: Arnala in 1737, Thane and Salsette, Dahanu and Mahim, then Vasai on 16 May 1739. KEY FACTS: the victory ended Portuguese dominance north of Goa and transferred forts, trade routes and military infrastructure to Maratha control. Recent military scholarship emphasizes logistics and siege adaptation, not just bravery. Do NOT treat later temple-bell or devotional anecdotes as certain, and do NOT use exact casualty totals without source caveats.

episodes.title: Guru Arjan Gathers the Many Voices
episodes.era: Compilation of the Adi Granth and first Sikh martyrdom, c. 1604-1606 CE
episodes.region: Amritsar, Goindval, Lahore and the Mughal Punjab
episodes.logline: To protect the songs from forgery, Guru Arjan gathers Gurus, bhagats and Sufi voices into the Adi Granth and places it at Harmandir Sahib.
episodes.moral: A true book can make room for many voices.

sources.citation: Adi Granth tradition; GNDU Manuscript 1245, c. 1599, and related early pothis
sources.note: Material evidence for pre-canonical recensions and compilation.

sources.citation: Jahangir, Tuzk-e-Jahangiri, early 17th century
sources.note: Contemporary Mughal account of Guru Arjan's arrest and death.

sources.citation: Gurinder Singh Mann, The Making of Sikh Scripture (2001); Pashaura Singh, Life and Work of Guru Arjan (2006)
sources.note: Recent manuscript and biography scholarship.

episodes.notes: Guru Arjan compiled the Adi Granth with Bhai Gurdas as scribe and installed it at Harmandir Sahib on 1 September 1604 with Baba Buddha as first granthi. It is a scholarly and artistic innovation: hymns arranged by ragas, including Sikh Gurus and saint-poets such as Kabir, Ravidas, Namdev and Sheikh Farid across languages and social backgrounds. Jahangir's memoir confirms Arjan's death in Mughal custody in 1606, while Sikh tradition remembers him as the first martyr. RECENT/ACCURACY FLAGS: Gurinder Singh Mann shows multiple drafts and pre-canonical manuscripts; the Kartarpur Bir is revered but debated, so do NOT assert its provenance as settled; do NOT state specific torture methods as proven by Jahangir's text.
episodes.chapter: The Sikh Gurus and Ranjit Singh
episodes.chapter_part: II. The Sacred Word and the Pool

episodes.title: Light Scatters in Raman's Calcutta Lab
episodes.era: Discovery of the Raman Effect, 1921-1930
episodes.region: Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science, Calcutta
episodes.logline: In a modest Calcutta laboratory, C.V. Raman and K.S. Krishnan catch light changing colour as it passes through matter.
episodes.moral: Great discovery can begin with simple tools and disciplined eyes.

sources.citation: C.V. Raman and K.S. Krishnan, A New Type of Secondary Radiation, Nature 121, 31 March 1928
sources.note: Primary discovery announcement of the Raman Effect.

sources.citation: C.V. Raman, The Molecular Scattering of Light, Nobel Lecture, 11 December 1930
sources.note: Raman's official Nobel account of the discovery and its meaning.

sources.citation: Abha Sur, Dispersed Radiance: Caste, Gender and Modern Science in India, Navayana, 2011
sources.note: Recent critique emphasizing laboratory hierarchies and K.S. Krishnan's role.

episodes.notes: Raman's voyage across the Mediterranean inspired questions about light scattering, but the discovery itself happened in the IACS laboratory in Calcutta in February 1928. The Nature paper of 31 March 1928 named both Raman and K.S. Krishnan; Raman received the 1930 Nobel Prize in Physics. This is a SCIENTIFIC innovation story: Raman spectroscopy now serves chemistry, medicine, materials science and forensics. Recent scholarship by Abha Sur and Rajinder Singh stresses Krishnan's under-credited work and the Russian parallel of Landsberg and Mandelstam. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT make the blue-sea moment the discovery. Do NOT present the Raman Effect as Raman's sole, unaided finding; Krishnan was a key co-worker even though the Nobel went only to Raman.

episodes.title: The Poem That Hid the Binary
episodes.era: Sanskrit prosody and combinatorics, c. 300-200 BCE
episodes.region: Scholarly circles of early Sanskrit learning
episodes.logline: Counting heavy and light syllables, Pingala discovers a binary way to map the music of verse.
episodes.moral: Patterns in art can open doors to mathematics.

sources.citation: Pingala, Chandahsastra; A. Weber edition in Indische Studien 8 (1863)
sources.note: Primary prosody text with metrical enumeration procedures.

sources.citation: Halayudha, Mrta-sanjivani commentary, c. 10th century CE
sources.note: Later commentary that makes the binary structure explicit.

sources.citation: B. van Nooten, Binary Numbers in Indian Antiquity, Journal of Indian Philosophy 21.1 (1993)
sources.note: Landmark modern argument for Pingala's binary enumeration.

episodes.notes: Pingala's Chandahsastra solves a poetic problem: how to enumerate patterns of heavy and light syllables. The procedures correspond to binary enumeration and the Meru-prastara, later known elsewhere as Pascal's triangle, though the clearest explanation comes from Halayudha many centuries later. Plofker and van Nooten identify this as an independent ancient combinatorial system born from prosody. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT claim Pingala invented binary computers or general electronic binary arithmetic; he used binary representation for meter. The tradition calling him Panini's brother is not historically secure.

episodes.title: Turbak's Cannon and the Kingdom's New Fire
episodes.figure: Ton Kham Borgohain and Turbak Khan
episodes.era: Battle of Hadira Chowki, 1532 CE
episodes.region: Hadira Chowki near the Brahmaputra and Bharali rivers
episodes.logline: When Bengal's artillery enters Assam, Ton Kham Borgohain defeats Turbak and turns captured guns into a lesson in military adaptation.
episodes.moral: Survival belongs to those who learn fastest from danger.

sources.citation: Satsari Assam Buranji, in G.C. Barua, Ahom Buranji (1930)
sources.note: Ahom chronicle account of the Turbak campaign and pursuit westward.

sources.citation: ASI protected monument documentation for Talatal Ghar and surviving Ahom cannon
sources.note: Material evidence for later Ahom artillery preserved at Sivasagar.

sources.citation: Jadunath Sarkar, History of Bengal, Muslim Period, 1200-1757
sources.note: Context from the Bengal Sultanate side of the frontier conflicts.

episodes.notes: The 1532 Turbak campaign is the chapter's military science episode: cannon, matchlocks and gunpowder entered the Ahom war story through a dangerous enemy. Buranjis say Ton Kham Borgohain's forces killed Turbak at Hadira Chowki and captured artillery, after which the Ahoms adapted gunpowder technology for later river and fort warfare. Surviving cannon at Sivasagar support the later material culture, though they do not prove every technical detail of the 1532 story. ACCURACY FLAGS: avoid claims about bamboo cannon or miraculous weapons unless labeled folklore; do NOT invent exact casting methods absent from sources.

episodes.title: Rajaraja's Sword: Kandalur to Lanka
episodes.era: Imperial Chola conquests, c. 985-1014 CE
episodes.region: South India, Kerala and Sri Lanka
episodes.logline: Rajaraja's armies and new-built navy break the Cheras at Kandalur Salai, humble the Pandyas, and cross the strait to take Anuradhapura in Lanka, forging a true empire.
episodes.moral: Strength is worthy only when it builds order, not just victory.

sources.citation: K. A. Nilakanta Sastri, The CōĻas, ch. on Rajaraja I
Rajaraja's meykkirti inscriptions (Kandalur Salai, Ilam/Lanka, the Pandya war)

episodes.title: Aryabhata Turns the Earth
episodes.era: Gupta science, the Aryabhatiya composed 499 CE
episodes.region: Kusumapura (Pataliputra), Magadha
episodes.logline: At twenty-three, Aryabhata writes that the sky only seems to spin because the Earth turns, that eclipses are shadows and not a demon swallowing the sun, and sets down the world's first sine table - the science of a golden age in 121 verses.
episodes.moral: Courage is trusting what reason and measurement reveal, even against old certainties.

sources.citation: Aryabhatiya (499 CE); W.E. Clark (tr.), The Aryabhatiya of Aryabhata (Chicago, 1930); K.V. Sarma ed. (INSA, 1976)
sources.note: The primary text, dated by Aryabhata himself.

sources.citation: Kim Plofker, Mathematics in India (Princeton, 2009)
sources.note: Definitive modern study; clarifies the pi/irrationality question.

sources.citation: Bhaskara I's Aryabhatiya-bhashya, c. 629 CE
sources.note: Earliest commentary.

episodes.notes: Aryabhata (b. 476 CE) wrote the Aryabhatiya in 499 CE at Kusumapura (=Pataliputra). ATTESTED: Earth rotates on its axis (the boat-and-riverbank analogy), lunar/solar eclipses are shadows (rejecting the Rahu/Ketu myth), the first systematic sine (jya) table (24 values), pi = 62832/20000 = 3.1416 which he calls 'asanna' (approximate). IMPORTANT / RECENT SCHOLARSHIP: do NOT claim he PROVED pi irrational - Kim Plofker and Takao Hayashi call that an over-reading; he only called it approximate. He used positional letter-numerals (a step toward place-value) but NO written '0' symbol yet - that comes in the next story. Do not confuse him with the 10th-c. 'Aryabhata II'.
episodes.chapter_part: III. The Age of Number, Iron and Healing

episodes.title: Ashoka Appoints the Dhamma Officers
episodes.era: Ashokan dhamma policy, c. 260s-230s BCE
