episodes.region: Across the Mauryan provinces from Pataliputra to the frontiers
episodes.logline: Ashoka sends officials across the roads and provinces, asking an empire of many faiths to practice mercy, restraint, respect and care for the vulnerable.
episodes.moral: A ruler's duty is not only to command, but to care.

sources.citation: Ashoka's Rock Edicts 2, 3, 5 and 7; E. Hultzsch, Inscriptions of Asoka (1925)
sources.note: Primary evidence for roads, welfare, mahamatras, dhamma-mahamatras and respect for sects.

sources.citation: Ashoka's Rock Edict 13 and Pillar Edict 7
sources.note: Dhamma conquest, moral works and the king's summary of policy; avoid retelling Kalinga here.

sources.citation: Romila Thapar, Asoka and the Decline of the Mauryas (1961; 3rd ed. 1997); Nayanjot Lahiri, Ashoka in Ancient India (2015)
sources.note: Modern interpretation of dhamma as imperial ethic as well as religious conviction.

episodes.notes: This story must NOT retell the existing flagship Kalinga change-of-heart episode. Focus on policy: dhamma as non-violence, respect for all sects, obedience to parents, generosity, humane treatment of servants, welfare for prisoners and women, wells, shade trees and medical care. Rock Edict 5 creates dhamma-mahamatras, a new class of morality/welfare officers with no exact Arthashastra parallel. CRITICAL ACCURACY: Ashoka's dhamma is not identical to Buddhist doctrine; Greek versions translate it as eusebeia, piety, and Thapar reads it as a non-sectarian imperial ideology. Recent scholarship debates sincere Buddhist faith versus pragmatic imperial glue; present both as compatible rather than reducing him to either saint or politician.

episodes.title: The Stone Chariot and Singing Pillars
episodes.era: Vijayanagara temple craft, 15th-16th centuries CE
episodes.region: Vittala Temple and Hazara Rama Temple, Hampi
episodes.logline: Granite becomes music, story and motion as Hampi's craftsmen carve the Vittala stone chariot, resonant pillars and Ramayana walls.
episodes.moral: Art endures when skill serves wonder.

sources.citation: Vittala Temple inscriptions and ASI monument reports
sources.note: Primary monument evidence for patrons, phases and architectural features.

sources.citation: Abdur Razzaq, 1443, and Domingo Paes, c. 1520-22
sources.note: Foreign descriptions of temples, festival streets and royal display.

sources.citation: Fritz and Michell, Hampi Vijayanagara (Marg, 2003)
sources.note: Definitive VRP documentation of the temple complexes.

episodes.notes: The Vittala Temple was begun in the Deva Raya II period and expanded under Krishnadevaraya and Achyuta Deva Raya; its Garuda shrine is now famous as the Stone Chariot, while the musical pillar clusters produce distinct tones. The Hazara Rama Temple served the Royal Centre and carries Ramayana friezes plus processional scenes useful to historians. RECENT FINDINGS: 2026 ASI excavations around Hazara Rama reported a stone canal, drainage channel, vyala sculpture, Jain roof remains and Alvar sculptures, underscoring religious plurality and ritual water management. Do NOT claim the stone chariot is a single monolith; it is assembled from granite blocks, and the wheels are now fixed by later conservation.
episodes.chapter_part: II. The Zenith of the Rayas

episodes.title: Water in the Desert
episodes.era: Dholavira's Harappan occupation, c. 2900-1500 BCE
episodes.region: Dholavira, Khadir Bet, Rann of Kutch, Gujarat
episodes.logline: On a dry island in Kutch, Dholavira's engineers catch monsoon runoff in stone reservoirs, channels and step-like tanks so a city can live between salt and drought.
episodes.moral: Ingenuity begins by respecting scarcity.

sources.citation: R.S. Bisht, Dholavira: Excavations 1989-90 to 2004-05 (ASI, 2015)
sources.note: Definitive excavation monograph for reservoirs, city layout and inscription panel.

sources.citation: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Decision 44 COM 8B.35: Dholavira (2021)
sources.note: Official inscription document summarising the site's significance.

sources.citation: J.M. Kenoyer, Ancient Cities of the Indus Valley Civilization (1998)
sources.note: Contextual synthesis of Dholavira within Harappan urbanism.

episodes.notes: Dholavira used at least 16 reservoirs, channels, bunds and spillways to harvest seasonal flows from the Manhar and Mansar streams; it also preserves a large signboard of 10 undeciphered Harappan signs. UNESCO recognition in 2021 highlighted its urban water system, while hydrological modelling continues to refine capacity estimates. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT read or translate the inscription, do NOT call Dholavira the capital of Harappa, and do NOT treat population numbers beyond broad estimates as certain.

episodes.title: The Giant Book of Heroes
episodes.figure: Mir Sayyid Ali and Abdus Samad
episodes.era: Akbar's Hamzanama project, c. 1562-1577
episodes.region: Agra and Fatehpur Sikri
episodes.logline: Akbar's painters turn the tales of Amir Hamza into huge cloth pages where Persian line meets Indian color.
episodes.moral: Art becomes new when skilled hands learn from one another.

sources.citation: Abul Fazl, Akbarnama, vol. I, trans. H. Beveridge, Asiatic Society, 1902
sources.note: Primary court description of Akbar's atelier and patronage of painters.

sources.citation: Victoria and Albert Museum, Hamzanama collection records, London
sources.note: Museum records for surviving folios from Akbar's great manuscript project.

sources.citation: Milo Cleveland Beach, The Imperial Image: Paintings for the Mughal Court, Freer Gallery, 1981
sources.note: Art-historical synthesis of early Mughal painting and artist workshops.

episodes.notes: The Hamzanama was Akbar's first great illustrated commission, likely planned as about 1,400 large paintings on cotton cloth under Persian masters Mir Sayyid Ali and Abdus Samad, with Indian artists including Daswant and Basawan shaping a new Mughal style. Recent material study suggests the cloth folios may have been displayed during oral performance, not only read privately. Folio attribution is often connoisseurial and the exact original count is debated; do NOT credit all creativity to imported Persian masters, and do NOT speak as if every surviving page has a signed artist.

episodes.title: Badami's Four Caves Test Sacred Art
episodes.era: Early Chalukya rock-cut art, c. 570-700 CE
episodes.region: Badami, Karnataka
episodes.logline: Across four caves, Chalukya workshops try Shiva, Vishnu and Jain images in sandstone, creating a living laboratory of Deccan sacred art.
episodes.moral: Innovation grows when many traditions are allowed to meet.

sources.citation: Badami Caves 1-4, in-situ sculptures and Cave 3 inscription; ASI site documentation
sources.note: Primary monument evidence for the iconographic program.

sources.citation: George Michell, Badami, Aihole, Pattadakal, INTACH / Oxford University Press (1990)
sources.note: Standard study of Early Chalukya architectural sequence.

sources.citation: Hemanth Kadambi, Sahapedia essays on Early Chalukya archaeology (2011-2018)
sources.note: Recent caution that monument dating and dynastic attribution need close site-by-site analysis.

episodes.notes: The Badami caves show a plural visual world: Nataraja and Ardhanarishvara, Vishnu as Trivikrama and Varaha, and Jain Tirthankaras carved into the same royal landscape over time. Recent scholarship has moved away from treating all Malaprabha monuments as one fixed Chalukya master plan and instead emphasizes separate commissions, workshop experiments and debated sequences. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say the four caves were planned together from the start; do NOT call Cave 4 simply the last Chalukya cave without dating caution; do NOT claim Badami is important because of size rather than iconographic innovation.

episodes.title: Alauddin Holds Siri Against the Mongols
episodes.era: Khalji wars with the Mongols, 1297-1306 CE
episodes.region: Delhi, Siri, Kili, Amroha and the Ravi frontier
episodes.logline: Five times the Mongols press toward Delhi, and Alauddin answers with forts, armies, hard discipline, and the city of Siri.
episodes.moral: A city survives when preparation outlasts panic.

sources.citation: Ziauddin Barani, Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi
sources.note: Main narrative source for the Mongol invasions and Kili.

sources.citation: Amir Khusrau, Nuh Sipihr, 1318
sources.note: Courtly celebration of Alauddin's victories and Delhi's world.

sources.citation: Banarsi Prasad Saksena, 'Alauddin Khalji', in A Comprehensive History of India, Vol. 5 (1970); Jackson (2003)
sources.note: Detailed modern analysis of chronology and exaggerated army figures.

episodes.notes: Between 1297 and 1306, Alauddin's forces faced repeated Chagatai Mongol attacks, including Kili in 1299, the siege of Siri in 1303, Amroha in 1305 and fighting near the Ravi in 1306. Zafar Khan's death at Kili became heroic memory, while the 1303 siege exposed Delhi's food vulnerability and helped drive later market controls. Recent historians treat Barani's huge numbers as symbolic or inflated and emphasize fortification, logistics and Chagatai politics. Do NOT claim Alauddin personally charged into battle or that he ended all Mongol danger forever.

episodes.title: Kanishka Raises the Sky Stupa
episodes.era: Kanishka's Buddhist monuments, c. 127-150 CE; excavated 1908-09
episodes.region: Shah-ji-Dheri near Peshawar and Surkh Kotal in Afghanistan
episodes.logline: At Purushapura, Kanishka's builders raise a gigantic stupa whose relic casket, pilgrim memories and ruined base still point upward.
episodes.moral: Great monuments should lift memory, not inflate pride.

sources.citation: D.B. Spooner, Excavations at Shah-ji-Dheri, Annual Report ASI 1908-09 (1912)
sources.note: Primary excavation report for the stupa base and Kanishka Casket context.

sources.citation: Faxian, Record of Buddhistic Kingdoms; Xuanzang, Great Tang Records on the Western Regions
sources.note: Chinese pilgrim descriptions of the Peshawar stupa centuries after Kanishka.

sources.citation: Kanishka Casket inscription; Surkh Kotal inscriptions, revised by Nicholas Sims-Williams (2012)
sources.note: Primary epigraphic evidence for patronage and Kushan building culture.

episodes.notes: At Shah-ji-Dheri near Peshawar, Spooner's excavations uncovered a massive cruciform base about 83 meters wide and the Kanishka Casket, a Kharoshthi-inscribed relic container associated with Sarvastivadin teachers. Faxian and Xuanzang later described an extraordinary stupa, but their height figures are probably exaggerated; modern estimates still make it one of ancient Asia's most ambitious Buddhist structures. RECENT FINDINGS: re-readings corrected the old Greek-name Agesilaos reading on the casket, while Surkh Kotal still preserves evidence of Kushan monumental architecture and a named architect Palamedes. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say the stupa still stands; do NOT call it the tallest building in the ancient world.
episodes.chapter: The Kushan Empire and the Silk Road

episodes.title: Paranjothi Carries Home Vatapi Ganapati
episodes.era: Vatapi campaign and Nayanar memory, c. 642 CE and later
episodes.region: Vatapi, Kanchipuram and Tiruchengattankudy
episodes.logline: The general Paranjothi returns from Vatapi with victory spoils and later memory transforms him into Siruthondar, a warrior among the Shaiva saints.
episodes.moral: Service can change its form without losing its discipline.

sources.citation: Kuram copper plates of the Pallavas
sources.note: Epigraphic basis for the Vatapi campaign and Paranjothi's military context.

sources.citation: Sundarar, Tiruthonda Thogai
sources.note: Earliest canonical list of Nayanmars, including Siruthondar before later full legends.

sources.citation: Indira Viswanathan Peterson, Poems to Siva (1989); Norman Cutler, Songs of Experience (1987)
sources.note: Modern scholarship distinguishing Bhakti hymns from later hagiography.

episodes.notes: Paranjothi, traditionally linked with the title Vikrama Kesari, is remembered as Narasimhavarman I's commander in the Vatapi campaign and as Siruthondar among the 63 Nayanmars. The Vatapi Ganapati tradition at Tiruchengattankudy preserves the idea of a religious trophy brought from the defeated Chalukya capital. KEY ACCURACY FLAGS: the identification of Paranjothi the general with Siruthondar is traditional, not epigraphically proven; the child-sacrifice test in the Periya Puranam is a 12th-century hagiographic legend and must not be narrated as fact. The useful historical point is the social breadth of Bhakti, where warriors, farmers, merchants, women and marginalized devotees all enter sacred memory.
episodes.chapter: The Pallavas and the Bhakti Dawn

episodes.title: Jyeshthadeva Writes Proofs in Malayalam
episodes.era: Yuktibhasa, c. 1530-1550
episodes.region: Parangngottu family area near Trikkandiyur and Tirur, Kerala
episodes.logline: Jyeshthadeva turns difficult Sanskrit astronomy into Malayalam reasoning, preserving proofs of the series in a language students could follow.
episodes.moral: Knowledge travels farther when proof is made speakable.

sources.citation: Jyeshthadeva, Yuktibhasa, tr. K.V. Sarma, K. Ramasubramanian, M.D. Srinivas and M.S. Sriram, Ganita-Yukti-Bhasa (Springer, 2008)
sources.note: Complete English translation of the Malayalam proof-text.

sources.citation: Acyuta Pisharati, Uparagakriyakrama, 1592 CE
sources.note: Mentions Jyeshthadeva as an aged teacher and helps anchor his chronology.

sources.citation: Kim Plofker, Mathematics in India (2009), pp. 237-248; K.V. Sarma, A History of the Kerala School (1972)
sources.note: Modern analysis of the text's proof structure and dating.

episodes.notes: Yuktibhasa is one of the world's most remarkable vernacular mathematical works: it gives extended explanations and proofs for results that many Sanskrit texts state in compressed verse. It covers arithmetic, geometry, spherical astronomy, eclipses, planetary computation and the Madhava series. ACCURACY FLAGS: c. 1530 is an inferred date, with some scholars preferring a wider c. 1530-1550 range; no extant manuscript colophon fixes the composition date. Do NOT exaggerate by calling it the first proof text in the world, but it is safely framed as the earliest known extended mathematical proof-text in an Indian vernacular.

episodes.title: The Last Standard Bearer
episodes.era: Late Satavahana power, c. 152-203 CE depending on chronology
episodes.region: Kanheri, Nasik, Nagarjunakonda and the Deccan coasts
episodes.logline: The last great Satavahana ruler reclaims western ground, leaves cave inscriptions far apart, and watches a dynasty's unity fray into successor states.
episodes.moral: A final rally can shine even as an old order fades.

sources.citation: James Burgess, Report on the Buddhist Cave Temples and Their Inscriptions (ASI, 1882)
sources.note: Kanheri inscriptions and western Deccan cave records.

sources.citation: E. Senart, 'Inscriptions at Nasik,' Epigraphia Indica Vol. 8 (1905)
sources.note: Nasik Cave 20 and related late Satavahana records.

sources.citation: Akira Shimada, Early Buddhist Architecture in Context (Brill, 2012)
sources.note: Recent chronology linking late Satavahanas, Amaravati and regional transitions.

episodes.notes: Yajna Sri Satakarni is treated by historians as the last major Satavahana king. Kanheri and Nasik inscriptions show his reach, while the Junagadh inscription of Rudradaman supplies context for earlier Satavahana-Satrap conflict, though its defeated Satakarni is not Yajna Sri. Ship types on related Satavahana coinage and find-spots point to maritime awareness, but the polity fragmented after him into Abhira, Ikshvaku, Chutu and other successor powers. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT give one exact date, do NOT say one battle ended the dynasty, and do NOT attribute Rudradaman's defeated Satakarni to Yajna Sri.
episodes.chapter: The Satavahanas and the Sangam Age

episodes.title: Panipat on Makar Sankranti
episodes.era: Third Battle of Panipat, 14 January 1761
episodes.region: Delhi, Panipat, Awadh, Rohilkhand and Pune
episodes.logline: A starving Maratha camp breaks out at Panipat, where a day of courage and miscalculation becomes a wound in imperial memory.
episodes.moral: Ambition without supplies and allies can become tragedy.

sources.citation: Kashi Raja's Bakhar, eyewitness account from Shuja-ud-Daula's circle
sources.note: Often treated as the strongest primary narrative for the battle.

sources.citation: James Grant Duff, A History of the Marathas, Vol. II (1826)
sources.note: Early history using survivor testimony, valuable but colonial in perspective.

sources.citation: Uday S. Kulkarni, Solstice at Panipat: 14 January 1761 (2011)
sources.note: Recent synthesis using primary narratives and later scholarship.

episodes.notes: Sadashivrao Bhau's northern army secured Delhi in 1760 but was blockaded by Ahmad Shah Durrani, Najib-ud-Daula and Shuja-ud-Daula before the breakout on 14 January 1761. KEY FACTS: Ibrahim Khan Gardi's artillery, Vishwasrao's death, mass casualties and prisoner killings are strongly attested, while precise numbers vary. Recent scholarship treats defeat as multi-causal: logistics, alliance failures, non-combatant burden and Confederacy structure. Do NOT claim Bhau certainly escaped; most scholars accept he died, but body-identification stories remain contested.

episodes.title: Guru Hargobind Raises Two Swords
episodes.era: Miri-Piri and early Sikh militarization, c. 1606-1644 CE
episodes.region: Amritsar, Gwalior Fort, Kartarpur and Kiratpur Sahib
episodes.logline: After his father's death, Hargobind wears two swords for spirit and worldly duty, then raises the Akal Takht across from the shrine.
episodes.moral: Justice needs prayer, courage and responsibility together.

sources.citation: Varan Bhai Gurdas, including Vaar 26
sources.note: Early Sikh testimony for Hargobind's age.

sources.citation: Early Sikh hukamnamas from Guru Hargobind's period
sources.note: Evidence for institutions and the evolving term Khalsa.

sources.citation: Louis E. Fenech and W.H. McLeod, Historical Dictionary of Sikhism (2014); Pashaura Singh's studies on early Sikh history
sources.note: Modern synthesis and dating cautions.

episodes.notes: Guru Hargobind succeeded Guru Arjan in 1606 and symbolized miri-piri by wearing two swords, linking spiritual authority with worldly protection. The Akal Takht at Amritsar made that idea architectural: a temporal throne facing the Harmandir Sahib. His Gwalior imprisonment and later armed conflicts with Mughal forces are broadly attested, and recent hukamnama work shows terms like Khalsa predate the famous 1699 formalization. ACCURACY FLAGS: dates for his birth and Gwalior imprisonment vary; the Bandi Chhor story of 52 freed princes and cloak threads is beloved Sikh tradition but not epigraphically confirmed, so present it as tradition, not a literal court record.
episodes.chapter: The Sikh Gurus and Ranjit Singh

episodes.title: Bose Writes the Statistics of Light
episodes.era: Birth of Bose-Einstein statistics, 1924-1958
episodes.region: Dhaka, Berlin and Calcutta
episodes.logline: Satyendra Nath Bose sends Einstein a rejected paper that teaches physics how to count light quanta as indistinguishable particles.
episodes.moral: A rejected idea may still change the rules of the universe.

sources.citation: S.N. Bose, Plancks Gesetz und Lichtquantenhypothese, Zeitschrift fuer Physik 26, 1924
sources.note: Primary paper translated and submitted by Einstein.

sources.citation: S.N. Bose's letter to Albert Einstein, 1924, Einstein Archives, Hebrew University of Jerusalem, catalogue 6-340
sources.note: Primary correspondence behind the publication.

sources.citation: Jagdish Mehra and Helmut Rechenberg, The Historical Development of Quantum Theory, vol. 5, Springer, 2000
sources.note: Modern quantum-history context for Bose's derivation and Einstein's extension.

episodes.notes: At Dhaka University in 1924, Bose derived Planck's law by counting photons as indistinguishable particles. After rejection by Philosophical Magazine, he sent the paper to Einstein, who translated it into German, endorsed it, and extended the idea to atoms; Dirac later named bosons for Bose. This is a SCIENTIFIC and MATHEMATICAL innovation story whose importance was renewed after the 1995 creation of Bose-Einstein condensates and the 2001 Nobel for that experimental work. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say Einstein stole Bose's idea; Einstein cited and extended it. Do NOT state Bose deserved a Nobel more than someone else; the omission is a historical debate, not a proof of theft.

episodes.title: The Blade from the Forest Furnace
episodes.era: Crucible steel and Indian Ocean trade, c. 500 BCE-300 CE
episodes.region: Tamil Nadu, Telangana, Sri Lanka and western trade routes
episodes.logline: Anonymous smelters seal iron and carbon in clay crucibles, sending Indian steel across seas and deserts.
episodes.moral: Great inventions may travel farther than their makers' names.

sources.citation: K. Rajan, Archaeology of Tamil Nadu: Kodumanal (2009)
sources.note: Excavation evidence for ironworking, crucibles, slag and trade links.

sources.citation: Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, trans. Lionel Casson (1989)
sources.note: Primary trade account for south Indian exports, including iron goods.

sources.citation: Sharada Srinivasan, Wootz Crucible Steel, Papers from the Institute of Archaeology 5 (1994)
sources.note: Archaeometallurgical study identifying south Indian crucible steel production.

episodes.notes: South Indian and Sri Lankan ironworkers developed high-carbon crucible steel, later called wootz, by sealing ore and carbon in clay crucibles. Excavations at Kodumanal and metallurgical studies since the 1990s tie production to trade networks that also carried Roman amphorae and Indian Ocean goods. Roman and Arabic texts praise Indian iron and swords, but the artisans remain unnamed. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say Indians invented all steel; many iron and steel traditions existed. Do NOT equate every Damascus blade with Indian wootz, because some were pattern-welded. The achievement is a specific high-quality crucible technology and its economic reach.

episodes.title: The Oath After Mir Jumla's Storm
episodes.era: Mughal invasion and recovery, 1662-1667 CE
episodes.region: Garhgaon, Charaideo, Ghilajharighat and the Brahmaputra valley
episodes.logline: After Mir Jumla occupies Garhgaon and imposes a humiliating treaty, Chakradhwaj rebuilds the kingdom for the struggle to come.
episodes.moral: Defeat can become a beginning if recovery is organized.

sources.citation: Shihabuddin Ahmad Talish, Fathiyya-i-Ibriyya, c. 1665, trans. Jadunath Sarkar
sources.note: Eyewitness Mughal account of Mir Jumla's Assam campaign.

sources.citation: Tungkhungia Buranji, ed. and trans. S.K. Bhuyan (1968)
sources.note: Ahom-side chronicle tradition for Jayadhwaj, Chakradhwaj and the aftermath.

sources.citation: ASI Excavation at Maidam No. 2, Charaideo (Guwahati Circle, 2002)
sources.note: Archaeological evidence relevant to Charaideo tomb disturbance and material culture.

episodes.notes: Mir Jumla's 1662-63 invasion is among the best documented Ahom events because Talish recorded the Mughal march, rivers, forts, forests and monsoon misery in detail. Garhgaon was occupied, Charaideo was plundered, and the Treaty of Ghilajharighat imposed indemnity and submission before Mir Jumla died on the return. Buranji tradition remembers Jayadhwaj dying in despair and Chakradhwaj vowing to remove the spear of humiliation. ACCURACY FLAGS: the famous deathbed wording is literary chronicle tradition; use it as remembered sentiment, not a stenographic quote. The episode should emphasize logistics, rebuilding and population recovery, not only revenge.

episodes.title: Kundavai, the Chola Princess
episodes.era: Imperial Chola age, c. 980-1010 CE
episodes.region: Thanjavur and Pazhaiyarai, Chola country
episodes.logline: Honoured above queens, Rajaraja's elder sister Kundavai endows temples and hospitals and nurtures the arts, the steady, gracious power beside the tiger throne.
episodes.moral: Power used to heal and build outlasts power used only to conquer.

sources.citation: Chola inscriptions recording Kundavai's endowments (temples and the atula-salai hospital)
K. A. Nilakanta Sastri, The CōĻas

episodes.title: The Dot That Became Zero
episodes.era: The Indian journey of zero, Gupta age to 628 CE
episodes.region: From a birch-bark manuscript in the northwest to Brahmagupta's Bhinmal
episodes.logline: A dot for 'nothing' in an old birch-bark manuscript grows, through Aryabhata's places and Brahmagupta's bold rules of 628, into zero the number - the small circle that would remake the mathematics of the whole world.
episodes.moral: The greatest ideas can begin as almost nothing - a single, patient dot.

sources.citation: Brahmagupta, Brahmasphutasiddhanta (628 CE), ch. 18; tr. H.T. Colebrooke (1817)
sources.note: First systematic arithmetic rules for zero as a number.

sources.citation: The Bakhshali manuscript, Bodleian Library MS Sansk. d.14; T. Hayashi, The Bakhshali Manuscript (1995)
sources.note: Birch-bark handbook using a dot (bindu) placeholder zero.

sources.citation: Kim Plofker, Agathe Keller, Takao Hayashi, Clemency Montelle & Dominik Wujastyk, 'A Response to the Bodleian Library's Radiocarbon Dating', History of Science in South Asia 5/2 (2017)
sources.note: Peer-reviewed rebuttal of the '3rd-century zero' claim.

episodes.notes: Tell the STAGES honestly: Aryabhata's positional logic (499) -> the Bakhshali manuscript's placeholder DOT -> Brahmagupta's Brahmasphutasiddhanta (628 CE) giving zero arithmetic rules (n+0=n, n*0=0; his n/0=0 was the first, imperfect attempt) -> the Gwalior inscription (876 CE), the earliest UNDISPUTED epigraphic '0'. CRUCIAL RECENT SCHOLARSHIP: the 2017 Bodleian radiocarbon claim that Bakhshali's zero is 3rd-4th century was REBUTTED by Plofker, Keller, Hayashi, Montelle & Wujastyk - the bark is old but the MATHS is 7th c.+ (a manuscript is dated by its LATEST folio). Do NOT assert the 3rd-century 'oldest zero' as fact; present the honest, contested story. Brahmagupta (598-668) is just after the imperial Guptas - frame him as the culmination of the golden age's mathematics.
episodes.chapter_part: III. The Age of Number, Iron and Healing

episodes.title: Prinsep Reads the Forgotten King
episodes.era: Decipherment of Ashoka's edicts, 1837-1838 CE
episodes.region: Calcutta, Sanchi, Bharhut, Maski and the Ashokan inscription network
episodes.logline: After a thousand years of silence, James Prinsep notices tiny repeated letters for 'gift' and unlocks Brahmi, revealing the voice of Devanampiya Piyadasi as Ashoka.
episodes.moral: Patience can make even silent stones speak again.

sources.citation: Ashoka's rock and pillar edicts; E. Hultzsch, Inscriptions of Asoka (1925)
sources.note: The physical inscriptions in Brahmi, Kharoshthi, Greek and Aramaic.

sources.citation: James Prinsep, articles in Journal of the Asiatic Society of Bengal, 1836-1838
sources.note: Published decipherment work on Brahmi and related inscriptions.

sources.citation: Richard Salomon, Indian Epigraphy (OUP, 1998); Harry Falk, Asokan Sites and Artefacts (2006)
sources.note: Modern epigraphic assessment and site catalogue.

episodes.notes: Ashoka's edicts became unreadable after Brahmi and Kharoshthi fell out of use. Prinsep, secretary of the Asiatic Society of Bengal, cracked Brahmi by studying repeated short Sanchi and Bharhut donation inscriptions ending in danam. By March 1838 his Brahmi alphabet was nearly complete, but the edict king called Devanampiya Piyadasi was linked to Ashoka only after George Turnour's Pali Mahavamsa evidence; Christian Lassen's 1836 coin work and Alexander Cunningham's help belong in the collaborative story. The Maski edict found in 1915 later confirmed the identification by naming Ashoka. RECENT/ACCURACY FLAGS: more than 30 edicts survive; Kandahar's Greek-Aramaic bilingual inscription was discovered in 1958 and proves a multilingual Mauryan frontier. Do not make Prinsep a lone genius without the network.

episodes.title: Four Travelers Enter the City
episodes.figure: Paes, Nunes, Abdur Razzaq and Nicolo de' Conti
episodes.era: Foreign eyewitness accounts, c. 1420-1537 CE
episodes.region: Vijayanagara, Calicut, Goa, Persia and Italy's travel circuits
episodes.logline: An Italian, a Persian ambassador and two Portuguese visitors leave dazzling reports of walls, bazaars, armies and festivals in the city of victory.
episodes.moral: Listen to eyewitnesses, but test every dazzling number.

sources.citation: Nicolo de' Conti in Poggio Bracciolini, De Varietate Fortunae, c. 1447
sources.note: Early European description of the city around 1420.

sources.citation: Abdur Razzaq, Matla-us-Sadain, 1443, trans. Elliot and Dowson
sources.note: Persian ambassador's detailed Sangama-era account.

sources.citation: Paes and Nunes in Robert Sewell, A Forgotten Empire (1900)
sources.note: Portuguese accounts from Krishnadevaraya and Achyuta Deva Raya's time.

episodes.notes: Nicolo de' Conti described Vijayanagara around 1420; Abdur Razzaq visited Deva Raya II's court in 1443; Domingo Paes saw Krishnadevaraya's capital around 1520-22; and Fernao Nunes wrote a later Portuguese chronicle around 1535-37. KEY FACTS: their accounts preserve walls, Mahanavami, markets, armies and the city's cosmopolitan population. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP in Textures of Time warns that foreign accounts are not transparent mirrors: Paes had commercial interests in the horse trade, Razzaq used Persianate literary conventions, and all numbers are estimates. Use them as vivid witnesses, not neutral statisticians.
episodes.chapter_part: III. Roads of Witness and Wealth

episodes.title: The Bead That Crossed the World
episodes.era: Mature Harappan craft production and export, c. 2600-1900 BCE
episodes.region: Chanhudaro, Lothal, Harappa, Gujarat quarries and Mesopotamian cities
episodes.logline: A carnelian bead begins as rough stone, passes through fire, drills and polish, and ends in a Mesopotamian tomb as proof of Harappan skill.
episodes.moral: Small works can carry a civilization across the sea.

sources.citation: S.R. Rao, Lothal: A Harappan Port Town (1955-62), ASI Memoir 78 (1979)
sources.note: Primary evidence for bead workshops and tools at Lothal.

sources.citation: J.M. Kenoyer, 'The Indus Bead Industry,' Ornament 10 (1986)
sources.note: Specialist study of bead technology.

sources.citation: M. Vidale, 'Specialized Producers and Urban Elites' in Old Problems and New Perspectives in the Archaeology of South Asia (1989)
sources.note: Analysis of craft specialisation and social context.

episodes.notes: Carnelian beads required heat treatment, grinding, polishing and drilling with hard micro-drills; etched carnelian beads of Harappan type are found from South Asia to Mesopotamia. Chanhudaro and Lothal show production stages, while recent sourcing and experimental studies clarify raw material movement and technique. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT claim formal guilds are proven, do NOT say all carnelian came only from Gujarat, and do NOT reduce artisans to nameless extras when their technology is the story.

episodes.title: Jahangir Watches the Birds
episodes.era: Jahangir's natural history court, c. 1605-1627
episodes.region: Agra, Lahore, Kashmir and Ajmer
episodes.logline: When rare animals reach court, Jahangir observes them closely and Ustad Mansur paints them before memory can fade.
episodes.moral: Wonder becomes knowledge when we look carefully.

sources.citation: Jahangir, Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri, trans. Alexander Rogers, rev. Henry Beveridge, Royal Asiatic Society, 1909-1914
sources.note: Primary royal memoir for Jahangir's nature observations and Mansur's title.

sources.citation: Victoria and Albert Museum and other museum records for Ustad Mansur animal and bird paintings
sources.note: Physical primary evidence for Mughal natural history painting.

sources.citation: Julian Pender Hume, The History of the Dodo Raphus cucullatus and the Penguin of Mauritius, Historical Biology 15, 2003
sources.note: Recent zoological-historical study using Mansur's dodo image.

episodes.notes: Jahangir recorded close observations of birds, animals and flowers while Ustad Mansur produced precise court paintings, including celebrated images of rare species such as the dodo and turkey. Modern zoological and conservation studies value some Mansur works as unusually accurate early modern natural history images. The Tuzuk covers only part of Jahangir's reign and individual painting dates can be inferred rather than certain; do NOT call Jahangir a modern scientist, and do NOT state that Mansur always painted from living specimens.

episodes.title: Lokamahadevi Builds in Two Stone Tongues
episodes.era: Pattadakal temple patronage, c. 733-745 CE
episodes.region: Pattadakal, Karnataka
episodes.logline: At Pattadakal, Queen Lokamahadevi sponsors Virupaksha temple, where northern and southern architectural forms meet in one royal masterpiece.
episodes.moral: Patronage can turn memory into beauty that lasts.

sources.citation: Virupaksha temple inscription of Lokamahadevi, Pattadakal, South Indian Inscriptions Vol. I
sources.note: Primary in-situ evidence for the queen's patronage and victory dedication.

sources.citation: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Group of Monuments at Pattadakal, List 239
sources.note: Official archaeological summary of Pattadakal and the Virupaksha temple.

sources.citation: Adam Hardy, The Temple Architecture of India (2007)
sources.note: Recent architectural analysis of Nagara-Dravida synthesis and Deccan forms.

episodes.notes: Lokamahadevi's Virupaksha temple is one of the clearest premodern Indian examples of a royal woman named as major architectural patron. The monument draws on Dravida forms associated with Pallava Kanchi and northern Nagara elements already tested in the Malaprabha region, while recent scholarship stresses gradual Deccan synthesis rather than a single invention moment. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say Lokamahadevi invented Vesara style alone; do NOT state that Kanchi craftsmen came to Pattadakal as documented fact, because it is an art-historical inference; do NOT confuse this Virupaksha with the later Hampi temple.

episodes.title: Muhammad bin Tughlaq Tests the Impossible
episodes.era: Tughlaq experiments, 1325-1351 CE
episodes.region: Delhi, Daulatabad, the Deccan, Sindh and Himalayan frontiers
episodes.logline: A brilliant sultan moves a capital, issues token coins, dreams across mountains, and leaves Ibn Battuta amazed by genius and terror in the same court.
episodes.moral: Vision without workable trust can ruin what it hopes to save.

sources.citation: Ibn Battuta, Rihla, India sections dictated c. 1355
sources.note: Eyewitness account from a qadi at Muhammad bin Tughlaq's court.

sources.citation: Billon and base-metal token coins of Muhammad bin Tughlaq in museum collections
sources.note: Physical evidence for the failed fiduciary currency experiment.

sources.citation: Peter Jackson, The Delhi Sultanate (2003), chapter on Muhammad bin Tughlaq
sources.note: Modern critique of the old 'mad sultan' caricature.

episodes.notes: Muhammad bin Tughlaq ruled from 1325 to 1351 and attempted a capital transfer to Daulatabad around 1327, a token currency around 1329-1332, and ambitious frontier campaigns. Ibn Battuta portrays a ruler of learning, generosity and cruelty; coins prove the currency experiment, and Deccan history shows the capital move helped seed durable Muslim communities even as it caused suffering. Recent scholarship rejects mental-illness caricatures and sees failed implementation of strategic ideas. Do NOT claim he killed his father as fact, that he reached China, or that he was simply insane.

episodes.title: The Council Tradition in Kashmir
episodes.era: Northern Buddhist memory of Kanishka's council, c. 2nd century CE tradition
episodes.region: Kashmir, Gandhara and later Chinese Buddhist libraries
episodes.logline: In northern Buddhist memory, scholars gather under Kanishka to systematize the Dharma, but history asks which parts are text, tradition and legend.
episodes.moral: Wisdom grows stronger when honest doubt guards it.

sources.citation: Xuanzang, Da Tang Xiyu Ji, trans. Samuel Beal (1884)
sources.note: Later Chinese pilgrim account of Kanishka's council tradition.

sources.citation: Mahavibhasha, Chinese translation by Xuanzang, Taisho 1545
sources.note: Massive Sarvastivada commentary associated with the northwestern scholastic tradition.

sources.citation: Richard Salomon, Ancient Buddhist Scrolls from Gandhara (1999); Mark Allon et al., Gandhari Manuscripts: The Senior Collection (2007-)
sources.note: Recent manuscript publications showing Kushan-era Buddhist textual culture.

episodes.notes: The Fourth Buddhist Council under Kanishka is preserved in northern Sanskrit and Chinese Buddhist traditions, usually placed in Kashmir with Vasumitra, Parsva and sometimes Ashvaghosha among the learned figures. The Mahavibhasha and Sarvastivada scholastic culture are real, and the British Library and Senior Gandharan manuscripts provide physical evidence of 1st-2nd century Buddhist textual activity in the Kushan world. RECENT FINDINGS: the Gandharan birchbark scrolls acquired and published since 1994 revolutionized the evidence base but do not directly prove the council. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT present the council, 500 monks or copper-plate storage as contemporary fact; Theravada tradition does not recognize this council.
episodes.chapter: The Kushan Empire and the Silk Road

episodes.title: Mamallapuram's Stone Theater
episodes.era: Mamallapuram monuments, c. 630-728 CE, with later discoveries in 2004-2005
episodes.region: Mamallapuram on the Coromandel Coast
episodes.logline: Granite outcrops become chariot temples, ocean shrines and a vast carved cliff where water may once have made the Ganga descend before festival crowds.
episodes.moral: Great art teaches stone to move.

sources.citation: UNESCO, Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram World Heritage nomination (1984)
sources.note: Heritage documentation for the monument group.

sources.citation: Shore Temple inscriptions naming Kshatriyasimha and Rajasimha Pallavesvara shrines
sources.note: Primary epigraphic basis for Rajasimha-period structural works.

sources.citation: NIOT/ASI Underwater Exploration off Mahabalipuram Coast, interim reports 2005
sources.note: Post-tsunami documentation of submerged structures linked cautiously to the Seven Pagodas tradition.

episodes.notes: Mamallapuram's Pancha Rathas, cave shrines, Descent of the Ganges or Arjuna's Penance relief, and Shore Temple span multiple Pallava reigns from Mamalla to Rajasimha. The great relief may have used a water channel in its central cleft, making sculpture, myth and hydraulic theater work together. RECENT FINDING: after the 2004 tsunami, NIOT and ASI surveys documented submerged stone structures offshore, supporting but not proving the Seven Pagodas tradition. Do NOT attribute the entire site to one king, and do NOT claim the underwater remains are fully dated Pallava temples until publication confirms it.
episodes.chapter: The Pallavas and the Bhakti Dawn
episodes.chapter_part: IV. Stone, Script and the Sea

episodes.title: Sankara Variyar Saves the Verses
episodes.era: Commentary culture after Tantrasangraha, c. 1500-1560
episodes.region: Kerala temple-service and scholarly communities
episodes.logline: A temple-service scholar comments line by line until Madhava's most fragile verses survive inside the margins of another book.
episodes.moral: Preservation is also a form of genius.

sources.citation: Sankara Variyar, Yukti-dipika or Tantrasamgraha-vyakhya
sources.note: Commentary preserving Madhava's quoted series verses and Nilakantha's text.

sources.citation: Sankara Variyar, Kriyakramakarini, ed. K.V. Sarma and S. Hariharan (1975)
sources.note: Commentary on Bhaskara II's Lilavati showing his broader mathematical learning.

sources.citation: C.T. Rajagopal and T.V. Vedamurti, Scripta Mathematica 17 (1951); Rajagopal and Rangachari, Archive for History of Exact Sciences 18 (1978)
sources.note: Modern recovery of the Sanskrit series material.

episodes.notes: Sankara Variyar was not a Nambudiri but a Variyar, from a temple-service community, which complicates any simple caste-only picture of the school. His Yukti-dipika is vital because it preserves verses explicitly attributed to Madhava, including the sine series and the Katapayadi pi value. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP FLAG: distinguish Yukti-dipika from the anonymous Tantrasamgraha-vakhya; manuscript attributions vary, and authorship of the anonymous commentary is unresolved. Do NOT merge Sankara Variyar with the later Sankara Varman of Sadratnamala.

episodes.title: The Jewel on the Krishna
episodes.era: Amaravati great stupa phases, c. 300 BCE-250 CE
episodes.region: Dharanikota-Amaravati on the Krishna River, Andhra Pradesh
episodes.logline: On the Krishna River, queens, merchants, monks and sculptors rebuild a great Buddhist sanctuary whose limestone reliefs travel from Andhra to the world.
episodes.moral: Great art is often the work of generations, not one hand.

sources.citation: James Burgess, The Buddhist Stupas of Amaravati and Jaggayyapeta (1887)
sources.note: Foundational documentation of the monument and inscriptions.

sources.citation: Robert Knox, Amaravati: Buddhist Sculpture from the Great Stupa (British Museum Press, 1992)
sources.note: Catalogue of major surviving sculptures.

sources.citation: Akira Shimada, Early Buddhist Architecture in Context: The Great Stupa at Amaravati (Brill, 2012)
sources.note: Modern stratigraphic and art-historical phasing.

episodes.notes: The monument known in inscriptions as the mahacetiya at ancient Dharanikota developed across centuries, with Satavahana-era patronage only one phase. Limestone reliefs in the Amaravati school influenced Buddhist art across Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia and now survive in Chennai, Amaravati and the British Museum after 19th-century removals. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP: Shimada's 2012 study is the key modern phasing, and Kanaganahalli offers important comparison. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say Ashoka founded Amaravati decisively, do NOT call it a single Satavahana royal project, and do NOT turn the modern repatriation debate into a settled historical claim.
episodes.chapter: The Satavahanas and the Sangam Age

episodes.title: Madhavrao Rebuilds the Broken Tent
episodes.era: Maratha recovery after Panipat, 1761-1772 CE
episodes.region: Pune, Rakshasbhuvan, Mysore, Dharwad and Delhi
episodes.logline: A teenage Peshwa inherits ruin and uses discipline, campaigns and revenue reform to make Maratha power stand again.
episodes.moral: Recovery begins when grief becomes disciplined work.

sources.citation: Peshwa Daftar records for Madhavrao I's administration and campaigns
sources.note: Primary administrative evidence for reform, orders and revenue discipline.

sources.citation: G.S. Sardesai, New History of the Marathas, Vol. III (1948)
sources.note: Detailed narrative of Madhavrao's recovery period.

sources.citation: Stewart Gordon, The Marathas 1600-1818 (Cambridge UP, 1993)
sources.note: Modern assessment of post-Panipat reconstruction and limits.

episodes.notes: Madhavrao I became Peshwa in June 1761 at age sixteen and, despite conflict with Raghunathrao and tuberculosis, restored authority against the Nizam at Rakshasbhuvan in 1763, pushed Mysore campaigns, and saw Mahadji Scindia restore Shah Alam II to Delhi in 1771. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP highlights fiscal discipline and officer accountability as much as battlefield success. Do NOT imply Punjab was recovered after Panipat, and do NOT turn every later praise of Madhavrao into contemporary evidence.

episodes.title: Guru Tegh Bahadur Stands at Delhi
episodes.era: Ninth Guru and religious freedom, c. 1664-1675 CE
episodes.region: Anandpur Sahib, Delhi, Punjab, Bihar, Bengal and Assam
episodes.logline: The quiet ninth Guru faces Aurangzeb's power at Delhi, choosing death rather than letting conscience be crushed.
episodes.moral: Freedom of faith is worth defending even for others.

sources.citation: Bachittar Natak, attributed to Guru Gobind Singh, c. late 17th century
sources.note: Primary Sikh framing of Guru Tegh Bahadur's sacrifice.

sources.citation: Guru Granth Sahib, hymns and salokas of Guru Tegh Bahadur
sources.note: Direct evidence of his thought and devotional voice.

sources.citation: Louis E. Fenech, Martyrdom in the Sikh Tradition (2000); Satish Chandra, Medieval India (2001)
sources.note: Modern analysis of Sikh and Persian source conflicts.

episodes.notes: Guru Tegh Bahadur, born Tyag Mal in 1621, became the ninth Guru in 1664 and travelled widely before his execution at Delhi on 11 November 1675 under Aurangzeb. Sikh tradition calls him Hind ki Chadar, the shield of India, because he died for the right of others to worship freely. The sources problem is central: Sikh accounts emphasize martyrdom and conscience, while later Persian accounts frame him as a political rebel or bandit; both agree that he was executed. RECENT/ACCURACY FLAGS: Fenech treats martyrdom narratives as theological as well as historical; the Kashmiri Pandit delegation appears in later tradition and is not in Bachittar Natak, so do NOT present it as independently proven.
episodes.chapter: The Sikh Gurus and Ranjit Singh

episodes.title: Chandra Finds the Weight of Dead Stars
episodes.era: The Chandrasekhar limit, 1930-1983
episodes.region: Madras, Cambridge and Chicago
episodes.logline: On a ship to England, young Chandrasekhar calculates that a white dwarf above a limit must collapse toward stranger fates.
episodes.moral: Truth may need patience when authority says no.

sources.citation: S. Chandrasekhar, The Maximum Mass of Ideal White Dwarfs, Astrophysical Journal 74, 1931
sources.note: Primary early publication of the stellar mass limit.

sources.citation: S. Chandrasekhar, On Stars, Their Evolution and Their Stability, Nobel Lecture, 8 December 1983
sources.note: Official retrospective by Chandrasekhar on the theory's meaning.

sources.citation: Kameshwar C. Wali, Chandra: A Biography of S. Chandrasekhar, University of Chicago Press, 1991
sources.note: Definitive biography drawing on interviews and correspondence.

episodes.notes: Chandrasekhar calculated the white-dwarf mass limit during his 1930 voyage from India to Cambridge and published the result in 1931; his 1935 Royal Astronomical Society presentation met famous resistance from Arthur Eddington. The result later became foundational for neutron stars, black holes and Type Ia supernovae, and Chandrasekhar received the 1983 Nobel Prize. This is a SCIENTIFIC innovation and a credit-resistance story. Recent biographies and Arthur Miller's Empire of the Stars debate whether Eddington's opposition included racial assumptions. ACCURACY FLAGS: present racial motivation as debated, not settled fact. Do NOT claim he would certainly have won the Nobel in 1935; scientific acceptance and Nobel politics were more complex.

episodes.title: The Man Who Read the Sky and the Soil
episodes.era: Astronomy and natural knowledge, c. 505-587 CE
episodes.region: Ujjain and the wider Sanskrit scholarly world
episodes.logline: Varahamihira gathers stars, storms, gems, buildings and omens into one vast manual of the observed world.
episodes.moral: Knowledge grows when specialists dare to compare fields.

sources.citation: Varahamihira, Panchasiddhantika; Neugebauer and Pingree edition (1970-71)
sources.note: Primary astronomical compendium with a self-stated 505 CE date.

sources.citation: Varahamihira, Brihat Samhita; M. Ramakrishna Bhat translation (1981)
sources.note: Primary encyclopaedia of astronomy, meteorology, architecture, gems and social knowledge.

sources.citation: Ajay Mitra Shastri, Varahamihira and His Times (1991)
sources.note: Modern study warning against the later Nine Gems legend.

episodes.notes: Varahamihira worked at Ujjain, compiled five astronomical systems in the Panchasiddhantika, and wrote the Brihat Samhita, an encyclopaedic text spanning eclipses, rainfall, earthquakes, water-finding, agriculture, architecture, perfumes and more. Recent scholarship values the text as natural philosophy and applied knowledge rather than forcing it into modern categories of science versus astrology. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT repeat the Nine Gems of Vikramaditya as fact; the Jyotirvid-abharan source is late and unreliable, and Varahamihira is not a contemporary of the legendary Vikramaditya or probably Kalidasa. Greek influence on some siddhantas is debated and should be presented cautiously.

episodes.title: Lachit Borphukan Holds the River at Saraighat
episodes.era: The Battle of Saraighat, 1671 CE
episodes.region: Saraighat, Guwahati and the Brahmaputra
episodes.logline: Gravely ill and outnumbered, Lachit Borphukan has himself rowed into the fight to rally a wavering Ahom navy and break the Mughal fleet on the Brahmaputra.
episodes.moral: Knowing your own land, and holding your nerve on it, can guard a border that arms alone cannot.

sources.citation: Assam Buranji, ed. and trans. S.K. Bhuyan
sources.note: Ahom-side chronicle tradition for the Saraighat campaign and Lachit Borphukan.

sources.citation: S.K. Bhuyan, Lachit Barphukan and His Times (1947)
sources.note: Standard modern reconstruction of the 1667-1671 Guwahati war and the naval battle.

sources.citation: Mughal accounts of Ram Singh I's Assam (Kamrup) expedition, 1667-1671
sources.note: Mughal-side perspective on the campaign and the defeat at Saraighat.

episodes.notes: After the Ahoms retook Guwahati in 1667, Aurangzeb sent Ram Singh I of Amber with a large force; the war culminated in the naval battle at Saraighat on the Brahmaputra in 1671. Lachit Borphukan, the Ahom Borphukan, blunted superior Mughal cavalry and artillery by fighting on the river and in the hills, using earthen ramparts, boat-bridges and guerrilla raids. Buranji tradition remembers Lachit, gravely ill, having himself rowed into the battle to shame his retreating navy into turning and winning. ACCURACY FLAGS: (1) the 'Momai-Kota' episode (Lachit beheading his maternal uncle over a half-built rampart, 'my uncle is not greater than my country') is Buranji discipline-tradition; present it as remembered legend, not documented fact. (2) Frame the war as geopolitical (Mughal expansion vs Ahom sovereignty), NOT Hindu-Muslim: Ram Singh I was a Rajput in Mughal service who reportedly praised Ahom valour, and Ahom command included Muslims (the artillery tradition of Rupai/Ismail). (3) Chronicle numbers are inflated; stress terrain, logistics and morale over a single duel.

episodes.title: Rajendra Brings the Ganges South
episodes.era: Imperial Chola, c. 1012-1044 CE
episodes.region: Gangaikonda Cholapuram, Bay of Bengal, and Southeast Asian sea routes
episodes.logline: Rajendra Chola I celebrated northern and overseas campaigns by founding Gangaikonda Cholapuram, 'the city of the Chola who took the Ganges.' The child-safe story can focus on envoys, ships, maps, and a ceremonial pot of river water.
episodes.moral: Ambition should be remembered through purposeful building and capable organization.

sources.citation: Tiruvalangadu Copper Plates of Rajendra Chola I
sources.note: Primary dynastic source for Chola lineage and Rajendra's northern campaign claims.

sources.citation: Tirumalai inscription/meikeerthi of Rajendra Chola I, listing Ganges and Kadaram-related achievements
sources.note: Primary inscriptional basis for the Ganges title and maritime campaign memory.

sources.citation: UNESCO/ASI, Great Living Chola Temples: Brihadisvara at Gangaikondacholapuram
sources.note: Material evidence for Rajendra's capital-temple complex and Chola architecture.

episodes.notes: Campaign lists are royal eulogies; the broad northern expedition and Kadaram campaign are inscriptionally attested, while route details require scholarly caution.

episodes.title: The Iron Pillar That Would Not Rust
episodes.figure: The Master Smith of the Iron Pillar
episodes.era: Gupta metallurgy, c. early 5th century CE
episodes.region: Forged for Vishnupadagiri (Udayagiri); now at Mehrauli, Delhi
episodes.logline: Gupta smiths hammer-weld a hundred glowing blooms into a single seven-metre shaft for King Chandra's Vishnu-standard - and sixteen centuries of monsoons cannot make it rust, a secret modern science has only just explained.
episodes.moral: Mastery of a craft can outlast empires - and even time itself.

sources.citation: The Mehrauli Iron Pillar inscription of King 'Chandra' (Gupta Brahmi); J.F. Fleet, Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum Vol. III (1888)
sources.note: Names 'Chandra' (widely identified as Chandragupta II) and calls the pillar a Vishnudhvaja.

sources.citation: R. Balasubramaniam, 'On the Corrosion Resistance of the Delhi Iron Pillar', Corrosion Science 42 (2000): 2171-2199
sources.note: Peer-reviewed explanation of the rust resistance.

sources.citation: R. Balasubramaniam, 'On the History of the Delhi Iron Pillar Revealed by Technical Analysis', Indian Journal of History of Science (2007)
sources.note: Forge-welded construction analysis.

episodes.notes: The pillar (~7.2 m, ~6 tonnes) was FORGED, not cast - roughly 20-30 iron blooms hammer-welded together. The inscription names only 'Chandra' (scholarly consensus: Chandragupta II), styles him parama-bhagavata, and calls the pillar a Vishnudhvaja set on Vishnupadagiri (now identified with Udayagiri); it was likely moved to Delhi later. RECENT FINDING (the heart of the story): R. Balasubramaniam (IIT Kanpur, Corrosion Science 2000) showed the rust resistance comes from the ancient iron's HIGH PHOSPHORUS (~0.15%), which in Delhi's wet-dry cycles forms a thin, self-sealing protective layer of iron-phosphate/oxyhydroxide ('misawite') - modern steel burns the phosphorus off. Hero is an anonymous master smith (like the Chola temple architect).
episodes.chapter_part: III. The Age of Number, Iron and Healing

episodes.title: The Four Lions of Sarnath
episodes.era: Ashokan pillar art, c. 250 BCE and modern national adoption in 1947-1950
episodes.region: Sarnath near Varanasi; Chunar sandstone routes; the Sarnath Museum
episodes.logline: A pillar raised where the Buddha first taught carries four roaring lions, a shattered wheel, and a polished message that one day becomes India's national emblem.
episodes.moral: Symbols endure when they speak to justice beyond one age.

sources.citation: Sarnath Lion Capital of Ashoka, excavated by F.O. Oertel, ASI, 1904-1905
sources.note: Physical monolithic Chunar sandstone capital, now in the Sarnath Museum.

sources.citation: Ashokan pillars and pillar edicts; Ashoka's own term dhamma-thambha
sources.note: Primary context for pillars as carriers of dhamma.

sources.citation: Frederick Asher, Sarnath: Buddhism, Art and Archives (2020); Vidya Dehejia, Indian Art (1997); John Boardman, The Diffusion of Classical Art in Antiquity (1994)
sources.note: Recent and classic scholarship on Sarnath, Mauryan polish and Achaemenid/Hellenistic influence.

episodes.notes: The Sarnath Lion Capital is 2.1 m high, carved from a single block of Chunar sandstone, with lotus base, animal abacus, four back-to-back lions and an originally large Dharma Wheel. It was excavated in broken pieces in 1904-05; the pillar shaft stayed in situ. The Mauryan polish should gleam visually, but its technique remains uncertain. KEY ART-HISTORY FLAG: do not frame it as simply Persian copying or purely isolated Indian invention; current consensus is synthesis, with Achaemenid/Hellenistic craft influence combined with Indian Buddhist symbolism. Nehru proposed the Ashoka Chakra for the flag in July 1947, and the Lion Capital became India's State Emblem on January 26, 1950, with Satyameva Jayate added below.

episodes.title: Diamonds Horses and Pagodas in the Bazaar
episodes.era: Vijayanagara trade networks, 15th-16th centuries CE
episodes.region: Hampi bazaars, Goa, Hormuz, Golconda, Malabar and Coromandel ports
episodes.logline: Jewels glitter in temple streets, horses arrive from the Arabian Sea, and gold pagodas carry Hampi into the Indian Ocean economy.
episodes.moral: Prosperity grows from exchange, trust and wise dependence.

sources.citation: Domingo Paes and Duarte Barbosa in Sewell, A Forgotten Empire (1900)
sources.note: Primary Portuguese descriptions of bazaars, horses and trade volumes.

sources.citation: Abdur Razzaq, Matla-us-Sadain, 1443
sources.note: Persian description of jewel bazaars and urban wealth.

sources.citation: R. Krishnamurthy, Vijayanagara Coins (Tamil Nadu Government Museum, 2005)
sources.note: Modern study of varaha, pagoda and related coinage.

episodes.notes: Vijayanagara's economy linked Hampi bazaars to diamond regions, textile producers, spice ports, Persian Gulf horse traders and Portuguese Goa. KEY FACTS: the varaha or pagoda was a high-value gold coin; imported Arabian and Persian horses were vital for cavalry; gems were traded in markets described by Razzaq and Paes. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP by Sanjay Subrahmanyam treats the Portuguese horse trade as structural interdependency, not background color. Accuracy flags: figures such as 13,000-14,000 horses per year come from foreign sources and need caution, and famous diamonds from Golconda belong to a larger regional history, so do NOT imply every named jewel passed through Hampi's bazaar.
episodes.chapter_part: III. Roads of Witness and Wealth

episodes.title: The Same Weight from Harappa to Shortughai
episodes.era: Mature Harappan metrology, c. 2600-1900 BCE
episodes.region: Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Lothal, Dholavira, Chanhudaro and Shortughai
episodes.logline: Tiny chert cubes keep the same ratios across deserts, rivers and ports, turning trust into a measurable Harappan invention.
episodes.moral: Fair exchange begins with a standard everyone can trust.

sources.citation: A.S. Hemmy, 'The Weight Standards of Mohenjo-Daro and Harappa' in Marshall, Vol. II (1931)
sources.note: Original metrological analysis of excavated weights.

sources.citation: S.R. Rao, Lothal: A Harappan Port Town (1979)
sources.note: Evidence for a scale-beam and possible measuring rule.

sources.citation: J.M. Kenoyer, Ancient Cities of the Indus Valley Civilization (1998)
sources.note: Modern synthesis of weights, trade and administration.

episodes.notes: Harappan weights are polished cubes and hemispheres, often chert, using binary lower units and decimal higher units around a base near 0.836 g. Their consistency across a huge area is measured fact and supports long-distance trade, but whether a state, city authorities or commercial convention maintained the standards remains debated. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT call them coins, do NOT make the base unit exactly 1 gram, and do NOT claim the system proves a single central government.

episodes.title: Nur Jahan's Name on Gold
episodes.era: Nur Jahan's political power, 1611-1627
episodes.region: Agra, Lahore, Ajmer and the Mughal mints
episodes.logline: Nur Jahan signs decrees, guides diplomacy, and sends coins through the empire bearing an empress's name.
episodes.moral: Authority can be proven in records, not just remembered in stories.

sources.citation: Jahangir, Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri, trans. Rogers and Beveridge, Royal Asiatic Society, 1909-1914
sources.note: Primary court evidence for Nur Jahan's presence, skills and influence.

sources.citation: Sir Thomas Roe, The Embassy of Sir Thomas Roe to India, ed. William Foster, Hakluyt Society, 1926
sources.note: Eyewitness diplomatic account noting Nur Jahan's political power.

sources.citation: Ruby Lal, Empress: The Astonishing Reign of Nur Jahan, W.W. Norton, 2018
sources.note: Recent biography grounding her authority in coins, farmans and court politics.

episodes.notes: Nur Jahan's authority is attested by farmans, Roe's diplomatic testimony, architectural patronage at Itimad-ud-Daula's tomb and rare Mughal coins bearing her name with Jahangir's. Ruby Lal's recent work corrects older romantic narratives and treats the coinage as public evidence of co-sovereignty. Later Shah Jahani histories had reasons to reduce her legacy and the Tuzuk ends before the last crisis years; do NOT explain her power as only a love story, and do NOT imply every Mughal queen shared this formal authority.

episodes.title: Krishna I Carves Kailasa Downward
episodes.era: Rashtrakuta Ellora patronage, c. 756-775 CE
episodes.region: Ellora, Maharashtra
episodes.logline: Instead of stacking stone upward, Krishna I's craftsmen cut a mountain from the top down until Kailasa temple stands free inside the rock.
episodes.moral: The impossible becomes possible when vision and skill work together.

sources.citation: Baroda Copper Plates of Karka II, c. 812 CE, Epigraphia Indica Vol. XIV
sources.note: Retrospective primary attribution of the great Elapura Shiva temple to Krishna I.

sources.citation: M.K. Dhavalikar, V.S. Gupte and S.A. Mate, Excavations at Ellora (1978)
sources.note: Major archaeological report on Ellora and its construction evidence.

sources.citation: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Ellora Caves, List 243; ASI Ellora documentation
sources.note: Official heritage and conservation context for Cave 16.

episodes.notes: Kailasa at Ellora, Cave 16, is the chapter's great engineering story: a monolithic rock-cut complex excavated from basalt by removing enormous quantities of stone from the top downward. Recent engineering and digital-survey work has sharpened appreciation of its precision, while art historians increasingly see its plan as an enlargement of Pattadakal's Virupaksha, showing Rashtrakutas building on Chalukya models. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT give a magical or exact eighteen-year construction timeline; do NOT say Krishna I personally designed it; do NOT call it India's largest temple generally--it is the largest monolithic rock-cut temple complex.

episodes.title: Timur Leaves Delhi Empty
episodes.era: Timurid invasion of north India, 1398-1399 CE
episodes.region: Delhi, Punjab, Gujarat and Samarkand
episodes.logline: Timur storms into a weakened Sultanate, sacks Delhi in December 1398, and marches away with treasure, captives and artisans for Samarkand.
episodes.moral: A city divided within is most vulnerable to the storm outside.

sources.citation: Yazdi, Zafar Nama, 1424-1425, translated in Elliot and Dowson, History of India, Vol. III
sources.note: Official Timurid account of the Indian campaign.

sources.citation: Tuzuk-i-Timuri / Malfuzat-i-Timuri traditions
sources.note: Timurid court memory of the campaign, including the prisoner massacre, with authenticity caveats.

sources.citation: Beatrice Forbes Manz, The Rise and Rule of Tamerlane (Cambridge University Press, 1989/1999)
sources.note: Standard modern biography for Timur's aims and methods.

episodes.notes: In 1398, after years of Tughlaq decline, Timur entered India, ordered a mass killing of prisoners before the battle, took Delhi in December, looted for days, enslaved artisans, and left rather than ruling. Nasir-ud-Din Mahmud Tughlaq fled, and Delhi's political center never regained the reach it had under earlier sultans. Modern scholarship accepts the catastrophe while warning that exact death totals come from rhetorical chronicles. Do NOT claim precise casualty figures as census data, and do NOT attach the Koh-i-Noor legend to Timur's Delhi sack as fact.

episodes.title: The First Human Face of the Buddha
episodes.era: Kushan-era Buddhist art, c. 1st-3rd century CE
episodes.region: Gandhara, Taxila, Peshawar, Swat and Mathura
episodes.logline: Under Kushan patronage, Gandhara and Mathura sculptors give the Buddha a human form that will travel across Asia in stone, stucco and faith.
episodes.moral: New beauty is often born where traditions meet without fear.

sources.citation: Inscribed Bala Bodhisattva and Kimbell Seated Bodhisattva, Kanishka-era Year 3 and Year 4
sources.note: Year-dated Mathura-school images anchoring the early Buddha image chronology.

sources.citation: John M. Rosenfield, The Dynastic Arts of the Kushans (1967)
sources.note: Foundational study of Kushan royal and religious art.

sources.citation: Robert DeCaroli, Image Problems: The Origin and Development of the Buddha's Image in Early South Asia (2015)
sources.note: Recent treatment of the aniconic-to-iconic transition and Gandhara-Mathura debate.

episodes.notes: Kushan-era patronage fostered two great image-making centers: Gandhara, with schist and stucco figures shaped by Hellenistic visual language, and Mathura, with red sandstone images growing from Indian yaksha traditions. The Bala Bodhisattva and Kimbell Bodhisattva have Kanishka-era inscriptions, making Mathura especially well dated, while Gandhara supplied forms that traveled widely into East Asia. RECENT FINDINGS: a Mathura-style red sandstone sculpture found at Taxila in 2008 suggests stronger exchange between the two schools than older models allowed. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say Greeks invented Buddhist art; do NOT claim Gandhara definitely preceded Mathura, because the primacy debate remains unresolved.
episodes.chapter: The Kushan Empire and the Silk Road
episodes.chapter_part: IV. Where Gods Met and Art Was Born

episodes.title: Rajasimha Builds the Kailasanathar
episodes.era: Rajasimha's reign, c. 695-728 CE
episodes.region: Kanchipuram and the Shore Temple at Mamallapuram
episodes.logline: Rajasimha turns Pallava experiment into structural stone, raising Kailasanathar as a royal shrine, icon gallery and prototype for South Indian temple building.
episodes.moral: A lasting tradition begins as someone's bold experiment.

sources.citation: Kailasanathar temple inscriptions, South Indian Inscriptions, Vol. I and later epigraphic editions
sources.note: Primary evidence naming Rajasimha's shrine and royal builders.

sources.citation: ASI conservation and mural documentation at Kailasanathar temple, Kanchipuram
sources.note: Material evidence for architecture, paintings and conservation history.

sources.citation: Padma Kaimal, studies of the Kailasanathar temple and Pallava art, 1990s-2010s
sources.note: Modern architectural and iconographic reassessment.

episodes.notes: The Kailasanathar temple, begun by Narasimhavarman II Rajasimha and completed or expanded by his son, uses granite foundations and carved sandstone superstructure, with subsidiary shrines and a wall of Shaiva iconography that influenced later Dravidian temples. Its old murals connect Pallava Kanchi to wider Indian painting traditions. RECENT DOCUMENTATION has refined the temple's c. 700-728 CE date and recorded fragile paintings. Do NOT claim with certainty that Rajaraja Chola personally copied it for Brihadisvara, though later Chola architecture clearly inherited Pallava structural experiments; and do NOT present popular tunnel stories as archaeology.
episodes.chapter: The Pallavas and the Bhakti Dawn
episodes.chapter_part: IV. Stone, Script and the Sea

episodes.title: The Illam That Remembered Everything
episodes.era: Household transmission across c. 1237-1621
episodes.region: Vatasseri, Kelallur, Parangngottu and related houses of the Nila valley
episodes.logline: Without a university building, Kerala's illams, teachers, palm leaves and memorized number-verses keep a scientific tradition alive for centuries.
episodes.moral: Institutions can be made from relationships as much as walls.

sources.citation: K.V. Sarma, A History of the Kerala School of Hindu Astronomy (1972)
sources.note: Standard reconstruction of the teacher-pupil chain from Govinda to Acyuta Pisharati.

sources.citation: K.V. Sarma, Science Texts in Sanskrit in Manuscripts Repositories of Kerala and Tamil Nadu (2003)
sources.note: Survey of manuscript holdings and repositories.

sources.citation: Romila Thapar, Early India (2002), pp. 442-445; Plofker (2009)
sources.note: Context for Brahmin settlements, land grants and mathematical manuscript culture.

episodes.notes: This social innovation story should show how knowledge was organized before modern universities. Sarma reconstructs a chain from Govinda Bhattathiri through Paramesvara, Damodara, Nilakantha, Jyeshthadeva, Sankara Variyar, Acyuta Pisharati and Melpathur. Palm leaves decayed and had to be recopied; Katapayadi verse and oral teaching helped numerical data survive. ACCURACY FLAG: the claim that inheritance customs directly caused mathematical creativity is an argued social explanation, not a primary-source statement. Do NOT invent charters, laboratories or royal academies; the institution was household, temple, teacher and manuscript together.
episodes.chapter_part: IV. The House and the Court

episodes.title: Most Excellent in Jambudvipa
episodes.era: Karla Great Chaitya, c. 50-70 CE with later Satrap and Satavahana gifts
episodes.region: Karla Caves near Lonavala, Maharashtra
episodes.logline: Merchants, monks, guilds and Yavana donors carve a vast rock-cut prayer hall whose banker patron boasts it is the finest in Jambudvipa.
episodes.moral: Shared faith and trade can cut beauty from stone.

sources.citation: H. Luders, A List of Brahmi Inscriptions, Epigraphia Indica Vol. 10 Appendix (1912)
sources.note: Catalogue of Karla donor inscriptions, including Yavana and merchant gifts.

sources.citation: Vidya Dehejia, Early Buddhist Rock Temples (Thames and Hudson, 1972)
sources.note: Chronological study of early western Deccan rock-cut architecture.

sources.citation: Akira Shimada, Early Buddhist Architecture in Context (Brill, 2012)
sources.note: Recent comparison of Buddhist architecture and patronage networks.

episodes.notes: Karla Cave 8 is among South Asia's largest early rock-cut chaitya halls, preserving wooden roof elements and a forest of inscribed pillars. Bhutapala, a setthi from Vaijayanti, declared the rock mansion 'most excellent in Jambudvipa'; several pillars were donated by self-described Yavanas from Denukakata. Later inscriptions by Ushavadata of the Western Satraps and Vasisthiputra Pulumavi show cross-political patronage. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say Ushavadata built the hall, do NOT assume Yavana means Alexandrian Greek by this date, and do NOT treat Bhutapala's boast as neutral measurement.
episodes.chapter: The Satavahanas and the Sangam Age

episodes.title: Forts Where the Mountains Fought
episodes.era: Maratha military landscapes, 1645-1818 CE; UNESCO inscription 2025
episodes.region: Raigad, Rajgad, Pratapgad, Sindhudurg, Suvarnadurg, Vijaydurg and the Sahyadris
episodes.logline: Cisterns, hidden gates, sea walls and mountain paths turn Maratha forts into an engineered network of survival.
episodes.moral: Good design can make courage endure.

sources.citation: Henry Oxienden's 1674 English report from Raigad
sources.note: Eyewitness description of Raigad during Shivaji's coronation context.

sources.citation: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Maratha Military Landscapes of India nomination and 2025 listing materials
sources.note: Recent archaeological and conservation survey of the fort network.

sources.citation: M.S. Naravane, Forts of Maharashtra (1995); Stewart Gordon, The Marathas 1600-1818
sources.note: Architectural and historical interpretations of the fort system.

episodes.notes: Maratha fort engineering combined hill forts, sea forts, cisterns, granaries, bent entrances, sally ports and coastal bases so a weaker field army could survive stronger imperial forces. KEY FACTS: Raigad, Sindhudurg, Suvarnadurg, Vijaydurg, Khanderi and other forts were surveyed in the Maratha Military Landscapes nomination and listed by UNESCO in 2025 after debate. RECENT FINDINGS: ICOMOS questioned whether the forts were proven as one integrated system, so present the network as a historical and conservation argument, not a settled engineering blueprint. Do NOT present Hirakani or handprint traditions as independently verified.

episodes.title: Guru Gobind Singh Calls the Five
episodes.figure: Guru Gobind Singh and the Panj Pyare
episodes.era: Birth of the Khalsa, 1699-1708 CE
episodes.region: Anandpur Sahib, Chamkaur, Sirhind and Nanded
episodes.logline: At Vaisakhi, Guru Gobind Singh calls five volunteers from distant regions and shapes the Khalsa into a fearless community of equals.
episodes.moral: Courage becomes stronger when shared by all.

sources.citation: Senapatii, Sri Gur Sobha, c. 1711
sources.note: Near-contemporary account of Guru Gobind Singh's final years.

sources.citation: Hukamnamas of Guru Gobind Singh, c. 1699-1708
sources.note: Primary documents for Khalsa identity and discipline.

sources.citation: W.H. McLeod, Sikhism (1997); Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh, The Birth of the Khalsa (2005)
sources.note: Contrasting critical and sympathetic scholarly readings.

episodes.notes: Guru Gobind Singh, born at Patna in 1666, became Guru after his father's martyrdom and formally shaped the Khalsa at Anandpur on Vaisakhi 1699. The Panj Pyare came from different regions and social backgrounds, and the rahit with the Five Ks made a visible, disciplined community; later events at Chamkaur, Sirhind and Nanded turned the story into one of sacrifice and succession to the Guru Granth Sahib. RECENT/ACCURACY FLAGS: the earliest near-contemporary Sri Gur Sobha does not contain the full dramatic tent-and-heads scene, which appears in later tradition; say Sikh tradition narrates it, not that every detail is proven. Also note that Khalsa language appears in earlier hukamnamas, so 1699 was formalization, not creation from nothing.
episodes.chapter: The Sikh Gurus and Ranjit Singh

episodes.title: Saha Reads the Temperature of Stars
episodes.era: Saha ionization equation and science advocacy, 1920-1956
episodes.region: Calcutta, Allahabad and Parliament in New Delhi
episodes.logline: Meghnad Saha turns heat, pressure and atoms into an equation that lets astronomers read the hidden temperatures of stars.
episodes.moral: A clear equation can turn scattered clues into understanding.

sources.citation: M.N. Saha, Ionisation in the Solar Chromosphere, Philosophical Magazine 40, 1920
sources.note: Primary first paper on the ionization equation.

sources.citation: M.N. Saha, On a Physical Theory of Stellar Spectra, Proceedings of the Royal Society A 99, 1921
sources.note: Primary fuller derivation and astrophysical application.

sources.citation: Virendra Nath Sharma, Meghnad Saha: His Life and Times, Rupa, 2019
sources.note: Recent full biography situating Saha's science and public policy work.

episodes.notes: Born near Dhaka, Saha used thermodynamics and atomic physics in 1920-21 to explain why stellar spectra vary with temperature and pressure. His ionization equation made modern stellar classification quantitative and later supported plasma physics. He also founded Science and Culture, helped establish the Institute of Nuclear Physics, and entered Parliament to argue for scientific planning. This is a SCIENTIFIC innovation story with institutional and civic dimensions. Recent scholarship stresses both Western textbook under-recognition and Saha's public role in river and energy planning. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say Saha worked without Western physics; his originality lay in combining existing thermodynamics and atomic theory. Do NOT frame Nobel non-recognition as a proven robbery; it is a documented recognition gap.
episodes.chapter_part: IV. Science for Land, Life and Numbers

episodes.title: The Book That Crossed Mountains
episodes.era: Medical synthesis and transmission, c. 6th-7th century CE
episodes.region: Northwestern India, Tibet and Kerala medical lineages
episodes.logline: Vagbhata condenses older medical schools into a portable handbook that journeys into Tibet and living Kerala practice.
episodes.moral: A clear synthesis can carry knowledge across mountains.

sources.citation: Vagbhata, Ashtangahridaya; K.M. Krishna Murthy translation (1991-96)
sources.note: Primary Sanskrit medical synthesis organised for clinical use.

sources.citation: Tibetan Yan-lag brgyad-pai snying-po translation tradition
sources.note: Evidence for the text's reception in Tibetan medicine.

sources.citation: G.J. Meulenbeld, A History of Indian Medical Literature, Vol. IIA (2000)
sources.note: Definitive analysis of Vagbhata dating, authorship and regional legends.

episodes.notes: The Ashtangahridaya condensed Charaka and Sushruta traditions into elegant verses covering the eight branches of Ayurveda, and it became a widely copied medical handbook. Its Tibetan translation and Kerala Ashtavaidya use show how a Sanskrit text could move through Buddhist and hereditary medical networks. Recent scholarship by Meulenbeld distinguishes the Hridaya and Sangraha traditions and corrects older regional myths. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT claim one certain biography for Vagbhata or single authorship of both major Vagbhata texts. The Pulamanthole and Kerala stories are living local traditions, not proof that the historical author retired there.

episodes.title: Gadadhar Drives the Mughals Beyond Manas
episodes.era: Battle of Itakhuli and the Tungkhungia restoration, 1682 CE
episodes.region: Itakhuli, Guwahati and the Manas frontier
episodes.logline: After a decade of turmoil, Gadadhar Singha takes power and expels Mughal authority from Guwahati to the Manas River.
episodes.moral: A wounded kingdom must first restore order before it can guard its borders.

sources.citation: Tungkhungia Buranji, ed. and trans. S.K. Bhuyan (1968)
sources.note: Primary chronicle for Gadadhar Singha, the Tungkhungia line and Itakhuli.

sources.citation: H.K. Barpujari, ed., The Comprehensive History of Assam, Vol. 2 (1992)
sources.note: Modern synthesis of the Mughal-Ahom frontier and the 1682 settlement.

sources.citation: J.F. Richards, The Mughal Empire (Cambridge, 1993)
sources.note: Context for Mughal limits in the eastern frontier zone.

episodes.notes: This episode deliberately does not retell the already famous Saraighat story. It follows Gadapani, later Gadadhar Singha, through the crisis after Lora Raja and into the 1682 Battle of Itakhuli, when Ahom forces drove Mughal power out of Guwahati and fixed the Manas River as the practical western boundary. The victory opened the Tungkhungia dynasty, which ruled until 1826. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT make Itakhuli a single heroic duel; it was the culmination of court recovery, frontier administration and Mughal weakness after years of pressure. Use Mughal and Buranji perspectives together.

episodes.title: Rajendra's Fleet to Srivijaya
episodes.era: Imperial Chola naval expedition, c. 1025 CE
episodes.region: Bay of Bengal, Srivijaya (Sumatra) and Kadaram (Malaya)
episodes.logline: Rajendra launches the greatest fleet India had ever sent across the eastern sea, striking Srivijaya and Kadaram, the one Indian emperor to carry conquest overseas.
episodes.moral: Vision dares where others dream, yet power reached far must be held with wisdom.

sources.citation: Rajendra's Tanjore inscription listing the Southeast Asian ports (Kadaram, Sri Vijaya)
George Coedes, The Indianized States of Southeast Asia

episodes.title: Sushruta and the Healer's Knife
episodes.era: The Gupta redaction of Ayurveda, c. 4th-5th century CE
episodes.region: Ancient Kashi (Varanasi) and the schools of Indian medicine
episodes.logline: In the age when a Chinese pilgrim marvels at India's free hospitals, its surgeons refine the Sushruta Samhita - a hundred and twenty instruments, three hundred operations, and a new nose rebuilt from a patient's own skin, one of the world's first plastic surgeries.
episodes.moral: To heal is the highest craft - knowledge turned to mercy.
