sources.citation: George Gheverghese Joseph, The Crest of the Peacock, 3rd ed. (2011)
sources.note: Modern account of Kerala mathematics and its priority claims.

episodes.notes: Madhava's own works mostly vanished, but later Kerala texts credit him with infinite series for pi, sine and cosine, motivated by more accurate astronomy. The Yuktibhasha, written in Malayalam by Jyesthadeva around 1530, preserves proofs and is a landmark recent scholarly edition in the history of Indian mathematics. Mainstream historians accept independent priority over comparable European discoveries for these specific results. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say India transmitted calculus to Newton or Leibniz; there is no documentary proof. Do NOT call it modern calculus as a complete system. Tell it as brilliant infinite-series mathematics within an astronomical school.
episodes.chapter_part: V. What India Gave the World

episodes.title: Rang Ghar, the Pavilion Built Without Cement
episodes.era: Royal sports architecture, c. 1696-1751 CE
episodes.region: Rupahi Pathar, Rangpur, modern Sivasagar
episodes.logline: A boat-roofed brick pavilion rises from rice, lime and craft, letting kings watch Bihu games on the fields of Rangpur.
episodes.moral: A civilization is known by what it builds for joy as well as war.

sources.citation: ASI, List of Centrally Protected Monuments in Assam, Rang Ghar entry
sources.note: Official protected monument record for the surviving brick pavilion.

sources.citation: Tungkhungia Buranji, ed. and trans. S.K. Bhuyan (1968)
sources.note: Chronicle context for royal construction under Rudra and Pramatta Singha.

sources.citation: S.L. Baruah, A Comprehensive History of Assam (1985)
sources.note: Modern synthesis of Tungkhungia architecture and cultural patronage.

episodes.notes: Rang Ghar is an engineering and cultural episode, not merely a postcard monument. The current brick structure is usually dated to Pramatta Singha's reign, 1744-1751, while Buranji tradition remembers an earlier wooden or bamboo pavilion under Rudra Singha. Its curved boat-like roof, arched openings, crocodile finials and sticky rice-lime-egg mortar show adaptive craft in a wet landscape. ACCURACY FLAGS: avoid the absolute claim 'oldest amphitheater in Asia'; safer wording is one of Asia's oldest surviving royal sports pavilions. The story should connect Bihu games, royal spectacle and material science without inventing untested chemical formulas.
episodes.chapter_part: IV. Courts of Craft and Code

episodes.title: Kulottunga, the King Who Abolished Tolls
episodes.era: Later Imperial Chola, c. 1070-1122 CE
episodes.region: The Chola empire, Kaveri to the Godavari
episodes.logline: Uniting Chola and Eastern Chalukya blood, Kulottunga wins a name no war could buy, 'Sungam Tavirtta', the king who abolished tolls, easing the burden on his people.
episodes.moral: A ruler is remembered less for what he takes than for what he lifts from his people.

sources.citation: Inscriptions granting Kulottunga I the title 'Sungam Tavirtta Cholan' (abolisher of tolls)
K. A. Nilakanta Sastri, The CōĻas, ch. on Kulottunga I

episodes.title: The Gods Take Shape at Deogarh
episodes.figure: The Master Sculptor of the Gupta Age
episodes.era: The classical moment of Indian art, 5th-early 6th century CE
episodes.region: Sarnath, Udayagiri and the Dashavatara temple at Deogarh
episodes.logline: Gupta stone-carvers give the Buddha his serene, wet-robed calm at Sarnath and raise Vishnu's temple at Deogarh with its soaring spire - setting the mould for sacred art across Asia for a thousand years.
episodes.moral: A true artist carves not just stone, but the way an age will imagine the divine.

sources.citation: The Sarnath Buddha (5th c.), Archaeological Museum, Sarnath
sources.note: Paradigm of classical Gupta Buddhist sculpture (dharmachakra mudra, transparent robes).

sources.citation: The Dashavatara (Vishnu) temple, Deogarh (early 6th c.); the Udayagiri Varaha relief (c. 401 CE)
sources.note: Early Nagara-style temple with sikhara; the earth-lifting Boar.

sources.citation: Michael Willis, The Archaeology of Hindu Ritual (2009); Walter Spink, Ajanta: History and Development (2005-2014)
sources.note: Recent scholarship on Udayagiri's meaning and Ajanta's compressed chronology.

episodes.notes: The 'classical' Gupta style synthesised the Mathura and Gandhara traditions into a serene, idealised norm copied across South and Southeast Asia. Key works: the Sarnath Buddha (clinging robes, downcast eyes, Wheel-of-Dharma gesture); the Deogarh Dashavatara temple (one of the earliest stone temples with a curvilinear sikhara - foundational for the NAGARA style; its Vishnu-on-the-serpent panel); the Udayagiri Varaha (Vishnu = Chandragupta II lifting the Earth - Michael Willis). RECENT: Walter Spink's compressed chronology dates Ajanta's great late phase to a burst c. 462-480 CE under the Gupta-allied Vakatakas. Hero is an anonymous master sculptor (craft theme, like the Chola bronze artists). Keep divine images reverent and accurate.

episodes.title: The Parade That Ended the Mauryas
episodes.era: End of the Maurya Empire, c. 185 BCE
episodes.region: Pataliputra and the fractured post-Ashokan empire
episodes.logline: At a military review, the general Pushyamitra kills the last Mauryan king Brihadratha, and the empire of Chandragupta and Ashoka gives way to the Shungas.
episodes.moral: An empire that cannot renew its bonds may fall from within.

sources.citation: Bana, Harshacharita, 7th century CE
sources.note: Later literary source for Pushyamitra assassinating Brihadratha during a military parade.

sources.citation: Ayodhya Inscription of Dhana
sources.note: Epigraphic evidence for Pushyamitra and his Ashvamedha sacrifices.

sources.citation: Romila Thapar, Asoka and the Decline of the Mauryas (1961; 3rd ed. 1997); Upinder Singh (2008)
sources.note: Modern analysis of decline, fragmentation and the persecution debate.

episodes.notes: After Ashoka, the king-list becomes poorly attested: Kunala/Dasharatha, Samprati, Shalishuka, Devavarman, Shatadhanvan and Brihadratha are known mostly from Puranic lists with differing details. Pushyamitra's coup around 185 BCE is the accepted end of Mauryan rule, but Bana's assassination scene is a 7th-century literary account, not an eyewitness report. ACCURACY FLAGS: do not blame the fall simplistically on Ashoka's pacifism; historians also cite over-extension, loose network control, economic strain, succession fragmentation and external Indo-Greek pressure. Buddhist texts accuse Pushyamitra of persecution, but Thapar and others stress the lack of firm archaeological proof, Roman denarii anachronisms in Ashokavadana, and Shunga-period expansion at Bharhut and Sanchi. Show a contested, multifactor decline.

episodes.title: Tenali Rama Between Poet and Folktale
episodes.era: Krishnadevaraya's court and later folklore, c. 1480-1528 CE and after
episodes.region: Tenali, Vijayanagara court and Telugu literary tradition
episodes.logline: Behind the laughing trickster of children's tales stands Tenali Ramakrishna, an attested Telugu poet whose wit later bloomed into folklore.
episodes.moral: Enjoy legends, but honor the real person beneath them.

sources.citation: Tenali Ramakrishna, Panduranga Mahatmyam, manuscripts in Tanjore Sarasvati Mahal Library tradition
sources.note: Primary literary evidence for the historical poet.

sources.citation: Rao and Shulman, Classical Telugu Poetry: An Anthology (University of California Press, 2002)
sources.note: Context for Telugu court poetry and Panduranga Mahatmyam.

sources.citation: Tanjore Sarasvati Mahal Library catalogue
sources.note: Manuscript repository evidence for pre-modern Telugu works.

episodes.notes: Tenali Ramakrishna, also called Tenali Ramalinga, was a real Telugu poet associated with Krishnadevaraya's literary world and remembered as Vikatakavi, poet of wit. KEY FACTS: Panduranga Mahatmyam gives hard literary evidence of his stature, and the Ashtadiggajas link belongs to retrospective tradition. Accuracy flag: the famous Tenali Rama tales of impossible riddles, jester tricks and outwitting priests are mostly 17th-19th century folklore, culturally meaningful but not contemporary biography. Do NOT present individual jokes as court records, and treat the snakebite death story as traditional but not independently verified.
episodes.chapter_part: IV. Songs, Wit and Shattered Walls

episodes.title: A Face in Stone a Body in Bronze
episodes.era: Mohenjo-daro sculpture and Harappan iconography, c. 2500-1900 BCE
episodes.region: Mohenjo-daro, with figurines and seals from many Harappan sites
episodes.logline: A bronze youth called the Dancing Girl and a steatite bust called the Priest-King reveal Harappan artistry while warning us how easily labels become legends.
episodes.moral: Wonder grows stronger when it tells the truth.

sources.citation: J.H. Marshall, Mohenjo-daro and the Indus Civilization, Vol. I (1931)
sources.note: Primary publication of figurines, seals and sculptures.

sources.citation: E.J.H. Mackay, Further Excavations at Mohenjo-daro (1938)
sources.note: Find context for major objects from Mohenjo-daro.

sources.citation: J.M. Kenoyer, Ancient Cities of the Indus Valley Civilization (1998)
sources.note: Modern analysis of Harappan art, technology and iconography.

episodes.notes: The bronze figure called the Dancing Girl is a 10.8 cm lost-wax casting from Mohenjo-daro; the steatite bust called the Priest-King is 17.5 cm and neither priesthood nor kingship is proven. Terracotta figurines, animal toys and the Pashupati seal show rich iconography, but religious readings remain provisional; recent studies of bangles and figurines broaden the possible social meanings. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT call the bronze figure a dancer as fact, do NOT call the bust a priest or king as fact, and do NOT present Pashupati as proto-Shiva with certainty.

episodes.title: The Port That Fed an Empire
episodes.figure: Virji Vora and the Surat merchants
episodes.era: Mughal Surat, c. 1572-1680
episodes.region: Surat, Gujarat and the Indian Ocean
episodes.logline: At Surat, merchants, pilgrims and European factories crowd a Mughal port whose customs and credit help feed an empire.
episodes.moral: Commerce can be as powerful as armies in shaping history.

sources.citation: British Library, India Office Records, IOR/G/36, Surat Factory Records
sources.note: Primary English East India Company records for Surat trade and merchants.

sources.citation: Sanjay Subrahmanyam, The Hidden Face of Surat: Reflections on a Cosmopolitan Indian Ocean Centre, 1540-1750, JESHO 61, 2018
sources.note: Recent revisionist study of Surat's cosmopolitan commercial life.

sources.citation: Ashin Das Gupta, Indian Merchants and the Decline of Surat, c. 1700-1750, Franz Steiner, 1979
sources.note: Foundational study of Indian merchant networks and Surat's later decline.

episodes.notes: After Akbar annexed Gujarat in 1572-73, Surat grew into the Mughal Empire's major oceanic port, Hajj embarkation center and customs gateway. Merchants such as Virji Vora could finance and frustrate European companies, while Bohra, Jain, Armenian, Jewish, Muslim and Hindu networks moved textiles, indigo, spices, horses and bullion across the Indian Ocean. Recent work by Subrahmanyam challenges Europe-centered narratives; do NOT inflate Virji Vora's wealth into a precise audited fortune, and do NOT treat English factory complaints as neutral descriptions of Indian merchants.
episodes.chapter_part: V. The Vast and Broken Realm

episodes.title: Amoghavarsha Opens Kannada's Royal Path
episodes.era: Rashtrakuta literary culture, c. 814-878 CE
episodes.region: Manyakheta and the Kannada-speaking Deccan
episodes.logline: In Amoghavarsha's court, Kavirajamarga maps a country of poets and gives Kannada literature a royal path beside Sanskrit learning.
episodes.moral: A language flourishes when scholars teach it how to sing.

sources.citation: Kavirajamarga, c. 850 CE, ed. R. Narasimhachar (1926)
sources.note: Primary poetics text associated with Amoghavarsha and Sri Vijaya.

sources.citation: Nilgund inscription of Amoghavarsha and Sanjan Copper Plates, Epigraphia Indica / CII Vol. IV
sources.note: Primary epigraphic anchors for Amoghavarsha's reign and patronage.

sources.citation: Sheldon Pollock, The Language of the Gods in the World of Men (2006)
sources.note: Recent influential account of Kannada's 'literization' and regional literary culture.

episodes.notes: Kavirajamarga is the earliest surviving Kannada poetics treatise and a landmark in the making of a regional literary culture, identifying a Kannada country and praising earlier poets whose works are now lost. Recent scholarship usually treats Sri Vijaya as the main literary author with Amoghavarsha as patron or collaborator, fitting Pollock's broader model of royal support for vernacular literary worlds. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say Amoghavarsha single-handedly wrote the book; do NOT call it the first Kannada literary work; do NOT turn Jain devotional traditions about his self-sacrifice into documented political events.

episodes.title: Amir Khusrau Sings Hind and Iran
episodes.era: Indo-Persian literary culture, 1253-1325 CE
episodes.region: Patiyali, Delhi, Multan, Bengal and Nizamuddin
episodes.logline: Serving eight sultans and loving one saint, Amir Khusrau writes Persian for courts, Hindavi for the street, and songs that still echo at Nizamuddin.
episodes.moral: A bridge of words can outlive empires.

sources.citation: Amir Khusrau, Khazain-ul-Futuh, Qiran-us-Sadain, Nuh Sipihr and Tughlaq Nama
sources.note: Surviving works that make Khusrau both poet and historical witness.

sources.citation: Amir Hasan Sijzi, Fawaid-ul-Fuad, compiled 1309-1322
sources.note: Conversations of Nizamuddin Auliya with references to the Chishti circle.

sources.citation: Sunil Sharma, Amir Khusraw: The Poet of Sultans and Sufis (Oneworld, 2005)
sources.note: Key modern English biography and literary guide.

episodes.notes: Khusrau, born in 1253 to a Turkic father and Indian mother, served courts from Balban's circle to the Tughlaqs, wrote major Persian masnavis and histories, celebrated India in Nuh Sipihr, and became inseparable from Nizamuddin Auliya's Chishti world. His Hindavi verses, riddles and musical memory helped shape later north Indian culture, while qawwali tradition keeps him alive at the dargah. Recent musicology warns that sitar and tabla invention stories are late. Do NOT claim he invented the sitar or tabla, and do NOT state Khaliq Bari is certainly his without caveat.
episodes.chapter_part: V. Words, Song and the Open Door

episodes.title: Vasudeva and the Long Unraveling
episodes.era: Late Great Kushan period, c. 191-232 CE and after
episodes.region: Mathura, Gandhara, Bactria and the Sasanian frontier
episodes.logline: As Vasudeva's coins turn toward Shiva and Nandi, Sasanian pressure in the west and new rivals in the east begin to pull the Kushan world apart.
episodes.moral: Decline is often a slow loosening, not a single fall.

sources.citation: Jongeward, Cribb and Donovan, Kushan, Kushano-Sasanian, and Kidarite Coins (2015)
sources.note: Coin sequence for Vasudeva, later Kushans and Kushano-Sasanians.

sources.citation: Shapur I, Ka'ba-ye Zartosht inscription, c. 262 CE, trans. M. Back (1978)
sources.note: Sasanian royal claim over Kushan territory or Kushanshar.

sources.citation: Khodadad Rezakhani, ReOrienting the Sasanians (2017)
sources.note: Recent study of East Iran, Kushano-Sasanian rule and late antique frontiers.

episodes.notes: Vasudeva I, often treated as the last Great Kushan, ruled as the empire's western holdings came under pressure from Ardashir I, Shapur I and later Kushano-Sasanian governors styling themselves Kushanshah. His coins strongly emphasize Shiva with Nandi, unlike the broader pantheons of Kanishka and Huvishka, while later eastern or Little Kushans persisted in reduced form until Gupta, Kidarite and other powers absorbed their territories. RECENT FINDINGS: newer numismatic work distinguishes Great Kushan, Kushano-Sasanian and Kidarite issues more carefully. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say the empire simply fell to the Guptas; western loss to Sasanians and northern pressure were central, and the process was gradual.
episodes.chapter: The Kushan Empire and the Silk Road

episodes.title: Appar Sings the King Toward Siva
episodes.era: Early Tamil Shaiva Bhakti, c. 600-650 CE
episodes.region: Kanchipuram, Tiruvathigai and Pallava Tamil country
episodes.logline: Appar's Tamil hymns carry devotion beyond elite ritual and later memory links his songs to Mahendravarman's turn from Jain patronage toward Siva.
episodes.moral: A song in the people's language can change public life.

sources.citation: Appar's Tevaram hymns, Tirumurai volumes 4-6
sources.note: Primary devotional corpus for Appar's voice and religious world.

sources.citation: Mandagapattu inscription of Mahendravarman I
sources.note: Royal Shaiva temple dedication consistent with a shift in patronage.

sources.citation: Indira Viswanathan Peterson, Poems to Siva (1989); Karen Pechilis, The Embodiment of Bhakti (1999)
sources.note: Modern scholarship on Bhakti sources, embodiment and social scope.

episodes.notes: Appar, a Vellalar devotee remembered as once Jain, composed Tamil hymns that helped make temple devotion emotionally direct and publicly performable. Later hagiography says he converted Mahendravarman I from Jainism to Shaivism; inscriptions instead show a religious shift in the king's patronage, not the dramatic prison-and-miracle story. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP emphasizes the hymns themselves over Periya Puranam biography and debates how far Bhakti should be called social reform. Do NOT say Bhakti abolished caste or that the king became intolerant; the Pallava religious landscape remained plural, with Jain, Buddhist and Brahmanical institutions present.
episodes.chapter: The Pallavas and the Bhakti Dawn
episodes.chapter_part: V. Villages, Voices and the Bhakti Dawn

episodes.title: K V Sarma Unlocks the School
episodes.figure: K V Sarma and C T Rajagopal
episodes.era: Modern recovery of Kerala mathematics, 1944-2008
episodes.region: Thiruvananthapuram, Madras, Hoshiarpur, Chennai and global scholarship
episodes.logline: After a century of neglect, Indian scholars edit manuscripts, translate proofs and give the Kerala school back to the history of mathematics.
episodes.moral: Recovery takes scholarship as dedicated as discovery.

sources.citation: K.V. Sarma, A History of the Kerala School of Hindu Astronomy (1972)
sources.note: Foundational modern monograph establishing authors, lineage and texts.

sources.citation: C.T. Rajagopal and M.S. Rangachari, Archive for History of Exact Sciences 18 (1978), pp. 89-102
sources.note: Key mathematical recovery and translation of Kerala series material.

sources.citation: K.V. Sarma et al., Ganita-Yukti-Bhasa, 2 vols. (Springer, 2008); Kim Plofker, Mathematics in India (2009)
sources.note: Complete English Yuktibhasa translation and authoritative modern synthesis.

episodes.notes: C.T. Rajagopal and colleagues translated the series into modern mathematical notation from the 1940s through the 1970s. K.V. Sarma began manuscript work in 1944, edited Venvaroha, Goladipika, Nilakantha's Aryabhatiya-bhasya, Jyotirmimamsa and many more texts, then produced the 1972 history that all later work relies on. His Yuktibhasa translation appeared posthumously in 2008 through Ramasubramanian, Srinivas and Sriram. RECENT FLAG: Plofker 2009 and Divakaran 2018 sharpened the source criticism; do NOT treat online summaries as substitutes for manuscript-based scholarship.

episodes.title: The 1610 Rules of a Language
episodes.era: Layered Tolkappiyam tradition, c. 2nd century BCE-5th century CE debated
episodes.region: Tamilakam and the Madurai literary tradition
episodes.logline: An unknown Tamil grammarian turns sounds, words, landscapes and emotions into a lasting literary system for love, war and public life.
episodes.moral: A language endures when people understand its patterns.

sources.citation: Tolkappiyam, Tamil critical text ed. K.R. Kovintarajan (Tamil University, 1994)
sources.note: Primary grammatical and poetic text in three books.

sources.citation: Kamil Zvelebil, The Smile of Murugan (Brill, 1973)
sources.note: Classic study of Tamil literature and Tolkappiyam dating.

sources.citation: Iravatham Mahadevan, Early Tamil Epigraphy (Harvard Oriental Series, 2003)
sources.note: Pulli mark and Tamil Brahmi arguments relevant to dating.

episodes.notes: The Tolkappiyam is the oldest extant Tamil grammatical work, with sections on letters, words and meaning, including the akam-puram division and tinai system linking landscapes to emotion, flora, fauna, time and poetic situation. Dating is highly contested: some layers may be early, while Mahadevan's pulli argument places important features no earlier than the 2nd century CE and Zvelebil saw later redaction. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP by Shulman and Tieken keeps the debate alive. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT date it to a legendary ancient Sangam, do NOT insist one historical Tolkappiyar wrote all of it, and do NOT treat the three Sangam academies as historical.
episodes.chapter: The Satavahanas and the Sangam Age

episodes.title: Mahadji Scindia Drills a New Army
episodes.figure: Mahadji Scindia and Benoit de Boigne
episodes.era: Maratha military modernization, 1784-1794 CE
episodes.region: Gwalior, Delhi, Agra, Hindustan and the Chambal region
episodes.logline: Mahadji Scindia hires de Boigne and forges drilled infantry that can guard Delhi with muskets, artillery and regular pay.
episodes.moral: Learning from rivals can become strength when guided by purpose.

sources.citation: James Grant Duff, A History of the Marathas, Vol. III (1826)
sources.note: Early narrative using Maratha and British materials for Scindia's late eighteenth-century power.

sources.citation: Benoit de Boigne memoir traditions and European accounts of Scindia's service
sources.note: Primary-adjacent testimony for the campoo brigades, read with caution.

sources.citation: Randolf Cooper, The Anglo-Maratha Campaigns and the Contest for India (Cambridge UP, 2003)
sources.note: Modern military analysis of European-drilled forces and Anglo-Maratha conflict.

episodes.notes: After restoring Mughal emperor Shah Alam II to Delhi in 1771 and becoming a northern kingmaker, Mahadji Scindia employed Benoit de Boigne from the mid-1780s to organize regular infantry brigades, artillery and disciplined campoo formations. KEY FACTS: this was a major military innovation inside the Confederacy, pairing Maratha finance and politics with European drill before Scindia's death in 1794. Recent scholarship warns that modernization was uneven and dependent on pay, commanders and regional revenue. Do NOT portray de Boigne as single-handedly modernizing all Maratha armies, and do NOT treat Delhi's Mughal emperor as holding independent power by this time.

episodes.title: The Army That Learned from Napoleon
episodes.era: Fauj-i-Khas and military modernization, c. 1822-1839 CE
episodes.region: Lahore, Peshawar, Jamrud and Manikyala
episodes.logline: Ranjit Singh hires veterans of Napoleon to train infantry, artillery and cavalry, while Sikh generals guard the road to the Khyber.
episodes.moral: Learning from others can strengthen your own house.

sources.citation: W.G. Osborne, The Court and Camp of Runjeet Sing (1840)
sources.note: Eyewitness source for the army and European officers.

sources.citation: Jean-Marie Lafont, Maharaja Ranjit Singh: Lord of the Five Rivers (2002); Charles Grey, European Adventurers of Northern India (1929)
sources.note: Studies of Allard, Ventura, Avitabile and Court.

sources.citation: Jean-Baptiste Ventura's Manikyala excavation reports, Journal of the Asiatic Society of Bengal, 1830s
sources.note: Primary scholarly record of an early stupa excavation by a Lahore officer.

episodes.notes: After 1809, Ranjit Singh modernized beyond cavalry. Jean-Francois Allard and Jean-Baptiste Ventura arrived in Lahore in 1822, later joined by Paolo Avitabile and Claude Auguste Court, and helped train the Fauj-i-Khas with European-style infantry, cavalry and artillery. Hari Singh Nalwa's frontier campaigns, including Peshawar and Jamrud, show that the empire combined imported drill with Sikh and Punjabi command. Ventura's 1830 Manikyala stupa excavation adds an unexpected scholarly innovation. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT portray Europeans as the sole creators of Sikh strength; the regular army worked because Ranjit Singh, local commanders, artillery workshops and Punjabi soldiers adapted foreign techniques to their own state.
episodes.chapter: The Sikh Gurus and Ranjit Singh

episodes.title: Sarabhai Launches from a Fisherman's Shore
episodes.era: Indian space research, 1947-1972
episodes.region: Ahmedabad, Thumba and Thiruvananthapuram
episodes.logline: Vikram Sarabhai turns a church near the magnetic equator into the launch site for India's first sounding rocket.
episodes.moral: Science reaches higher when it serves everyday life below.

sources.citation: INCOSPAR founding documents, 1962, Department of Space and ISRO records
sources.note: Primary institutional record for the committee that began India's space programme.

sources.citation: A.P.J. Abdul Kalam and Arun Tiwari, Wings of Fire, Universities Press, 1999
sources.note: Firsthand account of the Thumba years and early rocket work.

sources.citation: Amrita Shah, Vikram Sarabhai: A Life, Penguin Viking, 2007
sources.note: Standard biography using PRL archives and family records.

episodes.notes: Sarabhai founded the Physical Research Laboratory in Ahmedabad on 11 November 1947, led INCOSPAR from 1962, and chose Thumba because it lay near the magnetic equator. With local church support, St. Mary Magdalene Church became a rocket assembly space, and India launched a US Nike-Apache sounding rocket on 21 November 1963; the Indian-designed Rohini RH-75 followed in 1967. This is an ENGINEERING and DEVELOPMENT innovation story: Sarabhai argued space research should support communication, weather, education and agriculture. Recent ISRO and VSSC retrospectives preserve photographs and launch records, including the bicycle nose-cone tradition. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say the first rocket was Indian-designed. Do NOT say Sarabhai founded ISRO directly; INCOSPAR became ISRO in 1972 after his death.
episodes.chapter_part: V. Laboratories of a Free Nation

episodes.title: The Scholar Who Brought a Notebook
episodes.era: Arabic study of Indian knowledge, c. 1017-1030 CE
episodes.region: Ghazni, northwestern India and Sanskrit scholarly circles
episodes.logline: Al-Biruni learns Sanskrit and writes a careful outsider's map of Indian mathematics, astronomy and thought.
episodes.moral: Respectful study begins by learning another person's language.

sources.citation: Al-Biruni, Kitab al-Hind; Edward Sachau translation, Alberuni's India (1888)
sources.note: Primary external account of Indian science, religion, chronology and scholarship.

sources.citation: Seyyed Hossein Nasr, An Introduction to Islamic Cosmological Doctrines (2nd ed., 1993)
sources.note: Context for Islamic scientific exchange and al-Biruni's methods.

sources.citation: David Pingree, Indian Reception of Muslim Versions of Ptolemaic Astronomy (1996)
sources.note: Study of Indo-Islamic astronomical exchange.

episodes.notes: Al-Biruni accompanied the Ghaznavid world into India, learned Sanskrit, read Indian texts and wrote Kitab al-Hind around 1030 CE. His account is unusually critical and sympathetic: he praises Indian mathematics while noting social and intellectual barriers to exchange. Recent scholarship still relies on Sachau's translation while situating al-Biruni in a broader Arabic-Persian scientific network. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT claim he transmitted all Indian science to Europe; many translations, including the Sindhind stream from Brahmagupta, predated him. He is not neutral in a modern sense, but he is one of the best documented medieval observers of Indian knowledge.
episodes.chapter_part: V. What India Gave the World

episodes.title: The Underground Palace of Rangpur
episodes.figure: Rajeswar Singha and the Chang-Rung Phukan
episodes.era: Talatal Ghar and Kareng Ghar phases, 1698-1769 CE
episodes.region: Rangpur palace complex, modern Sivasagar
episodes.logline: Below Rangpur's palace, vaulted chambers, stores and rumored tunnels reveal a court that planned for ceremony, records and escape.
episodes.moral: Prudence designs exits as carefully as entrances.

sources.citation: Chang-Rung Phukanor Buranji, Assam manuscript tradition
sources.note: Architectural chronicle associated with palace and maidam construction offices.

sources.citation: ASI, List of Centrally Protected Monuments in Assam, Talatal Ghar entry
sources.note: Protected monument evidence for the standing palace complex.

sources.citation: R.D. Choudhury, Historical Architecture of Assam
sources.note: Specialist synthesis on Ahom secular architecture and construction methods.

episodes.notes: Talatal Ghar, the lower part of the Rangpur palace complex, lets the chapter show architecture as administration. Traditions associate Rudra Singha, Sunenphaa and Rajeswar Singha with phases of construction; the complex included council spaces, stores, archives, magazines and underground levels. Rice-lime mortar and brick vaulting tie it to wider Ahom craft knowledge. ACCURACY FLAGS: local and Buranji traditions describe tunnels to the Dikhow River and Garhgaon, but the full 16 km route is not archaeologically verified; say portions or traditions, not proven full length. The Chang-Rung Phukan should be presented as an office of architects and supervisors, not necessarily one named hero.
episodes.chapter_part: IV. Courts of Craft and Code

episodes.title: Kamban Sings the Tamil Ramayana
episodes.era: Later Chola cultural age, c. 12th century CE
episodes.region: Therazhundur, Chola Tamil country
episodes.logline: Under Chola patronage the poet Kamban composes the Ramavataram, giving Tamil its own soaring Ramayana, proof that an empire's truest monuments can be its words.
episodes.moral: Long after thrones fall, a people's stories keep them alive.

sources.citation: Kamba Ramayanam (Ramavataram) of Kambar
Studies of Tamil literature under the imperial Cholas

episodes.title: Skandagupta Holds Back the Huns
episodes.era: The Gupta twilight, c. 455-467 CE
episodes.region: The empire's frontiers; pillars at Bhitari and Girnar (Junagadh)
episodes.logline: The last great Gupta emperor meets the Huna horsemen in a battle that 'makes the earth tremble', repairs the burst Sudarshana dam even as the treasury drains, and holds the golden age together one last time before the long dusk.
episodes.moral: Some victories are measured not in conquest but in how long you hold the light against the dark.

sources.citation: The Bhitari Pillar inscription of Skandagupta
sources.note: Earliest secure Indian source naming the Hunas as invaders; his restoration of the dynasty.

sources.citation: The Junagadh (Girnar) Rock inscription of Skandagupta, Gupta Era 138 (c. 457 CE)
sources.note: Records the repair of the Sudarshana Lake dam under Parnadatta and Chakrapalita.

sources.citation: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Hunnic Coinage' (N. Sims-Williams); Upinder Singh (2008)
sources.note: Recent identification of the Hunas as the Alchon Huns.

episodes.notes: Skandagupta (r. c. 455-467) defeated both the internal Pushyamitras and the invading Hunas; the Bhitari pillar (earliest Indian mention of the Hunas) says the encounter 'made the earth tremble'. The Junagadh inscription shows administration still working under strain - his governor Parnadatta and son Chakrapalita repaired the burst Sudarshana Lake dam (the same lake repaired earlier under Rudradaman, 150 CE). RECENT NUMISMATIC SCHOLARSHIP identifies the Hunas as the ALCHON Huns (distinct from the Hephthalites; often conflated in older textbooks). After him the empire fragmented; Toramana and Mihirakula broke it by the early 6th c. Close the chapter on a heroic-but-poignant last stand, and let the age's gifts (numerals, learning, art) be its true legacy.

episodes.title: Chandragupta's Last Fast at Shravanabelagola
episodes.era: Digambara Jain tradition of Chandragupta's final years, after c. 297 BCE
episodes.region: Shravanabelagola and Chandragiri Hill, Karnataka
episodes.logline: In Jain memory, the conqueror lays down his crown, follows Bhadrabahu south, and ends his life in silent fasting on Chandragiri Hill.
episodes.moral: The greatest conquest may be mastery over oneself.

sources.citation: Harishena, Brihakatha Kosha (931 CE); later Bhadrabahu Charita and Jain traditions
sources.note: Late Digambara textual tradition for abdication, migration and sallekhana.

sources.citation: Shravanabelagola inscriptions from c. 600 CE onward linking Bhadrabahu and Chandragupta
sources.note: Late epigraphic evidence that the tradition existed at the site.

sources.citation: Sushma Jansari on Chandragupta and Bhadrabahu (2023); Paul Dundas, The Jains (2002); R.K. Mookerji, Chandragupta Maurya and His Times (1966)
sources.note: Modern critical analysis of the late and problematic evidence.

episodes.notes: Tell this explicitly as Digambara Jain tradition, not settled history. The story says Chandragupta abdicated to Bindusara, became a monk under Bhadrabahu, migrated during a 12-year famine to Shravanabelagola, and performed sallekhana on Chandragiri Hill. CRITICAL RECENT SCHOLARSHIP: Sushma Jansari (2023) argues the evidence is late and problematic, with no non-Jain support and no 3rd-century BCE corroboration; the earliest inscriptional link appears around 600 CE, roughly 900 years after the supposed events. There may be identity confusion with Prabhacandra or Samprati Chandragupta, and Svetambara tradition rejects the southern migration. The site and tradition are real, and Chandragupta's actual end is unknown, so frame it as a powerful remembered ending with clear caveats.

episodes.title: Hampi Becomes a World Heritage Memory
episodes.era: Aravidu afterlife and modern heritage, 1570-1646 CE and 1986 onward
episodes.region: Penukonda, Chandragiri and the Group of Monuments at Hampi
episodes.logline: After the capital falls, Aravidu rulers carry the empire onward, while Hampi's ruins later become a UNESCO World Heritage landscape.
episodes.moral: A fallen city can still guide the future.

sources.citation: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Group of Monuments at Hampi, inscribed 1986
sources.note: Official heritage listing and Outstanding Universal Value.

sources.citation: Phillip B. Wagoner, Sultan among Hindu Kings, Journal of Asian Studies 55:4 (1996)
sources.note: Revisionist study of Vijayanagara's cosmopolitan Islamicate court culture.

sources.citation: Richard M. Eaton, A Social History of the Deccan (2005); India in the Persianate Age (2019)
sources.note: Modern Deccan framework for Vijayanagara's political and cultural afterlife.

episodes.notes: Tirumala Deva Raya escaped after 1565, founded the Aravidu dynasty around 1570, and shifted power to Penukonda and later Chandragiri; Vijayanagara's political entity lasted in weakened form until about 1646. Hampi today preserves more than 1,600 monuments across a protected landscape and was inscribed as UNESCO's Group of Monuments at Hampi in 1986, placed on the Danger List in 1999 and removed in 2011. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP by Wagoner and Eaton stresses that the empire was a cosmopolitan cultural synthesizer with Islamicate dress, titles and court forms alongside major Shaiva and Vaishnava patronage. Do NOT close with 'last Hindu kingdom' as a simple truth; mention Sangama, Saluva, Tuluva and Aravidu as a long, changing imperial story.

episodes.title: When the Monsoons Changed
episodes.era: Harappan decline and genetic evidence, c. 2200-1300 BCE
episodes.region: Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Dholavira, Rakhigarhi and the Ghaggar-Hakra region
episodes.logline: As monsoons weaken and rivers change, the great cities shrink rather than fall in a single blow, while one Rakhigarhi genome proves the story was not an invasion massacre.
episodes.moral: Endings are rarely single events, and survival can change form.

sources.citation: Y. Dixit, D.A. Hodell and C.A. Petrie, 'Abrupt weakening of the summer monsoon in northwest India ~4100 yr ago,' Geology 42 (2014)
sources.note: Palaeoclimate evidence for monsoon weakening.

sources.citation: L. Giosan et al., 'Fluvial landscapes of the Harappan civilization,' PNAS 109 (2012)
sources.note: River and monsoon landscape study of Harappan settlement.

sources.citation: V. Shinde et al., 'An Ancient Harappan Genome Lacks Ancestry from Steppe Pastoralists or Iranian Farmers,' Cell 179 (2019)
sources.note: First published ancient DNA from a Harappan burial at Rakhigarhi.

episodes.notes: The urban decline from about 2000-1700 BCE was gradual and uneven, with Late Harappan cultures continuing to c. 1300 BCE in some regions. Palaeoclimate records from Kotla Dahar, isotope studies, Giosan's river work and recent modelling point to weakened monsoons, river changes, trade disruption and adaptation rather than one sudden catastrophe; the 2019 Rakhigarhi genome lacks Steppe ancestry but represents one individual, not an entire civilisation. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say Aryan invasion caused the collapse, do NOT say climate alone explains everything, do NOT say the civilisation ended sharply in 1900 BCE, and do NOT state that Ghaggar-Hakra is the Rigvedic Sarasvati as fact.

episodes.title: Aurangzeb's Last Tent in the Deccan
episodes.era: Aurangzeb's Deccan campaigns, 1682-1707
episodes.region: Bijapur, Golconda, Maratha country and Ahmadnagar
episodes.logline: Aurangzeb wins forts across the Deccan, yet spends his last decades in a moving camp while the empire strains beneath him.
episodes.moral: Conquest without sustainable peace can hollow out victory.

sources.citation: Saqi Mustad Khan, Maasir-i-Alamgiri, trans. Jadunath Sarkar, Royal Asiatic Society of Bengal, 1947
sources.note: Primary Mughal chronicle for Aurangzeb's Deccan campaigns.

sources.citation: Jamshid H. Bilimoria, trans., Letters of Aurangzeb (Ruqat-i-Alamgiri), Luzac, 1908
sources.note: Primary correspondence collection including late-life reflections attributed to Aurangzeb.

sources.citation: J.F. Richards, The Imperial Crisis in the Deccan, Journal of Asian Studies 35.2, 1976
sources.note: Structural study of the jagir and fiscal crisis created by Deccan expansion.

episodes.notes: Aurangzeb left north India for the Deccan in 1682, took Bijapur in 1686 and Golconda in 1687, then spent two decades fighting Maratha resistance under Sambhaji, Rajaram and Tarabai before dying near Ahmadnagar on 3 March 1707. Richards' work explains the structural crisis: more mansabdars needed payment than the annexed lands could sustainably support. Recent reassessment warns against explaining the Deccan war only as religious zeal; strategy, revenue, frontier control and imperial imagination all mattered. Do NOT claim Aurangzeb simply lost every battle, and do NOT quote the deathbed letter without noting manuscript and interpretation debates.
episodes.chapter_part: V. The Vast and Broken Realm

episodes.title: Mahaviracharya Counts the World
episodes.era: Rashtrakuta mathematics, c. 820-850 CE
episodes.region: Manyakheta and Jain scholarly circles of the Deccan
episodes.logline: Mahaviracharya gathers rules for fractions, measures, shadows and combinations into a dedicated mathematics book for a practical world.
episodes.moral: Knowledge grows when old rules are organized so new minds can use them.

sources.citation: Mahaviracharya, Ganita Sara Sangraha, trans. M. Rangacharya, Madras Government Press (1912)
sources.note: Primary mathematical text with dedication to Amoghavarsha I.

sources.citation: Kim Plofker, Mathematics in India (Princeton University Press, 2009)
sources.note: Authoritative modern analysis of Mahaviracharya's place in Indian mathematics.

sources.citation: George Gheverghese Joseph, The Crest of the Peacock, 3rd ed. (2011)
sources.note: Recent discussion of combinations, fractions and mathematical transmission.

episodes.notes: The Ganita Sara Sangraha is a surviving Sanskrit mathematical compendium of more than a thousand verses, dedicated to Amoghavarsha and organized around arithmetic, fractions, measurement, shadows, progressions and combinations. Modern historians value it because it treats mathematics as an independent discipline, building on Aryabhata and Brahmagupta while serving merchants, architects and scholars. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT call Mahaviracharya the father of Indian mathematics; do NOT say he invented combinations or negative numbers; do NOT detach the text from its practical applied problems.

episodes.title: Nizamuddin Opens the Khanqah Door
episodes.era: Chishti Delhi, c. 1270s-1325 CE
episodes.region: Badaun, Ghiyaspur, Delhi and the Nizamuddin Dargah
episodes.logline: While sultans summon and threaten, Nizamuddin Auliya keeps his khanqah open to the poor, the stranger and the singer at the edge of Delhi.
episodes.moral: Service can become a kingdom without a throne.

sources.citation: Amir Hasan Sijzi, Fawaid-ul-Fuad, translated as Morals for the Heart by Bruce B. Lawrence (1992)
sources.note: Primary record of Nizamuddin's conversations, ethics and social world.

sources.citation: Simon Digby, 'The Sufi Shaykh and the Sultan', Iran 28 (1990)
sources.note: Modern study of competing saintly and royal authority.

sources.citation: Carl W. Ernst and Bruce B. Lawrence, Sufi Martyrs of Love (Palgrave Macmillan, 2002)
sources.note: Context for the Chishti order in South Asia.

episodes.notes: Nizamuddin Auliya, born in Badaun in 1238 and dead in Delhi on April 3, 1325, made Ghiyaspur a Chishti center where food, counsel and song crossed lines of status and community. Fawaid-ul-Fuad records teachings on poverty, love, music and distance from rulers; later tradition dramatized his conflict with Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq through the phrase 'Delhi is still far away.' Recent scholarship treats the khanqah as both spiritual refuge and social institution, not an apolitical fantasy. Do NOT present the curse story as established fact, and do NOT claim the Chishtis had no links at all to Sultanate political economy.
episodes.chapter_part: V. Words, Song and the Open Door

episodes.title: Buddhism's Road to China
episodes.era: Silk Road Buddhist transmission, c. 148-400 CE
episodes.region: Gandhara, the Tarim Basin, Dunhuang and Luoyang
episodes.logline: Monks and merchants carry Gandharan manuscripts through Kushan roads to Luoyang, where Lokaraksha turns Mahayana ideas into Chinese words.
episodes.moral: Ideas travel farthest when roads, books and seekers meet.

sources.citation: Lokaraksha's early Chinese Buddhist translations in the Taisho canon, identified by Erik Zurcher and Jan Nattier
sources.note: Primary textual evidence for Gandharan and Kushan-era transmission to China.

sources.citation: British Library Gandharan manuscripts, published by Richard Salomon, Ancient Buddhist Scrolls from Gandhara (1999)
sources.note: Physical Kharoshthi birchbark evidence for early Buddhist scribal culture.

sources.citation: Faxian, Record of Buddhistic Kingdoms, trans. James Legge (1886)
sources.note: Later pilgrim account of Buddhist landscapes that inherited Kushan-era networks.

episodes.notes: Lokaraksha, active at Luoyang around 148-170 CE and associated with Gandhara/Yuezhi background, produced some of the earliest Chinese Mahayana translations, while An Shigao and other translators worked in the same Han world. The Gandharan birchbark manuscripts, acquired and published from the 1990s onward, physically demonstrate the scribal culture from which such texts could travel through Tarim oasis monasteries to China. RECENT FINDINGS: Salomon's Gandhari manuscript project and Jan Nattier's work on earliest Chinese translations have made the Kushan-era transmission map far sharper. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say Kanishka sent missionaries to China; evidence points to monks and merchants using protected trade routes. Do NOT say Buddhism began in China only with the Kushans.
episodes.chapter: The Kushan Empire and the Silk Road

episodes.title: Women Who Sang the Bhakti Dawn
episodes.era: Women poet-saints of Tamil Bhakti, c. 5th-8th centuries CE
episodes.region: Karaikal, Thiruvalangadu, Srivilliputhur and the wider Tamil country
episodes.logline: Karaikkal Ammaiyar and Andal turn Tamil poetry into a woman's devotional voice, from cremation-ground Siva songs to Krishna longing sung every Margazhi.
episodes.moral: A tradition is richer when every voice can sing.

sources.citation: Karaikkal Ammaiyar's Arpudath Thiruvandhadhi and Thiruvaalangadu hymns, 11th Tirumurai
sources.note: Primary Shaiva poems attributed to one of the earliest women Nayanmars.

sources.citation: Andal's Tiruppavai and Nachiyar Tirumoli, Naalayira Divya Prabandham
sources.note: Primary Vaishnava poems of the only woman Alvar.

sources.citation: Elaine Craddock, Siva's Demon Devotee (2010); Archana Venkatesan, The Secret Garland (2010)
sources.note: Recent critical studies separating poetry from later miracle biographies.

episodes.notes: Karaikkal Ammaiyar, probably among the earliest Nayanmars, used fierce poetic images of Shiva's cremation-ground dance and helped shape Tamil devotional form; Andal, active around the 8th century in most scholarly dating, composed the Tiruppavai and Nachiyar Tirumoli in a female voice of vow, longing and theology. RECENT STUDIES by Craddock and Venkatesan foreground their literary agency and distinguish primary poems from later hagiographies. Do NOT claim exact dates are certain, do NOT treat Andal's miraculous union with Ranganatha or Ammaiyar's bodily transformation as contemporary fact, and do NOT erase their different Shaiva and Vaishnava contexts.
episodes.chapter: The Pallavas and the Bhakti Dawn
episodes.chapter_part: V. Villages, Voices and the Bhakti Dawn

episodes.title: The Question Newton Never Answered
episodes.era: Transmission debate, 1990s-present, with roots in 1498-1834
episodes.region: Kerala, Portuguese India, European mathematics and modern historiography
episodes.logline: Kerala's series predate Gregory, Newton and Leibniz, but the missing bridge to Europe keeps historians arguing over possibility and proof.
episodes.moral: Priority matters, but evidence matters more.

sources.citation: George Gheverghese Joseph, The Crest of the Peacock, 3rd ed. (2011); D.F. Almeida, J.K. John and A. Zubair, Journal of Natural Geometry 20 (2001)
sources.note: Sources presenting the possibility of Kerala-to-Europe transmission.

sources.citation: David Bressoud, Was Calculus Invented in India?, College Mathematics Journal 33:1 (2002); Victor J. Katz, Mathematics Magazine 68:3 (1995)
sources.note: Careful skeptical assessments of the calculus and transmission claims.

sources.citation: Kim Plofker, Mathematics in India (2009), pp. 251-253
sources.note: Balanced modern statement: possible routes, but no direct manuscript evidence.

episodes.notes: The chronological facts are powerful: Portuguese ships reached Calicut in 1498, Jesuits were active in the 1500s, and Kerala's series predate Gregory, Newton and Leibniz by centuries. But no letter, translation, European citation or manuscript has yet shown that Newton, Leibniz or Gregory knew Kerala mathematics. ACCURACY FLAGS: present transmission as a debated hypothesis, not a proven theft or a settled fact; also do NOT erase Kerala priority for specific series. The strongest honest ending is that Kerala mathematicians achieved remarkable pre-calculus series independently within Indian astronomy, while the European calculus arose as a different, documented synthesis.

episodes.title: The Poet Who Guarded Pari's Daughters
episodes.era: Sangam poetic memory, c. 50-200 CE debated
episodes.region: Parambu Nadu and the courts of Tamilakam
episodes.logline: Kapilar sings for the generous Vel Pari, challenges the three crowned kings with poetry, and in later memory protects Pari's orphaned daughters.
episodes.moral: Loyal words can defend the vulnerable when armies fail.

sources.citation: George L. Hart and Hank Heifetz, Four Hundred Songs of War and Wisdom (Columbia University Press, 1999)
sources.note: Purananuru translations including poems linked to Kapilar, Pari and the three crowns.

sources.citation: George L. Hart, The Poems of Ancient Tamil (University of California Press, 1975)
sources.note: Standard introduction to the milieu of Sangam poetry.

sources.citation: David Shulman, Tamil: A Biography (Harvard University Press, 2016)
sources.note: Recent literary history of Tamil and its poets.

episodes.notes: Kapilar is credited by manuscript colophons with over 200 Sangam poems, including mountain-landscape mastery and poems for Vel Pari of Parambu. Purananuru traditions present Pari as a Velir chieftain famous for generosity and besieged by the three crowned kings; later stories say Kapilar sought marriages for Pari's daughters and died by vadakirrutal. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP treats the poems as precious but mediated evidence. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say every attributed poem is certainly by one historical Kapilar, do NOT give precise dates, do NOT call Pari a crowned king, and do NOT present Kapilar's ritual death as directly attested in Sangam poems.
episodes.chapter: The Satavahanas and the Sangam Age

episodes.title: Nana Fadnavis and the Twelve Pillars
episodes.era: Barabhai Council and late Confederacy diplomacy, 1773-1800 CE
episodes.region: Pune, Salbai, Wadgaon, Delhi and the Deccan courts
episodes.logline: After a palace murder, Nana Fadnavis builds a council, guards an infant Peshwa and keeps rival powers balanced for a generation.
episodes.moral: Patient diplomacy can hold a fragile house together.

sources.citation: Peshwa Daftar, Nana Fadnavis letters, roznishi and diplomatic dispatches
sources.note: Large primary archive for late Maratha governance and intelligence.

sources.citation: Treaty of Wadgaon, 1779, and Treaty of Salbai, 1782, in British and Maratha records
sources.note: Documented instruments marking First Anglo-Maratha War outcomes.

sources.citation: Prachi Deshpande, Creative Pasts (Columbia UP, 2007); Stewart Gordon, The Marathas 1600-1818
sources.note: Modern interpretations of Nana's memory, diplomacy and limitations.

episodes.notes: Nana Fadnavis helped form the Barabhai Council after Narayanrao Peshwa's assassination in 1773, protected Madhavrao II's claim, and managed diplomacy through the First Anglo-Maratha War, Wadgaon in 1779 and Salbai in 1782. KEY FACTS: his papers make this period unusually document-rich; Grant Duff's 'Maratha Machiavelli' label is influential but colonial. Recent scholarship stresses collective politics and Nana's failures as well as skill, including tensions with Tipu, Scindia and the British. Do NOT make him the sole brain of the Confederacy, and do NOT quote the famous Tipu-death remark as certain exact wording.

episodes.title: Ranjit Singh Clothes the Temple in Gold
episodes.era: Golden Temple restoration and sacred kingship, c. 1802-1839 CE
episodes.region: Harmandir Sahib, Amritsar
episodes.logline: After decades of rebuilding, Ranjit Singh covers Harmandir Sahib in gold and turns royal wealth into a shining offering for all pilgrims.
episodes.moral: The finest treasure is the one shared with everyone.

sources.citation: Sohan Lal Suri, Umdat-ut-Tawarikh, c. 1805-1849
sources.note: Court evidence for Ranjit Singh's patronage and costs.

sources.citation: Pardeep Singh Arshi, The Golden Temple: History, Art and Architecture (1989)
sources.note: Standard architectural study of Harmandir Sahib's phases and design.

sources.citation: W.G. Osborne, The Court and Camp of Runjeet Sing (1840); J.M. Honigberger, Thirty-Five Years in the East (1852)
sources.note: European eyewitness descriptions of the shrine and court.

episodes.notes: The Harmandir Sahib had been damaged and rebuilt through the 18th century before Ranjit Singh controlled Amritsar in 1802. He funded marble work and, by about 1830, the gold overlay that gave the shrine its popular name, while the four entrances and low sanctum expressed openness and humility. This is a craft, economic and devotional story: treasury, artisanship, Mughal-Sikh design synthesis and public sacred space. RECENT/ACCURACY FLAGS: conservation studies stress many rebuilding phases; gold quantities vary, so avoid exact weights; pre-1984 Akal Takht murals documented by Kanwarjit Singh Kang were later destroyed, so do NOT imply all older artwork survives unchanged.
episodes.chapter: The Sikh Gurus and Ranjit Singh

episodes.title: Bhatnagar Builds the National Labs
episodes.era: CSIR and national laboratory building, 1942-1958
episodes.region: Lahore, Delhi, Pune, Mysore, Dhanbad and Lucknow
episodes.logline: Shanti Swaroop Bhatnagar helps turn CSIR into a network of laboratories for food, fuel, drugs, physics and industry.
episodes.moral: A nation grows stronger when research is shared across many workshops.

sources.citation: CSIR founding records and annual reports, 1942-1954, CSIR Archives and Government of India records
sources.note: Primary institutional evidence for Bhatnagar's laboratory programme.

sources.citation: S.S. Bhatnagar and K.N. Mathur, Physical Principles and Applications of Magnetochemistry, Macmillan, 1935
sources.note: Primary scientific monograph representing Bhatnagar's research field.

sources.citation: INSA, Biographical Memoir of S.S. Bhatnagar, Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of INSA, vol. 4, 1960
sources.note: Institutional scholarly memoir with career chronology.

episodes.notes: Bhatnagar was a chemist, magnetochemistry researcher, poet and administrator. After becoming CSIR's first Director-General in 1942, he worked with Nehru to build national laboratories after independence, including the National Physical Laboratory, National Chemical Laboratory, Central Food Technological Research Institute, Central Fuel Research Institute and Central Drug Research Institute. This is an INSTITUTIONAL, ECONOMIC and INDUSTRIAL innovation story: science policy became a network of practical research centres. Recent postcolonial histories debate whether CSIR created independent research capacity or leaned too much on adaptation of foreign technology. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT claim every laboratory was world-class immediately; many began short of staff and equipment. His legacy is the framework, momentum and national laboratory vision.
episodes.chapter_part: V. Laboratories of a Free Nation

episodes.title: The Birch-Bark That Started a Debate
episodes.era: Mathematical manuscript and zero debate, c. 3rd-10th century CE folios; found 1881
episodes.region: Bakhshali near Mardan in ancient Gandhara; Bodleian Library, Oxford
episodes.logline: A bundle of birch bark reveals a dot for zero and forces historians to rethink how old a manuscript can be.
episodes.moral: A small mark can change a very large story.

sources.citation: Bakhshali Manuscript, MS. Sansk. d. 14, Bodleian Library Oxford
sources.note: Primary birch-bark mathematical manuscript with dot-form zero placeholders.

sources.citation: Takao Hayashi, The Bakhshali Manuscript (Egbert Forsten, 1995)
sources.note: Definitive pre-radiocarbon study of the mathematical content.

sources.citation: Bodleian Library and Oxford Radiocarbon Accelerator Unit AMS dating announcement (2017)
sources.note: Recent finding that sampled folios date to different centuries.

episodes.notes: Found near Bakhshali in 1881, the birch-bark manuscript contains practical arithmetic, algebra and dot-form zero placeholders. Oxford's 2017 AMS radiocarbon dating sampled folios with ranges around 224-383 CE, 680-779 CE and 885-993 CE, showing that the object is not one simple manuscript from one year. The finding pushed public debate about the written zero much earlier than the Gwalior inscription, but specialists caution that bark age is not the same as composition date. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT state flatly that India has the world's oldest zero; say this may be among the earliest known written zero placeholders, with dating and definition debates ongoing.
episodes.chapter_part: V. What India Gave the World

episodes.title: Sankaradeva's Song for Every Village
episodes.era: Neo-Vaishnava reform, 15th-16th century CE
episodes.region: Bordowa, Barpeta, the Koch court and the Brahmaputra valley
episodes.logline: Sankaradeva turns devotion into song, drama, prayer halls and Assamese verse that ordinary villagers can hear and share.
episodes.moral: Knowledge becomes powerful when people can sing it in their own language.

sources.citation: Srimanta Sankaradeva, Kirtan Ghoxa, standard Assam Publication Board editions
sources.note: Primary devotional text central to Ekasarana practice.

sources.citation: Sankaradeva and Madhavdeva, Borgeets, ed. Maheshwar Neog
sources.note: Primary song corpus of the Assamese Vaishnava movement.

sources.citation: Maheshwar Neog, Early History of the Vaisnava Faith and Movement in Assam (1980)
sources.note: Definitive scholarly study of Sankaradeva, texts, dates and institutions.

episodes.notes: This scholarly, literary and social innovation story belongs inside the Ahom chapter because the Sattra and Namghar world shaped Assamese society under and beside Ahom power. Sankaradeva's Kirtan Ghoxa, Borgeets, Ankia Naat and Bhagavata renderings widened sacred access through Assamese and Brajavali performance, while Sattra institutions preserved manuscripts, music, theatre and community authority. ACCURACY FLAGS: his traditional birth year 1449 and lifespan of about 120 years are debated; recent Assamese scholarship proposes c.1479-1484. Do NOT turn hagiographic miracles into facts, and do NOT ignore state tensions over paik labor and sectarian politics.

episodes.title: The Maidams of Charaideo Remember the Dead
episodes.figure: The Chang-Rung Phukan and Rudra Singha
episodes.era: Royal burials from the 13th to 18th centuries; UNESCO inscription 2023
episodes.region: Charaideo, Sivasagar district, Upper Assam
episodes.logline: Under grassy domes at Charaideo, archaeology, Buranji records and living ancestor rites reveal what the Ahom buried and what they chose to change.
episodes.moral: A society honors the past best when it also learns to leave cruelty behind.

sources.citation: ASI Guwahati Circle, Excavation at Maidam No. 2, Charaideo (2002)
sources.note: Recent excavation evidence for brick vaults, skeletal remains, ivory objects and looting.

sources.citation: UNESCO World Heritage Committee, Charaideo Maidams, Decision 45COM 8B.28 (2023)
sources.note: Most recent heritage documentation and inscription of the site.

sources.citation: Chang-Rung Phukanor Buranji, Assam architectural chronicle tradition
sources.note: Primary textual tradition for tomb construction procedures and materials.

episodes.notes: Charaideo's maidams are the chapter's archaeological finale. They combine Tai burial practice, vaulted brick chambers, earthen mounds, octagonal walls, ritual officers and living Me-Dam-Me-Phi ancestor worship. ASI's 2000-02 excavation of Maidam No. 2 found skeletal remains of five individuals, ivory panels, wooden ritual objects and evidence of looting, broadly matching chronicle descriptions; UNESCO inscribed the site in 2023. Social reform matters too: Buranji tradition credits Rudra Singha with abolishing live burial of attendants. ACCURACY FLAGS: most individual tomb identities are uncertain; do NOT claim all maidams are fully excavated or that archaeology has resolved every chronicle detail.

episodes.title: Shivneri Son and the Rohideshwar Oath
episodes.era: Maratha Swaraj formation, c. 1630-1645 CE
episodes.region: Shivneri fort near Junnar, Pune jagir, Maval foothills and Rohideshwar tradition
episodes.logline: Born at Shivneri in a fractured Deccan, young Shivaji grew among Maval companions and a remembered oath of Swarajya that later generations turned into a founding scene.
episodes.moral: Great public lives begin in private discipline and shared purpose.

sources.citation: Krishnaji Anant Sabhasad, Sabhasad Bakhar, 1697; tr. S.N. Sen as Siva Chhatrapati, 1920
sources.note: Earliest substantial Maratha biography; strong for the life arc but panegyric and posthumous.

sources.citation: Jedhe Shakavali, ed. V.K. Rajwade, Bharat Itihas Sanshodhak Mandal, Pune
sources.note: Near-contemporary Marathi annals; important for Shivneri birth date traditions.

sources.citation: Stewart N. Gordon, The Marathas 1600-1818, Cambridge University Press, 1993, pp. 58-62
sources.note: Critical modern synthesis of Shivaji's childhood and Deccan context.

sources.citation: James W. Laine, Shivaji: Hindu King in Islamic India, Oxford University Press, 2003, chs. 1-2
sources.note: Useful for source memory and the later making of the childhood legend.

episodes.notes: Birth at Shivneri is well attested in Maratha sources; the commonly observed date is 19 February 1630, while older scholarship sometimes used 1627. Present Shahaji as a Maratha general serving Deccan sultanates and Jijabai as a formative political and cultural influence. The Rohideshwar oath and the phrase Hindavi Swarajya belong to remembered tradition: do NOT quote a verbatim oath as contemporary evidence. Set the Deccan as a multi-power political world of Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda, Mughal pressure, Maratha landed families and local Maval networks, not a communal battlefield.
episodes.chapter_part: I. Birth, Youth and the Swarajya Idea

episodes.title: Torna Treasure and the Rajgad Design
episodes.era: First fort seizures and capital building, c. 1646-1650 CE
episodes.region: Torna, Rajgad, Purandar, Kondana, Chakan and the Pune hill country
episodes.logline: At about sixteen Shivaji seized Torna, turned its remembered treasure into Rajgad, and began a hill-fort system where engineering mattered as much as courage.
episodes.moral: A durable dream needs strong walls, honest officers and careful stores.

sources.citation: Sabhasad Bakhar, tr. S.N. Sen, accounts of Torna, Rajgad, Purandar and Kondana
sources.note: Primary Maratha narrative for the first fort seizures and the Torna treasure tradition.

sources.citation: Jedhe Shakavali, entries for the 1640s, ed. V.K. Rajwade, BISM
sources.note: Chronological anchor for early fort captures.

sources.citation: Stewart N. Gordon, The Marathas 1600-1818, pp. 60-65
sources.note: Emphasizes stratagem, bribery and Bijapur weakness rather than heroic pitched battles.

sources.citation: Jadunath Sarkar, Shivaji and His Times, 6th ed., 1961, chs. 4-5
sources.note: Classic account to balance with later critical scholarship.

episodes.notes: STATECRAFT/INNOVATION: fort engineering and territorial administration. Torna was likely taken by stratagem or bribery during Bijapur weakness, not by a grand battlefield victory. The Torna treasure is a strong bakhar tradition, but exact amounts vary and should not be dramatized as fact. Rajgad became a fortified capital with water, stores and defensive terraces; later Maratha statecraft used multiple officers per fort to reduce betrayal risk. Note Shahaji's arrest by Bijapur in 1648 as political pressure on Shivaji. Do NOT call these early captures an empire; this is the foundation of a kingdom.
episodes.chapter_part: I. Birth, Youth and the Swarajya Idea

episodes.title: Javali and the More Rivalry
episodes.era: Seizure of Javali valley, 1656 CE
episodes.region: Javali valley near Mahabaleshwar, Wai and the Ghats-Konkan passes
episodes.logline: When Shivaji took Javali from Chandrarao More, he defeated a fellow Maratha rival and opened the passes from the Sahyadris to the Konkan coast.
episodes.moral: Politics is often closest and hardest among rivals who share the same world.

sources.citation: Sabhasad Bakhar, tr. S.N. Sen, account of Javali and Chandrarao More
sources.note: Maratha narrative; the outcome is clear but the manner of More's death is disputed.

sources.citation: Stewart N. Gordon, The Marathas 1600-1818, pp. 66-70
sources.note: Critical account of intra-Maratha rivalry under Bijapur.

sources.citation: Richard M. Eaton, A Social History of the Deccan, 1300-1761, Cambridge University Press, 2005, ch. 7
sources.note: Non-communal Deccan context for mobile service elites and political competition.

sources.citation: G.S. Sardesai, New History of the Marathas, Vol. 1, 1946, pp. 70-75
sources.note: Classic synthesis from Maratha sources.

episodes.notes: This episode is essential for non-communal framing. Chandrarao More was a Maratha Hindu sardar and Bijapur feudatory; Shivaji's conflict with him was a political struggle for valleys, passes and local authority. Sources agree Shivaji seized Javali in 1656 and that this opened the Konkan route; they disagree on whether More died in battle, at a parley or by assassination. Do NOT frame the rise as only wars against Muslim rulers. Javali also helps explain why Bijapur escalated by sending Afzal Khan.
episodes.chapter_part: II. The Rise in the Ghats

episodes.title: Pratapgad and the Afzal Khan Parley
episodes.era: Battle of Pratapgad, 10 November 1659 CE
episodes.region: Pratapgad fort, Wai and the Javali-Mahabaleshwar hill country
episodes.logline: Below Pratapgad, Shivaji met Bijapur general Afzal Khan in a guarded parley whose death scene remains debated, while the Maratha victory that followed is beyond dispute.
episodes.moral: Courage is strongest when joined to preparation and caution.

sources.citation: Sabhasad Bakhar, tr. S.N. Sen, Afzal Khan episode
sources.note: Records hidden armor, bagh-nakh tradition and Maratha victory; detailed but partisan.

sources.citation: Tarikh-i-Ali, Bijapur chronicle, excerpts compared in Jadunath Sarkar, Shivaji and His Times
sources.note: Hostile Bijapur account saying Shivaji struck with sword or dagger; essential counter-source.

sources.citation: Akhbarat-i-Darbar-i-Mualla, entries for 1659, cited in Sarkar, History of Aurangzib, Vol. III
sources.note: Independent Mughal intelligence on the episode's aftermath.

sources.citation: Stewart N. Gordon, The Marathas 1600-1818, pp. 66-72
sources.note: Compares traditions and rejects communal simplification.

episodes.notes: Sources agree that the parley happened, Afzal Khan died and Shivaji's forces routed the Bijapur army; they disagree on who struck first and which weapon was used. The wagh-nakh or bagh-nakh is a remembered Maratha tradition, not a stenographic fact; Bijapur sources mention dagger or sword. Frame Afzal Khan as an Adilshahi political general, not as a religious symbol. If temple desecration en route is shown, explain it as a contested tactical provocation in a military campaign. Include Shivaji's post-battle clemency to many captured Bijapuri soldiers.
episodes.chapter_part: II. The Rise in the Ghats

episodes.title: Lal Mahal Raid on Shaista Khan
episodes.era: Night raid at Pune, 5 April 1663 CE
episodes.region: Lal Mahal, Pune, then Mughal Deccan administration
episodes.logline: After Shaista Khan occupied Pune from Shivaji's own palace, Shivaji led a night raid into Lal Mahal and left Aurangzeb's uncle wounded and humiliated.
episodes.moral: A precise strike can change what a larger enemy thinks is possible.

sources.citation: Akhbarat-i-Darbar-i-Mualla, April 1663 entries, cited in Sarkar, History of Aurangzib, Vol. III
sources.note: Near-contemporary Mughal confirmation of the raid and Shaista Khan's injury.

sources.citation: Alamgirnama of Muhammad Kazim, tr. in Elliot and Dowson, History of India as Told by Its Own Historians, Vol. VII
sources.note: Mughal court chronicle confirming Shaista Khan's humiliation.

sources.citation: Sabhasad Bakhar, tr. S.N. Sen, Shaista Khan raid
sources.note: Maratha account with operational detail.

sources.citation: Jadunath Sarkar, Shivaji and His Times, ch. 10; History of Aurangzib, Vol. III
sources.note: Classic comparison of Maratha and Mughal evidence.

episodes.notes: The raid, the loss of Shaista Khan's fingers, the death of his son and his transfer to Bengal are strongly cross-attested. The exact entry method, disguise and number of raiders vary by tradition; flag them as story details, not secure fact. Non-communal framing: the target was the Mughal viceroy occupying Pune, not Muslims generally. Name the wider mixed service world: Shivaji's own forces included Muslim commanders such as Siddi Ibrahim, Daulat Khan and Darya Sarang in different arms of service.

episodes.title: Surat Raid and the Rules of Plunder
episodes.era: First sack of Surat, January 1664 CE
episodes.region: Surat, Gujarat, Mughal port city and international factory town
episodes.logline: At Surat, Shivaji took the wealth of a Mughal port while sparing mosques, missionaries and charitable houses, making plunder a fiscal act rather than a communal one.
episodes.moral: Even in war, restraint is a form of power.

sources.citation: George Oxenden and EIC Surat Factory Records, January 1664, India Office Records, British Library
sources.note: Contemporary English account of the raid, factory defense and Shivaji's conduct.

sources.citation: Francois Bernier, Travels in the Mogul Empire, Amsterdam, 1670; English tr. A. Constable, 1891
sources.note: Contemporary traveller preserving the Capuchin mission and charity details.

sources.citation: Maasir-i-Alamgiri of Saqi Mustaid Khan, tr. J.N. Sarkar, 1947, entries for 1664
sources.note: Mughal chronicle confirming the raid and imperial impact.

sources.citation: G.S. Sardesai, New History of the Marathas, Vol. 1, pp. 146-160
sources.note: Synthesis of English, Dutch, Mughal and Maratha sources.

episodes.notes: STATECRAFT/INNOVATION: revenue and war finance. Surat was raided for wealth after years of Mughal pressure and treasury strain. English, Dutch, French, Mughal and Maratha sources make this one of the best documented episodes. Say clearly that wealthy Muslim and Hindu merchants were plundered for wealth, not religion; mosques were not attacked, Capuchin Friar Ambrose was spared, and the charitable broker Mohandas Parekh's house was protected. Do NOT claim all Muslim property was spared. Plunder totals vary widely, so avoid exact treasure claims.

episodes.title: Purandar Treaty and Jai Singh's Net
episodes.era: Treaty of Purandar, 11 June 1665 CE
episodes.region: Purandar fort, Mughal Deccan camp and Aurangabad correspondence
episodes.logline: Mirza Raja Jai Singh, a Rajput general in Mughal service, forced Shivaji to surrender twenty-three forts, showing that survival sometimes required tactical submission.
episodes.moral: Bending at the right moment can preserve the strength to rise again.

sources.citation: Shivaji's Persian letters to Aurangzeb, translated and cited in Jadunath Sarkar, History of Aurangzib, Vol. III, pp. 73-81
sources.note: Primary documents showing tactical submission and Mughal political language.

sources.citation: Akhbarat-i-Darbar-i-Mualla, 1665 entries, cited in Sarkar, History of Aurangzib, Vol. III
sources.note: Near-contemporary record of treaty terms.

sources.citation: Stewart N. Gordon, The Marathas 1600-1818, pp. 72-76
sources.note: Critical reading of the treaty and Jai Singh's role.

sources.citation: G.S. Sardesai, New History of the Marathas, Vol. 1, pp. 157-180
sources.note: Classic account of the campaign and negotiations.

episodes.notes: Jai Singh's identity is crucial: he was a Rajput Hindu serving Aurangzeb, so the conflict was political and imperial, not communal. Terms included surrendering 23 forts, retaining 12, sending Sambhaji as a mansabdar and accepting Mughal suzerainty. Shivaji's submissive letters survive and should be shown as tactical political language, not cowardice. Do NOT overclaim that he knew all along how he would reverse the treaty; his position was genuinely dangerous.

episodes.title: Agra Captive King Vanishes
episodes.era: Agra house arrest and escape, May-August 1666 CE
episodes.region: Agra, Mughal court, Mathura route traditions and the return toward the Deccan
episodes.logline: Humiliated at Aurangzeb's court and held under watch, Shivaji escaped from Agra in a real disappearance whose famous sweet-basket method remains a beloved but disputed tradition.
episodes.moral: Resourcefulness turns captivity into a doorway.

sources.citation: Akhbarat-i-Darbar-i-Mualla, May-August 1666 entries, cited in Sarkar, History of Aurangzib, Vol. III, pp. 83-105
sources.note: Best near-contemporary record of the durbar, detention and escape, but not the mechanism.

sources.citation: Alamgirnama of Muhammad Kazim, 1668, tr. Elliot and Dowson, Vol. VII
sources.note: Mughal official account of the Agra period.

sources.citation: Sabhasad Bakhar, tr. S.N. Sen, Agra episode
sources.note: Records the sweetmeat-basket tradition.

sources.citation: Stewart N. Gordon, The Marathas 1600-1818, pp. 76-80
sources.note: States that there is no contemporary evidence for the basket story and suggests bribery or disguise.

episodes.notes: This integrated life-arc episode intentionally retells the famous Agra escape with a distinct title from the standalone episode. The journey to Agra, the 12 May 1666 durbar humiliation, house arrest under Ram Singh and the escape around 17 August are attested. The basket mechanism is not contemporary; present it as Sabhasad tradition and say historians often prefer bribery, disguise or guard compromise. Do NOT give a definite route. Note Jai Singh and Ram Singh's protective role inside Mughal politics.

episodes.title: Sindhudurg and the Maratha Navy
episodes.era: Coastal fort and navy building, 1664-1673 CE
episodes.region: Sindhudurg, Vijaydurg, Kolaba, Khanderi and the Konkan coast from Daman toward Goa
episodes.logline: At Sindhudurg, Shivaji turned the Arabian Sea into a frontier of Swarajya, building coastal forts and fleets commanded by officers including Daulat Khan and Darya Sarang.
episodes.moral: Sovereignty must defend its shores as carefully as its hills.

sources.citation: EIC Bombay and Surat Factory Records, 1670-1674, India Office Records, British Library
sources.note: Contemporary English monitoring of Maratha naval activity and fleet size.

sources.citation: Sabhasad Bakhar, tr. S.N. Sen, naval commanders and Sindhudurg traditions
sources.note: Names commanders including Daulat Khan and Maynak Bhandari.

sources.citation: Jadunath Sarkar, Shivaji and His Times, ch. 24, The Navy and Maritime Forts
sources.note: Classic study of fleet and sea forts.

sources.citation: Stewart N. Gordon, The Marathas 1600-1818, pp. 79-85
sources.note: Critical assessment of a coastal navy built with Portuguese technical knowledge.

episodes.notes: STATECRAFT/INNOVATION: navy, coastal forts and maritime engineering. Sindhudurg's foundation is traditionally dated 25 November 1664 and the fort was completed around 1667. Name Muslim officers: Daulat Khan or Qasim Khan Pathari, Darya Sarang and other Muslim seamen served in command roles; Portuguese and Goan Christian sailors and technicians also mattered. Fleet-size claims range from dozens to hundreds, so avoid inflated numbers. Do NOT call this a blue-water navy; it was a coastal or green-water force built to resist Siddis, Europeans and rival states along the Konkan.

episodes.title: Raigad Coronation and the New Seal
episodes.era: Coronation at Raigad, 6 June and 24 September 1674 CE
episodes.region: Raigad fort, Mahad, Sahyadri-Konkan frontier
episodes.logline: At Raigad, Shivaji became Chhatrapati through ritual, coinage, calendar and seal, while the debated Sisodia genealogy showed how legitimacy itself could be engineered.
episodes.moral: Symbols make power visible, but honesty must explain how symbols are made.

sources.citation: Sabhasad Bakhar, tr. S.N. Sen, coronation account
sources.note: Detailed Maratha account of ritual, titles, Gaga Bhatt and costs.

sources.citation: Jedhe Shakavali, ed. V.K. Rajwade, entry for Jyeshtha Shukla 13, Shaka 1596
sources.note: Chronological confirmation of 6 June 1674.

sources.citation: EIC Bombay Factory Records, June 1674, India Office Records, British Library
sources.note: Contemporary European envoy account; Dutch VOC records also confirm the event.

sources.citation: Stewart N. Gordon, The Marathas 1600-1818, pp. 85-92
sources.note: Critical discussion of sovereignty, coinage, Ashtapradhan and the genealogy problem.

episodes.notes: STATECRAFT/INNOVATION: sovereignty, legitimacy, coinage and administrative architecture. The first coronation was on 6 June 1674; a second ceremony on 24 September 1674 addressed ritual objections. Gaga Bhatt's Sisodia-Rajput genealogy is widely treated by modern scholars as politically constructed, not documented descent; do NOT present it as fact. Mention new titles, the Rajyabhishek era, coins such as Shivrai and hon, the Sanskrit royal seal and Jijabai's death soon after coronation. European factory records make the event unusually well attested.

episodes.title: Eight Ministers and the Kosha of Rule
episodes.era: Administrative consolidation, c. 1674-1677 CE
episodes.region: Raigad capital, Deccan forts, Konkan revenue stations and royal archives
episodes.logline: Shivaji's mature kingdom ran through ministers, revenue surveys, justice orders, mosque protections and a Sanskrit-Marathi lexicon that gave Swarajya its own language of rule.
episodes.moral: The deepest victory is a just system that outlives the sword.

sources.citation: Rajya Vyavahara Kosha, compiled by Raghunath Pandit, 1677; V.K. Rajwade ed., BISM, 1927
sources.note: Surviving Sanskrit-Marathi administrative lexicon with 1,344 terms.

sources.citation: Farmans of Shivaji, BISM Archives, Pune; partly in V.K. Rajwade, Marathyanchya Itihasachi Sadhane, 1898-1924
sources.note: Royal orders on revenue, military discipline, mosque and Quran protection and civilian safeguards.

sources.citation: Sabhasad Bakhar, tr. S.N. Sen, Ashtapradhan membership and duties
sources.note: Names ministerial offices and functions.

sources.citation: A.R. Kulkarni, The Marathas, 1996, pp. 34-56; Sheldon Pollock, The Language of the Gods in the World of Men, 2006
sources.note: Kulkarni on administration and revenue; Pollock on Sanskrit political culture.

episodes.notes: STATECRAFT/INNOVATION: administration, justice, revenue, language patronage and religious tolerance. Name the Ashtapradhan offices: Peshwa, Amatya, Sachiv, Sumant, Senapati, Mantri, Nyayadhish and Panditrao. Revenue reforms used land measurement and direct state karkuns but built on Malik Ambar and Deccan Sultanate precedents, so do NOT call them wholly new. The Rajyavyavahara Kosha replaced many Persianate terms with Sanskrit-Marathi vocabulary; do NOT frame this as anti-Muslim, but as cultural sovereignty. Include surviving mosque and Quran protection orders, prohibitions on harming women and civilians, and Muslim officers including Siddi Ibrahim, Ibrahim Khan, Daulat Khan and Darya Sarang.

episodes.title: Karnataka Campaign and Deccani Alliance
episodes.era: Southern campaign, 1677 CE
episodes.region: Hyderabad, Golconda, Vellore, Gingee, Mysore plateau and Thanjavur
episodes.logline: In 1677 Shivaji allied with Abu Hasan Qutb Shah of Golconda, marched into Karnataka, took forts like Gingee and Vellore, and proved his diplomacy was political rather than communal.
episodes.moral: Wise strategy chooses allies by purpose, not by labels.

sources.citation: Sabhasad Bakhar, tr. S.N. Sen, southern campaign, Vellore, Gingee and Venkoji settlement
sources.note: Most detailed Maratha narrative for the expedition.
