sources.citation: R.C. Hiremath, ed., Akkamahadevi Vachana (Kannada Sahitya Parishat, 2006)
sources.note: Modern critical edition of the Kannada vachanas.

episodes.notes: Akka Mahadevi is one of the strongest named women voices in 12th-century Kannada literature, with roughly 430 vachanas attributed to her. KEY FACTS: her poems address Shiva as Chenna Mallikarjuna; Lingayat memory places her in the Anubhava Mantapa at Basavakalyana with Basavanna and Allama Prabhu; her verse challenged caste, gender convention and empty ritual. INNOVATION: the vachana form made philosophy a spare vernacular utterance with a signature deity, helping transform Kannada literary history and social reform. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP: Padigar, Amaladass-Talib and critical editions reassess hagiography against texts. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT overstate the Kaushika marriage, naked wandering, or death at Srisailam as documented fact; those come through later hagiography. Her poems are the firm base.

episodes.title: Lal Ded Gives Kashmir a Voice
episodes.era: Kashmiri mystical poetry, c. 1320-1373 CE
episodes.region: Pandrethan, Bijbehara and the Kashmir valley
episodes.logline: Ignored by court chronicles yet remembered in every valley, Lal Ded turns Kashmiri speech into a sacred literary voice.
episodes.moral: What power forgets, people may still sing.

sources.citation: Lal Ded's vakhs, in Ranjit Hoskote, I, Lalla: The Poems of Lal Ded (Penguin, 2011)
sources.note: Authoritative recent translation and critical apparatus for the poetic corpus.

sources.citation: Mulla Ali Raina, Tadhkirat-ul-Arifin (1587)
sources.note: Earliest written biographical record, later and hagiographic.

sources.citation: Susie Tharu and K. Lalita, Women Writing in India, Vol. 1 (1991)
sources.note: Modern recovery of Lal Ded among early women writers.

episodes.notes: Lal Ded, also called Lalla or Lalleshwari, is conventionally dated to the 14th-century Kashmir Sultanate period. KEY FACTS: about 150-170 vakhs are attributed to her; they translate Kashmir Shaiva and mystical insight into Kashmiri speech; Nund Rishi's later verses acknowledge her spiritual authority. INNOVATION: her vakhs are among the earliest substantial Kashmiri compositions and helped form a shared literary memory across Hindu and Muslim communities. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP: Hoskote's 2011 edition compares manuscript and oral traditions and warns against communal ownership claims. ACCURACY FLAGS: contemporary Kashmir chronicles are silent; do NOT call every biography detail proven, and do NOT force her into modern Hindu/Muslim categories. The poems and later acknowledgments are the evidence.

episodes.title: Savitribai Opens the Schoolroom Door
episodes.era: Girls' education and anti-caste reform, 1848-1897 CE
episodes.region: Bhidewada, Pune, Naigaon and colonial Maharashtra
episodes.logline: Carrying books through abuse, Savitribai Phule opens a girls' school and makes education an anti-caste revolution.
episodes.moral: A classroom can be a battlefield for dignity.

sources.citation: Savitribai Phule, Kavya Phule (1854), translated in Women Writing in India, Vol. 2 (1993)
sources.note: Her own published poetry, one of the earliest such works by an Indian woman.

sources.citation: Dnyanodaya newspaper and Bombay Education Department reports, c. 1848-1853
sources.note: Contemporary evidence for the Phule schools and enrollment.

sources.citation: Rosalind O'Hanlon, Caste, Conflict, and Ideology (Cambridge University Press, 2002 ed.)
sources.note: Modern scholarly account of the Phules' schools and anti-caste reform.

episodes.notes: Savitribai Phule, trained by Jyotirao Phule and missionary-linked normal schools, helped open a girls' school at Bhidewada in Pune in early 1848 and later helped run multiple schools. KEY FACTS: the curriculum included mathematics, science and social studies; she co-founded institutions for women, widows and oppressed castes, including Mahila Seva Mandal, Balhatya Pratibandhak Griha and Satyashodhak Samaj; she died nursing plague patients in 1897. INNOVATION: formal girls' education, civil-society schooling and anti-caste social institutions. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP: O'Hanlon, Chakravarti and Sperandio place her at the intersection of caste and gender reform. ACCURACY FLAGS: the spare-sari story is powerful but often later commemorative; mention it cautiously. Do NOT reduce her to Jyotirao's helper; her writings and organizing are independent evidence.

episodes.title: Pandita Ramabai Builds a House of Freedom
episodes.era: Women's education and institution building, 1858-1922 CE
episodes.region: Pune, Calcutta, Bombay, Kedgaon, England and the United States
episodes.logline: A Sanskrit scholar turns testimony, books and shelters into institutions where widows and girls can rebuild their lives.
episodes.moral: Learning becomes power when it opens doors for others.

sources.citation: Pandita Ramabai, The High-Caste Hindu Woman (Philadelphia, 1887)
sources.note: Primary English-language reform text written for an international audience.

sources.citation: Report of the Indian Education Commission (Hunter Commission), Calcutta, 1883
sources.note: Published record of Ramabai's testimony on female education.

sources.citation: Uma Chakravarti, Rewriting History: The Life and Times of Pandita Ramabai (Kali for Women, 1998)
sources.note: Authoritative modern biography using archives and Ramabai's writings.

episodes.notes: Pandita Ramabai Sarasvati was honored by Calcutta University in 1878 as a woman Sanskrit scholar, testified before the Hunter Commission in 1882, and built major institutions for women. KEY FACTS: Arya Mahila Samaj began in 1882; Sharada Sadan opened in 1889; Mukti Mission at Kedgaon from 1898 housed, educated and employed large numbers of women through farms, workshops, a press and industrial training. INNOVATION: social reform, scholarship and women-run economic institution building on a rare scale. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP: Uma Chakravarti, Meera Kosambi and Tanika Sarkar highlight her complex position between feminism, conversion, nationalism and caste. ACCURACY FLAGS: acknowledge her Christian conversion without making it the whole story; do NOT flatten her as either missionary pawn or nationalist saint. Her own books and institutions are primary evidence.

episodes.title: Anandi Joshi Crosses the Black Water
episodes.era: Women's medical education, 1883-1887 CE
episodes.region: Kalyan, Pune, Serampore, Philadelphia and Kolhapur
episodes.logline: After losing a child for lack of care, Anandi Joshi crosses the sea to earn a medical degree for women who need women doctors.
episodes.moral: Pain can become a promise to heal.

sources.citation: Caroline Healey Dall, The Life of Dr. Anandabai Joshee (Roberts Brothers, 1888)
sources.note: Near-contemporary biography preserving letters and the Serampore speech.

sources.citation: Woman's Medical College of Pennsylvania records and Anandi Joshi, Obstetrics Among the Aryas (1886)
sources.note: Graduation record and MD thesis held by Drexel University Heritage Collections.

sources.citation: Meera Kosambi, Crossing Thresholds: Feminist Essays in Social History (Permanent Black, 2007)
sources.note: Recent historical analysis of Anandi's life, marriage and education.

episodes.notes: Anandi Gopal Joshi, born Yamuna in 1865, resolved to study medicine after her infant son died for lack of medical care. KEY FACTS: her 1883 Serampore speech argued that Indian women needed women doctors; she graduated from the Woman's Medical College of Pennsylvania in 1886; her thesis, Obstetrics Among the Aryas, compared Indian obstetric knowledge with Western medicine; she was appointed to Kolhapur but died of tuberculosis in 1887. INNOVATION: she was the first Indian woman to receive a Western medical degree, though Kadambini Ganguly is the key parallel as the first Indian woman doctor to practice in South Asia. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP: Kosambi and Drexel archival work complicate older heroic narratives. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT present Gopalrao only as a benevolent husband; documented coercion must be acknowledged carefully. Do NOT call Anandi a long-practicing physician; she died before she could serve.

episodes.title: Kamala Sohonie Wins the Laboratory Bet
episodes.era: Indian women in modern biochemistry, 1933-1939 CE
episodes.region: IISc Bangalore, Newnham College Cambridge, Delhi and Coonoor
episodes.logline: Rejected by C.V. Raman because she was a woman, Kamala Sohonie earns her place and discovers a key clue in cellular respiration.
episodes.moral: A closed door is not the same as a final answer.

sources.citation: Indian National Science Academy, Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of INSA, Kamala Sohonie entry (2001)
sources.note: Source for her recollections, dates and Raman admission episode.

sources.citation: Rohini Godbole and Ram Ramaswamy, eds., Lilavati's Daughters: The Women Scientists of India (Indian Academy of Sciences, 2008)
sources.note: Modern collection documenting Indian women scientists including Sohonie.

sources.citation: IISc Archives and Newnham College Cambridge records, 1933-1939
sources.note: Institutional records for admission, Cambridge study and PhD chronology.

episodes.notes: Kamala Sohonie studied chemistry and physics, challenged C.V. Raman's refusal to admit women researchers to IISc, completed her MSc with distinction in 1936, and earned a Cambridge PhD in 1939. KEY FACTS: her Cambridge work identified the role of cytochrome C in plant electron transport; later Indian nutrition work on neera linked laboratory science to public health. INNOVATION: first Indian woman PhD in a scientific discipline and a pioneer of biochemistry in India. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP: Lilavati's Daughters and INSA memoirs recover her story within the gendered history of Indian science; the 2023 public revival did not add new archival proof. ACCURACY FLAGS: state the first-PhD claim precisely, distinguishing research doctorate from medical degrees. Do NOT turn Raman into a caricature, but do quote her documented memory of discrimination if used.

episodes.title: Vijayalakshmi Pandit Chairs the World
episodes.era: Indian diplomacy and United Nations leadership, 1937-1953 CE
episodes.region: United Provinces, New York, Moscow, London and New Delhi
episodes.logline: From prison and provincial office to the United Nations rostrum, Vijayalakshmi Pandit becomes the first woman to preside over the General Assembly.
episodes.moral: Representation matters most when the world is being rebuilt.

sources.citation: Vijayalakshmi Pandit, The Scope of Happiness: A Personal Memoir (Weidenfeld and Nicolson, 1979)
sources.note: Her own account of political life and diplomacy.

sources.citation: United Nations General Assembly, 8th Session official records, 1953
sources.note: Primary institutional record of her election as UNGA President.

sources.citation: Mrinalini Sinha, Suffragism and Internationalism, Indian Economic and Social History Review 36.4 (1999)
sources.note: Modern context for Indian women, suffrage and internationalism.

episodes.notes: Vijayalakshmi Pandit, born Swarup Kumari Nehru in 1900, was imprisoned during the freedom struggle, became a United Provinces minister in 1937, and represented independent India abroad. KEY FACTS: she served as ambassador to the Soviet Union and the United States, headed Indian delegations to the UN, and in 1953 became the first woman President of the United Nations General Assembly. INNOVATION: institutional firsts in Indian cabinet government and global diplomacy, giving a newly independent country a woman's voice in world governance. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP: Sinha and Thapar-Bjorkert situate her within Indian internationalism and women in the national movement. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT erase the Nehru-family connection, but do NOT reduce her career to it; her jail terms, cabinet post and diplomacy are independently documented. End this story at 1953; later politics belong elsewhere.

episodes.title: Ramanuja Opens Srirangam's Door
episodes.era: Sri Vaishnava theology, c. 1077-1157 CE (traditional dates contested)
episodes.region: Sriperumbudur, Kanchipuram, Srirangam and Melkote
episodes.logline: A philosopher turns Alvar devotion into rigorous theology and leaves a tradition that remembers temple access as a question of justice, not birth.
episodes.moral: Faith grows stronger when learning serves inclusion.

sources.citation: Ramanuja, Sri Bhashya, Vedarthasangraha and Gita Bhashya
sources.note: Primary Sanskrit works that anchor his theology, even when the biography remains difficult.

sources.citation: Koyil Olugu and later Sri Vaishnava guru-parampara hagiographies
sources.note: Temple memory for Srirangam reforms; valuable but late and legend-layered.

sources.citation: John Carman, The Theology of Ramanuja (1974); Vasudha Narayanan, The Way and the Goal (1987); Paul Sydnor, Brill's Encyclopedia of Hinduism entry on Ramanuja (2012)
sources.note: Modern scholarship on date debates, theology and social memory.

episodes.notes: Ramanuja's secure history is clearest in his philosophical works and temple associations, while precise birth dates and reform episodes come through much later tradition. KEY FACTS: he systematized Vishishtadvaita, linked Sanskrit Vedanta with Tamil Alvar devotion, and is associated with Srirangam and Melkote under Hoysala patronage. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP stresses that the traditional 1017-1137 lifespan and many dramatic caste-access stories are not contemporary records; a c. 1077-1157 range is often preferred. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT claim the mass ordination of outcastes is documented by contemporary inscription; do NOT present north Indian Bhakti as a simple relay race from Ramanuja to every later saint.

episodes.title: Basavanna's Parliament of Souls
episodes.figure: Basavanna, Akka Mahadevi and Allama Prabhu
episodes.era: Kalachuri Kalyana and the vachana revolution, c. 1130-1196 CE
episodes.region: Basavana Bagewadi, Kudalasangama and Basavakalyana, Karnataka
episodes.logline: At Kalyana, a royal minister and wandering mystics imagine a hall where cobbler, woman and Brahmin can debate God as equals.
episodes.moral: A just community lets every honest voice be heard.

sources.citation: Harihara, Basavarajadevara Ragale, c. 1180
sources.note: Near-contemporary Kannada account of Basavanna's circle.

sources.citation: Arjunavad inscription, 1260 CE, and Kalachuri-era records
sources.note: Epigraphic context for Basava's family and Bijjala's world.

sources.citation: A.K. Ramanujan, Speaking of Siva (1973); Jan Peter Schouten, Revolution of the Mystics (1991); R. Blake Michael, The Origins of Virasaiva Sects (1992)
sources.note: Translations and social-historical analysis of vachanas and Lingayat origins.

episodes.notes: The Anubhava Mantapa is remembered as a deliberative spiritual assembly, and the vachana corpus preserves a dazzling Kannada prose-poetry innovation by hundreds of sharanas, including Akka Mahadevi. KEY FACTS: Basavanna served in Bijjala II's court; kayaka made dignified labor into worship; ishtalinga devotion bypassed inherited ritual hierarchy. RECENT DEBATE asks whether Basavanna founded Lingayatism or energized older Veerashaiva currents, and how far anti-caste ideals changed social practice. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT call it literally the world's first parliament; do NOT say caste disappeared in 12th-century Karnataka; treat miracle stories and exact debate transcripts as hagiography.

episodes.title: Dnyaneshwar Writes the Song Sermon
episodes.era: Yadava Maharashtra and the Dnyaneshwari, 1290 CE
episodes.region: Apegaon, Paithan and Alandi, Maharashtra
episodes.logline: A teenager denied a secure place in Brahmin society turns the Gita into 9000 Marathi verses that ordinary pilgrims can sing.
episodes.moral: Wisdom belongs in the language of the people.

sources.citation: Dnyaneshwar, Dnyaneshwari or Bhavartha Deepika, with Eknath's 1599 recension
sources.note: Primary Marathi Gita commentary; the recension underlies modern editions.

sources.citation: Namdev abhangas and Mahanubhava Lilacharita, c. late 13th century
sources.note: Near-contemporary context for Dnyaneshwar and early Marathi devotion.

sources.citation: V.G. Pradhan and H.M. Lambert, Jnaneshvari (SUNY, 1987); Christian Lee Novetzke, The Quotidian Revolution (2016)
sources.note: Critical translation and recent work on vernacular public religion.

episodes.notes: The Dnyaneshwari's 1290 date is unusually firm for the chapter, supported by colophon traditions and Yadava context, but the text reached us through manuscript transmission and Eknath's later restoration. KEY FACTS: Dnyaneshwar translated philosophical argument into Marathi ovi verse, helping found Warkari literary culture, and died young at Alandi. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP treats the Warkari tradition as a vernacular public sphere, not just private mysticism. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT claim every modern verse is untouched since 1290; do NOT present buffalo-reciting-Vedas or moving-wall miracles as history; separate Dnyaneshwari from Amrutanubhava.

episodes.title: Chokhamela at the Temple Threshold
episodes.era: Warkari devotion, c. 1300-1350 CE
episodes.region: Mehuna Raja, Mangalvedha and Pandharpur, Maharashtra
episodes.logline: A Mahar farmhand barred from the shrine leaves songs so fierce that the temple gate itself becomes his memorial.
episodes.moral: Dignity can speak from the threshold until the doorway changes.

sources.citation: Chokhamela abhangas in Marathi manuscript tradition
sources.note: Primary devotional poems, though transmitted through later copying.

sources.citation: Mahipati, Bhaktavijaya, 18th century
sources.note: Important hagiographic narrative; useful only with caution.

sources.citation: Rohini Mokashi-Punekar, On the Threshold: Songs of Chokhamela (2002); Eleanor Zelliot, From Untouchable to Dalit (1992); Christian Lee Novetzke, History at God's Feet (2008)
sources.note: Modern translations and Dalit/Bhakti historiography.

episodes.notes: Chokhamela's surviving abhangas are among the earliest sustained devotional voices from a Dalit community in Marathi, and his family's poetry, including Soyarabai's, makes the story broader than one saint. KEY FACTS: the Pandharpur samadhi at the gate is a powerful physical memory, while Mahar village-service labor forms the economic background. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP and Ambedkarite recovery have restored Chokhamela as a social critic, not a harmless miracle saint. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT claim the wall-collapse and singing-bones story as fact; do NOT call him the first Dalit saint in all India; explain that many biographical details come from late hagiography.

episodes.title: Ravidas Dreams Begampura
episodes.era: North Indian Sant tradition, c. 15th-early 16th century CE
episodes.region: Varanasi and the Banaras leather-working world
episodes.logline: A cobbler-poet imagines Begampura, a city without caste, fear or crushing taxes, and his hymns enter Sikh scripture.
episodes.moral: The future begins when someone dares to name a fairer city.

sources.citation: Guru Granth Sahib, Ravidas bani, 41 hymns
sources.note: Best-authenticated early corpus of Ravidas's verses, fixed by 1604.

sources.citation: Panch Vani and related Dadu Panthi anthologies
sources.note: Additional Ravidas traditions with source-critical debates.

sources.citation: John Stratton Hawley and Mark Juergensmeyer, Songs of the Saints of India (1988/2004); Hawley, A Storm of Songs (2015); Purushottam Agrawal, Akath Kahani Prem Ki (2009)
sources.note: Critical studies of Sant poetry, manuscript transmission and social context.

episodes.notes: Ravidas's best-attested voice survives in the Guru Granth Sahib, while exact dates, birthplace details and guru relationships remain disputed. KEY FACTS: his Chamar/cobbler identity matters to the poem Begampura, which imagines no second-class citizenship, no anxious taxation and no caste exclusion. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP questions the Mirabai-discipleship tradition and examines Ravidassia identity as a living modern community. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT state a precise birth year as fact; do NOT claim Mirabai was definitely his disciple; do NOT use Begampura as proof that a literal city was founded.

episodes.title: Kabir's Three Manuscript Faces
episodes.era: Varanasi Sant poetry, c. 1440-1518 CE
episodes.region: Varanasi and Magahar, Uttar Pradesh
episodes.logline: A weaver's verses cut through Hindu and Muslim certainties, then survive as three different Kabirs in three manuscript worlds.
episodes.moral: Truth need not flatter any camp to serve everyone.

sources.citation: Kabir Bijak; Kabir Granthavali; Kabir hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib
sources.note: Three major textual traditions with sharply different emphases.

sources.citation: Charlotte Vaudeville, A Weaver Named Kabir (1993); Linda Hess and Shukdev Singh, The Bijak of Kabir (2002)
sources.note: Critical edition and translation work.

sources.citation: John Stratton Hawley, A Storm of Songs (2015); Purushottam Agrawal, Akath Kahani Prem Ki (2009)
sources.note: Recent scholarship on the constructed 'Bhakti movement' and Kabir's social world.

episodes.notes: Kabir is historically secure but textually elusive: the eastern Bijak, Rajasthani Granthavali and Sikh scripture preserve overlapping yet different corpora. KEY FACTS: his julaha/weaver identity, Varanasi setting and nirguna critique made him a cross-community figure claimed by Kabir Panthis, Sikhs and many others. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP rejects the tidy colonial label of Hindu-Muslim synthesizer and stresses manuscript plurality and caste economy. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT certify any individual doha as certainly original Kabir without qualification; do NOT assert Ramananda was literally his guru as documented fact; do NOT present Magahar death miracles as history.

episodes.title: Mirabai Refuses the Widow's Silence
episodes.era: Mewar, Merta and Krishna bhakti, c. 1498-1547 CE
episodes.region: Kudki, Merta, Chittor, Vrindavan and Dwarka traditions
episodes.logline: A Rajput princess turns widowhood into song, but the historian must follow her through a fog of beloved later legends.
episodes.moral: Courage can sing even when records fall silent.

sources.citation: Nabhadas, Bhaktamala, c. 1600, and Priyadas commentary, c. 1712
sources.note: Early but posthumous hagiographic references to Mira.

sources.citation: Fatehpur inscription, c. 1623
sources.note: One of the earliest physical references connected to Mirabai memory.

sources.citation: Nancy Martin-Kershaw, 'Mirabai: Inscribed in Text, Embodied in Life' (2000); John Stratton Hawley, A Storm of Songs (2015); Lindsey Harlan, Religion and Rajput Women (1992)
sources.note: Modern source criticism, corpus debates and Rajput gender context.

episodes.notes: Mirabai's cultural life is vast, but her documentary footprint is thin: no contemporary inscription and poem manuscripts mainly from much later. KEY FACTS: she likely came from the Merta Rathore line, married into Mewar, and became the center of a living bhajan tradition of female spiritual agency. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP sharply narrows what can be treated as plausibly her own compositions and contextualizes in-law conflict amid Mewar's political crises. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT claim Akbar and Tansen visited her; the chronology fails. Do NOT say Ravidas was definitely her guru, or that all popular Mira bhajans are authentically hers.

episodes.title: Lal Ded Walks Through Kashmir
episodes.era: Early Kashmiri vernacular mysticism, c. 1320-1392 CE
episodes.region: Pandrethan, Srinagar and the Kashmir Valley
episodes.logline: A Kashmiri woman leaves domestic life and gives the valley its first great vernacular poems, claimed by Shaiva and Sufi memory alike.
episodes.moral: A voice rooted in one place can cross many boundaries.

sources.citation: Lal Vakhs, preserved in oral and manuscript tradition
sources.note: Primary poetic corpus, written down significantly after her lifetime.

sources.citation: Tadhkirat-ul-Arifin, 1587; Waqiati-e-Kashmir, 1746; Tarikh-i-Azami, 1736
sources.note: Persianate references that help date and frame Lal Ded but remain late.

sources.citation: Jayalal Kaul, Lal Ded (1973); Ranjit Hoskote, I, Lalla (2011); Mridu Rai, Hindu Rulers, Muslim Subjects (2004)
sources.note: Literary translation, source criticism and politics of Kashmiri religious identity.

episodes.notes: Lal Ded's vakhs are foundational for Kashmiri literature, yet they reached writing through oral performance and competing religious memory. KEY FACTS: she is associated with Kashmiri Shaiva practice, female renunciation and early Sultanate Kashmir; both Hindu and Muslim communities later claimed her as Lalla or Lal Arifa. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP highlights how modern Kashmir politics shapes readings of her identity. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT claim she was definitely Sufi, Buddhist or only one community's possession; do NOT present specific husband, village or miracle stories as certain; treat the 'nursing Nund Rishi' tale as symbolic legend.
episodes.chapter_part: IV. Kashmir Between Mountain and Shrine

episodes.title: Nund Rishi Plants Kashmir's Ethic
episodes.era: Kashmir Rishi order, c. 1377-1438 CE
episodes.region: Kulgam, Charar-e-Sharif and the Kashmir Valley
episodes.logline: A Muslim saint preaches in Kashmiri, praises Lal Ded's wisdom, and builds an indigenous Sufi order around labor, restraint and mercy.
episodes.moral: Shared ethics can outlive arguments over labels.

sources.citation: Nund Rishi's Shruks in Kashmiri oral and manuscript tradition
sources.note: Primary verse tradition, without autograph manuscripts.

sources.citation: Khwaja Azam Diddamari, Tarikh-i-Azami, 1736, and Rishi Namah traditions
sources.note: Later Persian and hagiographic sources for the Rishi order.

sources.citation: Mohammad Ishaq Khan, Kashmir's Transition to Islam (1994); Mridu Rai, Hindu Rulers, Muslim Subjects (2004); Triloki Nath Raina, An Introduction to Kashmiri Language and Literature (1972)
sources.note: Modern work on Rishi Sufism and Kashmiri language history.

episodes.notes: Nund Rishi, also Sheikh Noor-ud-Din Noorani, is central to Kashmir's indigenous Rishi Sufi tradition rather than an imported Persian order. KEY FACTS: his shruks helped preserve Kashmiri as a religious-literary language; his remembered ethic emphasized honest labor, restraint, nonviolence and communal harmony. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP treats the Rishi order as one actor in Kashmir's gradual Islamization, not the whole explanation. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT claim Nund Rishi converted Kashmir to Islam by himself; do NOT assert the Lal Ded nursing legend as documentary fact; avoid turning a complex transition into a simple harmony fable.
episodes.chapter_part: IV. Kashmir Between Mountain and Shrine

episodes.title: Muinuddin Chishti Opens Ajmer
episodes.era: Early Chishti order in India, c. 1143-1236 CE
episodes.region: Sistan and Ajmer, Rajasthan
episodes.logline: A Chishti mystic makes Ajmer a doorway of hospitality, music and memory that even emperors later approach barefoot.
episodes.moral: Open doors can become stronger than forts.

sources.citation: Mir Khord, Siyar al-Auliya, c. 1350
sources.note: Key early Chishti hagiography, written more than a century after Muinuddin's death.

sources.citation: Hasan Sijzi, Fawa'id al-Fu'wad, early 14th century; Abdul Haqq Dehlawi, Akhbar ul-Akhyar, 1590s
sources.note: Chishti silsila memory and later compilation.

sources.citation: Bruce Lawrence, Notes from a Distant Flute (1978); Simon Digby, 'The Sufi Shaikh as a Source of Authority' (1986); Muzaffar Alam, The Languages of Political Islam (2004)
sources.note: Studies of early Indian Sufism, khanqah authority and political culture.

episodes.notes: The Ajmer dargah became South Asia's most influential Sufi shrine, but Muinuddin's biography is filtered through later hagiography. KEY FACTS: the Chishti khanqah model joined spiritual teaching, hospitality, sama and service to the poor; later Mughal pilgrimages to Ajmer are well documented. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP warns that institutional economics are clearer for later Chishti centers than for Muinuddin's own lifetime. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT claim he personally converted millions; do NOT treat miracle contests with Prithviraj's priests as history; do NOT present the Husaynid lineage claim as secure, since it appears late and is contested.
episodes.chapter_part: V. Sufi Doors and Sung Worlds

episodes.title: Baba Farid Sings Punjabi
episodes.era: Chishti Punjab, c. 1188-1266 CE
episodes.region: Multan, Hansi and Ajodhan or Pakpattan
episodes.logline: A Chishti saint chooses the speech of Punjab over courtly Persian, and his couplets find a permanent home in Sikh scripture.
episodes.moral: A mother tongue can carry the highest longing.

sources.citation: Guru Granth Sahib, Baba Farid slokas, compiled 1604
sources.note: Strong textual anchor for the Farid verse tradition.

sources.citation: Mir Khord, Siyar al-Auliya, c. 1350; Hasan Sijzi, Fawa'id al-Fu'wad
sources.note: Chishti lineage sources connecting Farid to Nizamuddin Auliya.

sources.citation: K.A. Nizami, The Life and Times of Shaikh Farid-ud-Din Ganj-i-Shakar (1973); J.S. Grewal, The Sikhs of the Punjab (1998)
sources.note: Historical context for Punjab, Chishti institutions and scripture.

episodes.notes: Baba Farid's authenticated poetic afterlife is unusually strong because his slokas were fixed in the Guru Granth Sahib. KEY FACTS: he settled at Ajodhan/Pakpattan, shaped the Chishti chain that led to Nizamuddin Auliya, and helped make local vernacular suitable for spiritual poetry. The Pakpattan khanqah also embodied hospitality, feeding and travel networks. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP notes dialect complexity: the language may reflect Multani/Punjabi forms later standardized by transmission. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say the extant verses are identical to modern standard Punjabi; do NOT call every austerity miracle factual; avoid duplicating the Sikh chapter's Adi Granth focus by centering Farid's Chishti and vernacular role.
episodes.chapter_part: V. Sufi Doors and Sung Worlds

episodes.title: Chaitanya Starts the Kirtan Storm
episodes.era: Gaudiya Vaishnavism, 1486-1534 CE
episodes.region: Navadvipa, Puri and Vrindavan
episodes.logline: A Bengal scholar turns ecstatic street kirtan into a public movement and sends disciples to rebuild Vrindavan through texts, temples and song.
episodes.moral: Joy becomes powerful when it steps into the street.

sources.citation: Vrindavana Dasa, Chaitanya Bhagavata, c. 1535; Krishnadasa Kaviraja, Chaitanya Charitamrita, c. 1612
sources.note: Major Gaudiya hagiographies, early but theological in purpose.

sources.citation: Shikshashtakam attributed to Chaitanya
sources.note: Small corpus traditionally treated as his own surviving composition.

sources.citation: Tony K. Stewart, The Final Word (2010); Edward C. Dimock, The Place of the Hidden Moon (1966); David Haberman, Acting as a Way of Salvation (1988)
sources.note: Source criticism and studies of Bengal-Vrindavan devotional practice.

episodes.notes: Chaitanya's importance lies in public nagara-sankirtana, Gaudiya theology and the Six Goswamis' scholarly recovery and reinvention of Vrindavan as a pilgrimage-literary center. KEY FACTS: his 1486 birth is tied to lunar-eclipse tradition, and his Puri and Vrindavan links are multiply attested in Gaudiya sources. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP, especially Tony Stewart, reads the Chaitanya Charitamrita as theological argument rather than modern biography. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT claim Chaitanya invented kirtan; earlier kirtan existed. Do NOT present miracle episodes or his mysterious death as settled history; avoid overclaiming the first public procession in Bengal.
episodes.chapter_part: V. Sufi Doors and Sung Worlds

episodes.title: Shah Latif Sings the Seven Heroines
episodes.era: Sindhi Sufi poetry, c. 1689-1752 CE
episodes.region: Hala Haweli, Bhit Shah and Sindh
episodes.logline: In Sindh, a Sufi poet turns folk heroines into maps of the soul and leaves a sung book that defines a language.
episodes.moral: A people's songs can preserve their deepest wisdom.

sources.citation: Shah Jo Risalo, oral corpus first printed in 1866; Nabi Bakhsh Baloch critical edition, 1958-1962
sources.note: Primary poetic tradition, with serious oral-transmission issues.

sources.citation: Mir Ali Sher Qani, Tuhfat al-Kiram, c. 1767, and Maqalat al-shu'ara
sources.note: Near-contemporary biographical evidence written after Latif's death.

sources.citation: H.T. Sorley, Shah Abdul Latif of Bhit (1940); Annemarie Schimmel, As Through a Veil (1982); Christopher Shackle's work on Sindhi and Siraiki traditions
sources.note: Biographical, mystical and linguistic scholarship.

episodes.notes: Shah Latif's Risalo is a literary, musical and devotional monument built around surs and heroines such as Marui, Sassi and Sohni. KEY FACTS: he drew on Sufi orders, Rumi, local Jogi/Hindu traditions and Sindhi-Rajasthani folk worlds; Bhit Shah became a major pilgrimage and urs economy. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP and critical editions emphasize that no autograph survives and the corpus was compiled from oral performance long after his death. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT claim the 1866 printed Risalo is exactly what Latif composed; do NOT present the Saida Begum love story or illiteracy tradition as fact; frame Sindh as historical subcontinent geography.
episodes.chapter_part: V. Sufi Doors and Sung Worlds

episodes.title: Sala Strikes the Tiger of Legend
episodes.era: Hoysala origins, c. 950-1098 CE
episodes.region: Malnad hills, Angadi, Belur and Dorasamudra in Karnataka
episodes.logline: A tiger-slaying emblem gives the Hoysalas a name, while inscriptions reveal hill chiefs turning into Chalukya feudatories and then regional kings.
episodes.moral: Identity can begin as legend, but power must be built in history.

sources.citation: Epigraphia Carnatica, Vol. 2 (Hassan), B.L. Rice, 1889
sources.note: Primary inscription corpus for early Hoysala genealogy, emblem and Hassan-region records.

sources.citation: S. Settar, Hoysala Heritage, Vol. 1 (Kala Yatra, 1992)
sources.note: Modern source-critical treatment of the origin legend and early rulers.

sources.citation: Suryanath U. Kamath, Karnataka: A History (1980)
sources.note: Standard Karnataka political history for Vinayaditya, Ereyanga and the Chalukya feudatory phase.

episodes.notes: The Sala tiger story appears in Hoysala identity and temple emblems, but it is an origin myth, not a contemporary eyewitness event. The safer historical frame begins with Malnad chiefs and better-attested rulers such as Vinayaditya, who operated within the Western Chalukya world before the dynasty asserted wider power. KEY FACTS: early Hoysala inscriptions cluster in Hassan/Malnad, Dorasamudra became the capital, and the emblem made the dynasty instantly recognizable. RECENT/ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT narrate Sala, Sudattamuni or Sosevur as proven biography; do NOT claim an exact founding date for the dynasty; treat Yadava/Krishna-Baladeva descent claims as prashasti legitimation, not independent genealogy.
episodes.chapter: The Hoysalas and the Temple Sculptors

episodes.title: Bittideva Takes Talakadu
episodes.era: Reign of Vishnuvardhana, c. 1108-1152 CE
episodes.region: Talakadu, Belur, Gangavadi and Melkote in Karnataka
episodes.logline: Bittideva becomes Vishnuvardhana, defeats Chola power at Talakadu, and raises Belur's Chennakesava as a monument to victory and new devotion.
episodes.moral: Change is strongest when it makes room for many loyalties.

sources.citation: Belur Chennakesava consecration inscription, 1117 CE, in Epigraphia Carnatica Vol. 2
sources.note: Primary evidence for the temple foundation and victory context.

sources.citation: Divyasuricharita and Prapannamritam, Sri Vaishnava hagiographies
sources.note: Primary sources for the Ramanuja-Vishnuvardhana conversion tradition, but late and sectarian.

sources.citation: Sheldon Pollock, The Language of the Gods in the World of Men (UC Press, 2006)
sources.note: Context for Hoysala-era Kannada vernacularization and court culture.

episodes.notes: Vishnuvardhana, originally Bittideva in later tradition, defeated the Cholas at Talakadu around 1117 and sponsored the Chennakesava temple at Belur. The Ramanuja connection belongs to Sri Vaishnava memory and may preserve real Hoysala-period contact with Melkote, but no contemporary Hoysala inscription proves a personal conversion ceremony by Ramanuja. General Ganggaraj's Jain patronage and Queen Shantala's Jain faith show pluralism after the king's Vaishnava turn. RECENT/ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT claim a forced religious shift or Jain persecution; do NOT treat the 103-year completion tradition as a single dated construction fact; present Belur as victory, devotion and political statement together.
episodes.chapter: The Hoysalas and the Temple Sculptors

episodes.title: Shantala Devi Keeps Her Faith
episodes.era: Early 12th-century Hoysala court, d. 1131 CE
episodes.region: Belur, Halebidu, Balligavi, Shivagange and Shravanabelagola
episodes.logline: A queen famed for music, dance and Jain devotion builds at Belur and leaves one of medieval Karnataka's clearest records of royal women's agency.
episodes.moral: Integrity can shine even inside a changing court.

sources.citation: Chandragiri Hill inscription, Shravanabelagola, 1131 CE
sources.note: Primary record of Shantala Devi's sallekhana, family, guru and grants.

sources.citation: Belur and Shravanabelagola inscriptions in Epigraphia Carnatica
sources.note: Primary evidence for royal women and Jain patronage.

sources.citation: S. Settar, Hoysala Heritage, Vol. 1 (1992)
sources.note: Modern documentation of Shantala Devi and Hoysala patronage.

episodes.notes: Shantala Devi, chief queen of Vishnuvardhana, is unusually visible through inscriptions: her family background, Jain guru Prabhachandra Siddhanta Deva, grants and death by sallekhana in 1131 are recorded at Shravanabelagola. She is associated with the Kappe Chennigaraya temple at Belur and with the Shantalesvara half of the Halebidu twin complex. RECENT/ACCURACY FLAGS: inscriptions praise her skill in music and dance, but do NOT invent court performances or a fixed modern dance form; do NOT reduce her to a converted king's wife; show her as an independent Jain donor in a plural royal household.
episodes.chapter: The Hoysalas and the Temple Sculptors
episodes.chapter_part: II. Queens, Warriors, and the Long Resistance

episodes.title: Halebidu Waits for Its Towers
episodes.era: Hoysala high power, c. 1173-1220 CE
episodes.region: Dorasamudra-Halebidu and Shravanabelagola
episodes.logline: Ballala II's capital fills with sculpted walls, merchant gifts and queenly authority, yet Halebidu's great twin temple remains famously uncrowned.
episodes.moral: Unfinished work can still become a masterpiece.

sources.citation: Hoysalesvara temple inscriptions at Halebidu, c. 1121 CE onward, EC Vol. 2
sources.note: Primary donor and construction records including merchant patrons.

sources.citation: Akkana Basadi inscription, Shravanabelagola, 1182 CE
sources.note: Evidence for Ballala II's Jain patronage and plural court culture.

sources.citation: Gerard Foekema, A Complete Guide to Hoysala Temples (Abhinav, 1996)
sources.note: Architectural guide for Halebidu plans, iconography and construction state.

episodes.notes: The Hoysalesvara-Shantalesvara temple complex at Halebidu, begun in the 12th century, reached extraordinary sculptural richness under the long Hoysala high period associated with Ballala II. Inscriptions preserve merchant patrons such as Ketamalla and Kesarasetti and record continuing Jain patronage at Shravanabelagola; other records credit Queen Umadevi with authority while the king campaigned. UNESCO's 2023 evaluation discusses the missing superstructures as an integrity issue but still recognizes outstanding value. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say the towers were certainly destroyed by Malik Kafur or certainly left unfinished by war; the reason remains debated. Do NOT make merchant donors a footnote: their names are central evidence for Hoysala patronage beyond kings.
episodes.chapter: The Hoysalas and the Temple Sculptors
episodes.chapter_part: II. Queens, Warriors, and the Long Resistance

episodes.title: Ballala III Holds the South
episodes.era: Last Hoysala resistance, c. 1292-1343 CE
episodes.region: Dorasamudra, Tiruvannamalai, Hosapattana and the Tungabhadra region
episodes.logline: After tribute, raids and exile, the last great Hoysala king fights to hold the south and leaves a contested bridge to the Vijayanagara age.
episodes.moral: Resilience can outlive defeat by shaping what comes next.

sources.citation: Amir Khusrau, Dewal Rani-Khizr Khan
sources.note: Sultanate perspective on the 1311 Dorasamudra campaign; use critically.

sources.citation: Ziauddin Barani, Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi
sources.note: Fourteenth-century Sultanate account for Khalji-Tughluq southern politics.

sources.citation: Cynthia Talbot, Precolonial India in Practice (OUP, 2001)
sources.note: Modern context for local agency and political change in the Sultanate period.

episodes.notes: Veera Ballala III ruled through crisis: Yadava, Pandya and Sultanate pressures, the 1311 Khalji raid, later Tughluq attacks, refuge and campaigns from the Tamil region, and death against the Madurai Sultanate around 1342-43. Hoysala inscriptions and later scholarship discuss Hosapattana on the Tungabhadra; some historians connect it with the later Vijayanagara site, but the identification is debated. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT retell the Malik Kafur raid in detail because the Delhi Sultanate chapter owns that story; do NOT claim Harihara and Bukka's Hoysala service as a simple documented fact; present the Hoysala-to-Vijayanagara transition as a political world, not a single founding myth.
episodes.chapter: The Hoysalas and the Temple Sculptors
episodes.chapter_part: II. Queens, Warriors, and the Long Resistance

episodes.title: Soapstone Stars Change the Temple
episodes.era: Hoysala architectural florescence, 12th-13th centuries CE
episodes.region: Belur, Halebidu and Somanathapura
episodes.logline: Architects turn soft soapstone, star plans and layered friezes into a new Karnata Dravida language of shadow, movement and carved detail.
episodes.moral: Innovation begins when craft understands its material.

sources.citation: Chennakesava, Hoysalesvara and Keshava temples as built primary evidence
sources.note: The buildings themselves document stellate plans, jagati platforms, friezes and material choices.

sources.citation: Adam Hardy, The Temple Architecture of India (Wiley, 2007)
sources.note: Key recent reclassification of Hoysala architecture as Karnata Dravida rather than simply Vesara.

sources.citation: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas, property 1670, 2023
sources.note: Recent OUV statement identifying stellate plan, soapstone and sculptural programs as exceptional.

episodes.notes: This is the core engineering innovation story: chloritic schist could be carved finely when fresh and hardened after exposure; stellate plans produced rhythmic projections; low jagati platforms became circumambulatory paths; and horizontal friezes turned temple walls into narrative surfaces. Adam Hardy's work reframes the style as Karnata Dravida, not merely a north-south hybrid, and UNESCO's 2023 inscription made this achievement globally visible. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT call the style purely isolated genius or purely copied from Chalukya/Kadamba models; it transforms inherited Deccan forms. Do NOT overstate exact workshop organization where inscriptions are silent.
episodes.chapter: The Hoysalas and the Temple Sculptors
episodes.chapter_part: III. The Art of the Star-Shaped Stone

episodes.title: Mallitamma Signs the Stone
episodes.era: Hoysala sculptor workshops, 12th-13th centuries CE
episodes.region: Halebidu, Belur and other Hoysala temple sites
episodes.logline: In a world where many artists stayed anonymous, Hoysala sculptors carved their names into temples and made artistic agency visible in stone.
episodes.moral: Honored craft gives makers a place in memory.

sources.citation: Halebidu and Belur sculptor-name inscriptions in Epigraphia Carnatica Vol. 2
sources.note: Primary evidence naming sculptors such as Ruvari Mallitamma, Dasoja, Chavana and Malloja.

sources.citation: S. Settar, Hoysala Heritage, Vol. 1 (1992)
sources.note: Definitive modern catalogue and analysis of Hoysala sculptor signatures.

sources.citation: UNESCO WHC 2023 OUV statement for Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas
sources.note: Highlights numerous artist signatures as evidence of artistic agency and prestige.

episodes.notes: Named sculptors are one of the Hoysala chapter's strongest innovation themes. Inscriptions preserve names including Ruvari Mallitamma, Dasoja, Chavana and Malloja, making workshops and individual agency unusually visible for medieval temple art. UNESCO's 2023 language explicitly values these signatures as evidence of prestigious artistic standing. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT claim signed artists are unique in all Indian history; say exceptional in frequency and documentation at Hoysala sites. Do NOT attribute every famous bracket figure or panel to a named sculptor unless the inscription specifically supports it; exact panel attribution can remain uncertain.
episodes.chapter: The Hoysalas and the Temple Sculptors
episodes.chapter_part: III. The Art of the Star-Shaped Stone

episodes.title: Soma Builds the Perfect Star
episodes.era: Keshava temple at Somanathapura, c. 1268 CE
episodes.region: Somanathapura near Mysore on the Kaveri
episodes.logline: A Hoysala general commissions Somanathapura's triple-shrined Keshava temple, preserving the dynasty's mature vision in one finished star of stone.
episodes.moral: Patronage can turn service into enduring beauty.

sources.citation: Somanathapura Keshava temple consecration inscription, c. 1268 CE, EC Vol. 5
sources.note: Primary old Kannada record naming Soma Dandanayaka and Narasimha III.

sources.citation: M.H. Krishna, Inscriptions of Somanathapura (Mysore Gazetteer, 1965)
sources.note: Dedicated inscriptional study for the site.

sources.citation: UNESCO WHC 2023 dossier, Somanathapura component
sources.note: Recent evaluation of Somanathapura as a high point of Hoysala style.

episodes.notes: The Keshava temple at Somanathapura is crucial because it was commissioned by Soma Dandanayaka, a general under Narasimha III, not directly by a king. Its triple shrines, intact towers, enclosure and surviving sculptural program show a mature, highly legible Hoysala design. The main Keshava image is missing, and scholars differ on whether dates should be read around 1268 or slightly later in some older works. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT claim all three original icons survive; do NOT make Narasimha III's Jain affiliation cancel the Vaishnava dedication; Hoysala patronage crossed sectarian lines and court ranks.
episodes.chapter: The Hoysalas and the Temple Sculptors
episodes.chapter_part: III. The Art of the Star-Shaped Stone

episodes.title: The Lake That Named Dorasamudra
episodes.era: Hoysala agrarian administration, 11th-13th centuries CE
episodes.region: Dorasamudra-Halebidu, Hulikere, Belur and Mysore-Hassan districts
episodes.logline: Reservoirs, grants and temple tanks reveal a kingdom where water management tied villages, shrines and local assemblies into power.
episodes.moral: A lasting state must learn to store and share water.

sources.citation: Hoysala copper-plate and stone grants in Epigraphia Carnatica Vols. 2 and 5
sources.note: Primary records of land, tanks, village rights and temple endowments.

sources.citation: Noboru Karashima, South Indian History and Society (OUP, 1984)
sources.note: Landmark inscription-based study of south Indian agrarian society.

sources.citation: Kesavan Veluthat, The Early Medieval in South India (OUP, 2009)
sources.note: Modern interpretation of temple, land-grant and state formation systems.

episodes.notes: Dorasamudra itself points to water: the capital was associated with a great reservoir, while inscriptions across Hoysala territory record tanks, kalyanis, village boundaries, devadana, brahmadaya and agrahara grants. Local bodies such as nagara, sabha and ur appear in administrative contexts, showing negotiated power below the king. RECENT/ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT model Hoysala assemblies as identical to the better-documented Chola Uttaramerur system; do NOT claim a fully mapped hydraulic system like Vijayanagara's without evidence. The innovation is the tank-land-temple nexus visible in epigraphy, not a modern-style bureaucracy.
episodes.chapter: The Hoysalas and the Temple Sculptors
episodes.chapter_part: IV. The Lake, the Guild, and the Gold Coin

episodes.title: Gold Coins and Merchant Guilds
episodes.era: Hoysala trade and coinage, 12th-13th centuries CE
episodes.region: Halebidu, Belur, Shravanabelagola, Malnad routes and coastal links
episodes.logline: Merchant donors, nagara guilds and Hoysala gadyana coins show how trade wealth helped fund the temples of Karnataka's interior.
episodes.moral: Prosperity becomes culture when wealth serves shared institutions.

sources.citation: Ketamalla-Kesarasetti donor inscription at Halebidu, EC Vol. 2
sources.note: Primary record linking merchant wealth to the Hoysalesvara temple.

sources.citation: R. Champakalakshmi, Trade, Ideology and Urbanization: South India 300 BC to AD 1300 (OUP, 1996)
sources.note: Major study of south Indian merchant guilds and urban-temple networks.

sources.citation: P.L. Gupta, Coins (National Book Trust, 1969)
sources.note: Accessible numismatic context for medieval Indian coinage including southern gold issues.

episodes.notes: The Hoysala economy was not only royal land grants: inscriptions preserve merchant patrons such as Ketamalla and Kesarasetti, local nagara bodies, and links to broader south Indian commercial networks. Gold gadyana or honnu issues, often associated with dynastic symbols and royal names, point to monetized exchange alongside agrarian revenue. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT duplicate the Chola chapter's Ainnurruvar oceanic guild story; mention pan-regional guilds only as background and keep focus on Hoysala nagara, donors and coinage. Do NOT specify coin types, routes or commodities beyond what sources support.
episodes.chapter: The Hoysalas and the Temple Sculptors
episodes.chapter_part: IV. The Lake, the Guild, and the Gold Coin

episodes.title: Kannada Learns New Metres
episodes.era: Hoysala Kannada literary age, c. 1160-1230 CE
episodes.region: Halebidu, Hoysala courts and literary Karnataka
episodes.logline: Poets in the Hoysala world make Kannada a courtly, ethical and experimental language through Jain stories, ragale verse and shatpadi metre.
episodes.moral: A language grows when poets dare to reshape it.

sources.citation: Janna, Yashodhara Charite, c. 1209 CE
sources.note: Primary Jain Kannada narrative poem of the Hoysala period.

sources.citation: Harihara, Ragalegalu and Basavarajadevara Ragale, c. late 12th century
sources.note: Primary works associated with the ragale form and early Basava biography.

sources.citation: Sheldon Pollock, The Language of the Gods in the World of Men (UC Press, 2006)
sources.note: Recent framework for Kannada vernacularization under the Hoysalas.

episodes.notes: Janna, Harihara, Raghavanka and Rudrabhatta represent a Hoysala literary flowering in Old Kannada. Janna's Yashodhara Charite uses Jain ethical narrative; Harihara's ragale loosened older metrical constraints; Raghavanka popularized the six-line shatpadi with Harishchandra Kavya. Pollock's scholarship frames this as vernacularization: Kannada becoming a major administrative and literary language. ACCURACY FLAGS: dates are conventional scholarly ranges, not birth certificates; do NOT claim Sanskrit vanished; Hoysala inscriptions often combine Sanskrit prashasti with Kannada practical clauses.
episodes.chapter: The Hoysalas and the Temple Sculptors
episodes.chapter_part: V. The Word, the Grammar, and the Moving Flame

episodes.title: The Grammar Mirror and Kannada Numbers
episodes.era: Hoysala scholarship, 12th-13th centuries CE
episodes.region: Hoysala Karnataka, Shravanabelagola and courtly literary circles
episodes.logline: Kesiraja codifies Kannada grammar while Rajaditya writes practical mathematics in Kannada, turning scholarship toward a living regional language.
episodes.moral: Knowledge spreads when it speaks the people's language.

sources.citation: Kesiraja, Shabdamanidarpana, 1260 CE
sources.note: Primary grammar text that systematized Kannada and quoted earlier literature.

sources.citation: Rajaditya, Vyavaharaganita, M. Mariappa Bhat ed., Madras, 1955
sources.note: Surviving Kannada practical mathematics text from the Hoysala-era scholarly tradition.

sources.citation: R. Narasimhacharya, History of Kannada Literature (1988)
sources.note: Foundational literary history for Kesiraja, Rajaditya and Hoysala scholarship.

episodes.notes: Kesiraja's Shabdamanidarpana, the 'Jewel-Mirror of Grammar,' made Kannada itself the object of systematic scholarly analysis, while Rajaditya's Vyavaharaganita brought practical/commercial mathematics into Kannada. This is an innovation story about scholarly vernacularization, not a claim that Sanskrit science disappeared. RECENT/ACCURACY FLAGS: Rajaditya's exact dates are uncertain and usually placed in the 12th century; do NOT confuse his Kannada Lilavati references with Bhaskara II's Sanskrit Lilavati covered elsewhere; do NOT say these texts prove mass literacy, only elite scholarly use of Kannada for technical subjects.
episodes.chapter: The Hoysalas and the Temple Sculptors
episodes.chapter_part: V. The Word, the Grammar, and the Moving Flame

episodes.title: The Moving Temple of Vachana
episodes.era: Vachana movement and Hoysala literary memory, 12th century CE
episodes.region: Kalyana, Halebidu and wider Karnataka
episodes.logline: Vachana voices challenge caste, ritual and gender limits, while a Hoysala poet preserves their fire in the language of the age.
episodes.moral: The deepest temple may be the courage to live truthfully.

sources.citation: Basavanna and Akka Mahadevi vachanas, in A.K. Ramanujan, Speaking of Siva (1973)
sources.note: Accessible translations of primary devotional poems.

sources.citation: Harihara, Basavarajadevara Ragale, c. 1180 CE
sources.note: Early biographical account of Basavanna by a Hoysala-world poet.

sources.citation: R. Blake Michael, The Origins of Virasaiva Sects (1992)
sources.note: Historical-critical analysis of the Vachana movement and founder/reviver debates.

episodes.notes: Basavanna, Akka Mahadevi and Allama Prabhu belonged mainly to the Kalyana/Kalachuri world, not directly to the Hoysala court. The Hoysala link is Harihara of Halebidu, whose Basavarajadevara Ragale is among the earliest biographical memories of Basavanna, and the wider circulation of vachanas through Karnataka. The movement challenged caste hierarchy, gender limits and empty ritual through brief, intense Kannada poems and the ideal of personal devotion. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT make Basavanna a Hoysala minister; do NOT treat the Anubhava Mantapa as documented by contemporary meeting minutes; do NOT claim Basava single-handedly founded Lingayatism without noting the modern debate over revival, refinement and earlier traditions.
episodes.chapter: The Hoysalas and the Temple Sculptors
episodes.chapter_part: V. The Word, the Grammar, and the Moving Flame

episodes.title: The Vassals Who Chose Telugu Stone
episodes.era: Kakatiya rise from feudatories to sovereignty, c. 956-1163 CE
episodes.region: Anumakonda, Hanamakonda and Warangal, Telangana
episodes.logline: From Rashtrakuta and Chalukya service, the Kakatiya chiefs rise until Rudradeva's 1163 inscription speaks in Telugu with a sovereign voice.
episodes.moral: A new identity can begin when people write their own future.

sources.citation: Mangallu copper-plate grant, 956 CE; Bayyaram tank inscription; Sanigaram inscription of Prola II, 1149 CE
sources.note: Primary epigraphic chain for early genealogy, vassal status and the village-name Kakati tradition.

sources.citation: Anumakonda inscription of Rudradeva, 19 January 1163 CE
sources.note: The key sovereignty declaration and Telugu-language state record at Hanamakonda.

sources.citation: Cynthia Talbot, Precolonial India in Practice, OUP, 2001; Richard M. Eaton, A Social History of the Deccan, CUP, 2005
sources.note: Recent scholarship on Kakatiya social origin, language shift and regional identity formation.

episodes.notes: Begin with the secure epigraphic trail: Mangallu names Rashtrakuta-linked ancestors, Sanigaram still shows Prola II as a vassal, and Rudradeva's Anumakonda record of 19 January 1163 marks sovereignty. KEY FACTS: early records often describe the family as Shudra; the Telugu official inscriptional turn helped form a wider Telugu political identity. RECENT FINDINGS: Talbot's work on hundreds of inscriptions treats later Kshatriya and solar-line claims as panegyric strategies. Do NOT claim the Kakatiyas were Kshatriya by birth, or treat Durjaya and solar ancestry legends as documentary fact.

episodes.title: Ganapati Builds the Long Kingdom
episodes.era: Kakatiya expansion and consolidation, 1199-1262 CE
episodes.region: Warangal, Palampet, Pakhal and coastal Andhra
episodes.logline: After captivity and danger, Ganapati Deva rebuilds power from Warangal, stretches toward the coast, and anchors rule in forts, tanks and loyal commanders.
episodes.moral: Steady rebuilding can turn crisis into strength.

sources.citation: Palampet inscription of Recherla Rudra, 31 March 1213 CE
sources.note: Records Ramappa Temple patronage, grants and Rudra's service under Ganapati.

sources.citation: Kanakadurga temple inscription, 1201 CE; Chenna-keshava temple inscription near Bapatla, 1209 CE; Ganapeshvaram inscription of Jayapa Senani, c. 1231 CE
sources.note: Evidence for coastal expansion and Ganapati's military world.

sources.citation: P.V.P. Sastry, The Kakatiyas of Warangal, 1978; Cynthia Talbot, Precolonial India in Practice, 2001
sources.note: Syntheses of Ganapati's chronology and the inscriptional political network.

episodes.notes: Ganapati's reign, 1199-1262, is the Kakatiya high point: after Yadava captivity traditions, Recherla Rudra helped hold the realm, coastal inscriptions show expansion into Andhra, and Palampet and Pakhal point to monumental and hydraulic statecraft. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP: Talbot reads this expansion as community-building through inscriptions, gifts and local chiefs, not merely conquest. Do NOT claim Ganapati personally built every tank or that Recherla Rudra's self-praise is neutral reporting; present the rescue and regency as inscription-backed but self-promotional.

episodes.title: The Nayankara Compact
episodes.era: Military service, land assignments and social mobility, 13th century CE
episodes.region: Warangal and the Kakatiya mandalas of Telangana and Andhra
episodes.logline: Land, honor and military service bind new chiefs to Warangal, creating a flexible nayaka order that lets non-royal families rise.
episodes.moral: Institutions are strongest when talent can climb.

sources.citation: Bothpur and Vaddamanu inscriptions of Malyala Gunda Senani; Palampet inscription, 1213 CE
sources.note: Evidence for Shudra descriptions, commander lineages and nayaka service.

sources.citation: Raya-sthapan-acharya title inscriptions of Kakatiya chiefs, c. 1275-1290 CE
sources.note: Records chiefs styling themselves restorers of the kingdom after supporting Rudrama Devi.

sources.citation: Burton Stein, Peasant State and Society in Medieval South India, 1980; Cynthia Talbot, Precolonial India in Practice, 2001
sources.note: The main debate over fiscal-segmentary versus martial-civic interpretations of nayaka power.

episodes.notes: This is the required SOCIAL INNOVATION story. Kakatiya nayankara assigned land and honor to commanders in return for service, while Recherla, Malyala and other families gained authority through war, gifts and temple patronage. KEY FACTS: the system prefigured, but was not identical to, Vijayanagara's later amara-nayaka order; it was fluid and tied to local honor networks. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP: Talbot revises older segmentary-state models by stressing networks of ambition and loyalty. Do NOT call it a simple feudal system, do NOT call it uniquely Kakatiya, and do NOT duplicate Vijayanagara's amara-nayaka story.

episodes.title: Rudrama Rules as Rudra-deva Maharaja
episodes.era: Kakatiya queen regnant, c. 1262-1289 CE
episodes.region: Warangal, Vengi, Tripuranthakam and Chandupatla
episodes.logline: Rudrama Devi takes power in a contested court, ruling as Rudra-deva Maharaja while chiefs, rebels and travelers learn to reckon with a queen as king.
episodes.moral: Leadership can remake the rules without hiding the truth.

sources.citation: Tripuranthakam inscription, 1266 CE; Duggi inscription, 1269 CE; Chandupatla inscription, before 27 November 1289
sources.note: Primary evidence for contested succession, royal designation and Rudrama's death date.

sources.citation: Marco Polo, Il Milione / Divisament dou Monde, c. 1298-1300
sources.note: External praise for the queen's rule, useful but factually imperfect.

sources.citation: Cynthia Talbot, Precolonial India in Practice, 2001, pp. 152-169; B. Satyanarayana Singh, 1999
sources.note: Recent analysis of gendered kingship and the Chandupatla evidence.

episodes.notes: Rudrama ruled c. 1262-1289 using the masculine title Rudra-deva Maharaja; the Tripuranthakam and Duggi records show a negotiated and contested transition, while Chandupatla fixes her death before 27 November 1289. KEY FACTS: Marco Polo praised a queen but misidentified her as Ganapati's widow; epigraphy identifies her as Ganapati's daughter. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP: Talbot treats the masculine regnal style as a political legitimation strategy, not disguise. Do NOT claim Marco Polo met her, do NOT say she disguised herself as a man, and do NOT rely on the late half-brother rebellion story as fact.
episodes.chapter_part: II. Heroes Under the Lion Gate

episodes.title: Recherla Rudra's Pillar at Palampet
episodes.era: Kakatiya regency, military service and temple patronage, c. 1199-1218 CE
episodes.region: Palampet, Warangal and Nattaramesvaram
episodes.logline: A commander who helped save a kingdom leaves a 201-line pillar at Palampet, turning service, land and art into stone memory.
episodes.moral: Service becomes lasting when it builds for others.

sources.citation: Palampet inscription of Recherla Rudra, 31 March 1213 CE
sources.note: The main record for Rudra's lineage, temple commission and village grants.

sources.citation: Ramakrishnapuram inscription; Nattaramesvaram inscription, 1218 CE
sources.note: Records the tradition of Rudra restoring Ganapati and suppressing rebels.

sources.citation: G.V. Lakshmi, Recherla Reddis, 2023; P.V.P. Sastry, The Kakatiyas of Warangal, 1978
sources.note: Modern and classic treatments of Rudra's inscriptional career.

episodes.notes: Recherla Rudra's Palampet pillar is one of the best Kakatiya windows into military service, local elite ascent and patronage. It records the Rudreshvara temple, grants to Nekkonda and other villages, and a lineage from Brahma-sena-pati rather than ancient kings. RECENT FINDINGS: recent Recherla-focused work revisits the inscription and related Godiasla material to show ministerial and commander networks. Do NOT make Rudra the king, and do NOT say Ramappa was the deity; the temple is Rudreshvara, while Ramappa is remembered as architect or sculptor.
episodes.chapter_part: II. Heroes Under the Lion Gate

episodes.title: Malik Kafur at the Granite Walls
episodes.era: First Delhi siege of Warangal, 1309-1310 CE
episodes.region: Warangal Fort, Telangana
episodes.logline: At Warangal's earthen and stone rings, Prataparudra faces Malik Kafur, negotiates survival, and sends tribute toward Delhi.
episodes.moral: Survival sometimes demands hard choices under pressure.

sources.citation: Amir Khusrau, Khazain-ul-Futuh, 1311 CE, ed. M. Wahid Mirza, 1950
sources.note: Near-contemporary account of Malik Kafur's campaign and Warangal's defenses.

sources.citation: Warangal Fort remains: outer earthen works, inner stone fortification and moat
sources.note: Material remains match Khusrau's description of concentric defenses.

sources.citation: K.S. Lal, History of the Khaljis, 1950; Asher and Talbot, India Before Europe, CUP, 2006
sources.note: Scholarly context for the 1310 siege, tribute and diamond economy.

episodes.notes: Tell the siege from Warangal's side, complementing any Delhi Sultanate account. Khusrau says Alauddin ordered the march on 31 October 1309, Kafur reached Warangal in early 1310, and the fort had an outer hardened mud circuit and inner stone fort with moat, matching archaeology. KEY FACTS: Prataparudra submitted with horses, elephants and treasure to preserve rule. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP links Delhi's interest to Deccan wealth and diamonds. Do NOT claim the Koh-i-Noor was certainly seized in 1310; say it probably passed from the Kakatiya treasury to Delhi around this period, because no inscription names it.
episodes.chapter_part: III. Sieges at the Granite Walls

episodes.title: Prataparudra's Last Road
episodes.era: Fall of Warangal and Kakatiya sovereignty, 1321-1323 CE
episodes.region: Warangal, Devagiri, the Narmada road and Sultanpur
episodes.logline: After one Tughlaq army fails, a second cuts Warangal off until Prataparudra surrenders and the Kakatiya capital becomes Sultanpur.
episodes.moral: Even a brave kingdom needs food, allies and time.

sources.citation: Isami, Futuh-us-Salatin, c. 1350 CE; Amir Khusrau, Tughlaq-nama
sources.note: Near-contemporary Persian sources for the Tughlaq campaigns and political context.

sources.citation: Kaluvacheru grant of Anithalli, 1423 CE
sources.note: Later regional evidence for the post-fall coalition of nayakas.

sources.citation: Richard M. Eaton, A Social History of the Deccan, 2005, pp. 19-26; Cynthia Talbot, Precolonial India in Practice, 2001
sources.note: Recent synthesis of Warangal's fall, Sultanpur coinage and Prataparudra's death tradition.

episodes.notes: In 1321 Jauna Khan's first Tughlaq siege failed after months of confusion, but the reinforced 1323 campaign cut Warangal's supplies and forced surrender after about five months. KEY FACTS: Warangal was renamed Sultanpur and imperial coins were minted there; Prataparudra died near the Narmada while being taken north. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP: Eaton and Talbot cautiously treat suicide as probable, not certain. Do NOT say he died fighting or was executed; do NOT frame the 1336 recovery as modern nationalism, but as a regional chiefs' coalition in a changed Deccan.
episodes.chapter_part: III. Sieges at the Granite Walls

episodes.title: The Temple with Floating Bricks
episodes.era: Ramappa or Rudreshvara Temple engineering, 1213 CE and after
episodes.region: Palampet, Mulugu district, Telangana
episodes.logline: At Palampet, light porous bricks, a sandbox foundation and black stone dancers make Ramappa a temple where engineering and art hold hands.
episodes.moral: Beauty lasts longest when imagination respects science.

sources.citation: Palampet inscription of Recherla Rudra, 31 March 1213 CE
sources.note: Primary date and patronage evidence for the Rudreshvara temple.

sources.citation: NIT Warangal geotechnical appraisal, 1991; Ghulam Yazdani restoration notes and chemical analysis of bricks
sources.note: Technical evidence for sandbox foundation and low-density porous bricks.

sources.citation: UNESCO World Heritage Committee Decision 44 COM 8B.21, 2021, Kakatiya Rudreshwara (Ramappa) Temple
sources.note: Recent global recognition of Kakatiya engineering and artistic value.

episodes.notes: This is the required SCIENTIFIC AND ENGINEERING INNOVATION story. The 1213 Palampet inscription anchors the temple; later technical studies explain its low-density tower bricks, material choices, sandbox foundation and polished dolerite madanikas. RECENT FINDINGS: UNESCO's 2021 inscription highlights Kakatiya engineering as Outstanding Universal Value, and NIT Warangal's 1991 work made the seismic-foundation argument systematic. Do NOT use the popular Marco Polo 'brightest star' quote as secure primary evidence, and do NOT call Ramappa the deity; the deity is Shiva as Rudreshvara.

episodes.title: The Thousand Tanks of Telangana
episodes.era: Kakatiya hydraulic engineering, 13th century CE
episodes.region: Pakhal, Ramappa, Bayyaram, Laknavaram and Telangana's plateau tanks
episodes.logline: Across a thirsty plateau, royal women, generals and local chiefs store monsoon water in tanks that feed fields for centuries.
episodes.moral: A wise society saves water before drought arrives.

sources.citation: Bayyaram tank inscription recording Mailama's Dharmakirti-samudra tank
sources.note: Primary source for both a major tank and Kakatiya genealogy.

sources.citation: Telangana Irrigation Department documentation for Ramappa Lake and related Kakatiya tanks; ICID World Heritage Irrigation Structure proposal, 2021
sources.note: Modern recognition of long-lived irrigation works.

sources.citation: Richard M. Eaton, A Social History of the Deccan, 2005; V. Ratna Reddy and CESS studies on Telangana cheruvu networks
sources.note: Scholarship on tank networks, agrarian economy and modern mapping.

episodes.notes: This is the required ECONOMIC AND ENGINEERING INNOVATION story. Ganapati's age is linked to Pakhal Lake, Recherla Rudra to Ramappa Lake, Mailama to Bayyaram's Dharmakirti-samudra, and many nayakas to local cheruvus that stored monsoon runoff. RECENT FINDINGS: modern irrigation surveys and satellite mapping show dense tank landscapes across old Kakatiya territory, though not every tank is medieval. Do NOT claim an exact number of Kakatiya tanks, do NOT say Ganapati built them all, and avoid the phrase 'first in the world' unless carefully qualified.

episodes.title: Three Shrines at Hanamakonda
episodes.era: Thousand Pillar Temple and Kakatiya craft, c. 1163-1175 CE
episodes.region: Hanamakonda, Telangana
episodes.logline: Rudradeva's craftsmen raise a triple-shrine temple where Shiva, Vishnu and Surya share polished pillars, a star platform and a stone Nandi.
episodes.moral: Shared spaces can turn difference into harmony.

sources.citation: Anumakonda inscription of Rudradeva, 1163 CE
sources.note: Sovereignty context for Rudradeva's Hanamakonda building age.

sources.citation: ASI documentation for Thousand Pillar Temple, Hanamakonda, Monument of National Importance
sources.note: Site record for the trikutalayam plan, pillars, Nandi and restoration history.

sources.citation: UNESCO Tentative List submission for Warangal Fort, Kakatiya Kala Thoranam and Thousand Pillar Temple, India, 2010
sources.note: Recent heritage framing of Kakatiya architectural serial sites.

episodes.notes: The Thousand Pillar Temple, or Veyyi Stambhala Gudi, is best told as CRAFT AND SOCIAL-RELIGIOUS INNOVATION: a trikutalayam combining Shaiva, Vaishnava and Saura shrines on one platform, with star planning, polished pillars and a monolithic Nandi. KEY FACTS: exact construction dates are usually placed c. 1163-1175, but the precise start year is not separately inscribed. RECENT CONSERVATION: ASI and state work have restored damaged mandapa elements, and the site remains on UNESCO's tentative list. Do NOT say there are literally exactly 1,000 pillars.

episodes.title: The Motupalli Promise
episodes.era: Maritime trade charter under Ganapati Deva, c. 1230s-1240s CE
episodes.region: Motupalli port, Andhra coast and the Indian Ocean
episodes.logline: At Motupalli, Ganapati promises merchants fixed duties, safe cargo and royal protection, making the coast a gateway for risk and reward.
episodes.moral: Trade flourishes when trust is protected by law.

sources.citation: Motupalli copper-plate inscription of Ganapati Deva, c. 1245 CE
sources.note: Primary charter for customs duties, shipwreck protection and merchant security.

sources.citation: Marco Polo, Il Milione / Divisament dou Monde, c. 1298-1300
sources.note: External evidence for the Andhra coastal trade world, used with caution.

sources.citation: Richard M. Eaton, A Social History of the Deccan, 2005; Catherine B. Asher and Cynthia Talbot, India Before Europe, 2006
sources.note: Modern context for trade, diamonds and Kakatiya wealth.

episodes.notes: This is the required ECONOMIC INNOVATION story. The Motupalli charter promises protection to maritime traders, curbs arbitrary exactions and fixes customs duties, making it a striking legal-commercial document from the Kakatiya coast. KEY FACTS: the port moved diamonds, textiles and other goods through Indian Ocean networks; horses may have entered via such ports, but specifics need caution. RECENT ARCHAEOLOGY and port studies place Motupalli in a long coastal trade history. Do NOT claim Marco Polo certainly visited Motupalli itself or that every horse-import detail is inscriptionally proven.

episodes.title: Jayapa Writes the Dance of War
episodes.era: Kakatiya scholarly, literary and performing arts, c. 1231-1320 CE
episodes.region: Warangal, Chebrolu, Nellore and Telugu literary country
episodes.logline: A general writes a dance manual, a poet expands the Telugu Mahabharata, and Kakatiya courts turn movement and language into memory.
episodes.moral: Learning can live in books, bodies and songs.

sources.citation: Jayapa Senani, Nrtta Ratnavali, c. 1231 CE; Chebrolu inscription, 21 April 1235 CE
sources.note: Primary textual and inscriptional evidence for dance theory and performance patronage.

sources.citation: Tikkana, Andhra Mahabharatam; Vidyanatha, Prataparudriyam, c. 1320 CE
sources.note: Major Telugu and Sanskrit works of the Kakatiya cultural sphere.

sources.citation: Velcheru Narayana Rao, David Shulman and Sanjay Subrahmanyam, Textures of Time, 2002; Richard Eaton, A Social History of the Deccan, 2005
sources.note: Recent scholarship on Telugu literary identity and Kakatiya-period culture.

episodes.notes: This is the required SCHOLARLY AND ARTISTIC INNOVATION story. Jayapa Senani's Nrtta Ratnavali describes marga and desi dance forms, including martial Perini traditions; Tikkana translated most of the Mahabharata into Telugu under a Kakatiya-affiliated Nellore Choda setting; Vidyanatha's Prataparudriyam shows Sanskrit poetics at Prataparudra's court. RECENT FINDINGS: Nataraja Ramakrishna's 20th-century Perini revival used Ramappa sculpture and Jayapa's text together. Do NOT call Tikkana a direct Kakatiya court poet; he served the Nellore Chodas and came to Ganapati's court as envoy.

episodes.title: The Gates of Telangana
episodes.era: Kakatiya afterlife and regional memory, 1323-2021 CE
episodes.region: Warangal, Telangana and the Deccan
episodes.logline: After Warangal falls, nayakas reclaim the city, poets reshape memory, and the Kakatiya stone gate becomes a symbol of modern Telangana.
episodes.moral: The past endures when people remember it responsibly.

sources.citation: Kaluvacheru grant of Anithalli, 1423 CE
sources.note: Evidence for the 75-nayaka coalition remembered after the fall of Warangal.

sources.citation: Ferishta, Tarikh-i-Firishta, c. 1606-1623; Prataparudra Caritramu, 16th century Telugu tradition
sources.note: Later narrative sources for liberation and Kakatiya memory, used with caution.

sources.citation: Government of Telangana state emblem records, 2014; UNESCO World Heritage inscription for Ramappa Temple, 2021
sources.note: Modern adoption of the Kakatiya Kala Thoranam and global heritage recognition.

episodes.notes: The legacy story runs from the 1323 fall to Musunuri Kapaya Nayaka's 1336 recovery of Warangal, from 16th-century Prataparudra Caritramu to Telangana's 2014 emblem using the Kakatiya Kala Thoranam, and to Ramappa's 2021 UNESCO inscription. KEY FACTS: Ferishta is late, and the Kaluvacheru grant is later still but closer to regional memory than modern retellings. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP: Eaton reads the post-Kakatiya world as political reorganization by former nayaka networks. Do NOT present late literary legends as eyewitness history, and do NOT make the liberation a modern communal slogan.

episodes.title: The Grammar That Watched a War
episodes.era: Indo-Greek pressure after the Mauryas, c. 185-150 BCE
episodes.region: Saketa, Madhyamika, Pataliputra and the northwestern routes
episodes.logline: A grammar lesson preserves the thunder of Yavana armies as post-Mauryan India learns that the northwest frontier has changed forever.
episodes.moral: A tiny line in a book can carry the sound of an age in crisis.

sources.citation: Patanjali, Mahabhashya, c. 150 BCE
sources.note: Near-contemporary Sanskrit grammatical examples mentioning Yavanas besieging Saketa and Madhyamika.

sources.citation: Gargi Samhita / Yuga Purana, probably compiled c. 1st century BCE-3rd century CE
sources.note: Later Indian prophetic-style account of Yavana advances toward Pataliputra.

sources.citation: Coins of Menander I and other Indo-Greek rulers; A.K. Narain, The Indo-Greeks (1957)
sources.note: Independent evidence for Indo-Greek power, chronology and reach.

episodes.notes: ERA PIVOT: before, Magadha's Mauryan successor states still imagined the Gangetic heartland as the center; after, Shunga power had to face mobile Indo-Greek rulers from the northwest. PRIMARY SOURCES: Patanjali's Mahabhashya is near-contemporary but is a grammar text, not an eyewitness war report; the Yuga Purana is later and schematic; coins give the independent political map. AGREEMENT: all sources support Indo-Greek pressure after the Mauryas. DISAGREEMENT: whether Menander himself reached Saketa or Pataliputra is debated. SOURCES PROBLEM: do NOT claim a fully described siege, fixed troop numbers, or a proven Shunga victory parade; the attested fact is frontier shock preserved in grammar and numismatics.

episodes.title: The Coins Go Silent in Ujjain
episodes.figure: Chandragupta II Vikramaditya and Rudrasimha III
episodes.era: Gupta expansion into western India, c. 395-415 CE
episodes.region: Malwa, Ujjain, Gujarat and the old Western Satrap lands
episodes.logline: When the last Western Satrap coins vanish and Gupta silver appears in their place, a battlefield without a chronicle reshapes India's western trade routes.
episodes.moral: Sometimes the clearest battle report is a coin that stops being minted.

sources.citation: Final Western Kshatrapa coins of Rudrasimha III and Gupta silver coinage of Chandragupta II
sources.note: Primary physical evidence for the end of Satrap rule and Gupta takeover.

sources.citation: Udayagiri inscriptions of Chandragupta II's circle, c. 401-402 CE
sources.note: Contemporary Gupta evidence for the king's western presence and imperial ambition.

sources.citation: D.C. Sircar, Select Inscriptions; R.C. Majumdar and A.S. Altekar on Gupta numismatics
sources.note: Modern reconstruction of the western campaign.

episodes.notes: ERA PIVOT: before, the Saka Western Satraps controlled Malwa-Gujarat and western sea trade; after, the Gupta empire reached Ujjain and the Arabian Sea economy. PRIMARY SOURCES are coins and inscriptions, not a narrative chronicle. AGREEMENT: coin sequences and Gupta records agree that Rudrasimha III's line ended and Gupta silver imitated Satrap types.
