DISAGREEMENT: the exact battle site and year are unknown, and literary fragments such as Devi-Chandraguptam are too late and dramatic to supply tactics. EYEWITNESS: none survives. Do NOT invent a duel, massacre, or single day; present a source-critical conquest reconstructed from numismatic silence.

episodes.title: The Victory Pillars at Sondani
episodes.era: End of Huna dominance in northwestern India, c. 528-532 CE
episodes.region: Sondani near Mandsaur, Malwa and the Huna frontier
episodes.logline: Two stone pillars boast that a Malwa king bent the Huna storm, but rival memories argue over who truly broke Mihirakula's power.
episodes.moral: Victory is strongest when pride is tested against other evidence.

sources.citation: Mandsaur/Sondani pillar inscriptions of Yashodharman, c. 532 CE
sources.note: Victor-side primary inscription claiming submission of rulers from the Lauhitya to the western ocean.

sources.citation: Gwalior inscription of Mihirakula, c. 6th century CE
sources.note: Huna-side evidence for Mihirakula's presence and status before defeat.

sources.citation: Xuanzang, Datang Xiyu Ji, c. 646 CE; Kalhana, Rajatarangini, 12th century
sources.note: Later accounts linking Mihirakula's defeat or survival to other kings and memories.

episodes.notes: ERA PIVOT: before, Toramana and Mihirakula's Hunas shook Gupta authority across Malwa and the northwest; after, Huna imperial momentum broke and regional powers replaced Gupta centrality. AGREEMENT: inscriptions and later accounts accept Mihirakula as a major Huna ruler and Yashodharman as a sudden victor. DISAGREEMENT: Xuanzang credits Baladitya with sparing Mihirakula, while Sondani centers Yashodharman; Kalhana preserves a darker Kashmir memory. SOURCES PROBLEM: the Sondani prashasti is triumphal propaganda, but the Huna record and later independent traditions confirm a real collapse. Do NOT claim exact troop numbers or that one battle alone ended all Huna influence.

episodes.title: The Oath by the Pyre
episodes.era: Rise of Harsha after the fall of Maukhari-Kannauj order, c. 606-612 CE
episodes.region: Thanesar, Kannauj, Gauda and the middle Ganga plain
episodes.logline: After a royal killing and a sister's rescue, Harsha turns grief into a northern campaign that remakes Kannauj as an imperial capital.
episodes.moral: Power born from grief must still answer to evidence and restraint.

sources.citation: Banabhatta, Harshacharita, c. 640 CE
sources.note: Near-contemporary court panegyric from Harsha's side, vivid but partisan.

sources.citation: Xuanzang, Datang Xiyu Ji, c. 646 CE
sources.note: Near-contemporary outsider account of Harsha's empire and the political map.

sources.citation: Banskhera and Madhuban copper plates of Harsha; seals and coins of Shashanka
sources.note: Primary administrative and numismatic evidence for both powers.

episodes.notes: ERA PIVOT: before, Thanesar, Maukhari Kannauj and Gauda competed after Gupta decline; after, Harsha made Kannauj the northern imperial center. PRIMARY SOURCES: Bana writes for Harsha and blames Shashanka; Xuanzang admires Harsha but is independent; Shashanka's coins and seals prove a strong Gauda kingdom. AGREEMENT: Rajyavardhana died in the crisis and Harsha rose rapidly. DISAGREEMENT: motive, treachery and battlefield detail come mainly from Harsha's court. NON-COMMUNAL FLAG: frame this as dynastic competition for Kannauj, not religious hatred. Do NOT demonize Shashanka or claim a neat single decisive battle where the sources give a campaign.

episodes.title: What the Chachnama Remembers
episodes.figure: Raja Dahir and Muhammad bin Qasim
episodes.era: Fall of Brahman dynasty Sindh and Umayyad provincial expansion, 711-712 CE
episodes.region: Debal, Rawar, Aror and the Indus valley
episodes.logline: In 711 an Umayyad frontier army takes Sindh from Raja Dahir - a conquest the Arabic and Persian chronicles record in blood, tribute and terms.
episodes.moral: A province changed hands through war, tribute and terms; the sources record its slaughter and its settlements alike.

sources.citation: Ali Kufi, Chachnama, c. 1216 CE
sources.note: Persian narrative claiming to translate an Arabic account; later, Sindh-centered and highly debated.

sources.citation: al-Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan, c. 892 CE
sources.note: Independent Abbasid-era account of the conquest from an Arabic imperial perspective.

sources.citation: Manan Ahmed Asif, A Book of Conquest (2016); Andre Wink, Al-Hind, Vol. I (1990)
sources.note: Modern source-critical readings of Chachnama, frontier politics and Sindh.

episodes.notes: ERA PIVOT: before, Dahir's Brahman dynasty controlled lower Sindh's river ports and inland forts; after, Sindh became an Umayyad/Abbasid province tied to the Indian Ocean and Iraqi administration. AGREEMENT: Arabic and Persian traditions agree on Debal, Dahir's defeat near Rawar/Aror, and Qasim's consolidation. DISAGREEMENT: Chachnama's speeches, betrayals and moral lessons are literary and possibly 13th-century politics in disguise. EYEWITNESS: none extant. SOURCES PROBLEM: do NOT frame this as religion versus religion; local Buddhist, Jat, merchant and elite choices were political. Do NOT repeat inflated numbers, miracle stories or communal blame. HARD FACTS TO STATE (do NOT omit or soften; attribute to source): al-Baladhuri (Futuh al-Buldan) and the Chachnama record Debal stormed with its fighting men killed, its temple (budd) cast down, and captives including women enslaved and sent to Hajjaj; jizya imposed on those who submitted; at Brahmanabad a massacre of the defenders (numbers disputed) followed by a settlement that left temples standing under a tax and restored Brahmin officials (dhimma terms); Muhammad bin Qasim recalled by Caliph Sulayman c.715 and died in prison. PRESENT NEUTRALLY: state the events and the motives the sources give (secure routes, plunder, a province, jizya/consolidation AND local Buddhist/Jat/merchant political choices) without lensing, whitewashing or demonising; let the audience judge. Do NOT editorialize that it 'was not about faith'.

episodes.title: The Blind Poet and the Captive King
episodes.figure: Yashovarman of Kannauj and Lalitaditya of Kashmir
episodes.era: Karkota-Kannauj struggle for northern paramountcy, c. 730-740 CE
episodes.region: Kannauj, Kashmir and the upper Gangetic routes
episodes.logline: A court poem sings Yashovarman's victories while a Kashmiri chronicle remembers Lalitaditya breaking the very king that poetry tried to make immortal.
episodes.moral: A ruler's praise-song is not the same thing as history.

sources.citation: Kalhana, Rajatarangini, Books IV-V, 1148-1150 CE
sources.note: Kashmir-side chronicle, centuries later, using older materials but glorifying Lalitaditya.

sources.citation: Vakpati, Gaudavaho, c. 730-740 CE
sources.note: Near-contemporary Kannauj court poem praising Yashovarman and silent about defeat.

sources.citation: Huichao, Memoir on the Five Indian Kingdoms, c. 727 CE; Tang annals
sources.note: Near-contemporary evidence for the political world around Kashmir and north India.

episodes.notes: ERA PIVOT: before, Yashovarman's Kannauj court claimed northern prestige after Harsha; after, Karkota Kashmir under Lalitaditya became the remembered mountain empire and Kannauj's moment faded. AGREEMENT: sources show both kings as major powers in the same generation. DISAGREEMENT: Kalhana inflates Lalitaditya's world conquest, while Gaudavaho omits any defeat. EYEWITNESS: Vakpati is near-contemporary but poetic and partisan; Kalhana is method-aware but four centuries late. Do NOT claim Central Asian conquests as secure, fixed troop numbers, or a named battlefield; foreground court poetry versus chronicle memory.

episodes.title: The Navsari Tablet Remembers
episodes.era: Repulse of Arab expansion beyond Sindh and rise of Gurjara-Pratihara power, c. 724-739 CE
episodes.region: Rajasthan, Malwa, Gujarat and Navsari
episodes.logline: A copper plate in coastal Gujarat records a coalition's hard stop to frontier armies pushing east from Sindh.
episodes.moral: A turning tide is often a chain of resistances, not one simple clash.

sources.citation: Navsari Copper Plate Grant of Avanijanashraya Pulakesiraja, c. 738-739 CE
sources.note: Near-contemporary Chalukya-side record of victory over the Tajika army near Navsari.

sources.citation: Gwalior Prashasti of Bhoja I, c. 840-850 CE
sources.note: Later Pratihara memory crediting Nagabhata with repelling a mlechchha army.

sources.citation: al-Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan, c. 892 CE; Andre Wink, Al-Hind, Vol. I
sources.note: Arabic-side and modern accounts of Arab setbacks east of Sindh.

episodes.notes: ERA PIVOT: before, Arab governors in Sindh raided into Rajasthan, Malwa and Gujarat; after, durable expansion east of the Indus halted and Pratihara power rose in the northwest. AGREEMENT: Indian inscriptions and Arabic accounts agree that frontier pressure met reverses. DISAGREEMENT: the popular 'Battle of Rajasthan' is a modern compression of several engagements, not one attested battlefield. EYEWITNESS: the Navsari plate is close in time but is a royal grant. Do NOT claim Bappa Rawal's bardic role as fact, do NOT compare simplistically to Tours, and do NOT give invented forces.

episodes.title: The King Who Turned Ally
episodes.figure: Aditya I Chola and Aparajita Pallava
episodes.era: End of Pallava rule and Chola expansion into Tondaimandalam, c. 897 CE
episodes.region: Kanchi frontier, Tondaimandalam and the Ariyil river zone
episodes.logline: The ally who once fought beside the Pallavas returns as their conqueror, opening the road to the Chola imperial age.
episodes.moral: Alliances shift when ambition outgrows yesterday's map.

sources.citation: Tiruvalangadu Copper Plates of Rajendra Chola I, c. 1018 CE
sources.note: Chola victor-side genealogy stating that Aditya killed Aparajita.

sources.citation: Leiden Grant of Rajaraja Chola I, c. 1006 CE
sources.note: Chola record confirming conquest of Tondaimandalam and Pallava eclipse.

sources.citation: K.A. Nilakanta Sastri, A History of South India; T.V. Mahalingam, Kanchipuram in Early South Indian History
sources.note: Modern reconstruction of the late Pallava-Chola transition.

episodes.notes: ERA PIVOT: before, Pallavas dominated Kanchi and Tondaimandalam for centuries; after, the Cholas absorbed the region and gained the base from which Rajaraja I's empire later rose. AGREEMENT: multiple Chola copper plates agree that Aditya I ended Aparajita's power. DISAGREEMENT: Pallava records fall silent, so the losing side's voice is missing and the rupture between former allies is unexplained. EYEWITNESS: none. SOURCES PROBLEM: all surviving narratives are victor-side dynastic memory. Do NOT invent betrayal motives, a named duel, or battlefield numbers.

episodes.title: Who Shot the Elephant
episodes.era: Rashtrakuta-Chola struggle at Takkolam, c. 948-949 CE
episodes.region: Takkolam, North Arcot region, Tamil Nadu
episodes.logline: Two enemy traditions agree that the Chola prince died on an elephant, but they leave history arguing over whose arrow brought him down.
episodes.moral: Even when defeat is certain, glory remains contested.

sources.citation: Atakur Inscription of Krishna III and Western Ganga Butuga II, c. 949-950 CE
sources.note: Near-contemporary Rashtrakuta/Ganga-side claim that Butuga killed Rajaditya.

sources.citation: Leiden Grant of Rajaraja I and Tiruvalangadu Copper Plates of Rajendra I
sources.note: Chola-side records remembering Rajaditya as the prince who died on an elephant.

sources.citation: K.A. Nilakanta Sastri, The Colas; A.S. Altekar, The Rashtrakutas and Their Times
sources.note: Modern synthesis of Takkolam and its consequences.

episodes.notes: ERA PIVOT: before, Parantaka I's Cholas pressed north as a major southern empire; after, Rashtrakuta Krishna III reduced Chola power for a generation, making the later Rajaraja revival more dramatic. AGREEMENT: all sides place Rajaditya's death at Takkolam and accept Rashtrakuta victory. DISAGREEMENT: the Atakur inscription names Butuga as killer, while Chola plates honor the death but do not name the archer. EYEWITNESS: no eyewitness prose, but Atakur is near-contemporary stone evidence. Do NOT claim exact forces, a cinematic single arrow as proven, or Chola extinction.

episodes.title: The Dynasty That Fell in the Dust
episodes.era: Fall of the Rashtrakutas and rise of the Western Chalukyas, 972-973 CE
episodes.region: Manyakheta, Malkhed and the Deccan heartland
episodes.logline: After one enemy sacks Manyakheta, a former vassal strikes the weakened throne and ends a Deccan empire that had ruled for two centuries.
episodes.moral: Empires often fall when old servants know where the walls are thin.

sources.citation: Tailapa II's Kauthem and related grants, late 10th century
sources.note: Victor-side Western Chalukya evidence for overthrowing Rashtrakuta power.

sources.citation: Ranna, Gadayuddham, c. 993 CE
sources.note: Near-contemporary Kannada court epic at Tailapa's court, valuable but heroic and partisan.

sources.citation: Paramara records of Siyaka's sack of Manyakheta; late Rashtrakuta copper-plate silence
sources.note: Independent evidence for the sequence of collapse.

episodes.notes: ERA PIVOT: before, Rashtrakutas ruled the Deccan as Balhara power known to Arab geographers; after, Western Chalukyas of Kalyani dominated and reshaped Deccan politics. AGREEMENT: inscriptions and literary memory agree that Manyakheta was weakened by Siyaka and that Tailapa II replaced Karka II. DISAGREEMENT: Tailapa's claimed ancient Chalukya lineage may be political legitimation, not secure genealogy. EYEWITNESS: Ranna is near-contemporary but writes epic praise. Do NOT reduce the fall to one glorious duel, do NOT ignore Siyaka's earlier blow, and do NOT present epigraphic silence as a detailed battle report.

episodes.title: The Secretary Who Was There
episodes.figure: Jayapala Shahi and Mahmud of Ghazni
episodes.era: Ghaznavid expansion against the Hindu Shahi frontier, 27 November 1001 CE
episodes.region: Peshawar, Waihind and the Khyber-Punjab frontier
episodes.logline: A court secretary's one-sided account preserves the defeat that cracked the old Shahi frontier and opened a century of raids.
episodes.moral: A surviving witness must be heard, but never obeyed blindly.

sources.citation: al-Utbi, Kitab-ul-Yamini / Tarikh-i-Yamini, c. 1021 CE
sources.note: Near-contemporary Ghaznavid court secretary's account, possibly from eyewitness information.

sources.citation: al-Biruni, Kitab-ul-Hind, c. 1030 CE
sources.note: Contemporary observer of India and Ghaznavid context, not a battle chronicle.

sources.citation: Hindu Shahi coins of Jayapala and Anandapala; Peter Jackson, The Delhi Sultanate (1999)
sources.note: Physical evidence for the dynasty and modern reconstruction.

episodes.notes: ERA PIVOT: before, the Hindu Shahi kingdom guarded the Khyber approaches; after, Jayapala's defeat and capture began the erosion of that frontier, though resistance continued under Anandapala. AGREEMENT: Persian-Arabic accounts and coins confirm the Shahi line, the 1001 defeat near Waihind/Peshawar and later frontier collapse. DISAGREEMENT: Utbi supplies tactics, ransom and numbers from the victor's side only. EYEWITNESS: Utbi is near-contemporary, not neutral; al-Biruni is contemporary but more analytical. NON-COMMUNAL FLAG: frame this as frontier statecraft, cavalry logistics and revenue raids. Do NOT repeat inflated casualty numbers or portray either side as a religious caricature.
episodes.chapter_part: V. Frontiers, Legends and New Maps

episodes.title: The Legend at the Dargah
episodes.era: Bahraich memory after Ghaznavid-era expansion, traditionally 1033-1034 CE
episodes.region: Bahraich and the Sarayu-Ghaghara basin
episodes.logline: A shrine, a late hagiography and many communities remember a battle whose details are far less certain than its afterlife.
episodes.moral: Legends can matter deeply without becoming literal records.

sources.citation: Abd-ur-Rahman Chishti, Mirat-i-Masudi, 1620 CE
sources.note: Very late Persian hagiography of Ghazi Miyan; the main narrative source for Suheldev.

sources.citation: Dargah of Ghazi Miyan at Bahraich and its long pilgrimage tradition
sources.note: Physical and social evidence for an enduring 11th-century-associated memory.

sources.citation: Shahid Amin, Conquest and Community: The Afterlife of Warrior Saint Ghazi Miyan (2015)
sources.note: Modern source-critical study of the legend's changing meanings.

episodes.notes: ERA PIVOT: if historically grounded, the tradition marks a check to Ghaznavid-linked movement into the Sarayu basin; more securely, it created a major memory site shared and reinterpreted by communities over centuries. AGREEMENT: sources agree that Bahraich became a powerful shrine-memory. DISAGREEMENT: almost every battle detail, Suheldev's identity, coalition size and tactics comes from a text written nearly six centuries later. EYEWITNESS: none. SOURCES PROBLEM: this episode must foreground uncertainty. Do NOT claim the 21 rajas, caste identities, exact tactics, or communal lessons as fact; cite both Suheldev memory and the dargah respectfully.
episodes.chapter_part: V. Frontiers, Legends and New Maps

episodes.title: The Last King on the Yamuna
episodes.figure: Jaichand Gahadavala and Muhammad of Ghor
episodes.era: Ghurid conquest of the middle Ganga plain, 1194 CE
episodes.region: Chandawar near Firozabad, Yamuna river and Varanasi-Kannauj zone
episodes.logline: On the Yamuna, the fall of the Gahadavala king completes the political opening from which the Delhi Sultanate will rise.
episodes.moral: A new map is drawn by campaigns, treasuries and roads as much as by one battle.

sources.citation: Hasan Nizami, Taj-ul-Maasir, c. 1220 CE
sources.note: Near-contemporary Sultanate-side court history describing Chandawar and Jaichand's defeat.

sources.citation: Minhaj-i-Siraj Juzjani, Tabaqat-i-Nasiri, completed 1260 CE
sources.note: Later but important Persian synthesis of Ghurid campaigns.

sources.citation: Gahadavala copper plates and inscriptions ending around 1193-1194; Peter Jackson, The Delhi Sultanate (1999)
sources.note: Epigraphic silence and modern political-military reconstruction.

episodes.notes: ERA PIVOT: before, the Gahadavala dynasty dominated Kannauj and Varanasi as the last great middle-Ganga power after Tarain; after, Ghurid authority extended across the plain and supplied the base for Delhi Sultanate consolidation. AGREEMENT: Persian chronicles and the collapse of Gahadavala records support the 1194 defeat at Chandawar and Jaichand's death. DISAGREEMENT: whether he died fighting, drowned while fleeing, or had earlier dealings with Ghor belongs to contested later tradition. EYEWITNESS: no direct eyewitness; Hasan Nizami is near-contemporary and court-side. Do NOT repeat elephant numbers as exact, do NOT call Jaichand a traitor, and do NOT frame conquest communally.
episodes.chapter_part: V. Frontiers, Legends and New Maps

episodes.title: Tarain Twice and the Year Between Victories
episodes.figure: Prithviraj Chauhan III and Muhammad of Ghor
episodes.era: Chahamana-Ghurid confrontation, 1191-1192 CE
episodes.region: Tarain, modern Taraori in Haryana
episodes.logline: On the same plain, Prithviraj first drove Muhammad of Ghor away and then lost to a returned army that had learned how to fight differently.
episodes.moral: A victory is unfinished if you do not learn from it.

sources.citation: Hasan Nizami, Taj-ul-Maasir, c. 1205-1228 CE, trans. in Elliot and Dowson, Vol. II
sources.note: Near-contemporary Ghurid-Delhi account, valuable but panegyric.

sources.citation: Minhaj-i-Siraj Juzjani, Tabaqat-i-Nasiri, 1260 CE; trans. H.G. Raverty, 1881
sources.note: Gives later details of the second battle and Ghurid tactics.

sources.citation: Jayanaka, Prithviraja Vijaya, c. 1191-1192 CE; Cynthia Talbot, The Last Hindu Emperor, 2016
sources.note: Near-contemporary Sanskrit court poem from the Chahamana side, incomplete but crucial.

episodes.notes: ERA PIVOT: before Tarain, the Chahamanas and other Rajput powers contested north Indian supremacy from Ajmer and Delhi; after the second battle, Ghurid commanders held Delhi and opened the path to the Delhi Sultanate. Sources agree on a Prithviraj victory in 1191 and a Ghurid victory in 1192, but differ on numbers, sequence and motive; Persian chronicles foreground Ghurid recovery, while Prithviraja Vijaya preserves a rare Indian court voice before the disaster. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP by Cynthia Talbot separates early evidence from later heroic accretions. Do NOT use Prithviraj Raso as an eyewitness source, do NOT claim Jaichand betrayed Prithviraj, and do NOT repeat the late story that Prithviraj killed Muhammad of Ghor in Ghazni with a sound-guided arrow.

episodes.title: Gwalior and the Fort Above the Plain
episodes.era: Ghurid consolidation in north India, c. 1196 CE
episodes.region: Gwalior fort, central India
episodes.logline: After Tarain, the cliff-fort of Gwalior showed how conquest became rule when a garrisoned rock could command the roads below.
episodes.moral: A fortress can be both a shield and a hinge of power.

sources.citation: Hasan Nizami, Taj-ul-Maasir, c. 1205-1228 CE, trans. in Elliot and Dowson, Vol. II
sources.note: Near-contemporary Ghurid-Delhi court account of Aibak-era campaigns, written from the victorious side.

sources.citation: Minhaj-i-Siraj Juzjani, Tabaqat-i-Nasiri, 1260 CE; trans. H. G. Raverty, 1881
sources.note: Delhi Sultanate chronicle that summarizes the early conquests after Muhammad of Ghor.

sources.citation: K. A. Nizami, Some Aspects of Religion and Politics in India during the Thirteenth Century, 1961; Peter Jackson, The Delhi Sultanate, 1999/2003
sources.note: Modern reconstructions of early Sultanate expansion and the limits of the Persian narrative evidence.

episodes.notes: ERA PIVOT: before the Gwalior campaign, Tarain had opened the road to Delhi and Ajmer but many hill-forts still made Ghurid power discontinuous; after the c. 1196 surrender/capture of Gwalior, Aibak could hold a strategic rock overlooking routes between the Doab, Rajasthan and Malwa. Hasan Nizami writes close to the Ghurid court and Minhaj writes a generation later from the Delhi side; they agree on the fort entering the new regime, but they do not give a balanced defender narrative and their numbers and triumphal language must be treated as court rhetoric. The local ruler is commonly identified as Sulakshanapala in modern reconstructions, while precise siege details are thin. State the hard fact of conquest and garrisoning; do NOT invent a jauhar, a heroic duel, exact casualty figures, or a detailed speech not in the sources.

episodes.title: Chittor Taken and the Queen the Sources Do Not See
episodes.era: Khalji expansion into Rajasthan, 1303 CE
episodes.region: Chittor Fort, Rajasthan
episodes.logline: When Alauddin Khalji captured Chittor, an eyewitness wrote of siege and power, while a queen who became famous appeared only in poetry centuries later.
episodes.moral: The loudest legend must still answer to the earliest evidence.

sources.citation: Amir Khusrau, Khazain ul-Futuh, c. 1311 CE; trans. Mohammad Habib, 1931
sources.note: Eyewitness court poet who accompanied Alauddin's campaigns and says nothing of Padmini.

sources.citation: Ziauddin Barani, Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi, c. 1357 CE, trans. in Elliot and Dowson, Vol. III
sources.note: Later Sultanate account; also no Padmini motive or 1303 jauhar story.

sources.citation: Malik Muhammad Jayasi, Padmavat, 1540 CE; Ramya Sreenivasan, The Many Lives of a Rajput Queen, 2007
sources.note: The later Sufi poem that made Padmini famous, and modern analysis of that legend's afterlives.

episodes.notes: HISTORIOGRAPHY PIVOT: before 1303, Mewar's fort blocked Khalji power in Rajasthan; after the siege, Chittor was occupied and Khalji reach looked formidable, though Sisodia power later returned. Khusrau and Barani agree on a political-military siege and aftermath, while Jayasi's Padmavat, written 237 years later, creates the Padmini romance. Sreenivasan's recent scholarship explains how poetry, court memory and politics transformed the story. Do NOT claim Padmini existed, do NOT claim Alauddin attacked because of her beauty, and do NOT claim the 1303 jauhar as contemporary fact; better-attested jauhars belong to later Chittor sieges.
episodes.chapter_part: III. Sultanate Forts and Ocean Fire

episodes.title: Siwana and the Chauhan Fort in the Desert
episodes.era: Khalji expansion in Rajasthan, 1308 CE
episodes.region: Siwana fort, Marwar, Rajasthan
episodes.logline: On the desert edge, Siwana resisted Alauddin Khalji until the fort fell and the road toward Jalore stood exposed.
episodes.moral: When a frontier fort falls, the map changes beyond its walls.

sources.citation: Amir Khusrau, Khazain-ul-Futuh, c. 1311 CE; trans. Mohammad Habib, 1931
sources.note: Contemporary Khalji court panegyric, useful for sequence but openly triumphalist.

sources.citation: Ziauddin Barani, Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi, c. 1357 CE; trans. in Elliot and Dowson, Vol. III
sources.note: Later Delhi Sultanate political history that records Alauddin Khalji's campaigns.

sources.citation: Padmanabha, Kanhadade Prabandha, 1455 CE; trans. V. S. Bhatnagar, Kanhadade Prabandha: India's Greatest Patriotic Saga of Medieval Times, 1991
sources.note: Later Jain/Rajput-side narrative preserving Jalore-Siwana memory with bardic and devotional embellishment.

episodes.notes: ERA PIVOT: before Siwana, Khalji pressure had taken Gujarat, Ranthambhore and Chittor but Marwar still had fortified nodes outside direct control; after Siwana fell in 1308, the line toward Jalore and western Rajasthan was exposed. Amir Khusrau writes as Alauddin's court poet, Barani writes later from the Delhi political tradition, and Padmanabha writes more than a century later from a Rajput-Jain memory world; they agree that the fort fell after hard resistance, but disagree in tone, motive and heroic detail. Khusrau and Barani must be used for attested chronology, while Padmanabha is valuable for memory but not for exact speeches or miracle-like scenes. State recorded siege, conquest and killing/defeat of the defenders soberly; do NOT claim exact troop totals, a single decisive duel, or that every later Kanhadade episode is contemporary fact.
episodes.chapter_part: III. Sultanate Forts and Ocean Fire

episodes.title: Diu and the Cannon That Sealed the Sea
episodes.figure: Francisco de Almeida and Amir Hussain Al-Kurdi
episodes.era: Portuguese Indian Ocean expansion, 1509 CE
episodes.region: Diu harbour on the Gujarat coast
episodes.logline: Off Diu, shipboard cannon and ocean tactics broke a united fleet and shifted the balance of Indian Ocean trade toward Portuguese sea power.
episodes.moral: Control of technology and routes can change the fate of ports and empires.

sources.citation: Joao de Barros, Da Asia, Decada II, Livro V, 1553
sources.note: Portuguese imperial chronicle based on records and testimonies, not an eyewitness memoir.

sources.citation: Zainuddin al-Malibari, Tuhfat al-Mujahidin, c. 1579-1580 CE; trans. S. Muhammad Husayn Nainar, 1942
sources.note: Malabar Muslim perspective on Portuguese disruption in the Indian Ocean.

sources.citation: Sanjay Subrahmanyam, The Portuguese Empire in Asia, 1500-1700, 1993/2012; Giancarlo Casale, The Ottoman Age of Exploration, 2010
sources.note: Modern commercial and Ottoman-Indian Ocean contexts.

episodes.notes: ERA PIVOT: before Diu, Gujarat, Mamluk Egypt, Calicut and Venetian-linked trade networks challenged Portuguese intrusion; after 1509, Portuguese naval artillery dominated key routes and the Estado da India's cartaz system gained force. Portuguese sources and Malabar accounts agree on the battle's significance but differ in moral framing and details; Gujarati voices are thinner and often indirect. Recent scholarship treats the fight as maritime technology, trade, Red Sea strategy and port politics. Do NOT frame Diu as a religious war: the allied fleet crossed communities and states, and the Portuguese were pursuing commercial empire, customs and sea lanes.
episodes.chapter_part: III. Sultanate Forts and Ocean Fire

episodes.title: Sarangpur and the Sultan Taken Alive
episodes.figure: Rana Kumbha and Mahmud Khalji of Malwa
episodes.era: Mewar-Malwa wars, 1437 CE
episodes.region: Sarangpur, Malwa
episodes.logline: At Sarangpur, Rana Kumbha broke the Malwa advance and made Mewar the power every neighbor had to measure.
episodes.moral: Victory can be remembered in stone, but stone still has to be read against rival chronicles.

sources.citation: Kumbhalgarh inscription of Rana Kumbha, 15th century CE, summarized in Epigraphia Indica and G. H. Ojha's studies of Mewar
sources.note: Mewar-side epigraphic evidence for Kumbha's victories and royal claims.

sources.citation: Nizamuddin Ahmad, Tabaqat-i-Akbari, c. 1593 CE; and Firishta, Tarikh-i-Firishta, early 17th century
sources.note: Later Indo-Persian accounts preserving the Malwa-Mewar conflict from Sultanate/Mughal-era historical traditions.

sources.citation: Dasharatha Sharma, Lectures on Rajput History and Culture, 1970; R. C. Majumdar, ed., The Delhi Sultanate, 1960
sources.note: Modern critical synthesis of the battle, captivity tradition and its political consequences.

episodes.notes: ERA PIVOT: before Sarangpur, the Malwa Sultanate pressed Mewar from Mandu; after Rana Kumbha's victory and the reported capture and later release of Sultan Mahmud Khalji, Mewar entered its strongest fifteenth-century phase. The Mewar inscriptions praise Kumbha, while later Persian chronicles preserve the conflict from a different political tradition; they broadly agree that Kumbha defeated Mahmud, but differ on emphasis, dates and the meaning of the sultan's captivity. The Vijay Stambha belongs to Kumbha's victory culture, but do NOT claim it was a simple newspaper-like monument for only one battle. Mark court praise and later bardic expansions as source problems; do NOT invent exact army strengths or turn Kumbha or Mahmud into a flawless hero or villain.
episodes.chapter_part: IV. Sultanates, Mewar and Written Memory

episodes.title: Champaner and the Hill That Became a Capital
episodes.era: Gujarat Sultanate expansion, 1482-1484 CE
episodes.region: Pavagadh-Champaner, Gujarat
episodes.logline: Mahmud Begada took Pavagadh after a long siege and turned Champaner into a planned capital of walls, water and trade.
episodes.moral: Conquest can destroy a court and build a city in the same breath.

sources.citation: Sikandar ibn Muhammad Manjhu, Mirat-i-Sikandari, c. 1611 CE; trans. Fazlullah Lutfullah Faridi, 1899
sources.note: Gujarat Sultanate chronicle for Mahmud Begada's siege of Pavagadh and the fate of the local ruler.

sources.citation: Ali Muhammad Khan, Mirat-i-Ahmadi, 18th century; trans. M. F. Lokhandwala, Baroda Oriental Institute, 1965
sources.note: Later Gujarat history preserving administrative and urban memory of Champaner.

sources.citation: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Champaner-Pavagadh Archaeological Park dossier, 2004; Mehrdad Shokoohy, Muslim Architecture of South Gujarat, 1986
sources.note: Archaeological and architectural evidence for the capital, water systems, mosques, fortifications and pre-Sultanate remains.

episodes.notes: ERA PIVOT and INNOVATION ANGLE: before the siege, Pavagadh was a Rajput-held hill-fort controlling routes in eastern Gujarat; after Mahmud Begada's 1484 victory, Muhammadabad-Champaner became a planned Sultanate capital with fortifications, mosques, stepwells, tanks and route-control that show the economic and hydraulic side of conquest. Mirat-i-Sikandari and Mirat-i-Ahmadi agree on the long siege and Mahmud's victory, while archaeology confirms a layered city with both pre-Sultanate and Sultanate phases. The Gujarat chronicles record Patai Rawal/Jayasimha being captured and killed after refusing Islam; state that as the chronicle's claim, soberly and attributed. Do NOT claim every monument is post-1484, do NOT erase the recorded execution/conversion motif, and do NOT treat later siege duration or numbers as exact.
episodes.chapter_part: IV. Sultanates, Mewar and Written Memory

episodes.title: Gagron and the Mewar High Tide
episodes.figure: Rana Sanga and Mahmud Khalji II
episodes.era: Rajput-Malwa-Gujarat struggle, 1519 CE
episodes.region: Gagron fort, Hadoti, Rajasthan
episodes.logline: At Gagron, Rana Sanga defeated Malwa and showed why north India watched Mewar before Babur crossed the plains.
episodes.moral: A high tide can look permanent until a larger storm arrives.

sources.citation: Zahir-ud-din Muhammad Babur, Baburnama, completed 1530; trans. Annette Beveridge, 1922
sources.note: Near-contemporary outsider memoir noting Rana Sanga's strength and prior victories in north India.

sources.citation: Nizamuddin Ahmad, Tabaqat-i-Akbari, c. 1593 CE; Firishta, Tarikh-i-Firishta, early 17th century
sources.note: Indo-Persian historical traditions for Mahmud Khalji II, Malwa and the conflicts with Mewar.

sources.citation: Muhnot Nainsi, Nainsi ri Khyat, 17th century; G. N. Sharma, Mewar and the Mughal Emperors, 1954
sources.note: Rajasthani memory and modern reconstruction of Sanga's campaigns.

episodes.notes: ERA PIVOT: before Gagron, Malwa and Gujarat still contested the Rajasthan-Malwa frontier; after Sanga's 1519 victory and the capture/release tradition around Sultan Mahmud Khalji II, Mewar stood at its widest influence just before the Mughal challenge. Babur is not an eyewitness to Gagron but is a near-contemporary observer of Sanga's reputation; Nizamuddin, Firishta and Rajasthani chronicles agree on Sanga's rise but differ in numbers, battlefield detail and courtly emphasis. Use the battle to show Mewar's pre-Khanwa high point, not as a prophecy of later events. Do NOT claim a permanent Rajput empire over all north India, do NOT invent casualty totals, and do NOT fold Gagron into Khanwa as if they were the same battle.
episodes.chapter_part: IV. Sultanates, Mewar and Written Memory

episodes.title: Narrai and the Rani Who Would Not Yield
episodes.era: Mughal conquest of Gondwana, 1564 CE
episodes.region: Narrai valley and Chauragarh, Madhya Pradesh
episodes.logline: At Narrai, Rani Durgavati chose a narrow valley against Mughal numbers, and her death ended the independence of the Gondwana kingdom.
episodes.moral: Dignity can survive even when a kingdom falls.

sources.citation: Abu'l Fazl, Akbarnama, completed c. 1602 CE, trans. H. Beveridge, account of the Gondwana campaign
sources.note: Principal Mughal court narrative, written decades later from imperial records and perspective.

sources.citation: Abu'l Fazl, Ain-i-Akbari, c. 1595 CE, trans. H. Blochmann, account of Kara and related resources
sources.note: Administrative context for the region absorbed after the campaign.

sources.citation: Nandini Sengupta, Durgavati: Warrior Queen of Gondwana, 2022; Prem Chowdhry on gender and memory, 2005
sources.note: Recent reconstruction separating Akbarnama evidence from later Gondwana legend.

episodes.notes: ERA PIVOT: before Narrai, the Garha-Katanga/Gondwana kingdom under Durgavati and her son Vir Narayan remained a major central Indian power; after the battle and Chauragarh's fall, it was absorbed into Mughal power and its treasure and elephants were seized. Akbarnama and local Gondwana memory agree on Durgavati's courage, death and the kingdom's fall, but disagree or remain uncertain on the exact manner of death and motives. No contemporary Gondwana chronicle survives. Do NOT claim Asaf Khan invaded because he desired the queen, do NOT claim the dagger death as proven, and do NOT erase her Chandel birth and Raj Gond rulership by using a single identity label.

episodes.title: Sammel and the Handful of Millet
episodes.figure: Sher Shah Suri and Rao Maldev Rathore
episodes.era: Sur Empire expansion into Rajputana, 1544 CE
episodes.region: Giri-Sumel near Jaitaran, Rajasthan
episodes.logline: Near Sammel, Sher Shah won the field but learned how costly a desert kingdom could be.
episodes.moral: A victory that nearly breaks the victor is still a warning from history.

sources.citation: Abbas Khan Sarwani, Tarikh-i-Sher Shahi, c. 1580 CE; trans. in Elliot and Dowson, Vol. IV
sources.note: Afghan-side history of Sher Shah, source for the forged-letter stratagem and the famous millet remark.

sources.citation: Muhnot Nainsi, Nainsi ri Khyat, 17th century
sources.note: Rajasthani account preserving Marwar memory of Maldev, Jaita and Kumpa.

sources.citation: Firishta, Tarikh-i-Firishta, early 17th century; Satish Chandra, Medieval India, 1997
sources.note: Later Indo-Persian synthesis and modern reassessment of Sur-Rajputana politics.

episodes.notes: ERA PIVOT: before Sammel, Sher Shah had expelled Humayun and was turning the Sur state into the dominant power of north India; after the battle, Marwar was checked but not erased, and Rajputana remained costly terrain for imperial armies. Sarwani, writing from the Afghan tradition, reports that forged letters caused Maldev to withdraw and that Jaita and Kumpa fought on; Nainsi preserves the Rajasthani memory of their last stand; Firishta repeats a later Indo-Persian version. The famous line about almost losing Hindustan for a handful of millet is attributed to Sarwani and should be presented as a reported saying, not stenography. Do NOT claim Sher Shah permanently annexed all Marwar, do NOT give exact troop numbers as fact, and do NOT turn the stratagem into proven verbatim correspondence.

episodes.title: Khanwa and the Rajput Wall
episodes.era: Mughal consolidation after Panipat, 16 March 1527
episodes.region: Khanwa near Agra and Mewar's northern frontier
episodes.logline: Babur fastens carts into a firing wall, calls the campaign a jihad in his own memoir, and breaks Rana Sanga's coalition at Khanwa.
episodes.moral: A victory can turn a raid into a state.

sources.citation: Babur, Baburnama, trans. W.M. Thackston, 1996
sources.note: Eyewitness commander account for the cart line, tulughma, jihad language and skull tower.

sources.citation: Abul Fazl, Akbarnama, c. 1596-1602, trans. H. Beveridge
sources.note: Retrospective Mughal court narrative drawing on earlier material.

sources.citation: Jos Gommans, Mughal Warfare, Routledge, 2002; Rima Hooja, A History of Rajasthan, 2006
sources.note: Modern reassessment of tactics, firearms and the Rajput source problem.

episodes.notes: Khanwa is the battle that made Babur's conquest a possession rather than a raid: after Ibrahim Lodi's fall, Rana Sanga's Rajput-Afghan-Mewati coalition remained the strongest northern challenge. The Baburnama, an eyewitness Mughal-side memoir, records Babur renouncing wine, using chained carts, matchlocks, artillery and tulughma flanking, and declaring the campaign a jihad; it also records a skull tower after Khanwa. Later Rajput perspectives survive only through much later works such as Nainsi ri Khyat, Tod and bardic tradition, so do NOT present them as contemporary. Numbers are inflated on all sides; do NOT claim exact troop totals, a proven prior alliance, or the one-eye-one-arm Rana Sanga image as a tactical fact.

episodes.title: Ghaghra and the Last Afghan Line
episodes.era: Babur's final Indian campaign, 6 May 1529
episodes.region: Ghaghra-Ganges confluence in Bihar
episodes.logline: At the Ghaghra, Babur turns river crossing, cannon and negotiation against Mahmud Lodi's eastern Afghan-Bengal alliance.
episodes.moral: A frontier can be won by battle and settlement together.

sources.citation: Babur, Baburnama, trans. W.M. Thackston, 1996
sources.note: Near-eyewitness account of Babur's last major campaign.

sources.citation: Abbas Khan Sarwani, Tarikh-i-Sher Shahi, trans. Askari and Ahmad, 1964
sources.note: Retrospective account of Sher Khan's early world and Afghan politics.

sources.citation: John F. Richards, The Mughal Empire, Cambridge University Press, 1993
sources.note: Modern synthesis of Babur's consolidation and eastern frontier.

episodes.notes: Ghaghra ended Mahmud Lodi's attempt to revive Afghan power under Bengal's shadow and secured Babur's eastern frontier before his death in 1530. The Baburnama gives the Mughal view of the river crossing, the Bengal fleet and the peace terms with Nusrat Shah; Abbas Khan Sarwani, writing later for Akbar's court, supplies the Afghan/Sher Shah context. Sources agree Babur won and Mahmud Lodi ceased to matter, but they disagree by silence on scale because no detailed Bengal-side chronicle survives. Treat the 100,000-style numbers as conventional inflation, and do NOT overstate Ghaghra as a clean annihilation when negotiation and withdrawal mattered.

episodes.title: Chausa in the Monsoon Night
episodes.era: Sur challenge to Mughal rule, 26 June 1539
episodes.region: Chausa near Buxar, Bihar
episodes.logline: Sher Shah waits through talks and floodwater, then strikes Humayun's camp at night until the emperor escapes across the Ganges.
episodes.moral: Delay can be a weapon when terrain is changing.

sources.citation: Gulbadan Begum, Humayun-nama, trans. A.S. Beveridge, 1902
sources.note: Mughal family memory, not a battlefield eyewitness, but close to exile traditions.

sources.citation: Abbas Khan Sarwani, Tarikh-i-Sher Shahi, trans. Askari and Ahmad, 1964
sources.note: Sher Shah narrative based on later interviews with Afghan veterans.

sources.citation: John F. Richards, The Mughal Empire, CUP, 1993; Dirk Kolff, Naukar, Rajput and Sepoy, CUP, 2002
sources.note: Modern context for Afghan military labor and Mughal collapse.

episodes.notes: Chausa wounded the Mughal empire fatally: Sher Shah used months of negotiation and monsoon conditions before a night attack on Humayun's flooded camp. Gulbadan Begum, Jawhar Aftabchi, Mirza Haidar Dughlat, Sarwani and Abul Fazl all write from different later positions; none is a simple battlefield diary. They agree on surprise, confusion and Humayun's narrow river escape, but differ on how he crossed and whether the cause was Sher Shah's engineering, Mughal disunity, or both. Do NOT claim exact forces, do NOT mock Humayun as cowardly, and treat the Nizam water-carrier episode as a later but important Mughal memory rather than a verified battlefield transcript.

episodes.title: Kannauj and the Silent Guns
episodes.era: Fall of Humayun's first empire, 17 May 1540
episodes.region: Kannauj and Bilgram on the Ganges plain
episodes.logline: At Kannauj, Sher Shah's attack scatters Humayun before the Mughal artillery can fire, sending the dynasty into exile.
episodes.moral: A weapon unused can decide a war as surely as a weapon fired.

sources.citation: Mirza Haidar Dughlat, Tarikh-i-Rashidi, trans. Elias and Ross, 1895
sources.note: Near-contemporary Timurid account preserving the silent-artillery detail.

sources.citation: Abbas Khan Sarwani, Tarikh-i-Sher Shahi, trans. Askari and Ahmad, 1964
sources.note: Retrospective Afghan-centered narrative of Sher Shah's strategy.

sources.citation: Irfan Habib, The Agrarian System of Mughal India, rev. ed., OUP, 1999
sources.note: Context for Sher Shah's administrative legacy later adapted by the Mughals.

episodes.notes: Kannauj, also called Bilgram, completed what Chausa began: Humayun lost Delhi and Agra and spent years in Sindh, Persia and Afghanistan before restoration. Mirza Haidar says the Mughal cannon and firearms were not discharged, while Sarwani emphasizes Sher Shah's planning; Mughal-family sources stress fraternal non-cooperation, especially Kamran's refusal to support Humayun fully. The Sur victory matters beyond the battlefield because Sher Shah's road, coinage and revenue measures shaped later Mughal practice. Do NOT give fixed army totals, and do NOT reduce the defeat to one man's incompetence when the sources show command, logistics, family politics and speed together.

episodes.title: Second Panipat and Hemu's Arrow
episodes.era: Restoration of Mughal power, 5 November 1556
episodes.region: Panipat, Haryana
episodes.logline: Hemu's elephant-led army nearly breaks the Mughals until an arrow strikes his eye and a disputed execution becomes a source problem.
episodes.moral: A single wound can open a century of rule.

sources.citation: Abul Fazl, Akbarnama, trans. H. Beveridge, 1902-1939
sources.note: Pro-Akbar court account saying Akbar struck Hemu and received ghazi status.

sources.citation: Abd al-Qadir Badauni, Muntakhab ut-Tawarikh, trans. W.H. Lowe, 1898
sources.note: Critical court historian who says Bairam Khan killed Hemu after Akbar refused.

sources.citation: Satish Chandra, Medieval India, Part II, Har-Anand, 2007; Jadunath Sarkar, Military History of India, 1960
sources.note: Modern synthesis of the battle and source contradiction.

episodes.notes: Second Panipat restored the Mughal line after Humayun's death and Hemu's capture of Delhi as Vikramaditya. Sources agree Hemu's elephant charge initially shook the Mughal line, that an arrow incapacitated him, and that his army broke when he disappeared from command. The central source problem is the execution: Akbarnama credits young Akbar with the final blow and the title ghazi, while Badayuni says Akbar refused and Bairam Khan killed the unconscious prisoner; both accounts have clear agendas. Do NOT state who killed Hemu as settled fact, do NOT invent Hemu-side chronicles, and do NOT treat later patriotic or courtly versions as equal to the conflicting sixteenth-century Persian record.

episodes.title: Chittorgarh and the Count of Thirty Thousand
episodes.era: Mughal-Rajput frontier war, October 1567-February 1568
episodes.region: Chittorgarh Fort, Rajasthan
episodes.logline: Akbar's siege trenches and matchlock break Chittorgarh, where the Mughal record itself names jauhar and a massacre after the fall.
episodes.moral: The hardest records are the ones that refuse to flatter memory.

sources.citation: Abul Fazl, Akbarnama, Vol. II, trans. H. Beveridge
sources.note: Mughal victor's court history for the siege, Akbar shooting Jaimal, jauhar, jihad language and the 30,000 figure.

sources.citation: Badauni, Muntakhab ut-Tawarikh, Vol. II, trans. W.H. Lowe
sources.note: Independent Mughal-era Persian source confirming the massacre and Jaimal episode.

sources.citation: John F. Richards, The Mughal Empire, CUP, 1993; Satish Chandra, Medieval India, Part II, 2007
sources.note: Modern context for Akbar's Rajput policy and Chittor's political stakes.

episodes.notes: Chittorgarh must be told from the sources without softening: Abul Fazl's Mughal court account says Akbar personally shot Jaimal, the defenders' women performed jauhar, and after the fort fell Akbar ordered a general massacre; the Akbarnama gives the figure of 30,000 Hindu civilians and also frames the campaign in jihad language. Badauni confirms the massacre, while no contemporary Mewar chronicle survives. The same Akbarnama also records Akbar honoring Jaimal and Patta with statues at Agra Fort, so the record contains both tribute and slaughter. Do NOT present 30,000 as exact without attribution, do NOT dismiss it as false without evidence, and do NOT narrate jauhar while omitting the massacre or the reverse.
episodes.chapter_part: III. Siege and the Rajput Frontier

episodes.title: Haldighati and the Missing Chronicle
episodes.figure: Maharana Pratap and Man Singh I
episodes.era: Mewar resistance after Chittor, 18 June 1576
episodes.region: Haldighati pass near Gogunda, Rajasthan
episodes.logline: In the yellow pass of Haldighati, Pratap charges Man Singh's line, escapes, and leaves a battle whose sources still disagree.
episodes.moral: A tactical result and a remembered struggle need not be the same thing.

sources.citation: Badauni, Muntakhab ut-Tawarikh, Vol. II, trans. W.H. Lowe
sources.note: Eyewitness combatant-scribe, hostile in tone, with the only first-person battle account.

sources.citation: Abul Fazl, Akbarnama, trans. H. Beveridge; Nizamuddin Ahmad, Tabaqat-i-Akbari
sources.note: Retrospective and near-contemporary Mughal accounts for comparison.

sources.citation: Rima Hooja, A History of Rajasthan, 2006; Satish Chandra, Medieval India, Part II, 2007
sources.note: Modern treatment of casualty inflation, outcome and later legend.

episodes.notes: Haldighati is a historiography episode: Badayuni was present and gives Pratap about 3,000 horse and 400 Bhil archers, while later Rajasthani and colonial-romantic accounts expand both numbers and legend. Sources agree Man Singh's Mughal-Rajput army held the field, Pratap escaped, and Mewar's resistance continued; they differ on date, casualties and the meaning of Akbar's later displeasure with Man Singh for not capturing Pratap. Badayuni's quoted remark about shooting Rajputs on either side must be attributed to him and his hostile perspective, not generalized as a narrator's judgment. Do NOT claim Pratap won tactically, do NOT present Chetak's elephant leap as sixteenth-century fact, and do NOT give exact casualties.
episodes.chapter_part: III. Siege and the Rajput Frontier

episodes.title: Swally and the Watching Mughals
episodes.era: English, Portuguese and Mughal sea trade, November-December 1612
episodes.region: Suvali anchorage near Surat, Gujarat
episodes.logline: English ships beat the Portuguese off Swally while Mughal officials watch, turning a sea fight into a Surat trade farman.
episodes.moral: An empire can be changed by a battle it did not fight.

sources.citation: Thomas Best, The Voyage of Thomas Best to the East Indies, ed. William Foster, Hakluyt Society, 1934
sources.note: English eyewitness sea-diary for the engagement.

sources.citation: Jahangir, Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri, trans. Rogers and Beveridge, 1909-1914
sources.note: Mughal court diary for the political consequence, not a battle eyewitness.

sources.citation: Om Prakash, European Commercial Enterprise in Pre-Colonial India, CUP, 1998
sources.note: Modern economic history of the Portuguese-English transition.

episodes.notes: Swally belongs in a Mughal battle chapter because the Mughals were the armed audience and political arbiters: after English guns repelled the Portuguese, Jahangir's government permitted the English factory at Surat. The eyewitness record is mainly Thomas Best's English diary and EIC papers; the Mughal side appears through Jahangir's court memory of the aftermath, while an equivalent Portuguese eyewitness account is not central in published English scholarship. Sources agree the English won local command of the anchorage and gained trading privileges, but not the exact ship composition or wider significance. Do NOT call this a Mughal military victory, and do NOT treat it as the instant end of Portuguese power.

episodes.title: Purandar Under Jai Singh
episodes.era: Aurangzeb's first high-pressure Maratha campaign, March-June 1665
episodes.region: Purandar Fort near Pune, Maharashtra
episodes.logline: Jai Singh surrounds Shivaji's fort network, Murarbaji dies defending Purandar, and treaty turns siege into imperial negotiation.
episodes.moral: A siege can end in terms that both sides use differently.

sources.citation: Mirza Raja Jai Singh's letters and Aurangzeb's farmans, cited in Jadunath Sarkar, Shivaji and His Times, 1973
sources.note: Besieging-side dispatches and imperial correspondence.

sources.citation: Sabhasad Bakhar, c. 1697, and Jedhe Shakavali
sources.note: Near-contemporary Maratha records for Murarbaji, forts and treaty memory.

sources.citation: Niccolao Manucci, Storia do Mogor, trans. William Irvine, 1907-1908
sources.note: Contemporary European observer of Mughal-Maratha politics, not a siege eyewitness.

episodes.notes: Purandar was the high point of Mughal pressure on Shivaji before the Agra episode: Jai Singh used coordinated siege warfare, not a single heroic assault, and the treaty of June 1665 transferred 23 forts while leaving Shivaji 12 and making Sambhaji a mansabdar. Mughal dispatches frame Jai Singh's success and his concern for a workable Deccan settlement; Sabhasad Bakhar frames Shivaji's acceptance as strategic survival and preserves Murarbaji Deshpande's defense. The sources agree on the siege, Murarbaji's death and the treaty, but differ on agency and troop scale. Do NOT retell Shivaji's Agra escape here, and do NOT present either side's political spin as the narrator's verdict.

episodes.title: Bijapur and the Malik-i-Maidan
episodes.era: Annexation of the Adil Shahi Sultanate, 1685-1686
episodes.region: Bijapur Fort, Karnataka
episodes.logline: Aurangzeb's army grinds against Bijapur's walls and the Malik-i-Maidan gun until the Adil Shahi sultanate surrenders.
episodes.moral: A conquest can enlarge a map while deepening a war.

sources.citation: Muhammad Mustaid Khan, Maasir-i-Alamgiri, trans. Jadunath Sarkar, 1947
sources.note: Archive-based Mughal court history for Aurangzeb's later reign.

sources.citation: Bhimsen Saxena, Nuskha-i-Dilkusha, ed. V.G. Khobrekar, 1972; selections used by Sarkar
sources.note: Eyewitness Mughal cavalry officer for Deccan campaign conditions.

sources.citation: John F. Richards, The Mughal Empire, CUP, 1993; Jadunath Sarkar, History of Aurangzib, vols. 3-4
sources.note: Modern and classic syntheses of Deccan overextension.

episodes.notes: The Bijapur siege extinguished the Adil Shahi state after nearly two centuries, but it did not solve the Maratha war. Maasir-i-Alamgiri and Bhimsen Saxena record the long siege, hard walls, moat, supply problems, Maratha disruption under Sambhaji, and the symbolic presence of the Malik-i-Maidan cannon; they differ on how much Aurangzeb's personal arrival versus his commanders' encirclement decided the end. The sources also show the material scale of Deccan war: guns, trenches, hunger, disease and huge logistical cost. Do NOT make the surrender instantaneous, do NOT erase Maratha supply attacks, and do NOT claim Mughal annexation meant stable Deccan control.

episodes.title: Golconda and the Opened Gate
episodes.figure: Aurangzeb and Abul Hasan Qutb Shah
episodes.era: Fall of the Qutb Shahi Sultanate, January-September 1687
episodes.region: Golconda Fort and Hyderabad, Telangana
episodes.logline: Mughal mines fail, monsoon and disease bite the camp, and Golconda falls only when a gate opens from inside.
episodes.moral: The strongest wall can fall to the weakest trust.

sources.citation: Muhammad Mustaid Khan, Maasir-i-Alamgiri, trans. Jadunath Sarkar, 1947
sources.note: Mughal archive-based source for mines, Muazzam's arrest and fall of the fort.

sources.citation: Bhimsen Saxena, Nuskha-i-Dilkusha; Khafi Khan, Muntakhab ul-Lubab
sources.note: Deccan eyewitness/near-contemporary Persian accounts with administrative and camp perspectives.

sources.citation: John F. Richards, 'The Imperial Crisis in the Deccan,' Journal of Asian Studies 35.2, 1976
sources.note: Source-critical modern argument about Deccan overextension.

episodes.notes: Golconda completed Aurangzeb's annexation of the Deccan sultanates, but the records make it a siege of failure before betrayal: Mughal mines misfired or were countermined, disease and monsoon weakened the army, Prince Muazzam was accused of leaking tactics and food to the defenders, and the fort finally fell when an insider opened a gate. Maasir-i-Alamgiri, Bhimsen and Khafi Khan agree on betrayal and Abul Hasan's capture, while manuscript traditions and later historians vary on the traitor's exact name. Mention Golconda's treasury and diamond economy soberly, but do NOT claim the Koh-i-Noor was specifically seized at the 1687 siege as a documented fact.

episodes.title: Jajau and the First Crown After Aurangzeb
episodes.figure: Bahadur Shah I and Azam Shah
episodes.era: Mughal succession war after Aurangzeb, 20 June 1707
episodes.region: Jajau between Agra and Dholpur
episodes.logline: Aurangzeb's sons race toward Agra, and at Jajau one battle leaves Azam Shah dead and Muazzam wearing a fragile crown.
episodes.moral: A throne inherited by battle inherits the battle's fractures.

sources.citation: Khafi Khan, Muntakhab ul-Lubab, trans. S. Moinul Haq, 1975
sources.note: Near-contemporary Mughal administrative account of post-Aurangzeb politics.

sources.citation: Kamwar Khan, Tazkirat us-Salatin Chaghata, c. 1724-1725
sources.note: Later Persian court account of the succession wars.

sources.citation: William Irvine, Later Mughals, ed. Jadunath Sarkar, 1922; J.F. Richards, The Mughal Empire, 1993
sources.note: Modern source-based synthesis using Persian and European materials.

episodes.notes: Jajau began the final Mughal century by making Muazzam Bahadur Shah I after Azam Shah and his sons were killed. Khafi Khan and Kamwar Khan agree on the dynastic result and the death of Azam's line, while numbers and the tactical weight of Guru Gobind Singh's small supporting contingent remain uncertain; Sikh chronicles preserve the alliance memory but are later than the battle. The source problem is succession politics: each account writes after the winner is known. Do NOT overstate Guru Gobind Singh's contingent as the decisive battlefield factor, do NOT give fixed troop totals, and do NOT present Aurangzeb's proposed division of empire as if it had legal force after battle settled the matter.

episodes.title: Karnal and the Three Hour Rout
episodes.era: Afsharid invasion and Mughal collapse, 24 February 1739
episodes.region: Karnal and Delhi
episodes.logline: Nadir Shah breaks the Mughal army in three hours at Karnal, then Delhi pays in massacre, plunder and imperial humiliation.
episodes.moral: A hollow empire may stand until one hard blow shows the hollowness.

sources.citation: Anand Ram Mukhlis, Mirat ul-Warid, cited in Jadunath Sarkar, Nadir Shah in India, 1925
sources.note: Near-eyewitness Indian court perspective on Delhi's aftermath and massacre.

sources.citation: Mirza Mahdi Khan Astarabadi, Tarikh-i-Jahangushay-i-Nadiri, c. 1757; Rustam Ali, Tarikh-i-Hindi
sources.note: Persian/Afsharid and near-contemporary accounts for Nadir's side and force estimates.

sources.citation: Michael Axworthy, The Sword of Persia, I.B. Tauris, 2006; Alam and Subrahmanyam, The Mughal State 1526-1750, OUP, 1998
sources.note: Modern source-critical scholarship on Nadir and late Mughal power.

episodes.notes: Karnal exposed the Mughal military collapse: Nadir Shah's mobile cavalry and zanburak fire drew Mughal commanders into piecemeal action, Khan Dauran was mortally wounded, Saadat Khan was captured, and the battle was over in about three hours. The aftermath must be stated plainly from the sources: after Nadir occupied Delhi, a crowd attack on his soldiers preceded his order for a general massacre; Anand Ram Mukhlis gives about 30,000 killed, while Persian court sources give lower figures, so all casualty numbers must be attributed. Sources agree the Peacock Throne, treasury and Koh-i-Noor were taken, but do NOT claim the Tehran throne is Shah Jahan's original or that every later Koh-i-Noor chain detail is uncontested. Do NOT make Nizam-ul-Mulk's negotiation either treason or wisdom without source attribution.

episodes.title: The Last Confederacy at Chach
episodes.era: Ghaznavid-Shahi war, c. 1008-1009 CE
episodes.region: Chach plain near Hund/Waihind, Punjab frontier
episodes.logline: Anandapala gathers a last Shahi-led confederacy at Chach, where a fierce Gakhar charge nearly breaks Mahmud's line before discipline and rout decide the day.
episodes.moral: Valor can be real even when the field is lost.

sources.citation: al-Utbi, Kitab-ul-Yamini / Tarikh-i-Yamini, c. 1021 CE
sources.note: Near-contemporary Ghaznavid court account; pro-Mahmud and rhetorical, but central for the campaign.

sources.citation: al-Biruni, Kitab al-Hind, c. 1030 CE
sources.note: Near-contemporary scholar in the Ghaznavid orbit; useful for Shahi context rather than battle detail.

sources.citation: M.A. Rehman, The Last Two Dynasties of the Shahis (1976); Peter Jackson, The Delhi Sultanate (1999)
sources.note: Modern reconstruction and military context for the northwest frontier.

episodes.notes: State that Anandapala's coalition fought Mahmud around Chach in 1008-09 and was defeated, reducing the Hindu Shahis to tributary status. Utbi, from Mahmud's side, records the tribal/Gakhar assault and Ghaznavid counterstroke; al-Biruni gives independent near-contemporary context for the Shahi decline; Ferishta preserves the elephant-panic detail much later. AGREEMENT: battle, Shahi defeat and severe weakening. DISAGREEMENT: exact numbers, and whether Anandapala's elephant caused the rout. STATE the valor of the Gakhar/Khokhar infantry and the cost of defeat. DO NOT claim casualty totals as census data, do NOT say Anandapala won, and do NOT present Ferishta's elephant story as certain.
episodes.chapter: The Resistance Front: India's Stand Against the Invaders

episodes.title: Somnath's Last Watch
episodes.figure: Bhima I and the Somnath defenders
episodes.era: Mahmud of Ghazni's Somnath raid, 1025-1026 CE
episodes.region: Somanatha-Pattan, Prabhas Patan, Saurashtra coast
episodes.logline: At Somnath, local defenders and temple guardians face Mahmud's desert raid, and the shrine falls to plunder, desecration and disputed slaughter.
episodes.moral: A truthful record must name both resistance and ruin.

sources.citation: Gardizi, Zainu'l-Akhbar, c. 1048-1050 CE
sources.note: Near-contemporary Ghaznavid-side account of the Somnath campaign.

sources.citation: Ibn al-Athir, Al-Kamil fi'l-Tarikh, c. 1231 CE; al-Biruni, Kitab al-Hind, c. 1030 CE
sources.note: Independent Islamic historical and scholarly streams for the raid and shrine context.

sources.citation: Romila Thapar, Somanatha: The Many Voices of a History (2004); A.K. Majumdar, Chaulukyas of Gujarat (1956)
sources.note: Source-critical analysis of competing Somnath traditions and Bhima I's reign.

episodes.notes: State plainly that Mahmud reached Somnath in January 1026, the shrine was captured, the linga was broken, wealth was plundered, and the defenders lost; these facts appear across Gardizi, Ibn al-Athir and other Islamic chroniclers. Gardizi reports the fort commander fled to an island; later accounts inflate slaughter into the famous 50,000 figure. AGREEMENT: raid, desecration and plunder. DISAGREEMENT: casualty totals, defender composition, and whether the later 'Param Dev' who threatened Mahmud's return was Bhima I or Bhoja of Malwa. STATE Delavada massacre where Gardizi/al-Biruni attest it. DO NOT claim Bhima personally fought at Somnath, do NOT repeat 50,000 dead as fact, and do NOT turn later memory into eyewitness evidence.
episodes.chapter: The Resistance Front: India's Stand Against the Invaders

episodes.title: The Hills That Would Not Yield
episodes.era: Last Hindu Shahi resistance, c. 1021-1026 CE
episodes.region: Salt Range, Siwalik hills and Kashmir-Punjab borderlands
episodes.logline: Driven from the plains, Trilochanapala carries the last Shahi resistance into the hills until the dynasty that guarded the passes disappears.
episodes.moral: Some defeats matter because of how long people endured them.

sources.citation: Kalhana, Rajatarangini, Book VII, c. 1150 CE
sources.note: Independent Kashmiri Sanskrit chronicle preserving the Shahi-Kashmir connection.

sources.citation: al-Biruni, Kitab al-Hind, c. 1030 CE
sources.note: Near-contemporary account of Shahi genealogy and political decline.

sources.citation: M.A. Rehman, The Last Two Dynasties of the Shahis (1976); R.C. Majumdar, The Struggle for Empire
sources.note: Modern synthesis of the Shahi collapse.

episodes.notes: Tell this as an ending, not a victory: Trilochanapala resisted Mahmud from the Salt Range and Siwalik refuges, sought or worked through Kashmir-linked alliances noted by Kalhana, and by about 1026 the Hindu Shahi state had vanished. al-Biruni gives near-contemporary genealogy and decline; Kalhana, writing later from Kashmir, is independent of the Ghaznavid court. AGREEMENT: Shahi extinction in the 1020s. DISAGREEMENT: Trilochanapala's exact death date and whether he died by battle, flight or treachery. STATE the dynastic cost and refugee dispersal. DO NOT claim he defeated Mahmud, and do NOT overstate guerrilla organization beyond the sources.
episodes.chapter: The Resistance Front: India's Stand Against the Invaders

episodes.title: The Khokhars Rise on the Jhelum
episodes.era: Khokhar revolt and Ghurid crisis, 1204-1206 CE
episodes.region: Punjab, Jhelum river and Dhamiak in the Salt Range
episodes.logline: The Khokhar revolt blocks the roads between Lahore and Ghazni, draws Muhammad of Ghor into a brutal campaign, and leaves his death wrapped in contested memory.
episodes.moral: A source problem can be as important as a battlefield.

sources.citation: Minhaj al-Siraj Juzjani, Tabaqat-i-Nasiri, c. 1260 CE
sources.note: Delhi Sultanate insider source close to the Ghurid world.

sources.citation: Ibn al-Athir, Al-Kamil fi'l-Tarikh, c. 1231 CE; Ferishta, Gulshan-i-Ibrahimi, c. 1606 CE
sources.note: Independent near-contemporary account and much later Persian synthesis.

sources.citation: A.B.M. Habibullah, The Foundation of Muslim Rule in India (1961); Peter Jackson, The Delhi Sultanate (1999)
sources.note: Modern discussion of the revolt, massacre and transition to Delhi rule.

episodes.notes: State that the Khokhars revolted in 1204-05, blocked Punjab communications, and were crushed by Muhammad of Ghor in 1206 with massacre and enslavement/conversion of survivors recorded in the Persian tradition. Minhaj and Ibn al-Athir agree on revolt, suppression and Muhammad's assassination at Dhamiak, but attribute the killers to Ismaili/Batini assassins; later Ferishta strengthens the Khokhar-revenge tradition. AGREEMENT: revolt, punitive violence, death of the sultan. DISAGREEMENT: who killed him. DO NOT claim Khokhars definitely killed Muhammad of Ghor, do NOT make it a simple revenge legend, and do NOT omit the massacre recorded after the Jhelum fighting.
episodes.chapter: The Resistance Front: India's Stand Against the Invaders
episodes.chapter_part: II. The Ghurid Conquest and Its Costs

episodes.title: Kalinjar Falls and Returns
episodes.era: Ghurid siege of Kalinjar, 1202-1205 CE
episodes.region: Kalinjar Fort, Bundelkhand
episodes.logline: Kalinjar's rock fort surrenders to Aibak after siege and temple damage, yet inscriptions show the Chandelas back in control within a few years.
episodes.moral: A captured fort is not always a finished story.

sources.citation: Hasan Nizami, Taj-ul-Maasir, c. 1205-1228 CE
sources.note: Near-contemporary early Sultanate court account of Aibak's campaigns.

sources.citation: Paramardi's Kalinjar inscription, 1201 CE; Trailokyavarman inscription, 1205 CE
sources.note: Defender-side epigraphy before the siege and after Chandela recovery.

sources.citation: Syed Ali Nadeem Rezavi, 'Kalinjar: A Medieval Fortress-City' (Indian Historical Review, 2002)
sources.note: Modern fortress-city study using inscriptions and chronicles.

episodes.notes: Tell the hard sequence: Aibak besieged Kalinjar in 1202-03; Paramardi negotiated or died around the surrender; the garrison fell; Sultanate sources record looting and temple damage; then a 1205 inscription shows Trailokyavarman had restored Chandela control. Hasan Nizami and Minhaj give the conqueror-side narrative; inscriptions provide the defender-side check. AGREEMENT: siege and fall. DISAGREEMENT: Paramardi's death and the surrender mechanics. STATE both defeat and recovery. DO NOT claim Paramardi died heroically in combat, and do NOT treat the fall as permanent.
episodes.chapter: The Resistance Front: India's Stand Against the Invaders
episodes.chapter_part: II. The Ghurid Conquest and Its Costs

episodes.title: Zafar Khan's Last Charge at Kili
episodes.era: Chagatai Mongol invasion of Delhi, 1299 CE
episodes.region: Kili near Delhi
episodes.logline: Against orders, Zafar Khan rides into the Mongol wing at Kili, refuses surrender, and dies in an ambush as Delhi survives.
episodes.moral: Courage and discipline can collide on the same battlefield.

sources.citation: Ziauddin Barani, Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi, c. 1357 CE
sources.note: Delhi Sultanate historian preserving the main Zafar Khan narrative.

sources.citation: Amir Khusrau, Khaza'in-ul-Futuh, c. 1311 CE; Isami, Futuh-us-Salatin, c. 1350 CE
sources.note: Near-contemporary court poet and later Deccan narrative with casualty claims.

sources.citation: Peter Jackson, The Delhi Sultanate (1999)
sources.note: Modern analysis of Qutlugh Khwaja's wound and Mongol withdrawal.

episodes.notes: This is a defender-focused companion to the existing Sultanate episode, not a repeat: center Zafar Khan's disobedient charge, ambush, refusal of surrender, and death. Barani and Khusrau agree on the charge and death; Isami gives vivid but suspect casualty numbers; Jackson notes the Mongol retreat may owe as much to Qutlugh Khwaja's mortal wound as to fear of Zafar Khan. AGREEMENT: Zafar died fighting and the Mongols withdrew. DISAGREEMENT: casualties and reason for withdrawal. DO NOT claim Zafar alone saved Delhi, do NOT claim Alauddin celebrated him, and do NOT treat Barani's large numbers as exact.
episodes.chapter: The Resistance Front: India's Stand Against the Invaders
episodes.chapter_part: III. Standing Against the Mongol Storm

episodes.title: The Dipalpur Line
episodes.era: Northwest frontier against Mongol raids, c. 1305-1316 CE
episodes.region: Dipalpur, Multan and the Punjab frontier
episodes.logline: Ghazi Malik holds Dipalpur as a frontier wall, where repeated victories over Mongol raiders become memory, inscription and dynasty-making claim.
episodes.moral: A frontier is held by logistics as much as by sword strokes.

sources.citation: Amir Khusrau, Tughluq Nama, c. 1320 CE
sources.note: Near-contemporary celebratory account of Ghazi Malik's frontier career.

sources.citation: Ibn Battuta, Rihla, c. 1355 CE
sources.note: Reports a Multan mosque inscription claiming twenty-nine victories over Tatars.

sources.citation: Barani, Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi, c. 1357 CE; B.P. Saksena in The Delhi Sultanate (1960)
sources.note: Later court history and modern synthesis.

episodes.notes: Make this a frontier-resilience and evidence story: Khusrau says eighteen victories, Barani says twenty, and Ibn Battuta says he saw an inscription at Multan claiming twenty-nine; none lists the battles. The solid attested point is repeated Mongol frontier defense, including Ghazi Malik's role in the 1306 campaign. AGREEMENT: he became famous as a Mongol-fighter at Dipalpur and Multan. DISAGREEMENT: number and details of victories. STATE his mixed Mongol-Jat background as complexity, not a slogan. DO NOT claim all twenty-nine victories are documented, and do NOT say the inscription survives or has been archaeologically verified.
episodes.chapter: The Resistance Front: India's Stand Against the Invaders
episodes.chapter_part: III. Standing Against the Mongol Storm

episodes.title: Hammira's Guest at Ranthambhore
episodes.era: Siege of Ranthambhore, 1299-1301 CE
episodes.region: Ranthambhore Fort, Rajasthan
episodes.logline: Hammira shelters Mongol rebels, refuses to surrender them, loses Ranthambhore after siege, and dies in a last sortie amid jauhar and famine.
episodes.moral: An oath may outlive the ruler who keeps it.

sources.citation: Amir Khusrau, Khaza'in-ul-Futuh, c. 1311 CE; Barani, Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi, c. 1357 CE
sources.note: Sultanate-side accounts of Alauddin Khalji's siege.

sources.citation: Nayachandra Suri, Hammira Mahakavya, c. 1400-1420 CE
sources.note: Later Jain/Sanskrit heroic poem preserving Rajput memory, not an eyewitness chronicle.

sources.citation: Dasharatha Sharma, Early Chahamana Dynasties (1959); Aditya Malik on Hammira memory
sources.note: Modern source-critical readings.

episodes.notes: State the attested core: Hammira sheltered Mongol fugitives, refused extradition, Nusrat Khan was killed during the siege, Ranthambhore suffered famine, Hammira died in defeat, and jauhar is recorded. Khusrau/Barani give Sultanate-side conquest; Hammira Mahakavya preserves later defender memory with literary embellishment. AGREEMENT: asylum issue, siege, fall, Hammira's death. DISAGREEMENT: heroic speeches and exact battle scenes. This episode also prevents communal simplification because a Hindu ruler died protecting Mongol Muslim guests. DO NOT claim Hammira won, do NOT rely on the Mahakavya as eyewitness, and do NOT invent jauhar numbers.
episodes.chapter: The Resistance Front: India's Stand Against the Invaders
episodes.chapter_part: III. Standing Against the Mongol Storm

episodes.title: Bhatner to Delhi Against Timur
episodes.era: Timur's invasion of north India, 1398 CE
episodes.region: Bhatner, Meerut and Delhi
episodes.logline: From Bhatner's walls to Delhi's elephant line, defenders resist Timur before his own victory books record prisoner killing and a city-wide qatl-i-am.
episodes.moral: A record can honor resistance without hiding catastrophe.

sources.citation: Sharaf al-Din Ali Yazdi, Zafarnama, c. 1424 CE
sources.note: Near-contemporary Timurid court account, panegyric but detailed on the India campaign.

sources.citation: Malfuzat-i-Timuri / Tuzuk-i-Timuri traditions
sources.note: Attributed memoir tradition; authenticity disputed, but key details are corroborated elsewhere.

sources.citation: Justin Marozzi, Tamerlane (2004); Irfan Habib, Medieval India I (1992)
sources.note: Modern readings of the campaign and economic devastation.

episodes.notes: This is a defender-focused companion to the existing Timur episode: emphasize Bhatner's resistance, Delhi's battle with war elephants, and the cost. Yazdi and the Malfuzat/Tuzuk tradition record the killing of about 100,000 prisoners before Delhi; treat the number as a rounded claim but the massacre as attested in pro-Timur sources. They also record sack, enslavement/deportation of artisans, and mass killing after the city revolt. AGREEMENT: prisoner massacre, Delhi battle, sack and deportations. DISAGREEMENT: exact casualty totals and Tuzuk authenticity. DO NOT claim precise death figures, do NOT call Tuzuk Timur's literal diary, and do NOT claim Bhatner stopped the invasion.
episodes.chapter: The Resistance Front: India's Stand Against the Invaders
episodes.chapter_part: IV. Timur and the Broken City

episodes.title: The Moving Shield at Kup
episodes.era: Vadda Ghallughara, February 5, 1762 CE
episodes.region: Kup, Rahira, Malerkotla and Barnala, Punjab
episodes.logline: Sikh misls fight while moving around a convoy of families at Kup, losing thousands in the Vadda Ghallughara yet surviving Abdali's attempt to break them.
episodes.moral: Survival can be the only victory left after massacre.

sources.citation: Rattan Singh Bhangu, Sri Gur Panth Prakash, c. 1809-1841 CE
sources.note: Sikh narrative based on family and oral testimony; later than the event.

sources.citation: Tahmas Khan Miskin, Tahmasnama, 18th century
sources.note: Afghan-side near-contemporary participant account noting Sikh resistance.

sources.citation: Ganda Singh, Ahmad Shah Durrani (1959); Khushwant Singh, A History of the Sikhs, Vol. 1 (1963)
sources.note: Modern syntheses of Abdali's campaigns and Sikh recovery.

episodes.notes: State the event as catastrophe with resistance: Abdali's forces caught the Sikh vahir near Kup on 5 February 1762; the Sikhs fought as a moving cordon around women, children and elders; many non-combatants died; the community survived and rebuilt power within months. Bhangu gives the Sikh memory and casualty range; Tahmasnama provides rare Afghan-side confirmation of repeated Sikh resistance. AGREEMENT: encirclement, moving fight, mass casualties, survival. DISAGREEMENT: exact dead, often estimated around 20,000-30,000 but not census data. DO NOT call it a military victory, do NOT give a precise death toll, and do NOT retell Third Panipat.
episodes.chapter: The Resistance Front: India's Stand Against the Invaders
episodes.chapter_part: V. Later Invasions, Resilience and Memory

episodes.title: Delhi's Six Hours of Blood
episodes.era: Nader Shah's sack of Delhi, 1739 CE
episodes.region: Shahjahanabad, Delhi
episodes.logline: Inside Shahjahanabad, residents kill Afsharid soldiers after a false rumor, and Nader Shah answers with six hours of qatl-i-am.
episodes.moral: Eyewitnesses make denial harder than memory alone.

sources.citation: Anand Ram Mukhlis, Tazkira, 18th century
sources.note: Contemporary Delhi court voice recording local opposition and massacre.

sources.citation: Abdul Karim Khan Kashmiri, Bayan-e-Waqai; Rustam Ali, Tarikh-e-Hindi
sources.note: Contemporary Indo-Persian accounts of the invasion and qatl-i-am.

sources.citation: Michael Axworthy, The Sword of Persia (2006); Jadunath Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire, Vol. 1
sources.note: Modern and classic reconstructions of Nader Shah in India.

episodes.notes: Frame this only as Delhi's civilian resistance and the qatl-i-am aftermath, not the Karnal battle already covered in the Mughal battle chapter. After Nader entered Delhi, a false rumor of his death led residents to kill roughly 3,000 Afsharid soldiers; Nader ordered qatl-i-am from Sunehri Masjid. Anand Ram Mukhlis says some opposition was offered, but most were butchered unresistingly; Abdul Karim, Rustam Ali and European dispatches agree on massacre, looting and enslavement, while totals vary around 20,000-30,000 in contemporary estimates. STATE the Peacock Throne/Koh-i-Noor plunder and indemnity as aftermath facts. DO NOT retell Karnal, do NOT claim organized citywide resistance, and do NOT give casualty estimates as exact counts.
episodes.chapter: The Resistance Front: India's Stand Against the Invaders
episodes.chapter_part: V. Later Invasions, Resilience and Memory

episodes.title: The Shrine They Rebuilt
episodes.era: Somnath rebuilding traditions, 1026 CE onward
episodes.region: Prabhas Patan and Chaulukya Gujarat
episodes.logline: After Somnath's sack, builders, patrons and pilgrims restore the shrine economy again and again, turning recovery into a quieter form of resistance.
episodes.moral: Rebuilding can answer destruction without pretending destruction did not happen.

sources.citation: M.A. Dhaky in Encyclopaedia of Indian Temple Architecture, Vol. II, Part 3 (1998)
sources.note: Architectural analysis of Somnath fragments and rapid rebuilding evidence.

sources.citation: Hemachandra, Dvyashraya Kavya, 12th century; Merutunga, Prabandha Chintamani, 1305 CE
sources.note: Chaulukya/Jain literary traditions on Kumarapala and temple patronage.

sources.citation: Romila Thapar, Somanatha: The Many Voices of a History (2004); A.K. Majumdar, Chaulukyas of Gujarat (1956)
sources.note: Source-critical history of sack, rebuilding and memory.

episodes.notes: This is economic and spiritual resilience, not a battle. Dhaky's architectural analysis supports quick rebuilding after 1026; Jain and Chaulukya traditions connect later Kumarapala-era patronage to Somnath, though their hagiographic goals must be marked. AGREEMENT: the shrine did not remain dead and the pilgrimage economy recovered. DISAGREEMENT: which king rebuilt exactly what, and how literally to read Jain claims about Kumarapala's conversion. STATE that temple destruction happened and rebuilding followed. DO NOT claim Kumarapala's full Jain conversion as established fact, and do NOT call rebuilding an organized military defiance.
episodes.chapter: The Resistance Front: India's Stand Against the Invaders
episodes.chapter_part: V. Later Invasions, Resilience and Memory

episodes.title: The Source Battlefield
episodes.era: Memory and historiography of resistance, c. 1030-1600 CE
episodes.region: Ghazni, north India and Rajasthan's bardic archives
